For audio with unknown surroundings add deepening-by-linkage and breath-deepener, because they turn whatever happens into depth. For a strong step change use fractionation; for a long slow slide use staircase-deepener, heaviness-lightness or cognitive-quieting. Use two or three different deepeners in a row instead of one long one, and stop when the script has what it needs: the suggestions do the work, not the depth.

not_this.why: induction starts trance from ordinary attention; deepening presupposes it has started
that is the section of the script; this family is the devices used inside it
a convincer proves the state to the listener; a deepener asks for more of it

evidence.note: Deepening is standard in clinical texts, but controlled work finds that the induction adds only modestly to suggestibility and gives little sign that extra deepening raises responding much beyond what expectancy explains.

entries.name: Countdown deepener
entries.summary: Count down, usually from ten or five, and tell the listener that each number takes them deeper.
entries.definition: A count in which every number is tied to an increase in depth, with a stated end point at the last number. The numbers do no work themselves; they give the listener a fixed series of moments at which to respond and a known finish. It differs from a counting induction only in position: the listener is already in trance when the count starts.
entries.how_to: Announce the rule first ('I will count from ten to one; with each number you go deeper'), then count. Put one or two short suggestions between numbers and keep them different from each other so the count does not turn into noise. Say what happens at the last number. 'Twice as deep' at every step is common, but a listener who checks will not feel a doubling; 'deeper still' is safer. Count down, not up, so the direction cannot be confused with the wake-up count.
examples: I'm going to count from ten down to one. With every number, you sink a little further. Ten. Letting go. Nine. Deeper still.
Five... drifting down. Four... heavier now. Three... further than before. Two... almost there. One... all the way down.
By the time I reach one, you will be as relaxed as you have ever been. Starting now. Ten.
cues: a descending number series (ten, nine, eight / 5, 4, 3) inside an established trance
'with each number', 'with every number I say'
'by the time I reach one', 'when I reach zero'
number followed directly by a depth word: 'Seven. Deeper.'
'twice as deep', 'ten times deeper' attached to a count

not_this.why: same form used to start trance; choose this entry only when trance has already been declared before the count begins
numbers only pace other content; here the script says each number itself takes the listener deeper
there the listener does the counting and the numbers are made to disappear
labels the stated multiplier ('twice as deep' per count); add it to this label when a count carries one, and use this label alone when the numbers bring only 'deeper'

evidence.note: Found in nearly every clinical and stage script; no controlled study shows counting deepens more than any other credible instruction, and its effect is best explained by expectancy.

entries.name: Descent imagery
entries.summary: Have the listener imagine moving downward, by stairs, lift or slow sinking, and map each bit of descent onto going deeper.
entries.definition: An imagined downward movement in which distance travelled stands for depth of trance. It rests on the down-is-deeper metaphor that the word 'deep' already carries. The vehicle (stairs, elevator, escalator, sinking through water or a mattress) is scene and can be swapped; the device is the mapping of descent onto depth.
entries.how_to: Describe the start point, give the rule ('each step takes you deeper'), then move down in stages, usually with a count. Keep the scene sparse so any listener can picture it, and give a non-visual version too ('or just feel yourself sinking') for people who do not visualise. Say what is at the bottom, since arrival is where the next section starts. Avoid falling, lifts or water for a general audience without offering an alternative: some listeners fear them.
examples: Picture a staircase with ten steps leading down. With each step you take, you go deeper. Take the first step now.
The lift doors close, and you feel it begin to go down. Floor by floor, each floor takes you deeper than the last.
If stairs are hard to picture, just feel yourself drifting down, level after level, like a leaf settling through still air, each level deeper than the one above.
cues: 'staircase', 'steps leading down', 'elevator', 'escalator', 'lift'
'down, and down', 'sinking', 'drifting down', 'descending'
'each step takes you deeper', 'floor by floor'
'at the bottom you find', 'when you reach the bottom'
a count paired with steps or floors

not_this.why: a bare count with no imagined movement; a counted staircase takes both labels
a scene used to start trance, not built on descent
a body sensation of weight, with no journey or scene

evidence.note: A stock deepener in clinical texts; imagery raises reported depth in people who absorb easily, but nothing shows descent imagery beats other deepeners.

entries.name: False bottom
entries.summary: When the listener reaches the announced bottom of a descent, declare that it is only the top of a deeper level, or that there is no bottom at all.
entries.definition: A turn applied to descent imagery or a countdown: the end point the listener was promised is reached and then redefined as a new starting point. The listener has just taken the bottom as the deepest they could go, so the extension reads as going beyond their own limit. It comes in two forms: a further level revealed below (a door, a second staircase, a floor that gives way), or a plain statement that the descent has no bottom.
entries.how_to: Run an ordinary descent with a clear end point and let the listener arrive and settle for a line or two. Then reveal the next level and take them down it, usually faster than the first. Use it once, or twice at most; after that the listener stops believing any stated end point and the counts lose their pull. A revealed floor is safer than a bottomless fall: say the listener is held and comfortable, because endless falling frightens some people. If later sections need a stable place to work from, end on a real bottom.
examples: One. All the way down. And now that you are at the bottom, you notice a door. Behind it, another staircase, going deeper still.
You thought that was as deep as you could go. It was only the first floor.
And you find there is no bottom here. Only deeper, and deeper, safely held, for as long as you like.
cues: 'you thought that was the bottom', 'that was only', 'this is just the beginning'
'another staircase', 'a door at the bottom', 'a level below this one', 'the floor opens'
'there is no bottom', 'bottomless', 'no limit to how deep'
'deeper than you thought possible', 'deeper than the bottom'
a second descent or count that starts immediately after a completed one

not_this.why: the parent is any mapped descent; this is the specific move of revoking its stated end point
that runs a second induction inside the imagined scene; this extends the same descent with no new induction
fractionation brings the listener partly up before each drop; here there is no rise, only a further drop

evidence.note: A stock move in stage, recorded and erotic hypnosis scripts with no controlled test; that judgments of depth shift against a just-set reference point is plausible from contrast research, but untested here.

entries.consent_note: It works by breaking a stated end point, so it should not be used on a limit the listener agreed to in advance (session length, how far the content goes); keep it to the depth image.

entries.name: Fractionation
entries.summary: Bring the listener partly up, then send them back down, several times, saying each return goes deeper than the last.
entries.definition: Repeated interruption and resumption of trance, with each re-entry suggested to be deeper. The interruption can be as small as opening the eyes for a second or as large as a full wake and chat. It is credited to Oskar Vogt in the 1890s and is the core of Elman's eyes-open, eyes-closed routine. What marks it out is the cycle: at least two up-and-down passes, with a comparison between them.
entries.how_to: State the rule before the first lift: 'each time you close your eyes you go twice as deep'. Keep the up phase short and incomplete, a second or two with eyes open is enough, and make the down command a single word or short phrase used identically each time. Three cycles are usual; more works if each is quicker than the last. Ratify after each drop. Make the final emergence clearly different from the partial lifts (a full count up), or the listener will stay half down.
examples: In a moment I'll ask you to open your eyes, and then close them again. When they close, you drop twice as deep as you are now. Open. And close. Deeper.
One, two, three, eyes open, halfway back. And sleep. All the way down, further than before.
Every time you come up, it gets easier to go back down. Up a little now. And drop.
cues: 'open your eyes ... and close them' repeated two or more times
'each time', 'every time you go back', 'further than before', 'deeper than last time'
a short count up followed immediately by 'sleep', 'drop' or 'down'
'halfway up', 'just to the surface', 'not all the way awake'
the same drop word used at the end of each cycle

not_this.why: fires an installed cue once; fractionation is the repeated cycle, though it often uses and builds such a cue
wakes the body and stops there, with no drop back
the whole session built on wake-and-drop cycles; label the unit for a passage

evidence.note: Taught as one of the most reliable deepeners. No controlled study isolates fractionation as raising suggestibility more than the same time spent on another deepener; quicker re-entry with repeated cycles is a practitioner observation.

entries.name: Breath-linked deepening
entries.summary: Tell the listener that every breath out takes them a little deeper, so their own breathing does the deepening.
entries.definition: A contingent suggestion whose trigger is the breath: each exhale, which is certain to come, is tied to an increase in depth. The listener's body supplies the repetition, so the deepening continues without the writer saying anything more. It differs from a breath induction in that it does not direct or pace the breathing; it only gives the breath a meaning.
entries.how_to: Link depth to the exhale, not the inhale: the out-breath is when the body slackens, so the suggestion matches what is felt. Say it once or twice, then leave it and move on; it keeps running under whatever follows. Do not tell the listener to breathe in any special way at this stage, since effortful breathing brings them up. It combines well with a silence or with any other deepener.
examples: And with every breath you let out, you sink just a little deeper.
Each time you breathe out, you settle a little further down. Nothing to change about your breathing. Just notice where each breath out leaves you.
You don't have to do anything. Your breathing takes you deeper all by itself, one exhale at a time.
cues: 'with each breath', 'with every breath'
'every time you exhale', 'each breath out', 'as you breathe out'
breath phrase followed by a depth comparative: 'deeper', 'further', 'more relaxed'
'your breathing takes you', 'let each breath carry you'

not_this.why: directs or paces the breath to start trance; this only attaches depth to breathing that is already happening
gives the in-breath one thing to take in and the out-breath another to let go; this ties the breath to depth only, with no paired content
names any and every stimulus; this names the breath only
a delivery choice about timing the voice, not a suggestion in the text

evidence.note: Slow exhalation does lower arousal, which is well studied; that tying 'deeper' to it increases hypnotic responding has not been tested separately.

entries.name: Everything deepens
entries.summary: Declare that whatever the listener hears, feels or thinks from now on sends them deeper.
entries.definition: A blanket contingent suggestion: an open class of stimuli (the voice, each word, outside sounds, body sensations, passing thoughts) is declared to cause deepening. Because the class is open, nothing that happens can count against the trance. It is the deepening form of utilization, and differs from incorporation in that it does more than neutralise distractions; it makes them fuel.
entries.how_to: Place it early in the deepener, before other techniques, so it covers everything after. Name two or three concrete things the listener is sure to notice (your voice, sounds in the room, their own breathing), then generalise to 'everything'. In a recording, include thoughts and the urge to move or swallow, because those are what listeners take as failure. Leave real alarms out of 'everything': say that anything needing attention will get it.
examples: Every word I say takes you deeper. Every sound you hear, inside the room or outside it, just helps you sink.
Any thought that drifts through only carries you further down. Even wondering whether this is working takes you deeper.
From now on, everything you notice, a sound, a shift, a swallow, becomes one more reason to let go.
cues: 'every word', 'every sound', 'each word I say' followed by a depth result
'anything you hear', 'everything you notice', 'whatever happens'
'only takes you deeper', 'sends you further down', 'becomes a signal to sink'
a list of stimuli ending in a generalisation ('...everything')
'even' + a likely distraction or doubt + a depth result

not_this.why: names particular likely interruptions and says they will not disturb or simply belong; choose this entry when the class is open ('every', 'any', 'everything') and the stated result is going deeper
one named trigger, the breath
narrows attention to the voice without claiming the voice deepens

evidence.note: Standard practice with a clear rationale (it removes reasons to judge the session as failing); its separate effect has not been measured.

entries.consent_note: Exclude genuine emergencies from 'everything': a listener told that every sound deepens should also be told that anything needing attention will rouse them.

entries.name: Silence / pause deepener
entries.summary: Announce a stretch of silence, say that depth grows during it, then stop talking.
entries.definition: A marked gap in the speech, framed in advance as time in which the listener goes deeper unaided. Two parts make it a device: the instruction before the gap and the gap itself. A pause with no framing is just delivery. It hands the work to the listener, which suits people who find constant talk distracting.
entries.how_to: Say how long the silence will be, what happens in it, and what ends it ('when you hear my voice again, you will be deeper still'). Without that the listener wonders whether the recording stopped and comes up. Twenty seconds to a minute is typical for audio; longer needs a music bed or a tone so the gap is not dead air. Resume quietly and ratify the depth reached. In a written script, mark the duration as a stage direction.
examples: I'm going to be quiet for a little while. In that silence, you drift deeper on your own. When you hear my voice again, it won't disturb you at all. [pause 30 seconds]
For the next minute there is nothing to listen to and nothing to do. Just sinking. [silence, 60s]
...That's right. Deeper than before I stopped speaking.
cues: 'I'm going to be quiet', 'I'll stop talking for a moment'
'in the silence', 'during this quiet time'
'when you hear my voice again', 'when I speak again'
stage directions: [pause], [silence 30s], (long pause)
a ratification straight after a marked gap: 'that's right, deeper'

not_this.why: the delivery choice of leaving gaps; this entry needs the spoken frame that gives the gap a job
short written pauses for rhythm, not a framed stretch of silence
also uses a gap, but suggests the gap feels far longer than it is

evidence.note: Common in clinical and recorded work; no controlled comparison exists, and unframed silence is known to bring some listeners up.

entries.name: Losing the numbers
entries.summary: Have the listener count backward from one hundred, relaxing after each number, until the numbers fade and cannot be found.
entries.definition: The listener does the counting, aloud in person or inwardly on a recording, and is told that each number doubles mental relaxation and that after a few the numbers will be gone. It is the final step of the Elman induction, where it stands for relaxing the mind after the body. It is both a deepener and a test: stopping the count is the sign it worked. The listener's own effortful task is what is suggested away, which separates it from a countdown the writer speaks.
entries.how_to: Give the whole instruction before they start: count back from one hundred, say 'deeper relaxed' after each number, and let the numbers fade by the time you reach ninety-seven or so. Tell them to make it happen, to push the numbers out, which gives them something to do. In person, ask 'are they all gone?' and accept a nod. On a recording there is no check, so add a fallback: 'and if a number is still there, let it drift further away'. Do not ask for more than three or four numbers; a long count wakes people up.
examples: In a moment, begin counting backward from one hundred, slowly. After each number say the words 'deeper relaxed', and let the numbers grow fainter. After a few, they'll be gone.
Ninety-nine... deeper relaxed... and already they are harder to find. Let them go. Push them right out.
And when the numbers have gone completely, just let your counting stop.
cues: 'count backward from one hundred' given as a task to the listener
'deeper relaxed' after each number
'let the numbers fade', 'relax them away', 'push them out'
'are they all gone?', 'when the numbers are gone'
'double your relaxation' with each number

not_this.why: the writer counts and the numbers stay; here the listener counts and the numbers vanish
a convincer staged to prove trance by forgetting an item; here the forgetting is the route to depth
gives the mind a counting job to occupy it; here the job is suggested away

origin.source: Elman, Hypnotherapy (1964)

evidence.note: Central to the Elman method and widely taught; suggested amnesia is real and studied, but the claim that losing the numbers marks 'somnambulism' has no independent support.

entries.name: Depth scale
entries.summary: Give depth a number, level or dial, then move the number and tell the listener their depth moves with it.
entries.definition: Depth is turned into a quantity on a named scale: one to ten, zero to a hundred, levels A to C, a dial or a gauge. Once it has a number the writer can report it, raise it, or hand the control to the listener. The scale gives the listener a way to judge 'how deep', which otherwise has no reference. It is a reference-point device applied to trance, and differs from a countdown in that the number names a position, not a step in a series.
entries.how_to: Define the ends first ('ten is wide awake, one is as deep as you can go'), say where the listener is now, then move them a few points at a time. Put the present reading somewhere in the middle so there is room both ways. Letting the listener turn the dial themselves gives a sense of control and suits self-hypnosis; the writer naming the number is quicker. Keep the same scale for the whole session and series, and never run it the opposite way round from your wake-up count.
examples: Imagine a dial numbered from ten down to one. Right now you're at about six. Watch it turn slowly down to five... and feel yourself go with it.
On a scale where one hundred is wide awake and zero is completely asleep, let a number come to mind for where you are now. Then let it drop by ten.
You are at level two. Level three is deeper and quieter. Going there now.
cues: 'on a scale of', 'from one to ten' applied to depth or relaxation
'dial', 'meter', 'gauge', 'needle', 'level' with a number
'you are at a six', 'level three', 'down to a four'
'turn it down', 'watch the number fall'
'what number are you at?' (interactive scripts)

not_this.why: numbers there are steps in a spoken series, not readings of a position
offers a value before asking the listener to estimate a quantity; this entry names a depth scale and moves its current reading, whoever moves it
the general imagined dial or switch for any quantity; label both when the dial sets depth

origin.source: Charles T. Tart, Self-report scales of hypnotic depth, International Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hypnosis (1970)

evidence.note: Self-reported depth numbers were studied as a measure and track responsiveness moderately; using the scale as a control that the listener turns is clinical practice without controlled tests.

entries.name: Mind-blanking
entries.summary: Suggest that thoughts slow down, drift off or stop, leaving the mind quiet and blank.
entries.definition: A suggestion aimed at thinking itself: inner talk gets slower, fainter, further away, or switches off. Body relaxation is its usual precursor and this is the matching step for the mind. It differs from occupying the mind with a task (which adds content) and from bypassing the critic (which names the judging faculty); here the content is simply reduced.
entries.how_to: Do not command 'stop thinking'; trying to suppress a thought brings it back. Let thoughts go by instead: give them an image to leave on (clouds, leaves on water, words dissolving) or describe them slowing and thinning. Say that any thought that does come is fine and passes. Put it after the body is settled. In scripts with later instructions, say that the listener still hears and understands, or a literal-minded listener will worry about missing them.
examples: Your thoughts are slowing down now. Each one a little fainter than the last, with more and more space in between.
If a thought comes, let it drift past like a cloud. You don't need to follow it. Soon there is only quiet.
Nothing to think about. Nothing to work out. A calm, empty mind.
cues: 'thoughts slowing', 'thoughts fading', 'thoughts drifting away'
'blank', 'empty', 'quiet mind', 'mind goes still'
'nothing to think', 'no need to think', 'thinking is too much effort'
'let it drift past', thought-as-cloud or thought-as-leaf images
'switch off', 'turn down the chatter'

not_this.why: says the analytical or judging part steps aside; this reduces all thought
gives the mind a job to do; this takes jobs away
a lasting change in the ability to think; this is a passing quiet inside the session

evidence.note: Reduced spontaneous thought is a commonly reported feature of hypnosis in responsive people; direct commands to suppress thoughts are experimentally shown to backfire, so phrasing matters.

entries.consent_note: State that the blankness lasts only for the session unless the listener has agreed to more, and restore clear thinking at emergence.

entries.name: Heaviness / floating
entries.summary: Suggest the body growing heavy and sinking, or weightless and floating, and treat that feeling as a sign of depth.
entries.definition: A suggested change in felt body weight, used as both a deepener and a marker. Heaviness borrows from what relaxed muscle really feels like, so it is easily confirmed; floating is the dissociative version, where the body is felt less. Either direction works, and some scripts offer both. It differs from progressive relaxation in that it does not go region by region or ask for release; it names one whole-body quality and builds on it.
entries.how_to: Use heaviness for most listeners and early on, since they can verify it; move to floating later or offer it as an alternative ('heavy, or so light you hardly feel the bed'). Tie the feeling to depth with a the-more-the-more link. Name the surface holding the body, which makes the weight concrete. Do not mix heavy and light for the same body part in one passage unless you say it is a choice. Restore normal body feeling at emergence.
examples: Your arms and legs are growing heavy now. So heavy they sink into the bed, and it would be too much effort to lift them.
Or perhaps you feel light instead, as if you were floating just above the mattress, drifting.
The heavier your body becomes, the deeper you go.
cues: 'heavy', 'heavier', 'like lead', 'limp', 'loose'
'sinking into the bed / chair / floor'
'floating', 'weightless', 'light as', 'drifting'
'too heavy to move', 'too much effort to lift'
weight word linked to depth: 'the heavier ... the deeper'

not_this.why: works through body regions in order; this names one whole-body weight feeling
sinking down through levels, steps or floors is descent imagery; sinking into the surface under the body, with no levels and no distance travelled, is this entry
a convincer where the arms visibly drift apart as proof
the body is made distant, numb or not one's own, beyond a feeling of weight

evidence.note: Limb heaviness is a standard item in autogenic training and suggestibility scales and most people can produce it; its value as a deepener rests on practice, not controlled tests.

entries.name: Physical drop deepener
entries.summary: Lift the listener's arm, say that when it drops they go deeper, and let it fall.
entries.definition: A deepener in which a real physical event, a limb falling limp into the lap, is announced in advance as the moment of deepening. In person the hypnotist lifts the arm by the wrist; in a recording the listener lifts it or imagines it. The landing is a sharp, felt, undeniable instant to hang the suggestion on, and a limp fall also shows the hypnotist how relaxed the arm is. It is one event, not a cycle, and it happens inside trance, not as the way in.
entries.how_to: Say what will happen before touching or lifting: 'I'm going to lift your hand; when it drops into your lap you go much deeper'. Let it fall a short distance onto something soft. If the listener helps lift or lowers the arm slowly, tell them to let it be loose and repeat. For audio, have the listener raise a hand a few centimetres themselves and let it fall. Touch needs prior agreement.
examples: I'm going to pick up your hand by the wrist. When I let go, it falls like a wet cloth into your lap, and as it lands you go ten times deeper.
Lift your right hand just a little off your leg. Hold it. Now let it drop, and drop with it.
[lift subject's arm, release] ...and all the way down.
cues: 'when your hand drops', 'as it lands', 'the moment it touches your lap'
'lift your arm / hand' followed by 'let it drop / fall'
'limp', 'like a wet cloth', 'dead weight'
stage directions for touch: [lift arm], [release wrist]
'drop with it'

not_this.why: a rapid induction from waking, using surprise; this is an announced drop inside trance
repeated up-and-down cycles of the trance itself; this is one physical event
the arm is made rigid as proof; here it is made limp and falls

evidence.note: A staple of stage and Elman-style practice; no controlled work, and the effect is plausibly the same expectancy and timing as any contingent suggestion.

entries.consent_note: In-person versions involve touch; agree on it in the pre-talk.

entries.name: Pleasure as deepener
aliases: the better it feels the deeper you go
entries.summary: Tie depth to pleasure, so that going deeper feels good or feeling good takes the listener deeper; often stated both ways.
entries.definition: A deepener in which pleasure, comfort, or in erotic scripts arousal, is linked to depth so that each increases the other. It makes going deeper rewarding in itself, which gives the listener a motive beyond following instructions. It is the the-more-the-more form with pleasure as one term, and works as reinforcement as well as suggestion. The pleasure may be mild (warmth, relief, contentment); the device does not depend on erotic content.
entries.how_to: Start from a pleasant feeling the listener really has at that point, usually the relief of relaxing, and name it before linking it. State the link in both directions and repeat it at each later deepening step. Keep the pleasure word matched to the script's register: 'good', 'comfortable', 'lovely' for general work. Because it trains the listener to find trance itself rewarding, it also raises the pull to relisten; say so in the description if the file is meant for repeated use.
examples: Notice how good it feels to let go. And the better it feels, the deeper you go.
Every step down brings a warm wave of comfort, and that comfort carries you down another step.
Going deeper feels wonderful. Feeling wonderful takes you deeper.
cues: 'the better it feels, the deeper you go' and its reverse
'feels so good to' + sink / drop / let go
'wave of pleasure / comfort / warmth' attached to a depth step
pleasure and depth words in the same clause, joined by 'and', 'as' or 'the more'
'deeper feels better'

not_this.why: the general one-way yoke of any two quantities; choose this entry when one term is pleasure, comfort or arousal and the other is depth, in whatever grammatical form
defined by the stated return (A feeds B and B feeds A) with any terms; a pleasure-depth link stated in both directions takes both labels, a one-way link takes only this one
a burst of pleasure given after a specific act of compliance; here pleasure is tied to depth itself
pairs pleasure with a word, act or idea to change its value; here the partner is trance depth
uses arousal as the focus that starts trance

evidence.note: Near-universal in recreational and erotic scripts and consistent with reinforcement principles; never tested as a deepener.

entries.consent_note: It makes trance itself rewarding and so encourages repeat listening; erotic versions need the listener's agreement to that content beforehand.

entries.name: Vicarious deepening
entries.summary: Describe another person going into trance, step by step, and let the listener follow along with them.
entries.definition: The trance signs and deepening suggestions are attached to a third party: a character in a story, a person the listener is asked to watch, a previous client. The listener, attending closely to someone relaxing, tends to do the same, and can do so without being told to. It is the deepening use of modelling. In live work it also covers watching another subject be hypnotized.
entries.how_to: Describe the other person's outward signs in the order the listener would feel them: breathing slows, shoulders drop, eyelids grow heavy. Use present tense and enough detail to picture. Then either leave the parallel unstated or close the gap with a line such as 'and you may notice the same in yourself'. It suits listeners who resist direct instruction and scripts already inside a story. Quoted speech addressed to the character ('she heard him say: deeper now') doubles as suggestion to the listener.
examples: Watch her as she listens. Her breathing slows. Her shoulders loosen. Her eyes are closing now, and she lets them.
He could feel himself sinking with every word the voice spoke, and the further he sank, the easier it became.
And as you watch them drift down, you might find you are drifting too.
cues: third-person pronouns (he, she, they) as the subject of trance verbs: sinks, drifts, goes under
'watch as', 'picture someone', 'imagine a person who'
a described character showing relaxation signs in sequence
a bridging line from the character to 'you': 'just like', 'the same way', 'you too'
quoted deepening suggestions spoken to the character

not_this.why: suggestions are addressed to a stand-in as a whole induction or sequence, often from a cold start; here a person is described going deeper after the listener's own trance has been established
shows someone performing a target act and being rewarded for it, as a pattern for later behavior; here what is narrated is the other person's trance signs and descent, for the listener to mirror now
the listener becomes the character; here they watch from outside and follow
cites what others do as a reason; here the other's experience is narrated for the listener to mirror

evidence.note: Watching a responsive model does raise hypnotic responding in controlled studies; the scripted, narrated version in recordings has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: The listener is deepened without being addressed, so they may not notice it happening; when the passage sits inside a story, say in the description that the piece is hypnotic.

entries.name: Trance within trance
entries.summary: Inside the imagined scene of the trance, have the listener be hypnotized again, so the second trance stacks on the first.
entries.definition: A second induction carried out within the imagery of the first: the imagined self lies down, closes its eyes, watches a pendulum, or is hypnotized by a figure in the scene. Each layer is framed as deeper than the one containing it. The defining feature is the frame-within-a-frame; an ordinary second deepener addresses the listener directly, while this one addresses the listener's imagined self.
entries.how_to: Establish the outer scene firmly first, with the listener placed in it in the first person. Then run a short, complete induction on the imagined self, plainly marked ('in this place, you close your eyes again'). Two layers is usual; three risks losing people. Deliver the main suggestions at the innermost layer. Come out in reverse order, one layer at a time, and finish with a normal emergence, or the listener may wake feeling one layer short.
examples: In this quiet room, you lie back on the couch and close your eyes again. And you go into a trance inside this trance, twice as deep.
The figure beside you begins to count, and you feel yourself being hypnotized here too, sinking beneath the place you had already sunk to.
A dream inside the dream. Further in. Further down.
cues: 'close your eyes again' when eyes are already closed
'a trance within this trance', 'inside this dream', 'hypnotized here too'
an induction (count, fixation, eye closure) performed on the listener inside an imagined scene
an in-scene hypnotist or voice hypnotizing 'you'
layered exits: 'first, come back to the room in your mind, then...'

not_this.why: repeats exit and re-entry at the same level; this adds a level without leaving
declares the reached bottom to be the top of a further descent; here a new induction is run on the imagined self inside the scene
stories opened inside stories to carry suggestions, with no second induction
someone else is described going under; here the listener's own imagined self is induced

evidence.note: Used by clinicians and popular in recreational scripts, with good subjective reports from people who absorb easily; no controlled evidence that layers add depth.

entries.consent_note: Bring the listener out through every layer and finish with a full reorientation; a skipped layer can leave them feeling not quite awake.

entries.name: Approach deepener
entries.summary: Tie depth to something coming steadily closer, such as a light, footsteps or a voice, and promise full depth at the moment it arrives.
entries.definition: A deepener in which the listener stays still and something else moves toward them; the shrinking distance stands for growing depth, and arrival is the stated end point. It is the mirror of descent imagery, where the listener does the travelling. What approaches (a light, a tide, footsteps, the speaker's voice) is scene and can be swapped; the device is the mapping of nearness onto depth with a defined moment of contact.
entries.how_to: Name the thing while it is still far off, state the rule ('the closer it comes, the deeper you go'), then bring it nearer in three to six marked stages. Say what happens on arrival and deliver it on time: the listener is waiting for that moment, and a drawn-out or missing arrival wastes the build. Choose something welcome or neutral for a general audience; an approaching person or footsteps can alarm, so give them a friendly identity or use light, warmth or a tide instead. In audio, rising volume or a voice moving closer in the stereo field supports it.
examples: Far off, there is a soft light. It is coming slowly toward you, and the closer it comes, the deeper you go.
The tide is a long way out. Each wave reaches a little nearer, and each one takes you a little further down. When the water touches your feet, you let go completely.
My voice is getting closer now. Closer. And when it is right beside you, you will be as deep as you need to be.
cues: 'closer and closer', 'nearer and nearer', 'coming toward you'
'the closer it comes, the deeper you go'
'when it reaches you', 'when it touches you', 'when it arrives' followed by a depth or letting-go statement
a distant object or sound named first, then restated at shorter distances
the listener is stationary while the described thing moves
stage directions for a voice or sound moving nearer

not_this.why: there the listener moves downward; here the listener is still and something moves toward them
anticipation announces an event and delays it to raise wanting; here the approach itself is mapped onto depth step by step
a count ties depth to numbers; an approach ties it to distance, and a counted approach takes both labels

evidence.note: Common in recorded and erotic hypnosis scripts and absent as a named technique from clinical texts; nothing shows it deepens more than any other credible instruction, and its effect is best explained by expectancy and absorption in the image.

entries.name: Emergence
entries.summary: Ways of ending a session, or of deliberately leaving it open: waking, handing off to sleep, looping, and the suggestions placed at the exit.
entries.definition: Emergence groups devices that end a session or govern its ending. Its exits include count-up wake, self-paced wake, reorientation check, drift into sleep, loop back and partial wake. Conditional wake sets a condition for ending trance and may be stated earlier in the session. Sealing states what carries over after waking, and next-time-deeper suggests how future sessions will go; the latter may also be stated before the exit. Amnesia on waking is placed at the exit but filed as a variant of amnesia suggestion in the memory family. The emergence section is the place in a script where the ending occurs, rather than a family of devices.
entries.how_to: First choose the exit by how the file will be used: a count-up wake or self-paced wake for daytime listening, drift into sleep for bedtime files, loop back only for files built to repeat. Add a reorientation check whenever the session suggested heaviness, numbness, immobility, time distortion or strong emotion; a count alone does not cancel those. Place sealing and next-time-deeper just before the exit, not inside it, so the wake itself stays clean. Treat partial wake, amnesia on waking, drift into sleep and loop back as choices that leave something open, and say so in the file description. A complete default ending is: seal, cancel what should not persist, count up, check orientation.

not_this.why: the section is the place in the script; the family is the set of devices used there
a wake that exists only to be followed by another drop is deepening, not an ending
an emergency wake is a standing instruction given early, not the planned exit

evidence.note: Every standard clinical procedure and research scale ends with an explicit termination; which wording works best has not been compared in controlled studies.

entries.consent_note: The ending decides what the listener leaves with; any exit that leaves trance, suggestions or forgetting in place should be disclosed before the session starts.

entries.name: Count-up wake
entries.summary: Count upward, usually one to five, giving each number a step of returning alertness, and end on a clear wake instruction.
entries.definition: A counted exit in which each number is tied to a named piece of waking: energy returning, breath deepening, eyes opening. The count usually runs upward, opposite to the script's induction or deepener count, but some scripts and the standard research scales wake on a downward count; what defines the device is numbers tied to returning alertness, not their direction. It differs from a self-paced wake in that the writer sets the timing, and from a reorientation check in that it restores alertness without itemizing what must be cancelled.
entries.how_to: Announce the count and what happens at the last number before you start. Give every number one concrete change, moving from body to breath to head to eyes. Let sentences get shorter and the wording brisker as the count climbs, and finish with an unambiguous terminal phrase such as 'wide awake'. Do not slip new suggestions between the numbers; put them before the count. If the induction counted down, count up, and use the same range if you can.
examples: In a moment I will count from one to five. At five your eyes open and you are fully awake.
One, energy coming back into your arms and legs. Two, your breathing gets deeper and stronger. Three, your head is clearing.
Four, eyes ready to open. Five. Eyes open, wide awake, feeling good.
cues: ascending number sequence near the end of the script (one... two... three... four... five)
'I will count from one to', 'on the count of five', 'when I reach five'
'wide awake', 'fully alert', 'eyes open' on or after the last number
each number followed by a returning-alertness clause ('energy returning', 'more awake with each number')
'coming up', 'coming back', 'all the way up'

not_this.why: counts toward depth, not toward alertness, whatever direction the numbers run
a count-up followed by another drop is one cycle of fractionation, not the ending
the listener sets the timing there; here the count does

evidence.note: Counted termination is standard in clinical scripts and research scales; no studies show a count wakes better than a plain instruction to wake, and the direction of the count is convention.

entries.name: Sealing suggestions before waking
entries.summary: Just before waking, state that the session's suggestions stay in place and keep working afterward.
entries.definition: A closing statement about the session's suggestions as a set: they remain, they are locked in, they go with the listener. It adds no new content; it asserts the persistence of what was already given. That separates it from a recap, which restates the suggestions, from a posthypnotic suggestion, which specifies one later response, and from a permanence claim, which asserts that a change can never be undone.
entries.how_to: Place it after the last suggestion and before the count-up. Refer to the suggestions collectively ('everything you have accepted here') and say where they go ('with you', 'deep in your mind') and for how long. One or two sentences is enough; it leans on what came before and cannot rescue suggestions that did not land. In files with bounded effects, seal only what should persist and name what ends with the session in the same passage.
examples: Everything you have learned here stays with you, long after you open your eyes.
These suggestions are locked in now, working quietly in the background of your day.
Whatever was useful to you here goes with you when you wake. Everything else stays behind in this session.
cues: 'stays with you', 'carry this with you', 'bring this back with you'
'locked in', 'sealed', 'fixed in place', 'settling in permanently'
collective reference to prior suggestions ('everything I have said', 'all of these suggestions', 'what you learned here')
'even after you wake', 'long after this session ends'
position: last passage before the wake count or sleep handoff

not_this.why: a recap restates the suggestions; sealing only says they persist
that specifies a particular later response, usually on a cue; sealing is a blanket persistence statement
that asserts irreversibility of a change; sealing says the suggestions carry past the wake

evidence.note: Posthypnotic suggestions can persist without it; no study has tested whether a sealing statement adds durability beyond the suggestions themselves.

entries.consent_note: Sealing extends effects past the session, so the file description should say what is meant to persist and for how long.

entries.name: Partial wake
entries.summary: Bring back the eyes, body or speech while stating that the trance, or the responsiveness to suggestion, continues.
entries.definition: A wake that is explicitly incomplete: some faculties are restored (eyes open, able to move, talk, read) and the script states that the listener remains in trance or remains as suggestible as before. The defining feature is the pairing of a restoring instruction with a continuation statement. It is not fractionation, because no drop follows, and it is not an ending by itself unless the writer intends the session to end with trance left open.
entries.how_to: State exactly what returns and what stays: 'your eyes open; the trance stays'. Give the listener something to do in that state (follow instructions, look at a screen, carry out a task) so the continuation has content. Decide how it closes and write that in: a later full wake in the same file, a time limit, or a cue that completes the wake. A file that ends on a partial wake with no completion leaves the listener to shake it off alone, and should include a reorientation instruction or emergency wake they can use.
examples: In a moment your eyes will open, and you will stay exactly as deep as you are now.
You can move and speak and look around the room, and every word of mine still sinks straight in.
Eyes open. Still relaxed, still focused, still listening. You stay this way until I count you all the way up.
cues: 'open your eyes' or 'wake' paired with 'still', 'remain', 'stay' ('eyes open, still deep')
'without waking', 'while staying in trance', 'only your eyes wake'
'awake but', 'your body wakes while your mind stays'
'just as suggestible', 'still under', 'still mine' after a wake instruction
a wake count that stops short of its announced end, or is followed by continued suggestions

not_this.why: fractionation brings the listener up in order to drop them again; a partial wake holds them up and under
that withholds the wake until a command or condition and restores nothing; a partial wake restores eyes, movement or speech and says trance continues. A span that does both takes both labels
that induces and runs trance with eyes open from the start; a partial wake begins from an established eyes-closed trance and contains a wake or eye-opening instruction
that follows a full wake and fires later on a cue; here the trance itself is declared ongoing

evidence.note: Hypnotized subjects respond to suggestion with eyes open and moving about, and waking suggestion without any induction also works; whether a declared 'continuing trance' is a distinct state is not established.

entries.consent_note: The listener goes on acting while told they are still suggestible, so this needs prior agreement, a stated end condition, and a full wake available on demand.

entries.name: Drift into sleep
entries.summary: End with no wake-up: invite the listener to pass from trance into ordinary sleep and wake naturally later.
entries.definition: An ending for bedtime files in which the script hands the listener to natural sleep and puts the wake at the next morning. It is recognized by an invitation to sleep at the close together with the absence of a wake count. It differs from a file that simply stops, because the handoff is stated, and from sleep as a trance word ('sleep now'), which is an induction command and not an ending.
entries.how_to: Say in the pretalk and the description that the file ends in sleep, so nobody uses it in the daytime. Before the handoff, cancel anything that should not run overnight (heaviness, immobility, open triggers) and say that the listener will wake normally if anything needs them. Then slow down, lengthen the pauses, and let the last lines thin out; do not end on a sharp sound or a bright instruction. Add a morning line: waking at the usual time, rested and clear. Consider offering an optional wake for those not sleeping.
examples: There is nothing more to do tonight. Let this trance turn into ordinary, restful sleep.
You sleep through the night and wake at your usual time, rested and clear-headed.
I will not count you up tonight. My voice fades, and you go on drifting into sleep.
cues: 'drift into sleep', 'natural sleep', 'sleep through the night' in the closing passage
'when you wake in the morning', 'wake at your usual time'
no count-up and no 'wide awake' anywhere in the ending
'no need to wake', 'I will not wake you', 'my voice fades as you sleep'
closing lines that shorten and trail off, often into silence or music

not_this.why: also has no wakener, but returns to the start instead of releasing the listener into sleep
that hands over the timing of waking; this replaces waking with sleep
'sleep' as a command there means trance, at the start, not real sleep at the end

evidence.note: Hypnosis and relaxation recordings for sleep have some controlled support; whether unterminated suggestions behave differently after sleep than after a formal wake has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: The session is never formally closed, so nothing that should be cancelled may be left running, and the description must say the file ends in sleep.

entries.name: Loop back
entries.summary: Write the last lines to lead straight into the first lines, so the file can repeat with no wake and no seam.
entries.definition: An ending that is a join: the final passage matches the opening in wording, state and sound, or explicitly sends the listener back to the start. There is no wake; the listener leaves by stopping the file or by falling asleep. It is the ending device of a loop structure, and differs from a refrain, which returns within a script, and from drift into sleep, which releases the listener instead of returning them.
entries.how_to: Make the state at the last line equal the state the first line assumes; a loop that opens with a full induction from alertness will jar on the second pass, so start loop files already settled or make the opening work at any depth. Close on a line that can precede the opening line grammatically and in tone, or echo the opening words. Keep the audio level and bed continuous across the join. Because there is no wake, put an emergency wake and a stop rule early in the loop (stop the file, take a breath, open your eyes, fully alert), and state a suggested number of repeats in the description.
examples: And as you sink again, you hear the words that started all of this, and follow them down once more.
Every ending is a beginning. So begin again. Just listen, and breathe.
Round and round, back to the top, each pass a little easier than the last.
cues: last lines repeat or closely echo the first lines of the script
'again', 'once more', 'begin again', 'back to the beginning', 'around and around' in the closing passage
no wake count and no sleep handoff at the end
'each time through', 'every loop', 'with every repeat'
stage or production notes: 'loop', 'loopable', 'repeat', 'seamless'

not_this.why: the structure is the whole file built to repeat; this is the join at its end
a refrain recurs inside one pass; a loop back restarts the whole script
that repeats a short phrase to induce; this repeats the entire file

evidence.note: Repetition increases familiarity and recall of the repeated lines; no study has compared looped files with terminated ones, and nothing shows looping adds effect beyond the extra exposure.

entries.consent_note: A loop has no built-in exit, so the listener must be told how to stop and should have an emergency wake inside the loop.

entries.name: Next-time-deeper suggestion
entries.summary: Before waking, suggest that every future session will take hold faster and go deeper than this one.
entries.definition: A posthypnotic suggestion about future trance itself: its speed, depth and ease. It names no specific cue; it sets an expectation for all later sessions. That separates it from a re-induction trigger, which installs and fires a specific cue, and from a prescribed listening schedule, which says when to listen and not what listening will be like.
entries.how_to: Place it after the main suggestions and before the wake, when the listener has just experienced whatever depth they reached. Anchor it to that experience ('as deep as you went today, and then further') and phrase it as an ordinary skill improving with practice. Limit its scope: this voice, this series, or times the listener chooses to go into trance. Do not promise instant or unlimited depth; a claim the next session contradicts costs credibility.
examples: Each time you choose to listen, you return to this place more quickly and settle more deeply.
Next time, you begin where you are leaving off today.
Like any skill, this gets easier with practice. Every session, a little faster, a little deeper.
cues: 'next time', 'each time', 'every time you listen', 'whenever you return'
comparatives of depth or speed in future tense ('faster', 'deeper', 'more easily', 'twice as deep')
'begin where you left off', 'pick up from this depth'
practice framing ('like any skill', 'the more you practise')
position: late in the script, before the wake count

not_this.why: the trigger is a specific installed cue that drops the listener at once; the seed only sets expectation for future sessions
the general form; when the later response is trance itself coming faster or deeper and no cue is named, label only the seed
that strengthens one named trigger with each use, not trance in general
that tells the listener when to listen, not that listening will go deeper

evidence.note: Routine in clinical scripts, and practitioners report that returning subjects go under more quickly; this has not been measured with the suggestion separated from simple familiarity, and hypnotizability scores are fairly stable, so the promise of ever-greater depth outruns the evidence.

entries.consent_note: It shapes future sessions, so it should be limited to occasions the listener chooses and to the intended voice or series.

entries.name: Self-paced wake
entries.summary: Tell the listener to come back in their own time, when they are ready, instead of waking them on a count.
entries.definition: A permissive exit in which the writer gives the instruction to return and leaves the timing to the listener. It may be bare ('when you are ready, open your eyes') or conditional, tying the return to the listener's own sense that the work is done. It differs from a count-up wake in who sets the pace, and from drift into sleep in that waking is still the stated outcome.
entries.how_to: Use it after gentle or emotionally heavy sessions, in live work where you can watch the listener, and in recordings that can end in silence or music. Say what 'ready' looks like and give the last step concretely: a deeper breath, a stretch, eyes opening. In a recording, leave real time after the instruction and do not talk over it. If the session included heaviness, numbness or immobility, cancel those explicitly first, because a self-paced wake has no built-in steps to do it. A good fallback is to offer both: 'come back in your own time, or on my count if you prefer'.
examples: Take all the time you need. When you are ready, and not before, let your eyes open.
In your own time, take a deeper breath, stretch, and come back to the room.
You return only as quickly as your mind finishes settling what you have learned.
cues: 'when you are ready', 'in your own time', 'at your own pace', 'take all the time you need'
'whenever you like', 'no hurry', 'not before' governing eye opening or return
wake instruction with no count attached
'only as quickly as', 'as soon as your mind has' followed by a return
long pause, silence or music-only stage direction after the instruction

not_this.why: the writer sets the timing there with numbers
there the speaker's command or a set condition must be met and waking is stated as unavailable until then; here the only condition is the listener's own readiness
that replaces waking with sleep; here the listener still wakes, on their own clock
label the exit as self-paced wake; add implied directive only when the sentence has all three parts (time clause, inner task, outward signal such as the eyes opening)

evidence.note: Common in permissive and Ericksonian practice; no controlled comparison with counted wakes exists, and claims that it integrates the work better are untested.

entries.name: Reorientation check
entries.summary: Explicitly restore normal body feeling, time, place and alertness, and cancel any session effect that should not continue.
entries.definition: An itemized return to baseline: the script names what goes back to normal (weight and feeling in the limbs, movement, sense of time, awareness of the room, a clear head) and removes whatever was suggested only for the session. Its mark is the list of restored functions and the cancelling language. A count-up wake restores alertness in general; the reorientation check says what is restored and makes sure nothing unwanted is left.
entries.how_to: Go back through the session and list every suggested alteration: heaviness, lightness, numbness, immobility, time distortion, altered perception, roles, strong emotion. Reverse each one by name, in plain direct wording, before or during the wake. Then orient outward: the surface under the body, sounds in the room, the day and time. Finish with a check the listener can act on (move fingers and toes, look around, wait a few minutes before driving). Keep the tone matter-of-fact; this is housekeeping, and vague wording defeats its purpose.
examples: All normal feeling and movement return to your arms and legs now. Any heaviness is gone.
Feel the chair under you. Hear the sounds of the room. You know where you are and what day it is.
Your mind is clear and your body is back to normal in every way. Wiggle your fingers and toes, and take your time before you stand.
cues: 'back to normal', 'return to normal', 'in every way' applied to body, mind or sensation
'any heaviness / numbness / stiffness is gone', 'all feeling returns'
outward orientation ('the room around you', 'the surface beneath you', 'here and now', 'what day it is')
movement checks ('wiggle your fingers and toes', 'stretch', 'look around')
'clear-headed', 'fully present', 'fully back'
post-wake cautions ('take a moment before you stand', 'before driving')

not_this.why: a count restores alertness by steps; the check itemizes what is restored and cancels leftovers
aftercare is emotional settling and reassurance after waking; this is restoring function and orientation
that cancels something meant to act after the session, a trigger or posthypnotic suggestion, by name; this returns in-session alterations (heaviness, numbness, immobility, time sense) to normal
that declares the scene's claims and roles fiction that ends with the session; this restores body, senses and orientation

evidence.note: Clinical texts require cancelling suggested effects before ending, and surveys report transient after-effects such as drowsiness or headache in a minority of subjects; whether explicit reorientation reduces them has not been tested directly.

entries.name: Wellbeing suggestions
entries.summary: Before waking, give general suggestions of calm, good sleep, confidence and feeling well for the rest of the day.
entries.definition: Wellbeing suggestions are general, non-specific positive suggestions for rest, calm, self-regard and coping, added so the listener leaves better than they arrived. In clinical hypnosis they are called ego strengthening. They differ from suggestion sealing, which locks in the session's specific suggestions, and from aftercare, which settles the immediate reaction to intense content.
entries.how_to: Place them near the end, after the main work and before the count-up. Keep them broad and kind: sleep well, feel calm, think clearly, like yourself. Avoid tying them to the speaker or to relistening, which turns them into dependency. A short set of three or four lines is enough.
examples: Tonight you'll sleep deeply and wake rested.
You'll carry a quiet sense of calm with you, and find you handle the day with more ease.
Each day you notice a little more that you are capable and steady.
cues: 'you'll sleep deeply'
'feel calm / confident / refreshed'
'each day ... more'
general positive suggestions just before waking
'carry this calm with you'

not_this.why: specifies a particular response to occur after the session, with or without a cue; wellbeing suggestions give general wishes for calm, rest or confidence after waking
says the session's own suggestions stay, and adds no new content
settles the reaction to intense content now, not lasting wellbeing
a closing suggestion about the next session (faster, deeper), not about the listener's day

origin.source: John Hartland, The Value of ‘Ego-Strengthening’ Procedures Prior to Direct Symptom-Removal under Hypnosis, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1965)

evidence.note: Ego strengthening is standard in clinical texts; its specific added benefit over the rest of a session has little controlled evidence.

entries.consent_note: These suggestions are meant to last past the session, so the content note should say the file includes them. Keep them general; tying the good feeling to the speaker or to listening again turns them into dependency.

entries.name: Conditional wake
entries.summary: State that the listener stays in trance, and cannot leave it, until the speaker gives the wake command or a named condition is met.
entries.definition: A suggestion about the exit, given before the exit: waking is made to depend on one thing the writer names, such as a command, the end of a count, a finished task or the end of the file. Until then the script declares that the listener stays under, often adding that trying to wake only takes them deeper. It differs from a partial wake, which restores some faculties while trance continues, and from an eyelid lock, which blocks one movement and invites a test. Here the whole state is declared closed from the inside, with the key held by the speaker or the condition.
entries.how_to: Place it after the induction has taken, usually at the end of deepening, and state the condition in one plain sentence so there is no doubt what ends it. Make sure the condition is actually delivered later in the same file: a lock with no key is an unfinished script. Pair it with an emergency wake that the lock does not override, and say so in the same passage. In a recording the listener can always stop the file, so the lock works as agreed fantasy and as a deepener; write it that way and do not claim more. It fails when the condition is vague, or when the listener was not told beforehand that the file contains it.
examples: You stay this deep until you hear me say the words 'wide awake'. Nothing else brings you up.
Until I count from one to five, there is no way out of this calm, and nothing in you is looking for one.
If anything needs your attention, you wake at once. Otherwise you stay under until the task is done and I tell you to come back.
cues: 'until I say', 'until I wake you', 'until you hear', 'not before' attached to waking or coming up
'you cannot wake', 'you can't come up', 'no way out', 'locked in', 'held here'
'only my voice can wake you', 'only when I count', 'only I can bring you back'
'you stay in trance until' followed by a task, a count, a word or the end of the session
'trying to wake only takes you deeper'
a wake condition stated in the induction, deepening or suggestion section, well before the emergence section

not_this.why: that returns eyes, movement or speech while trance continues; this returns nothing and makes the full wake depend on a condition
that locks one movement and stages a test of it; this locks the state and usually stages no test
that attaches dread to stopping; a conditional wake asserts the listener cannot stop yet, with no threat attached

evidence.note: Common in recreational and stage scripts; there is no evidence that anyone can be held in hypnosis against their wish, and in research where the hypnotist stopped without ending the session, subjects came out on their own within minutes.

entries.consent_note: It tells the listener they cannot stop, so it needs agreement beforehand, an emergency wake that overrides it, and a condition the script actually delivers; never leave it unresolved at the end of a file.

entries.name: Suggestion forms
entries.summary: The ways a single suggestion can be worded: as a command, an offer, a link, a question, a quotation or a hint.
entries.definition: This family covers the sentence-level shape of one suggestion, independent of what is being suggested. The same content ('your arm is heavy') can be commanded, permitted, linked to a breath, asked as a question, put in someone else's mouth or hidden in a story. Entries here differ in grammar and in how much the listener is told that a suggestion is being made. Two nested families hold the largest sub-groups: Presupposition and implication (`presupposition`), where the claim is built into the background of a sentence, and Artful vagueness (`vague-language`), the Milton-model patterns that leave content unspecified.
entries.how_to: Pick the form from three things: how much authority the listener has agreed to, how likely the response is, and how deep they are. Use direct suggestion when the listener wants to be told and the response is easy; use permissive, open-ended or contingent forms early, with analytical listeners, or when a failed response would cost credibility. Link forms (contingent, compound, the more the more, implied directive) carry a suggestion on something already happening. Question forms prompt an inner search. Follow any response with ratification, and use repetition and compounding to hold what has been accepted. Mix forms; a script written in one form only goes flat.

not_this.why: nested family for claims carried in a sentence's background, not its main assertion
nested family for patterns that work by leaving content unspecified
figures of repetition and sound shape the texture of a passage, not the form of one suggestion

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Clinical texts list these forms in detail; controlled comparisons of direct and indirect wording have not shown one form to be reliably more effective than another.

entries.name: Direct suggestion
entries.summary: Say plainly what the listener will do or feel, as an instruction or a statement of fact.
entries.definition: A direct suggestion names the response openly and tells the listener to produce it or states that it is happening. There is no hedge, no choice and no disguise: the listener knows a suggestion has been given and what it asks. It is the default form of the standard hypnotizability scales and of authoritarian styles.
entries.how_to: Use short sentences in the imperative or the plain present or future: one response per sentence. It lands when the listener has accepted the speaker's role and the response is within reach; it fails when it demands something the listener can check and find untrue, so start with easy responses and build. Follow each one with ratification or a pause long enough to respond. With wary listeners, soften the first few into permissive form and move to direct once responses are coming.
examples: Close your eyes.
Your right arm is growing heavy. Heavy and still.
You feel completely calm now.
cues: second-person imperative: 'close', 'relax', 'let go', 'sink'
unhedged declaratives: 'you are', 'you will', 'your X is becoming'
no modal softeners ('may', 'might', 'perhaps', 'can') in the sentence
'now' attached to a command
one named response per short sentence

not_this.why: permissive wording offers the response ('you may'); direct wording tells
indirect suggestion never states the wanted response as an instruction
an embedded command is an imperative hidden inside a sentence about something else

evidence.note: Direct verbal suggestions are the items on the standard hypnotizability scales and reliably produce responses in a proportion of people; response depends far more on the listener's suggestibility and expectancy than on wording.

entries.name: Indirect suggestion
entries.summary: Get the response across by hint, story, general remark or possibility, without ever telling the listener to do it.
entries.definition: An indirect suggestion points at the response without commanding it and often without addressing it to the listener at all. The wanted response is something the listener infers or drifts into, so it tends to feel self-generated. It is an umbrella label: when a more specific form applies (truism, embedded question, metaphor, implication, open-ended suggestion), label that; use this entry for indirect phrasing that fits none of them.
entries.how_to: Talk about the response in general terms, about other people, or as one possibility among several, and leave the application to the listener. Use it where a command would invite checking or pushback: early in a session, with analytical listeners, or for responses that cannot be forced, such as forgetting or involuntary movement. It fails when it is so oblique that nothing is suggested; make sure a listener who took the hint would know what to do. Follow up with a direct or contingent line once the response starts.
examples: Some people find that their hands grow warm before anything else changes.
There's a particular quiet that comes over a room once the last job of the day is done.
A person can be surprised by how quiet the mind becomes when nothing is asked of it.
cues: third-person or generic subjects: 'some people', 'a person', 'many listeners'
a remark about the room, the hour or the speaker's own state that names the wanted state without attributing it to the listener
possibility words: 'perhaps', 'might', 'sooner or later'
the response is described but no sentence instructs the listener to do it
talk about a topic (a garden, a journey) whose terms match the wanted state

not_this.why: permissive wording still names the listener's response openly; it only softens the demand
implication is the specific case where the listener must infer an unstated claim from what is said
metaphor carries the suggestion in a parallel story or image; label that when a story is present

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: The claim that indirect wording works better or gets past resistance is not supported; controlled comparisons generally find direct and indirect suggestions about equally effective, though indirect ones may feel less effortful.

entries.consent_note: Because the listener may not register that a suggestion was made, tell them beforehand what the session is for.

entries.name: Permissive suggestion
entries.summary: Offer the response as something the listener can, may or might do, instead of ordering it.
entries.definition: A permissive suggestion names the response openly but frames it as an ability or an option the listener is free to take. The marker is a modal of possibility or a verb of allowing in the place where a command would be. It differs from indirect suggestion in that the response is stated outright and addressed to the listener.
entries.how_to: Replace the imperative with 'you can', 'you may', 'you might', 'allow', 'let'. Use it at the start of a session, for listeners who dislike being told, and for any response that might not happen, since nothing is contradicted if it does not. Too many in a row sound hesitant; firm up to contingent or direct wording once the listener is responding. Keep the response itself specific even though the demand is soft.
examples: You can let your shoulders drop whenever you're ready.
You might notice your breathing slowing by itself.
Allow that calm to spread as far as it wants to go.
cues: 'you can', 'you may', 'you might', 'you could'
'allow yourself to', 'let yourself', 'let your'
'if you like', 'whenever you're ready', 'when you want to'
'feel free to'
a named response with no imperative verb governing it

not_this.why: permission-giving lifts a restraint on something the listener is holding back ('it's okay to'); this is a general soft form for any suggestion
modal-operator labels the modal word itself wherever it occurs; this labels a whole suggestion offered as optional
indirect suggestion does not state the response to the listener at all

evidence.note: Standard in clinical texts; studies comparing permissive and authoritarian wording find little overall difference in response, with some listeners preferring one style.

entries.name: Contingent suggestion
entries.summary: Tie the wanted response to something already happening or sure to happen, so one brings the other.
entries.definition: A contingent suggestion makes the response depend on an ongoing or inevitable event: 'as you breathe out, your shoulders drop'. The link is made with a time or condition word (as, while, when, each time, with every), not with a claim of causation. The certain event supplies both the timing and the credibility for the uncertain one.
entries.how_to: Choose a first half the listener cannot fail to do or notice: a breath, a blink, hearing a word, a count. Put it in a subordinate clause and the suggestion in the main clause. Keep the pair plausible in size; a breath can carry a little more relaxation but not a large change in one step. Recurring events ('each time', 'with every') make the suggestion repeat itself without more words.
examples: As you breathe out, your shoulders sink a little lower.
Each time you blink, your eyelids feel a little heavier.
When your hand touches your lap, you can let go completely.
cues: 'as you ..., you ...'
'while', 'when', 'as soon as' joining an ongoing act to a response
'each time', 'every time', 'with every breath/word/number'
first clause is a verifiable or inevitable event; second clause is the suggested response
'and as it does', 'and when that happens'

not_this.why: compound suggestion joins with plain 'and' and states no dependence between the halves
cause-effect claim asserts that X makes or causes Y; contingent wording only ties them in time
there the time clause holds the suggested thing as a given; here the time clause holds the real event and the main clause the suggestion

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: A standard clinical form; the linking has not been tested in isolation, though tying a response to a cue is well supported in other fields.

entries.name: Stepwise doubling
entries.summary: Attach a stated multiplier or increment of the state, such as twice as deep or ten percent more, to each count, breath or repetition.
entries.definition: A contingent suggestion whose second half is a quantified increase of a state the listener already has: each recurring event doubles it, multiplies it by ten, or adds a fixed share. The recurring event supplies the timing, as in any contingent suggestion; what makes this variant is the explicit arithmetic and the fact that it compounds across steps. The number is not meant to be checked. It tells the listener the size of step to aim for and makes each step visibly larger than the last.
entries.how_to: Establish the state first, since a multiplier needs something to multiply. Pick the recurring event (a count, an exhale, a snap, each return in fractionation) and state the rule once, then repeat the multiplier at each step in the same words. Doubling suits three to five steps; over a long count use a small increment ('ten percent more', 'one notch') because repeated doubling soon outruns anything the listener can feel and invites checking. Analytical listeners take a modest number better than a large one. Finish with a plain statement of where the listener now is, not with one more multiplier.
examples: With each number I count, you go twice as deep as you were the moment before. Three. Twice as deep. Two. Twice as deep again.
Every breath out relaxes you ten percent more.
Each time I snap my fingers, that calm feeling doubles. Snap. Double. Snap. Double again.
cues: 'twice as', 'double', 'doubling', 'ten times', 'a hundred times' applied to a felt state
'ten percent more', 'one notch more', 'another level' as a fixed increment
the multiplier joined to a recurring event: 'with each number', 'every breath', 'each time I say'
the same multiplier phrase repeated at successive counts or beats
'twice as deep as before', 'again', 'and double that' - each step measured from the previous one

not_this.why: a reference point is a single stated value that judgment adjusts from; this is a multiplier re-applied at every step of a recurring event
that yokes two continuous quantities with comparatives and no numbers; this ties a numbered increase to discrete events
the countdown is the count with depth attached; label this as well only when a multiplier or increment is stated at the steps
that says an installed cue grows stronger with each use; this multiplies the present state, not the strength of a cue

evidence.note: Standard wording in stage and Elman-style scripts; no study tests the multiplier, listeners cannot verify a doubling, and any effect is best explained by expectancy and by numeric anchoring of reported depth.

entries.name: Compound suggestion
entries.summary: Join a statement the listener can verify to a suggestion with 'and', so acceptance of the first carries to the second.
entries.definition: A compound suggestion is one sentence with two halves joined by a plain conjunction: the first is true or obvious, the second is the suggestion. No reason or dependence is stated; the 'and' simply runs them together. It is the smallest unit of pacing and leading, done inside one sentence.
entries.how_to: Write the undeniable half first, then 'and', then the suggestion, and keep both halves short and similar in rhythm. Use it early, when the listener is still checking each statement. The join works best when the two halves are loosely related in topic; an obvious jump draws attention to the trick. Do not stack more than one suggestion after the 'and'.
examples: You're sitting in that chair and you can begin to relax.
You hear my voice and your breathing slows.
Your eyes are closed now and your mind is growing quiet.
cues: single sentence: verifiable clause + 'and' + suggested clause
first clause describes present posture, hearing, breathing or position
'and' (or 'and so', 'and now') with no 'as', 'because' or 'when'
the second clause could not be checked the way the first can

not_this.why: contingent wording states that the response happens as or when the first event does
pacing and leading runs several verifiable statements across sentences before the lead; this is one of each inside a sentence
compounding is a claim that suggestions strengthen each other, not a sentence shape
polysyndeton is a long run of 'and' clauses for rhythm, without the true-then-suggested pairing

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Described in Ericksonian texts; whether the conjunction itself transfers acceptance has not been tested.

entries.name: Truism
