entries.summary: State something so plainly true about people or experience that the listener can only agree.
entries.definition: A truism is a general statement the listener cannot reasonably dispute: about how bodies work, how time passes, or what everyone has experienced. It asks for nothing; its job is to be accepted. Erickson and Rossi count it as a suggestion form because a truism about a response ('everyone knows what it's like to feel warmth in the hands') tends to evoke that response.
entries.how_to: Pick a truth that sits next to the response you want and state it without 'you must'. Truisms about sensation recall the sensation; truisms about time ('sooner or later') make the timing unarguable. Use two or three before a suggestion, or attach one with 'and' to make a compound suggestion. A truism that is merely probable invites disagreement, so test each one: could any listener honestly say no?
examples: Everyone knows what it's like to drift off without deciding to.
Sooner or later, tired eyes want to close.
Most people have nodded their head yes without even noticing.
cues: generic subjects: 'everyone', 'most people', 'we all', 'anyone'
'you already know', 'you know what it's like to'
'sooner or later', 'at some point'
statements of ordinary fact about the body, sleep, learning or time
no instruction and no claim about what the listener is doing right now

not_this.why: pacing states what this listener can verify right now; a truism is a general truth that needs no checking
normalizing says a response is ordinary and expected, to remove worry about it; a truism is true whether or not the response occurs
that labels the 'every/always' word and need not be true

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian texts; acquiescence after agreement has some experimental support, but truisms as a hypnotic form have not been tested alone.

entries.name: Embedded command
entries.summary: Place a command inside a longer sentence that is on its face about something else.
entries.definition: An embedded command is a string of words that would be an imperative if lifted out ('relax deeply', 'let go now') sitting inside a sentence whose grammar makes it a report, question or description. The surface sentence asks nothing of the listener. The claim is that the inner string is still received as an instruction, especially when set apart by voice.
entries.how_to: Write the command first, then build a carrier around it: 'I wonder how soon you'll [command]', 'people can [command]', 'I knew someone who learned to [command]'. Keep the command two to five words, starting with a bare verb, and place it at the end of the clause where a pause can follow. In audio, pair it with analog marking; in text, some writers italicize or capitalize it. One per sentence; a carrier stuffed with commands reads as awkward and gives the game away.
examples: Some evenings it takes no effort at all to sit back and relax completely.
A person can, you know, feel at ease here.
My teacher used to say that anyone can learn to let go now, given a little time.
cues: a bare-verb phrase inside a subordinate clause that reads as an imperative on its own
carrier frames: 'I wonder if you'll', 'you don't have to', 'people can', 'I'm not going to tell you to'
the embedded phrase is italicized, capitalized or set off by commas or dashes
'now' placed oddly at the end of the embedded phrase
a name or 'you know' inserted just before the verb phrase

not_this.why: analog marking is the vocal or typographic setting-apart; the embedded command is the wording being set apart
interspersal scatters single words or phrases across a narrative; an embedded command is a whole imperative inside one sentence

an embedded question folds a question into a statement; an embedded command contains a phrase that reads as an imperative when lifted out, and a question carrier can contain both only when that separate imperative phrase is present
a direct suggestion is an imperative standing as its own sentence

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Widely taught, but there is no controlled evidence that an embedded phrase is processed as a separate command or works outside awareness.

entries.consent_note: It is meant to work without the listener noticing a command, so use it only where the listener has agreed to receive suggestions of that kind.

entries.name: Interspersal
entries.summary: Scatter the words and phrases of the suggestion through a narrative that is about something else.
entries.definition: Interspersal threads suggestion words (comfort, ease, resting, letting go) at intervals through a stretch of unrelated talk, such as a story about a plant growing or a walk by a river. No sentence addresses the suggestion to the listener; the words accumulate. It works at passage scale, which separates it from the single-sentence embedded command.
entries.how_to: Choose three to six target words or short phrases, then write a narrative on a neutral, mildly interesting topic that can use them naturally. Place a target every sentence or two, vary its grammatical role, and let some attach to the story's subject ('the leaves rest'). Give the targets a slight vocal marking in audio. It needs length to work, a paragraph at least; it fails when the story is so thin that it is plainly a wrapper, or when the listener has no idea why they are hearing it.
examples: A seed lies in the warm soil, comfortable, in no hurry. It rests. The rain comes and it can simply take in what it needs, feeling at ease.
The river slows where it widens. It lets go of its hurry, grows calm and settles deep between the banks.
Old houses settle at night. The beams relax, the boards rest, everything inside grows quiet and still.
cues: narrative about an unrelated subject (plant, river, house, journey) with no 'you' instructions
recurring state vocabulary (comfort, rest, ease, calm, deep, let go) at a rate the topic does not need
non-human subjects given verbs of resting, relaxing or feeling
target words italicized or marked for emphasis across a passage
the same handful of words recurring every one to two sentences

not_this.why: an embedded command is one full imperative in one sentence; interspersal is words spread over a passage
seeding mentions an idea early so it is familiar later; interspersal is the delivery of the suggestion itself
metaphor relies on the story's structure matching the change; interspersal relies on the scattered words and the story can be arbitrary
that labels one sentence giving a thing a human feeling; interspersal is the pattern across the passage

origin.source: Erickson, 'The interspersal hypnotic technique for symptom correction and pain control', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1966)

evidence.note: Rests on Erickson's case reports; semantic priming is real but small and short-lived, and interspersal has not been shown in controlled work to produce the clinical effects claimed.

entries.consent_note: It is designed to be missed, so the listener should have agreed beforehand to what is being suggested.

entries.name: Embedded question
entries.summary: Fold a question into a statement about the speaker's wondering, so the listener searches for an answer without being asked.
entries.definition: An embedded question is grammatically a statement ('I wonder how soon your eyes will close') that contains a question as its object. Because nothing is asked, no reply is owed, yet the listener tends to consider the question inwardly. The question usually presupposes the response and leaves only its manner or timing open.
entries.how_to: Open with a frame of speaker curiosity or ignorance ('I wonder', 'I'm curious', 'I don't know', 'I'd like to know') and follow with what, how, when, which or whether. Put the response in the presupposed part of the question and leave something harmless open. Leave a pause after it. Use it where a direct question would pull the listener into answering aloud or into analysis.
examples: I wonder which hand will feel lighter first.
I'm curious how deeply you'll relax today.
I don't know whether you've noticed yet how slow your breathing has become.
cues: 'I wonder', 'I'm wondering', 'I'm curious', 'I don't know', 'I'd like to know', 'I ask myself'
followed by 'whether', 'if', 'how', 'when', 'which', 'what'
sentence ends in a full stop, not a question mark
the subordinate question takes the wanted response for granted

not_this.why: that is a question asked outright, with a question mark and a turn handed to the listener
a conversational postulate is a direct yes/no question that works as a request to act
an embedded command hides an imperative, not a question
mind reading claims to know what the listener thinks; this states what the speaker does not know

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume I, Meta Publications (1975)

evidence.note: Indirect questions do carry their presuppositions, which is well studied; that the embedded form prompts a stronger or less guarded inner search than a plain question is untested.

entries.name: Conversational postulate
entries.summary: Ask a yes/no question about ability or willingness that the listener answers by doing the thing.
entries.definition: A conversational postulate is a question that literally asks whether the listener can or will do something and conventionally means 'do it': 'Can you close your eyes?' The expected response is the act, not the word yes. It is the ordinary polite-request form of everyday speech, borrowed for suggestion because it commands without the grammar of a command.
entries.how_to: Take the instruction and front it with 'can you', 'could you', 'will you', 'would you' or 'are you able to'. Use it for simple acts the listener can plainly do, early in a session or wherever an imperative would feel too hard. It works less well for involuntary responses, where 'can you' becomes a real question and invites the answer no; use an embedded question there.
examples: Can you let your eyes close now?
Would you take one slow breath for me?
Could you imagine a door in front of you?
cues: question opening with 'can you', 'could you', 'will you', 'would you', 'are you able to', 'do you mind'
followed by an action verb the listener could carry out at once
question mark, but the script goes on as though the act was done, not answered
'for me', 'now' or 'please' appended

not_this.why: a tag question is a short question fixed to the end of a statement, seeking agreement
that asks a real question whose consideration produces an experience; this is a request to act dressed as a question
'you can' as a statement offers; 'can you' as a question requests
agreement harvest wants a stated yes; this wants the action

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume I, Meta Publications (1975)

evidence.note: Indirect requests are thoroughly studied in pragmatics and are simply understood as polite requests; no evidence shows they get more compliance in hypnosis than a plain instruction.

entries.name: Tag question
entries.summary: Add a short question to the end of a statement to invite agreement and soften the claim.
entries.definition: A tag question is a two- or three-word question appended to a statement, usually reversing its polarity: 'You're beginning to relax, aren't you?' The statement makes the claim and the tag asks the listener to confirm it. In hypnosis it is credited with drawing out a yes and with giving a contrary listener a negative to attach to.
entries.how_to: Write the suggestion as a statement, then add the matching tag: auxiliary verb, opposite polarity, pronoun. Use it on statements the listener is likely to agree with, and say it with falling intonation so it sounds like confirmation, not doubt. Use sparingly: one every few sentences. A tag on every line sounds unsure, and a tag on a doubtful claim invites the answer no.
examples: That feels better already, doesn't it?
You can hear how quiet it's become, can't you?
And it's easy to keep listening, isn't it?
cues: sentence-final ', isn't it?', ', doesn't it?', ', aren't you?', ', can't you?', ', don't you?', ', haven't you?'
', right?', ', yes?', ', is it not?' after a statement
comma + auxiliary + (n't) + pronoun + question mark
positive statement with negative tag, or the reverse

not_this.why: that is a whole question asking for an act; a tag hangs on a statement and asks for agreement
a rhetorical question is a full question asked for effect, not a tag on a statement
agreement harvest explicitly asks the listener to say or nod yes
a yes set is a run of items each getting a yes; a tag is one device that may be used inside it

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume I, Meta Publications (1975)

evidence.note: The hypnotic claim (it displaces resistance) is untested; persuasion research on tag questions is mixed, and they can make a speaker sound less certain.

entries.name: Negative suggestion
entries.summary: Name the response inside a negation ('don't relax yet') so the listener has to picture it to understand the sentence.
entries.definition: A negative suggestion states the wanted response under 'don't', 'not', 'no need to' or 'try not to'. To understand what is being ruled out, the listener must represent it, and the prohibition is usually partial or temporary ('yet', 'too quickly'), which implies it will happen. The mark is that the negated thing is what the writer wants.
entries.how_to: Negate the response and add a limiter that leaves the door open: 'yet', 'too soon', 'until', 'more than you want to'. It suits moments where a command would be premature, and it gives a contrary listener something to defy in the wanted direction. Do not rely on the idea that negatives are ignored; listeners understand 'don't'. For that reason avoid accidentally naming what you do not want ('you won't feel anxious') when a positive wording exists.
examples: Don't relax too quickly.
You don't have to close your eyes just yet.
Try not to notice how heavy your hands are getting.
cues: 'don't', 'do not', 'no need to', 'you needn't' + the target response
limiters: 'yet', 'too quickly', 'too soon', 'until', 'before you're ready'
'try not to' + response
'I'm not going to tell you to' + response
the surrounding script goes on to assume the negated response happened

not_this.why: that releases the listener from effort or understanding; this names the target response itself under a negation
reverse psychology is the strategy of instructing the opposite to exploit opposition; negative suggestion is a sentence form that may or may not serve it
stacked negation aims at confusion by piling negatives up; this uses a single clear negation

when the target response itself sits under a negation, with or without 'yet', label it here; keep implication for inferences carried some other way (a limit, a remark about other people, a permission)

evidence.note: Trying to suppress a thought can make it more frequent (ironic process research), but the popular claim that the unconscious cannot process negatives is false, and no study shows 'don't X' works as a suggestion to X.

entries.consent_note: It asks for one thing while seeming to ask for its opposite, so the listener should know the session uses indirect wording.

entries.name: Not doing / not knowing
entries.summary: Tell the listener they need not try, do, understand or even listen, so the response is left to happen automatically.
entries.definition: This form removes the listener's job: they do not have to make anything happen, know how it works or pay attention. What is negated is effort and understanding, not the target response. It defines the response as something that occurs without the listener doing it, which is the experience of involuntariness that marks a hypnotic response.
entries.how_to: List the things the listener does not have to do (talk, move, try, listen, understand), then say or imply that the response goes on anyway. Use it at the start of an induction to take off performance pressure, and before any response that trying would spoil, such as arm levitation or forgetting. Follow with wording that hands the work to the body, the breath or 'the back of your mind'. It fails if followed straight away by demands for effort.
examples: You don't have to do anything at all. You don't even have to listen.
You don't need to know how your breathing slows. It simply does.
There's nothing to figure out and nothing to get right.
cues: 'you don't have to', 'you don't need to', 'no need to' + try / do / know / understand / listen / think / make an effort
'without knowing how', 'without trying', 'without any effort'
'it doesn't matter whether/if you'
'nothing to do', 'nothing to get right'
followed by 'by itself', 'all on its own', 'automatically'

not_this.why: negative suggestion negates the target response to evoke it; this negates effort and knowledge
automaticity framing describes a response as happening by itself; this releases the listener from trying, which usually comes just before
permission says a held-back response is okay; this says no action is required at all

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Standard clinical form; research supports that hypnotic responses are experienced as involuntary and that expectancy shapes this, but the wording itself has not been tested alone.

entries.name: Open-ended suggestion
entries.summary: Suggest that something will happen without saying what, so whatever the listener does counts as the response.
entries.definition: An open-ended suggestion leaves the content of the response to the listener: something will change, be learned or be noticed, in the listener's own way. Because no particular response is named, none can fail. It differs from its variant, covering all possibilities, which names the options one by one.
entries.how_to: State that a response will occur and decline to specify it: 'in your own way', 'whatever you need', 'something'. Use it at the start of a section to see what the listener does, then pick up whatever appears and build on it; in recorded scripts, where you cannot see the listener, it protects against a mismatch. Follow it with something specific. A script made only of open-ended suggestions suggests nothing.
examples: Your mind can find its own way of settling.
Something will change over the next minute, and you can be curious about what.
You'll take from this whatever is most useful to you.
cues: 'in your own way', 'at your own pace', 'in whatever way'
'whatever', 'however', 'whichever' + response
'something', 'a certain feeling', 'some change' with no further description
'your own' + nominalization ('your own kind of comfort')
no specific sensation, action or timing named

not_this.why: the variant lists the possible responses explicitly; the open-ended form names none
no-fail framing declares after or about the outcome that anything counts as success; this is a suggestion worded so no outcome is specified
a bind offers named alternatives that all lead to one outcome; here the outcome itself is left open

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Standard Ericksonian form; its value is avoiding visible failure, and it has not been tested against specific suggestions for effect.

entries.name: Covering all possibilities
aliases: covering all possibilities of a class of responses
entries.summary: List every way the listener might respond, including not at all yet, and treat each one as correct.
entries.definition: The writer names the full range of responses within one class (lift, press down, move sideways, stay still) and presents each as a valid form of the response. Whatever the listener does has been predicted, so it confirms the speaker. Unlike a double bind, the options are not steering to one result; the aim is that no outcome falls outside the suggestion.
entries.how_to: Pick one response class, such as hand movement, speed of going under or which sensation comes first, and list its options with 'or', ending with the null case ('or nothing at all just yet'). Keep the list to one sentence or two and say it evenly, giving no option more weight unless you want to steer. Then watch or, in a recording, continue with wording that fits any of them. Use it for a first ideomotor or sensory response, where the result is hard to predict.
examples: Your hand may feel lighter, or heavier, or warm, or it may feel no different at all yet.
You might go quickly, or slowly, or in steps, or so gradually you only notice afterward.
One finger may twitch, or the whole hand may lift, or it may simply rest there and wait.
cues: three or more alternatives joined by 'or' within one response class
a null option: 'or not at all', 'or nothing yet', 'or stay just as it is'
'may ... or ... or ... or'
paired opposites in the list (left/right, faster/slower, lighter/heavier)
closing phrase: 'whichever happens', 'any of these is fine'

not_this.why: a bind's alternatives all lead to the one wanted outcome; here the alternatives are different outcomes, all accepted
that offers a choice only of manner, with the response presupposed; this includes the response not happening
no-fail framing is a blanket statement that anything is right, without listing the possibilities

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Described in Ericksonian texts as a way to make any response count; not tested separately.

entries.name: Implied directive
aliases: when your unconscious is ready, your finger will lift
entries.summary: Say that when an inner response is complete, a small outward signal will occur by itself.
entries.definition: The implied directive has three parts: a time-binding opening ('as soon as', 'when'), an internal response the listener is to carry out, and a behavioral signal that it is done. The internal task is never commanded; it is implied by being placed in the 'when' clause. The signal gives the operator, or the listener, evidence that something internal happened.
entries.how_to: Build it in order: 'As soon as' + the inner work ('your mind has found a calmer way to see this') + the signal ('one finger will lift', 'you'll take a deeper breath', 'your eyes will open'). Choose a signal that is small, visible and plausible as automatic. Then stop talking and wait; the form needs silence. In a recording, give a generous pause and a fallback line that accepts the signal having come or still being on its way.
examples: As soon as your mind has settled on a place to rest, your head will nod, just slightly.
When the back of your mind has finished sorting that through, you'll notice yourself take one deeper breath.
And when you know you can keep this calm with you, your eyes will open by themselves.
cues: 'as soon as', 'when', 'once' + an internal, unobservable process
main clause naming a small behavior: finger lifts, head nods, deeper breath, eyes open
'your unconscious', 'the back of your mind', 'some part of you' as subject of the inner work
perfect aspect in the when-clause: 'has finished', 'has found', 'has decided'
marked pause or silence after the sentence

not_this.why: contingent suggestion ties a response to an event that is already happening; here the trigger is an inner task that is itself the hidden suggestion
ideomotor signal is the movement used as an answer; the implied directive is the three-part sentence that may call for one
that labels the time clause alone; the implied directive adds the behavioral signal of completion

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: A named Ericksonian form; ideomotor movement is real, but a signal shows only that the listener responded, not that the inner work described took place.

entries.name: Posthypnotic suggestion
entries.summary: Suggest during the session a response that is to occur after it ends, usually when a named cue appears.
entries.definition: A posthypnotic suggestion is defined by timing: it is given in trance and aimed at a later moment. It normally has two parts, a cue (a time, place, event or signal) and the response the cue will bring. Any content can be posthypnotic; this entry labels the after-the-session reach, while the installing of a cue as such is covered by trigger installation.
entries.how_to: State the cue and the response in one clear sentence: 'After you wake, whenever X, you will Y.' Choose a cue that is specific and will actually occur, and a response the listener wants. Repeat it two or three times, rehearse it in imagination with future pacing, and say how long it lasts and where it applies. Place it late in the suggestion section, before emergence. Vague cues and unwanted responses are the usual reasons it does not carry over.
examples: After you open your eyes, each time you sit down at your desk you'll feel this same steady focus.
Tonight, when your head touches the pillow, your body will remember exactly how to let go.
Later today, the first time you hear a door close, you'll notice your shoulders drop.
cues: 'after you wake', 'when you open your eyes', 'once this session is over'
'later today', 'tonight', 'tomorrow', 'from now on' + a response
'whenever you', 'each time you', 'the next time you' + everyday cue + response
future tense reaching past the end of the session
placed shortly before the wake-up count

not_this.why: trigger installation is the setting-up of a cue-response pair, which can be tested in session; posthypnotic labels any suggestion aimed at after the session
future pacing is the imagined walk-through of the later moment, used to rehearse the suggestion
sealing is the closing statement that suggestions stay; it does not specify a later cue and response
habit stacking attaches a deliberate behavior to a daily cue as a plan; the posthypnotic response is suggested as automatic

evidence.note: Posthypnotic responding is documented in the laboratory, mainly in highly hypnotizable people; it depends on context and expectation, usually fades over days to weeks, and is not irresistible.

entries.consent_note: The effect is meant to persist after the session, so the listener must know before starting what is being set, and the script should state its limits and how it ends.

entries.name: Extended quotes
entries.summary: Deliver the suggestion as something another person said, so it is heard without being addressed to the listener.
entries.definition: The suggestion sits inside quotation: the speaker reports what someone else said, often to a third party. The listener hears the exact words of a direct suggestion, but the speaker is only telling a story. Quotes can be nested (someone who told someone who said) until it is unclear who is speaking to whom.
entries.how_to: Introduce a speaker ('my first teacher', 'a woman on the train'), give them a reason to say the line, then quote the suggestion in full, in the second person and present tense so it lands on the listener. For the extended form, nest two or three reporting frames before the quote. Keep the quoted line short and deliver it as the character would, directly. Return to the story afterward; do not explain.
examples: My old instructor would look at a nervous student and say, 'Stop. Breathe out. You already know how to do this.'
She told me her grandmother used to say, 'Close your eyes, the day is done.'
A man once told me his coach told the whole team, 'You are calmer than you think.'
cues: reporting verbs: 'said', 'told me', 'used to say', 'would whisper'
quotation marks around a second-person imperative or 'you' statement
nested reports: 'who told me that her teacher said'
a named or sketched third person introduced only to speak the line
tense shifts to present inside the quote

not_this.why: the variant describes or addresses a third person receiving and responding to suggestions; the base form only reports someone's words
an embedded command hides the imperative in the grammar of the speaker's own sentence; a quote attributes it to someone else
a testimonial reports what others experienced as evidence; a quote carries a suggestion aimed at the listener
citing an expert lends weight to a claim; the quotes pattern uses the citation as cover for a direct suggestion

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975)

evidence.note: An NLP pattern without controlled tests; narrative research shows that content met inside a story draws less counterarguing, which is consistent with it but does not establish it.

entries.consent_note: It lets a direct suggestion pass as storytelling, so use it only where the listener has agreed to be given suggestions.

entries.name: My friend John
entries.summary: Hypnotize or instruct an imagined or described third person in the listener's hearing, and let the listener respond in their place.
entries.definition: The speaker directs a full induction or set of suggestions at someone else: an imagined person in an empty chair, or a character whose session is being described. Every suggestion is addressed to or reported about that person, and the listener, following along, carries them out. It differs from plain quoting in that the third person is shown receiving and responding to the suggestions step by step.
entries.how_to: Set up the stand-in: ask the listener to picture a friend in a chair, or begin a story about someone being hypnotized. Then give that person the suggestions directly, by name, and describe their responses as they occur. Use it with listeners who say they cannot be hypnotized or who watch themselves too closely; it gives them the role of observer. Keep the stand-in's responses ordinary and gradual so they are easy to follow, and decide in advance whether you will later switch to addressing the listener.
examples: Imagine my friend John is sitting in that chair. I say to him, 'John, let your hand rest on your knee and watch it. It's getting lighter.' And John's hand begins to lift.
I told her, 'Just look at the spot on the wall, Maria,' and I watched her blinking slow down, the way blinking does.
So I say to John, 'Now that hand is stuck to the arm of the chair,' and you can watch him tug at it and smile.
cues: a named third person addressed with induction or suggestion language
'I say to him/her', 'I told him' + quoted suggestion, repeated across a passage
description of the third person's responses in sequence (eyes closing, hand lifting, shoulders dropping)
setup line: 'imagine someone sitting in that chair', 'let me tell you how I'd hypnotize someone'
present tense narration of a session that is not, on its face, the listener's

not_this.why: the parent is any suggestion placed in a quote; this is a whole induction or sequence run on a stand-in
vicarious deepening uses a described person going under to deepen an existing trance; this uses the stand-in as the route for the suggestions themselves, often from a cold start
there the listener is asked to be the character; here the listener only watches someone else
covert induction is any induction framed as something else; this is one specific way of doing it

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson, The ‘Surprise’ and ‘My-Friend-John’ Techniques of Hypnosis: Minimal Cues and Natural Field Experimentation, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964)

evidence.note: Rests on Erickson's own demonstrations and case descriptions; observational learning and modeling are well supported, but the technique has not been tested in controlled work.

entries.consent_note: The listener may not realize the session is aimed at them, so agree beforehand that hypnosis is what is taking place.

entries.name: Challenge suggestion
entries.summary: Suggest that something cannot be done, then invite the listener to try, so the failed attempt proves the suggestion.
entries.definition: A challenge suggestion pairs a suggested inability (eyes will not open, arm will not bend, a name will not come) with an invitation to test it. The listener's own failed effort becomes the evidence. The wording usually builds the failure into the invitation: 'try' already implies not succeeding, and 'the harder you try, the more stuck it is' turns effort against itself.
entries.how_to: First install the inability with several lines of direct suggestion and an image (glued, locked, welded). Then challenge briefly: 'try, and find you can't', and end the test within a few seconds with 'stop trying'. Release the effect in plain words before moving on. Start with the easiest item, eyelids, and use it only once the listener is responding to simpler suggestions. If the listener succeeds, credibility takes a hit, so have a no-fail line ready or leave the challenge out.
examples: Your eyelids are so relaxed they simply won't work. Try to open them, and find they stay shut. Now stop trying and go deeper.
That arm is a bar of steel now. Go ahead, try to bend it, and feel it stiffen the harder you try.
Try to remember the number that comes after six, and notice it just isn't there.
cues: 'try to ...' + 'and find that you can't' / 'but you cannot'
'the harder you try, the more/less' placed inside or straight after an invitation to try
'go ahead and test it', 'test them and make sure they won't work'
'stop trying' shortly after
preceded by images of locking, gluing, freezing or forgetting

not_this.why: convincer is any staged proof of trance; a challenge is the specific try-and-fail wording, which most but not all convincers use
eyelid lock and the other convincer variants name the phenomenon; label the variant on the whole passage (install, test, release) and this entry on the try-and-fail sentence inside it
that claims resisting the whole process strengthens it; a challenge sets a single concrete test
reverse psychology instructs the opposite of what is wanted; here the speaker wants the attempt to fail and says so
a 'the harder you try, the...' line with no invitation to test a named inability is the comparative yoke, not a challenge

evidence.note: Challenge items are part of the standard hypnotizability scales and are passed by a minority to about half of people depending on the item; the 'law of reversed effect' is a slogan, not an established law.

entries.consent_note: It stages a loss of control, so the listener should have agreed to that kind of demonstration and the effect must be released explicitly.

entries.name: The more... the more
aliases: the more aroused the more you agree
entries.summary: State that as one thing increases, another increases or decreases with it.
entries.definition: This form yokes two quantities with a correlative comparative: 'the more you listen, the calmer you feel'. The first term is usually something already happening or under the listener's control, and the second is the suggested response. It differs from a contingent suggestion in being a matter of degree, not of occurrence, so it keeps working for as long as the first term continues.
entries.how_to: Choose a first term that is sure to grow or continue (breathing, listening, time passing) and yoke the response to it. 'The more X, the less Y' turns an obstacle into fuel: the more the mind wanders, the less it matters. Keep both halves short and parallel. With resisting as the first term the form is the separate entry 'The harder you resist'. One or two per passage is enough; a string of them reads as a formula.
examples: The more you listen, the easier it becomes to let everything else go.
The slower you breathe, the quieter your thoughts.
The longer you listen, the less the rest of the day matters.
cues: 'the more ..., the more ...'
'the more ..., the less ...'
'the + comparative ..., the + comparative ...' ('the deeper, the better')
'more and more ... as ...'
first half names an ongoing act; second half names the response

not_this.why: the self-reinforcing loop is circular (A feeds B and B feeds A); this is a one-way yoke
contingent suggestion links occurrence to occurrence ('as', 'when'); this links amount to amount
cause-effect asserts 'X makes Y'; this asserts co-variation with a comparative
that labels a lone comparative with no standard ('deeper'); this pairs two comparatives
when the first term is resisting, fighting or trying not to respond, label that entry; this one covers every other pairing

evidence.note: A common form in Ericksonian and NLP scripts; not tested as a form.

entries.name: Self-reinforcing loop
entries.summary: State a circle: A increases B, and B increases A, so the state keeps feeding itself without further input.
entries.definition: Two the-more-the-more links joined end to end so the second term feeds back into the first: the more you relax, the further down you drift, and the further you drift, the more you relax. What makes it a loop and not a single link is the stated return. Once set up it is declared to run on its own, which lets the writer move on while deepening is presumed to continue. The terms can be anything; depth and relaxation are only the commonest.
entries.how_to: Pick two things that are both already present and both easy to feel. Say the link forward, then back, in matching grammar, and then say it continues by itself. Two terms is clearest; three is the limit before the listener loses the circle. Use it once per section as a hand-off before the suggestions, not repeatedly. Be careful what goes in the loop: a loop on a compulsion or on need is hard for the listener to step out of, and that is a different decision from deepening.
examples: The more you relax, the further down you drift. And the further you drift, the more you relax.
Listening makes it easier to let go, and letting go makes it easier to listen. Round and round, all by itself.
Each one feeds the other: calm into quiet, quiet into calm.
cues: 'the more X, the more Y' followed by 'the more Y, the more X'
the same two terms appearing in swapped order in adjacent clauses
'round and round', 'feeding itself', 'a circle', 'a spiral', 'on and on'
'and that makes you ... which makes you ...' returning to the first term
'all by itself', 'without you doing anything' after a reciprocal pair

not_this.why: one-way link from one thing to another, with no return
the same ABBA shape as a figure of style, with no claim that the terms cause each other
says each accepted suggestion strengthens the others, not that two states feed each other

evidence.note: A common pattern with an obvious logic; no study tests whether a stated loop keeps deepening going after it is said.

entries.consent_note: Harmless for relaxation; when the looped terms are need, arousal or obedience, the loop is meant to be hard to exit and should be disclosed and bounded.

entries.name: The harder you resist
entries.summary: Declare that the effort of resisting itself strengthens the effect, so fighting it feeds it.
entries.definition: A claim that links resisting to the opposite of its aim: the more you fight, the deeper you go. It is a the-more-the-more statement with resistance as the first term. It differs from inevitability, which says the outcome is certain without tying it to effort, and from resistance as participation, which calls resistance helpful without saying it backfires.
entries.how_to: State the link plainly and early, before resistance shows, then point to any sign of effort as proof. Pair it with a challenge so the listener tests it and finds the effort tiring. It suits playful dominance scenes and listeners who enjoy struggling. It fails when the listener feels no effort to point at.
examples: The harder you try to stay awake, the heavier your eyes become.
Every time you fight it, you sink a little further.
Struggle all you like. Each push just pulls you deeper.
cues: 'the harder you try/resist/fight..., the...'
'every time you fight it'
'struggle all you like'
resisting or fighting as the cause of deepening

not_this.why: inevitability asserts certainty; this links certainty to the effort of resisting
the general comparative form; this is the case where the first term is resistance
resistance as participation calls resistance useful without claiming it backfires

evidence.note: Echoes Coue's 'law of reversed effort' and fits ironic-process findings on suppression, but the stated claim that resisting deepens trance is untested.

entries.name: Ratification
entries.summary: Confirm a response the moment it happens, marking it as real and as the right thing.
entries.definition: Ratification is a short acknowledgment placed directly after a response: 'that's right', 'good', 'just like that'. It tells the listener that what just happened was the response and that it was noticed. It differs from praise in that it certifies the event rather than rewarding the person, though one phrase can do both.
entries.how_to: Put it immediately after the point where the response should occur: after a breath instruction, a pause, a count. In live work, time it to what you see; in a recording, time it to what almost certainly happened (an exhale, a swallow, stillness). Keep it to two or three words in a level voice. Unearned ratification, saying 'that's right' to nothing, is noticed by alert listeners, so tie each one to something specific.
examples: Breathe out slowly... that's right.
And there it is. Just like that.
Good. You felt that shift.
cues: 'that's right', 'that's it', 'good', 'very good', 'just like that', 'there you go', 'perfect'
standalone short sentence following an instruction and a pause
'you felt that', 'there it is', 'you noticed'
ellipsis or line break before the phrase
repeats at regular intervals through a passage

not_this.why: that describes specific bodily signs as evidence of trance; ratification is the brief confirmation of any response
praise rewards the listener ('good girl', 'well done') to make the response more likely again; ratification marks the response as having occurred
naming the state says what the condition is called; ratification only confirms that something happened
a tag asks the listener to confirm; ratification is the speaker confirming

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Standard practice; consistent with research on expectancy and on feedback raising response to later suggestions, but not tested as a wording.

entries.name: Pacing trance signs
entries.summary: Describe the ordinary signs of settling, such as slower breathing and stillness, as evidence that trance is happening.
entries.definition: The writer names small bodily changes that occur whenever someone sits quietly with attention held: slower breathing, heavier limbs, less blinking, swallowing, stillness, a smoother face. These are then presented as signs of trance. It is pacing, because the signs are real, joined to an interpretation the listener did not supply. It differs from a convincer, which stages a special phenomenon, in that it only points at what is already there.
entries.how_to: Use it a few minutes in, once the signs are likely to be present. Describe first, interpret second: 'your breathing has slowed' before 'which tells you something is changing'. Live, name only what you see. In a recording, use 'you may notice' or 'perhaps already' and choose signs that almost always occur. Do not overclaim; calling a slight heaviness 'deep trance' invites the listener to check and disagree.
examples: You may notice your breathing has become slower and a little deeper. That is one of the first signs.
Your hands have been still for some time now. You haven't needed to move them. That stillness tells you trance has already begun.
Perhaps you've swallowed or felt your eyelids flutter. Those small changes can be signs that you're settling into trance.
cues: named physiological signs: breathing slower, swallowing, eyelids fluttering, stillness, heavy limbs, face relaxing
perfect or progressive aspect marking a change that has occurred: 'has slowed', 'has become', 'are becoming'
interpretive clause: 'that is a sign', 'that tells you', 'that means you are going into trance'
noticing frames: 'you may notice', 'perhaps you've already'
the word 'sign', 'signal' or 'evidence' near a body description

not_this.why: ratification briefly confirms a response as it occurs ('that's right'); this entry names a sign of settling and presents it as evidence of trance
complex equivalence is the general claim that X means Y; when an ordinary bodily or behavioral sign of settling is presented as evidence of trance, use this narrower entry
sensation relabeling gives a felt sensation a new cause or meaning; when the meaning is simply that trance or relaxation is occurring, use this entry
a convincer stages a suggested phenomenon as proof; this entry interprets an ordinary sign of settling as evidence of trance

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Standard in clinical texts; the signs named are those of ordinary relaxation and are not specific markers of hypnosis, though telling people they are responding does raise expectancy, which predicts response.

entries.consent_note: It presents normal relaxation as proof of trance; this is fair inside an agreed session, but should not be used to persuade someone they are more affected than they are.

entries.name: Apposition of opposites
aliases: as one hand rises the other sinks
entries.summary: Pair two opposite experiences in one suggestion so each makes the other clearer and stronger.
entries.definition: Two opposed states are suggested together and tied to each other: one hand lighter as the other grows heavier, the body more relaxed as the mind grows more alert. Each side gives the other a reference point, and the pairing presents the two as a balanced system. Both sides are experiences being suggested, which separates it from a rhetorical contrast between ideas.
entries.how_to: Choose a real pair of opposites along one dimension (heavy/light, warm/cool, tense/loose, remembering/forgetting, inner/outer) and assign each to a different place or part. Link them with 'as' or 'while' so they move together. It is useful when one side is easy and the other hard: the easy side lends its reality to the other. Keep the two halves parallel in wording.
examples: As your right hand grows lighter, your left sinks heavier into your lap.
Let the warmth gather in your hands while your forehead stays cool.
Tension in the fist, ease in the shoulders; as one tightens, the other lets go.
cues: antonym pair in one sentence applied to experience: heavy/light, warm/cool, tense/relaxed, up/down, remember/forget
'as one ..., the other ...'
'while your X ..., your Y ...' with opposite predicates
left/right or body/mind assigned opposite states
parallel clauses differing mainly in the opposed terms

not_this.why: antithesis is a balanced contrast of ideas for effect; this suggests two opposite experiences at once
contrast shifts judgment by presenting a more extreme comparison first; here both sides are wanted responses
book and balloon is a specific convincer that uses this form; label the convincer when the test is staged
tense-and-release is a sequence of doing one then the other; apposition holds both together

that yokes any two amounts with 'the more..., the more/less'; label this entry only when the two halves are opposite experiences that are both being suggested, and both labels when such a pair is written in the comparative form

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: A named Ericksonian form; perceptual contrast is well established, but this use of it has not been tested.

entries.name: Question as suggestion
entries.summary: Ask a direct question that the listener can only answer by having or checking for the response.
entries.definition: A question is put to the listener whose answer requires turning attention to the wanted experience: 'Which hand feels warmer?' Considering the question does the work; the answer itself hardly matters. It is asked outright, with a question mark, and concerns the listener's experience, which separates it from the embedded question and from a question used only for rhetorical effect.
entries.how_to: Ask about the experience you want, in a form that presupposes it and leaves a detail open: which, where, how much, how soon. Ask one question, then pause long enough for an inward look. Questions suit the early part of a session and any moment where you want attention directed without telling. Avoid yes/no questions about whether the response is present unless a no is acceptable.
examples: Which of your hands feels warmer right now?
Where in your body do you notice the relaxation first?
How much heavier can your eyelids get before they close?
cues: direct question with a question mark addressed to 'you'
wh-words about experience: 'which', 'where', 'how much', 'how soon', 'what do you notice'
the question presupposes the response and asks only about a detail
followed by a pause, not by the speaker's own answer
the listener is not expected to reply aloud

not_this.why: the embedded question is wrapped in a statement ('I wonder which') and has no question mark
a rhetorical question makes a point and expects no inner search; this one needs the listener to check their experience
a loaded question forces a contested assumption about facts or character; this directs attention to a sensation or response
that is a request to act phrased as 'can you'; this is a question about experience
ask-and-answer has the speaker answer at once; here the answer is left to the listener

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Clinical use is standard; research on leading questions shows that question wording can shape reports and memory, but effects on hypnotic response specifically are not measured.

entries.name: Suggestion repetition
entries.summary: Give the same suggestion several times, word for word or in fresh words.
entries.definition: The writer returns to one suggestion more than once within the session, either verbatim or reworded. What is repeated is a specific suggestion with content, not a depth word, a rhythmic figure or a chant. Repetition is the oldest and most general way of giving a suggestion weight.
entries.how_to: State the key suggestion at least three times: once plainly, once in other words or another form (contingent, question, image), and once near the end. Space the repeats out, with other material between, and keep the core phrase stable enough to be recognized. Too little repetition is a commoner fault in scripts than too much, but exact repeats back to back turn into a mantra, which is a different device with a different feel.
examples: You sleep deeply through the night. [...] All night long, your sleep is deep and unbroken. [...] And tonight you sleep deeply, right through until morning.
Your focus holds. Whatever comes up, your focus holds.
You speak calmly. Calm in your voice. Calm in every word you say.
cues: the same suggestion content appearing three or more times in a script
a key phrase recurring verbatim at intervals
paraphrase runs: 'in other words', 'again', 'once more'
restatement immediately after a pause or a ratification
the suggestion returning in the closing passage

not_this.why: that repeats depth words to deepen trance; this repeats a content suggestion
a mantra is one short phrase repeated many times in a row as the activity itself
a refrain is a fixed line returning for structure; label refrain when the line is identical and placed at regular points
epizeuxis is a single word repeated with nothing between

evidence.note: Repeated statements are judged more true and more familiar (illusory truth, mere exposure), and practice strengthens responses; the 'law of concentrated attention' is a teaching slogan, and how many repeats a hypnotic suggestion needs is not established.

entries.name: Deeper and deeper
entries.summary: Repeat depth words such as deeper, down, further, sinking many times through a passage, with no other mechanism.
entries.definition: Deepening by saturation: the direct suggestion 'deeper' is restated over and over, plainly, often as the tail of otherwise unrelated sentences. No count, image or contingency is involved. It is the base layer most other deepeners sit on, and by itself it is what makes a passage read as a deepener at all.
entries.how_to: Spread the words out; do not stack them in one line. Vary the word (deeper, down, further, sinking, dropping) and its position in the sentence so it stays rhythmic and does not grate. Drop the voice and slow down on each one. Used alone for long it becomes wallpaper; give it thirty seconds to a minute, or run it under another deepener. A comparative with no end point ('deeper', never 'deep enough') keeps the direction open.
examples: Deeper now. Just drifting deeper. Every moment, a little deeper down.
That's it. Down. Further down. Deeper and deeper, with nothing to do but sink.
Going deeper. Feeling it. Deeper still.
cues: 'deeper and deeper', 'down and down', 'further and further'
high density of depth words (deeper, down, sink, drop, further) with no count or scene
'deeper still', 'even deeper', 'deeper now'
short sentences or fragments ending in a depth word

not_this.why: the general device of repeating any suggestion; this is its depth-word case, so label this one alone
labels 'deeper' when its comparison standard is omitted, even once; use this entry when depth words recur across a passage with no count, scene or contingency carrying them
a word repeated back to back as a figure; this is repetition spread across a passage
a repeated phrase or loop used to start trance

evidence.note: Repetition of suggestions is standard and repeated statements are experimentally rated as more true; whether repeating 'deeper' changes responsiveness has not been tested.

entries.name: Compounding
entries.summary: Tell the listener that each suggestion they accept makes the earlier and later ones stronger.
entries.definition: Compounding is a stated rule about the suggestions themselves: every one that takes effect reinforces the others. In Elman's teaching it is a principle (a second suggestion strengthens the first); in a script it appears as an explicit line saying so. It is a suggestion about suggestions, which separates it from simply repeating one.
entries.how_to: After the first clear response, say that it has made the next one easier and the last one firmer, and repeat the point briefly after later responses. It needs real responses to point at, so place it after a convincer or a ratified response, not at the start. Keep the claim modest in wording ('a little more each time') so it is not contradicted by experience.
examples: Every suggestion you accept makes the next one easier to accept.
And each thing I say settles in on top of the last, making all of it stronger.
That worked, so the next one works even better.
cues: 'each suggestion', 'every suggestion', 'everything I say' + 'stronger', 'easier', 'deeper'
'builds on', 'adds to', 'reinforces', 'locks in' applied to suggestions
'each time you follow/accept/respond' + increase
'the next one' + comparative
placed just after a response has been confirmed

not_this.why: compound suggestion is a sentence joining a true statement and a suggestion with 'and'; the names are alike but the devices are not
repetition restates a suggestion; compounding claims that suggestions strengthen one another
trigger strengthening says one trigger gains force with each use; compounding is about the whole set of suggestions
the self-reinforcing loop yokes two states to feed each other; compounding is about acceptance of suggestions

origin.source: Dave Elman, Findings in Hypnosis, Westwood Publishing (1964)

evidence.note: Elman's principle is taught widely; success on early suggestions does raise expectancy and later responding, but the stated rule has not been tested as a suggestion.

entries.name: Giving a reason
entries.summary: Attach 'because' and a reason to a suggestion, even a thin one.
entries.definition: The suggestion is followed, or preceded, by a stated reason. The form of a justification is what marks the device; the reason may be sound, circular or beside the point. It differs from a cause-effect claim in that the reason is offered as grounds for accepting or doing something, not as a statement that one event produces another.
entries.how_to: Add 'because', 'since' or 'so that' and a reason the listener will not stop to dispute: something true about the situation, their own aim, or what has just happened. Use it for small steps and for the moment a suggestion might otherwise prompt 'why?'. The more that is being asked, the better the reason has to be; an empty reason only carries a trivial request. A reason drawn from the listener's own goals does more than one drawn from the speaker's.
examples: You can let your eyes close now, because there's nothing here you need to look at.
Take a moment to settle in, because you've earned a few minutes to yourself.
Let that breath go slowly, since slow is how the body likes to settle.
cues: 'because', 'since', 'so that', 'which is why' attached to an instruction, request or offer ('close your eyes, because...', 'you can..., since...')
the causal clause gives grounds for doing or accepting the thing, not a mechanism by which a response happens
a reason that restates the suggestion or the obvious
'for the simple reason that'
instruction + comma + causal clause

not_this.why: if the 'because' clause explains why a response happens ('because you are sitting still, calm comes'), it is cause-effect; if it justifies an instruction, request or offer ('close your eyes, because there is nothing to look at'), it is reason-giving
values-linking ties the suggestion to something the listener cares about; label that when the reason is specifically their value
there the support is a cited source, not a 'because' clause
contingent wording links by time ('as', 'when'), not by justification

origin.source: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, 'The mindlessness of ostensibly thoughtful action', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1978)

evidence.note: In the original study an empty reason raised compliance only for a small request; with a larger request only a real reason helped, so the popular claim that 'because' works on anything overstates the finding.

entries.name: Sensory language
entries.summary: Word the suggestion in concrete terms of sight, sound, touch, smell and taste so the listener simulates it.
entries.definition: The suggestion is phrased in specific sensory terms instead of abstract ones: 'a slow warmth spreading across your shoulders' in place of 'relaxation'. The listener has something definite to imagine and so to feel. As a suggestion form it concerns the wording of a single suggestion; sustained multi-sense description of a scene is sensory immersion.
entries.how_to: Take the abstract word and ask what it would look, sound and feel like, then write that. Give location, temperature, weight, texture, direction of movement. Cover more than one sense across a passage, since listeners differ in which they imagine easily, and lead with body sensation for trance work. Do not try to diagnose and match a listener's 'preferred system'; that idea has not held up. Too much detail contradicts what the listener is imagining, so leave some gaps.
examples: A slow warmth spreads across your shoulders, like sun through a window.
The sounds of the room thin out and grow soft at the edges.
Your hands rest heavy and loose, palms warm against the fabric.
cues: concrete sense words: warm, heavy, soft, bright, dim, hum, smooth, cool
body locations paired with a sensation ('across your shoulders', 'behind your eyes')
sensory similes: 'like warm water', 'like sun through a window'
verbs of perceiving: see, hear, feel, smell, taste
abstract state nouns are absent or immediately given a physical form

not_this.why: immersion is a passage with three or more senses within a few sentences, written to hold attention; with fewer senses, or inside a single suggestion, label this entry
nominalization is the opposite choice: an abstract noun the listener fills in
guided imagery leads through a scene step by step; sensory language is the vocabulary it is written in
sense crossing describes one sense in terms of another; this stays within each sense
that is the suggested phenomenon of a felt sensation; this is a way of wording any suggestion

evidence.note: Imagery-rich suggestions are standard and concrete language is easier to imagine and remember; the NLP claim that people have a preferred representational system to be matched has failed controlled tests.

entries.name: First-person suggestion
entries.summary: Write the suggestion with 'I' as the listener, so hearing or reading it is the same as saying it.
entries.definition: The suggestion is phrased in the listener's own grammatical person: 'I am calm', 'my breathing is slow'. The speaker's voice stands in for the listener's inner voice, or the listener reads or repeats the lines. On a second voice running under a second-person lead it plays as the listener's inner monologue: nobody asks them to say it, which makes it the quiet form of repeat-after-me. The mark is the pronoun: 'I', 'me' and 'my' refer to the listener, not to the hypnotist.
entries.how_to: Write short present-tense statements with 'I' or 'my', positive in wording and plausible enough to be said without an inner objection. Signal the switch of person clearly, by a lead-in ('and the thought comes: ...'), a change of voice or track, or a repeat-after-me, or the listener will hear 'I' as the speaker. It suits self-hypnosis scripts, text to be read, and lines the listener will carry away. Statements far from what the listener believes tend to be rejected; step toward them. As an inner-monologue track, give it a different voice from the lead, keep it quieter, and write it as the answer to what the lead is saying at that moment.
examples: I am calm. My breathing is slow and even.
I notice my shoulders loosening, and I let them.
I can handle this. I have handled harder things.
cues: 'I', 'me', 'my' referring to the listener in suggestion lines
short present-tense statements: 'I am', 'I feel', 'I can', 'my ... is'
lead-ins: 'say to yourself', 'the thought comes', 'you hear yourself think'
a section headed affirmations or written as a list of I-statements
second-person narration switching to first person for key lines
a second voice or track in 'I' running under a lead voice in 'you'

not_this.why: affirmations are first-person positive statements repeated as a practice; this is the pronoun choice wherever it occurs, repeated or not
repeat-after-me is the instruction to say the line; first-person wording is the form of the line said
inner-voice suggestion claims in the second person that the speaker's words become the listener's thoughts; this writes the thoughts directly
pronoun shift is the change of pronoun partway through as a device; this is sustained first-person wording
autogenic phrases are the specific heavy-and-warm formulae used as an induction

evidence.note: Self-generated and self-referent material is better remembered, but studies of positive self-statements show mixed results, and they can backfire in people who do not believe them.

entries.consent_note: Lines written as the listener's own thoughts can blur whose idea they were, so the listener should know the script uses this form.

entries.name: Affirmations
entries.summary: Have the listener repeat positive first-person statements about themselves, usually in the present tense.
entries.definition: Affirmations are first-person statements the listener is asked to repeat, or that the script repeats as a block, describing a desired quality, ability, or outlook. They are usually positive and present-tense. A general mantra can use other wording or content. An identity statement can also be an 'I am' line; repeated or prescribed self-voicing makes that line an affirmation as well.
entries.how_to: Write each one in the first person and present tense, short enough to say on one breath. Keep the claim within reach: statements the listener finds plainly false tend to provoke counter-argument, so 'I am learning to speak calmly' is safer than 'I am fearless'. Use three to five affirmations and repeat the set, in the session and as daily practice. Tell the listener whether to say them aloud, silently, or just hear them.
examples: Say them with me, three times through: I am calm. I am capable. I am calm. I am capable. I am calm. I am capable.
Each morning, repeat three times: I speak clearly, and people listen.
I am learning to rest. I am learning to rest. I am learning to rest.
cues: first-person present-tense self-statements: 'I am ...', 'I can ...', 'I choose ...', 'I deserve ...'
positive wording with no negation
the same I-statement, or a short set of them, repeated
the word 'affirm' or 'affirmation'
an instruction to repeat daily or a set number of times
the classic formula 'every day, in every way ...'

not_this.why: any suggestion written in the listener's voice; affirmations are specifically positive self-descriptions that are repeated
a single 'you are X' or 'I am X' said as fact; label affirmation only when the I-statement is repeated or the listener is told to repeat it, and then both labels apply
first-person formulae about body sensations used as an induction, not self-evaluations

origin.source: Coue, Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion (1922)

evidence.note: Popular claims outrun the evidence: studies of repeating positive self-statements show mixed results, including worse mood in people with low self-esteem, and the better-supported 'self-affirmation' research concerns writing about one's values, which is a different procedure.

entries.name: Breathe in, breathe out
aliases: breathing in calm, breathing out tension
in with the good, out with the bad
entries.summary: Give the in-breath something to take in and the out-breath something to let go, so each breath carries a paired suggestion.
entries.definition: A two-part suggestion laid over one breath cycle: the inhale brings in a wanted quality and the exhale releases an unwanted one. What makes it this entry is the pairing of opposite directions, in and out, with opposite contents, gain and loss. A breath-linked deepener ties only the exhale to depth, and a breath-focus induction directs attention to breathing without loading it with content.
entries.how_to: Name one thing to take in and one thing to let go, and keep both to a word or two so they fit inside a breath. Put the wanted quality on the inhale and the release on the exhale; the body already loosens on the way out, so that half is confirmed by itself. Repeat the pair for three or more breaths, then either leave it running ('with every breath') or swap in a new pair. It fails when the lines are longer than a breath or when the script's rhythm fights the listener's own breathing.
examples: Breathe in calm. Breathe out tension. In with the calm, and out with whatever you no longer need.
Each breath in brings a little more focus. Each breath out carries a little more of the day away.
Breathe in my words. Breathe out your own thoughts. In, and they settle. Out, and there is more room.
cues: 'breathe in X ... breathe out Y' with two different objects
'inhale' and 'exhale' each followed by an abstract noun (calm, tension, doubt, confidence)
'in with the ..., out with the ...'
'each breath in brings ...' paired with 'each breath out takes / carries away ...'
bare 'In, ... Out, ...' lines alternating a gain and a release
the pair repeated over several consecutive breaths

not_this.why: the deepener ties each exhale to going deeper and gives the inhale no content; this entry loads both halves with paired contents
the induction makes breathing the object of attention or guides its pace; it need not attach anything to the breath
apposition sets two opposite experiences side by side in any wording; here the opposites are mapped onto the two halves of the breath

evidence.note: Routine in relaxation, meditation and clinical hypnosis scripts; slow breathing itself lowers arousal, but whether attaching paired contents to the two halves of the breath adds anything has not been tested.

entries.name: Presupposition and implication
entries.summary: Get a claim accepted by placing it in the background of a sentence, where it is taken for granted, instead of stating it where it can be judged.
entries.definition: Every sentence has a main point and things it takes for granted. Listeners weigh the main point and usually let the rest through, because rejecting background content means stopping the conversation to object. This family covers the ways a writer moves the target claim into that background: by grammar (presupposition), by a question (loaded question), by inference (implication), by a gap in an argument (unstated premise), or by treating it as already agreed (assumed common ground). It differs from direct suggestion, which asserts the claim, and from artful vagueness, which leaves content empty instead of smuggling specific content in.
entries.how_to: Choose by where the claim hides. If a grammatical trigger carries it and it survives negation, use Presupposition and pick the variant by trigger: time clause, ordinal, awareness verb, adverb, change-of-state verb, already-happened framing, or 'or'. If the carrier is a question the listener must answer, use Loaded question. If the listener has to work the claim out and could be told 'I never said that', use Implication, or If-then implication when a voluntary act is made to stand for agreement. If an argument is missing a step, use Unstated premise. If the claim is flagged as shared knowledge ('of course', 'as you know'), use Assumed common ground. Presuppose only what is plausible or about to be true; a presupposition the listener can plainly see is false gets noticed and costs trust.

not_this.why: asserts the response as the main point instead of taking it for granted
leaves content unspecified for the listener to fill; this family slips specific content in
binds are about the choice offered; the presupposition is the grammar that makes every option assume the outcome

origin.source: Stalnaker, 'Pragmatic Presuppositions', in Munitz & Unger (eds.), Semantics and Philosophy (1974)

evidence.note: That presupposed and implied content is accepted and remembered with less scrutiny than asserted content has controlled support; that it deepens hypnotic response more than direct wording does is not established.

entries.consent_note: The whole family works by keeping a claim out of the listener's direct view, so use it only for outcomes the listener has already agreed to pursue.

entries.name: Presupposition
entries.summary: Phrase the sentence so it only makes sense if the target claim is already true.
entries.definition: A presupposition is what a sentence takes for granted in order to mean anything. It is carried by a specific word or construction (the trigger) and it survives negation and questioning: 'you will notice the heaviness' and 'you won't notice the heaviness yet' both assume heaviness. That survival test separates it from implication, which can be cancelled, and from direct suggestion, which puts the claim up for judgment.
entries.how_to: Decide the claim you want accepted, then write a sentence about something else that needs it: its timing, its degree, its order, or the listener's awareness of it. Put the open question on a detail that does not matter (when, how easily, which first). Keep the presupposed claim plausible at that moment; use it after pacing or just as the response is starting, not cold. Do not stack several large presuppositions in one sentence, because one visible false assumption makes the listener re-read all of them.
examples: The heaviness in your hands can spread at its own pace.
It's the quiet part of your mind that does the listening now.
Your trance can take whatever shape suits you today.
cues: target response sits in a subordinate clause or noun phrase, not the main verb
the claim survives if the sentence is negated or turned into a question
definite or possessive noun phrase for a state not yet established: 'the heaviness', 'your trance', 'that calm'
cleft or pseudo-cleft: 'it's the ... that ...', 'what you'll find is ...'
no variant trigger carries the claim; if before/after/when, first/another/again, notice/realize, already/still/easily, begin/continue/stop or 'or' does, label the variant
a direct question (with a question mark) that carries the assumption is a loaded question, not this unit

not_this.why: an implication is inferred and can be denied; a presupposition is required by the grammar and survives negation
direct suggestion states the response as the main point
when the assumption rides on a direct question the listener is expected to answer, label loaded question; this unit covers statements
'I wonder how/when/which' is the embedded question; add a presupposition label only for the trigger inside it, by variant
a bind is the offer of options; presupposition is the mechanism that makes each option assume the outcome

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Experiments on question wording and memory show presupposed content is accepted and later recalled as fact; no controlled work shows it raises hypnotic responding over plain suggestion.

entries.consent_note: It works because the listener does not stop to evaluate the assumed claim, so presuppose only responses the listener has agreed to.

entries.name: Time-clause presupposition
entries.summary: Put the wanted response inside a before, after, while, when or as clause, so the sentence treats it as something that will happen.
entries.definition: A time clause locates one event relative to another and takes the event in the clause as given. 'Before you go deeper, take a breath' is about the breath; going deeper is assumed. The trigger is the time conjunction. It differs from a contingent suggestion, where the clause holds something already true and the suggestion sits in the main clause.
entries.how_to: Put the response you want in a time clause and an easy instruction or observation in the main clause. 'After', 'once', 'while' and 'since' can present the response as a temporal landmark, but a future clause does not guarantee it will occur. 'Before' is especially weak: 'stop before you fall' is coherent even if no fall occurs. 'When' and 'as' can sound like predictions or descriptions. Use these clauses where the response is plausible, and keep the main clause something the listener can do or verify at once. Avoid claiming a response the listener clearly is not having.
examples: Before you drift all the way down, notice the weight of your hands.
After your eyes close, the sounds in the room can fade into the background.
While that calm spreads through your chest, your shoulders can drop a little.
cues: 'before you ...'
'after you ...' / 'once you have ...'
'while you ...' / 'during ...'
'when you ...' / 'as you ...' followed by a response not yet established
'until you ...' / 'since you began ...'
wanted response in the time clause, minor instruction in the main clause

not_this.why: there the clause holds a fact already true and the main clause is the suggestion; here the suggestion is in the clause
a time bind offers a choice of when; a time clause offers no choice
an implied directive adds an internal response and a signal that it has happened

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Time clauses are established presupposition triggers in linguistics and standard in Ericksonian texts; their specific effect on hypnotic response has not been tested on its own.

entries.consent_note: The assumed response passes without being offered for agreement, so keep it within what the listener signed up for.

entries.name: Ordinal presupposition
entries.summary: Use first, next, another or again so the sentence assumes a series of responses, of which this is only one.
entries.definition: An ordinal or repetition word places an item in a sequence and takes the rest of the sequence as given. 'The first thing you'll notice' assumes there will be several things noticed; 'another wave of calm' assumes an earlier wave; 'again' assumes it happened before. The open question is the order or the identity of the item, never whether the series exists.
entries.how_to: Use 'first' at the start of a phase to promise more to come, and 'another', 'again' or 'once more' when one response has shown, so it reads as one of many. Pair it with uncertainty about which item comes first ('I don't know which hand will feel it first'); the not-knowing draws attention away from the assumption. Do not say 'again' or 'another' about something that has not happened once in the session; the listener can check, and describing an earlier occasion that never took place is suggested memory, with its own cautions.
examples: The first thing you might notice is a change in your breathing.
I wonder which hand will begin to feel heavy first.
And here comes another wave of that calm, moving down through you again.
cues: 'the first thing you'll notice'
'which ... first' in a question or 'I wonder' clause
'next', 'the next time', 'second', 'last'
'another', 'again', 'once more', 'one more'
'also', 'too', 'as well' adding a response to one already named

not_this.why: 'still', 'already' and 'even more' comment on one response in progress; 'first', 'another' and 'again' count it as one of a series
'which first, left or right' adds listed alternatives; label both when alternatives are named
'again' alone stays here; label suggested memory when the script goes on to describe an earlier occasion that did not happen

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Ordinals and repetition words are recognized presupposition triggers in linguistics; the claim that they increase hypnotic response comes from NLP teaching and is untested.

entries.consent_note: It works by the listener not questioning the assumed series, so use it only for responses the listener has agreed to.

entries.name: Awareness predicate
entries.summary: Ask the listener to notice, realize or become aware of the response, so its existence is assumed and only their awareness is in question.
entries.definition: Awareness verbs such as notice, realize, discover and be aware are factive: they can only be used of something true. 'Notice how heavy your arms are' therefore takes the heaviness as fact and makes the instruction about attention. This differs from pacing trance signs, which asserts the sign directly as evidence, and from mind reading, which claims to know what the listener is thinking.
entries.how_to: Write the response as the object of an awareness verb: 'notice how ...', 'you may realize that ...', 'become aware of the ...'. It suits responses that are faint, ambiguous or just beginning, because a listener who goes looking for a sensation usually finds something to count.
