Soften with 'may', 'might' or 'not yet' so a listener who feels nothing concludes they have not noticed yet, not that it is absent. Avoid it for gross, checkable claims (an arm that is plainly not lifting).
examples: Notice how heavy your arms have become.
You may be surprised to discover how easy it is to let that thought go.
At some point you'll realize your breathing slowed down a while ago.
cues: 'notice how/that ...'
'realize', 'discover', 'find that', 'recognize'
'be aware of', 'become aware that', 'are you aware'
'you may not have noticed yet ...'
'know that', 'remember that', 'it's nice to know that' followed by the target claim
awareness verb in the main clause, target response in its object clause

not_this.why: that names an observable sign and calls it evidence; this assumes the response and asks only for attention
mind reading claims knowledge of the listener's thoughts; this directs their attention to an assumed fact
'I wonder whether you notice' is an embedded question; label both when the object is an assumed response

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Factive presupposition is well established in linguistics and the pattern is standard in clinical scripts; its effect on hypnotic response has not been isolated experimentally.

entries.consent_note: The listener is led to search for and confirm a state without being asked whether it exists, so use it for agreed outcomes only.

entries.name: Adverb / adjective presupposition
entries.summary: Attach an adverb or adjective of manner, degree or attitude to the response, so the response is assumed and only its quality is open.
entries.definition: A sentence that asks or comments on how a response happens takes for granted that it happens. 'How easily you relax' assumes relaxing and leaves only its ease open; 'fortunately, you don't need to try' assumes the not-needing and comments on its luck. Three groups do this work: manner and degree words when they are the open element of a question or 'how' clause (how easily, how deeply), phase words (already, still, yet, even more), and commentary words that give the speaker's attitude to a clause taken as fact (fortunately, luckily, curiously). A manner adverb in a plain statement ('you relax easily') asserts the response and is not this variant.
entries.how_to: Write the response as a plain verb or clause, then add the modifier and make the modifier the point of the sentence: 'I wonder how quickly ...', 'it's interesting how deeply ...'. Choose modifiers the listener would be glad to accept (easily, comfortably), since accepting the adverb accepts the verb. 'Already' and 'still' are the strongest and the easiest to falsify; use them once there is something to point at. Too many adverbs in a row reads as padding and weakens each one.
examples: I wonder how easily you can let your shoulders drop.
Fortunately, you don't have to do anything for this to work.
You're still relaxing, even more deeply now.
cues: 'how easily / quickly / deeply / completely you ...'
'already', 'still', 'yet', 'anymore' with a response verb
'even more', 'even deeper', 'so much more'
sentence-opening evaluative word: 'fortunately', 'luckily', 'happily', 'curiously', 'interestingly'
'it's interesting / nice / surprising how ...'
question or wonder-clause whose only open element is a manner or degree word

not_this.why: 'more relaxed' with no standard is comparative deletion; it need not assume a response is under way
'it's good to let go' is a value judgment with no judge; it does not assume the letting go is happening
'already' alone overlaps; label already-happened framing when the whole clause reports the effect as done

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Phase words (already, still) and commentary adverbs are recognized triggers in linguistics. Manner and degree adverbs background the verb only when they are the open element of a question or 'how' clause; in a plain statement the verb is asserted. The claim that any of these improves hypnotic response is NLP teaching without independent tests.

entries.consent_note: The response is assumed while attention goes to its quality, so use it only for responses the listener has agreed to.

entries.name: Change-of-state verb
entries.summary: Use begin, continue, keep, stop or return with the response, so the sentence assumes the state that came before the verb.
entries.definition: Verbs of starting, continuing and stopping take a prior state for granted. 'Continue to relax' assumes relaxing is under way; 'stop holding on' assumes the listener was holding on; 'begin to notice' assumes they were not noticing and now will. The trigger is the phase verb, and what it presupposes is a state before the moment of speaking, where already-happened framing reports the effect itself as present or done.
entries.how_to: Use 'begin' and 'start' to open a response gently: the listener only has to accept a beginning, which is hard to disprove. Switch to 'continue', 'keep' and 'go on' once any sign has appeared; these turn one small response into a process in motion. Use 'stop' and 'no longer' to assume an effort or tension the listener can now drop. Avoid 'continue' as the first mention of a response; with nothing before it, the false assumption is easy to hear.
examples: You can begin to notice the weight of your eyelids.
And just continue relaxing, the way you have been.
You can stop trying to follow every word now.
cues: 'begin to', 'start to', 'starting to'
'continue to', 'keep', 'keep on', 'go on', 'carry on'
'stop', 'quit', 'no longer', 'not anymore'
'return to', 'go back to', 'resume'
'become', 'change into', 'turn into' with a state

not_this.why: that reports the effect itself as present or finished; a phase verb assumes only the state before it
'relax' asserts; 'continue to relax' assumes relaxing and instructs only its continuation
progressive tense is a tense choice; this needs a phase verb

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Phase verbs are textbook presupposition triggers and routine in clinical scripts; no study isolates their effect on hypnotic response.

entries.consent_note: The prior state is assumed, not offered for agreement, so keep it to responses the listener has consented to.

entries.name: Already-happened framing
entries.summary: Speak of the effect as already under way or finished, so the listener's only task is to recognize it.
entries.definition: The writer uses past or perfect tense, 'already', or a result state to report the response as an accomplished fact: 'something has already shifted'. Nothing is requested, so nothing can be refused; the listener is left checking for evidence. It differs from a change-of-state verb, which assumes only a prior state, and from inevitability framing, which predicts a future outcome instead of reporting a present one.
entries.how_to: Place it right after a stretch where some response is likely to have occurred (a long exhale, a silence, a deepener), then report the response as done and send attention to finding it. Keep the claimed effect internal and hard to check: 'something has shifted', 'part of you has already decided'. Follow with an awareness predicate or ratification so the listener confirms it. Do not claim completed effects that are visibly absent, and do not use it in place of the work; it harvests a response, it does not create one from nothing.
examples: It has already begun, and you don't need to do anything to help it along.
Somewhere in the last few breaths, your body decided to let go.
That change is made now. All that's left is to notice it.
cues: 'already' with perfect or past tense: 'has already begun', 'you've already'
'it's done', 'that's settled', 'the decision is made', 'that change is made'
'all that's left is to ...', 'the only thing left is ...'
past or perfect tense for a response the script never requested
'somewhere back there', 'at some point', 'in the last few breaths' locating the effect in the session's past
'by the time you notice, it has ...'

not_this.why: direct suggestion states the response in the present or future ('your eyes are closing', 'you will relax'); this reports it in the past or perfect and leaves only noticing it
'continue' assumes a prior state; this states the effect itself as accomplished
inevitability says it will happen; this says it has
retroactive framing says the trait was always true, across the listener's life; this covers the session's recent past
future progression moves the listener to a later date to look back; this stays in the present

evidence.note: Common in Ericksonian and clinical scripts and consistent with expectancy research, but not tested as a separate technique.

entries.consent_note: It removes the moment at which the listener could decline, so use it only for effects agreed before the session.

entries.name: Loaded question
entries.summary: Ask a question that cannot be answered, yes or no, without accepting an assumption built into it.
entries.definition: A loaded question carries a claim the listener has not agreed to, and every direct answer grants it. 'How long have you wanted to let go?' assumes the wanting whatever number comes back. It is the question form of presupposition, set apart because the listener must respond, and responding is what commits them. A leading question pushes toward one answer; a loaded question makes all answers concede the same thing.
entries.how_to: State the claim you want conceded, then ask about one of its details: how long, how much, when it started, what it feels like. Open questions (how, when, what) load better than yes/no questions. In recorded scripts, leave a pause so the listener answers inwardly; the inner answer is the concession. It is more exposed than a statement, because a question invites a reply and 'I don't' is an available one; keep the assumption close to something the listener has already shown or said.
examples: How long have you been needing a rest like this?
What made you decide to come back tonight?
When did you first realize you were good at this?
cues: direct wh-question ('how long', 'when did', 'what is it about', 'why do you') with a question mark
what it assumes is a wish, need, motive, history or trait of the listener, not a sensation they can check right now
'how much do you want ...', 'why do you keep coming back to ...'
'do you still ...', 'have you stopped ...'
no direct answer denies the assumption; denying it takes 'I don't' or 'it isn't'

not_this.why: label that when the question directs attention to a present sensation or response ('which hand feels warmer?'); label this when it assumes a wish, motive, history or trait
the same assumption in a statement is presupposition; loaded question needs a direct question the listener is expected to answer
'I wonder how long you've wanted this' owes no answer; label embedded question, with the presupposition variant for its trigger
a direct 'X or Y?' that offers two versions of the response is a bind, or a time bind when only timing differs; the or-presupposition variant covers alternatives inside a statement
a tag asks for agreement with a stated claim; a loaded question leaves the assumed claim unstated
a rhetorical question makes a point without seeking an answer; a loaded question solicits an answer that concedes its assumption

evidence.note: Studies of leading questions show that wording which presupposes a detail changes answers and later memory; whether an inward answer during trance commits the listener the same way is untested.

entries.consent_note: Answering concedes something the listener was never asked to agree to, and can alter what they later remember wanting, so load only what they have told you is true.

entries.name: Implication
entries.summary: Say one thing so that the listener infers another, and holds the inferred thing as their own conclusion.
entries.definition: An implication is content a sentence does not state or grammatically require, but which a listener can infer from its wording and context. 'You can keep your eyes open for the first minute or two' suggests that closing them later is expected, without saying that it will happen. The inference can be cancelled without contradiction. Indirect suggestion is the broad style; implication is the particular inference left for the listener to draw. When the target response itself is negated ('you don't have to close your eyes yet'), label negative suggestion.
entries.how_to: Write down the conclusion you want, then write a sentence that is only worth saying if that conclusion is true, and stop. Useful levers: a limit that implies what lies past it ('for now', 'only as fast as', 'for the first minute'), a mention that implies relevance ('some people find their hands tingle first'), and emphasis that implies a contrast ('your conscious mind can keep listening'). Leave a beat afterwards; the inference needs time. If the inference takes more than one step, most listeners will not make it, and spelling it out afterwards turns it into a direct suggestion.
examples: You can keep your eyes open for the first minute or two.
Most people find their eyelids start to feel it somewhere around the third breath.
You can keep that steady, ordinary breathing for now.
cues: a limit on a permission or description: 'for now', 'so far', 'at first', 'for the first minute or two'
a ceiling that only makes sense if the response is coming: 'only as deep as', 'no faster than'
one statement about other people or about one option, with the application to the listener left unsaid
target response never stated as instruction or fact, and not named under 'don't' or 'not', anywhere in the span
the inferred claim can be named in a sentence and could be denied without contradiction ('I didn't say that')

not_this.why: a presupposition is required by the grammar and survives negation; an implication is inferred and can be cancelled
when the target response is named under 'don't', 'not' or 'won't', label negative suggestion, even with 'yet' or 'until'; implication covers inferences from sentences that do not negate the target
one statement with its application left open is implication; an unstated premise needs two stated parts (a rule and a case, or a reason and 'so') with the last step missing
indirect suggestion is the general style, covering story and possibility; implication is one specific inference left to the listener

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Memory research shows listeners often recall pragmatic inferences as if they had been stated; studies comparing indirect with direct hypnotic suggestion have found no reliable advantage for indirect wording.

entries.consent_note: The listener experiences the conclusion as their own and the writer keeps deniability, so imply only what you would be willing to say outright.

entries.name: If-then implication
entries.summary: State a conditional whose 'if' is an easy act the listener controls, so doing the act counts as accepting the 'then'.
entries.definition: The writer ties a response to a simple voluntary act with 'if ... then'. The conditional is stated; what is implied is that by performing the act the listener has agreed to the consequence. It differs from a contingent suggestion, whose first half is already happening or certain to happen, so no act of acceptance is involved. Here the listener's own move closes the deal.
entries.how_to: Choose an 'if' the listener is about to do anyway or can do with no effort: sit back, close the eyes, take a breath, keep listening. State the 'then' as the response you want, with 'can' or 'will'. Say it before the act, and ratify the act when it comes. It works best early, as the listener settles, and at decision points. If the act and the response have no plausible connection, say so lightly or build one; an arbitrary link is noticed.
examples: If you settle back in the chair, that is your signal to let this begin.
If you close your eyes now, you're telling yourself you're ready to go deeper.
If you take one more slow breath, that breath is your signal to release the tension.
cues: 'if you [simple voluntary act], (then) you will / can [response]'
the 'if' clause names something the listener does on purpose, not something happening to them
the act has not been done yet; the sentence comes before it
the act is one the listener is about to do anyway: sit back, close the eyes, take a breath
ratification ('that's right', 'good') in the lines right after

not_this.why: its first half is already true or inevitable ('as you breathe out'); here the first half is a choice whose taking signals agreement
an implied directive has the internal response first and a behavioral signal after; here the act comes first and the response follows
'X means Y' asserts the meaning outright; label both when a conditional also says what the act means
that points back at something already done; this sets the meaning before the act

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Described in Ericksonian texts and consistent with commitment research, but not tested as a distinct technique.

entries.consent_note: It converts an ordinary act into consent without asking for consent, so do not treat the act as agreement to anything the listener has not been told about.

entries.name: Unstated premise
entries.summary: Give an argument with one step left out, so the listener supplies the missing premise or conclusion themselves.
entries.definition: An enthymeme is an argument in which a premise or the conclusion is not stated. The listener fills the gap to make the reasoning hold, and in doing so adopts the missing piece without examining it. It needs argument structure, a 'so', 'because' or 'which means' linking a reason to a claim, which separates it from implication. The unstated part is usually the general rule that would be the weakest point if said aloud.
entries.how_to: Write the full argument first: general rule, particular case, conclusion. Then delete the rule if it is the contestable part, or delete the conclusion if you want the listener to reach it and own it. Keep the gap one step wide. State the remaining parts plainly and join them with a connective so the listener knows an argument is being made. Check the deleted premise yourself: if it is false or you would not defend it, the device is doing dishonest work.
examples: Tense muscles can't hold on once the breathing slows. And your breathing slowed a while ago.
People who can imagine vividly respond well to this. And you pictured that room in detail.
You came back to listen again, which tells you something.
cues: general statement followed by a particular case, conclusion left unsaid
'which tells you something', 'and you know what that means', 'you can work out the rest'
two stated parts of an argument (rule and case, or fact and pointer) with the last step missing from the text
a pause or line break where the conclusion would go
if the reason and the claim are both stated and joined by 'so' or 'because', label giving a reason

not_this.why: when the reason and the claim are both on the page, label giving a reason; label this only when a step, usually the conclusion, is visibly left for the listener
implication is one statement with an inference left open; this needs two stated parts of an argument with a step missing
when the stated fact is the listener's own act and the point is what they want or are, label your-actions-prove-it; add this label only if the conclusion is left unsaid
an unfinished sentence breaks off the grammar; here the sentences are whole and the logic has the gap
a cause-effect link asserts that X causes Y; this argues from X to Y through an unspoken rule

origin.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric

evidence.note: A classical figure. Persuasion studies comparing stated and unstated conclusions do not establish an advantage for leaving the conclusion unsaid; the result varies with the message and audience.

entries.consent_note: The listener adopts a premise they never heard stated, so leave out only premises you could state and defend.

entries.name: Assumed common ground
entries.summary: Mark a claim as something speaker and listener already agree on, so it passes as a reminder instead of a new assertion.
entries.definition: The writer attaches a marker of shared knowledge ('of course', 'as you know', 'we both know', 'obviously') to a claim the listener has not agreed to. The claim is stated in the open, which separates this from grammatical presupposition; what is slipped in is its status as settled. Objecting now means denying something one supposedly already knows, which costs more than doubting a fresh claim.
entries.how_to: Use it on a claim that is close to true for the listener or that they would like to be true, and say it lightly, in passing, on the way to another point. Put the marker at the start or as an aside, then move on without pausing for agreement. It is strongest after real common ground has been built by pacing or earlier sessions. Overuse or use on a clearly new claim reads as pressure and invites the reply 'no, I don't know that'.
examples: As you already know, your body remembers how to do this.
Of course, the body does most of this by itself.
We both know you do this better when you stop trying.
cues: 'as you know', 'as you already know', 'as we both know', 'we both know'
'of course', 'obviously', 'naturally', 'clearly', 'needless to say'
'between us', 'as we agreed', 'you and I both know' presenting a claim as shared
'remember, ...' introducing something not said earlier in the script
'after all', 'as always', 'as we agreed' with no earlier agreement in the text
marker is an aside or sentence opener, or invokes shared agreement; the claim itself is stated in full

not_this.why: a truism really is undeniable; this dresses a contestable claim as already agreed
'you know / realize that X' with the claim as the verb's object is the awareness predicate; label this entry for an aside or opener ('as you know', 'of course') or a 'we' subject ('we both know')
mind reading claims knowledge of what the listener thinks or feels now; this claims they already hold a belief in common with the speaker
social proof cites what other people do; this cites agreement between speaker and listener

evidence.note: Common ground and accommodation are well described in pragmatics, and discourse studies document these markers in persuasive talk; their effect on acceptance has little direct experimental testing.

entries.consent_note: It tells the listener they already agreed to something they did not, which shades into rewriting their history; use it only for things actually established with them.

entries.name: Artful vagueness
entries.summary: Leave out or blur the specifics of a sentence so the listener supplies them from their own experience.
entries.definition: A group of sentence-level patterns, catalogued by Bandler and Grinder from Erickson's speech, that remove or blur information: who, what, how, compared with what, according to whom. The listener has to complete the sentence to understand it, and completes it with material that fits them. The family covers three kinds of pattern: deletions (missing content), unsupported links and generalizations (cause-effect, equivalence, mind reading, quantifiers, modals), and ambiguities (one wording, two readings). It differs from presupposition, which smuggles a specific claim into the background; vagueness leaves the claim open.
entries.how_to: Use deletions (nominalization, unspecified verb, unspecified referent, comparative deletion, simple deletion, lost performative) when you write for many listeners and cannot know their details; they keep statements unfalsifiable. Use the linking patterns (cause-effect link, complex equivalence, mind reading) when you need to connect something observable to the response you want. Use universal quantifiers and modal operators to set how certain or how permitted a response is. Use the ambiguities (sound-alike, syntactic, scope, run-on, double meaning) sparingly, as a light second channel; they are the weakest-supported members. Vagueness suits induction and general suggestion; switch to specific wording for triggers, safety statements and anything the listener must carry out exactly. Presupposition patterns are a separate nested family (presupposition), and the remaining Milton-model items live elsewhere: tag-question, conversational-postulate, embedded-command, embedded-question, quoted-suggestion, double-bind, pacing, utilization.

not_this.why: presupposition builds in a specific claim; vagueness leaves the content open for the listener to fill
indirect suggestion is the broader stance of not commanding; these are the specific wording patterns often used to do it
confusion makes the sentence hard to process on purpose; vague language is easy to process and simply under-specified

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: The patterns are real features of language and listeners do fill gaps with self-relevant content, but the claim that this catalogue makes suggestions more effective than plain wording has not been shown in controlled studies.

entries.consent_note: Vague wording makes statements hard to disagree with; do not use it to blur what a session will do or what the listener is agreeing to.

entries.name: Nominalization
entries.summary: Name a process or feeling with an abstract noun so the listener fills it with their own meaning.
entries.definition: A verb or adjective turned into a noun: relaxing becomes relaxation, learning becomes a learning, being comfortable becomes comfort. The noun drops who does it, how, and to what, so it cannot be checked against the listener's actual experience. The standard test: it is a noun, but you could not put it in a wheelbarrow. It differs from an unspecified verb in that the process is frozen into a thing the listener can have, find or go into.
entries.how_to: Use nominalizations where you need a statement every listener can accept: early in an induction, in general suggestions, and when naming resources ('your own understanding'). Pair them with verbs of having, finding or allowing. A long run of them reads as empty; follow with concrete sensory language when you want a specific experience.
examples: You can find a certain comfort in this stillness.
Let that relaxation bring with it a new understanding.
There is a learning here, and it belongs to you.
cues: abstract nouns ending in -tion, -ment, -ness, -ance, -ity (relaxation, awareness, surrender, clarity)
noun forms of state or process words: comfort, peace, focus, trust, change, learning, understanding, control
'a certain ...', 'a sense of ...', 'a feeling of ...', 'that ...' before an abstract noun
abstract noun as object of have, find, discover, allow, enjoy
the noun could be replaced by a verb phrase ('your relaxation' = 'you relaxing')

not_this.why: there the process stays a verb with its manner left out; here it has become a noun
that gives the state a physical substance (fog, warmth); a nominalization stays abstract
that tells the listener what their present state is called; a nominalization only refers to a state loosely

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Nominalization is a standard linguistic category, but no controlled study shows that abstract nouns produce stronger hypnotic response than concrete wording.

entries.name: Unspecified verb
entries.summary: Use a verb that says something happens without saying how, so the listener does it their own way.
entries.definition: A verb that names an internal process but gives no manner or mechanism: change, learn, experience, notice, let go, allow, drift. The listener must supply the how, and any way they do it counts. It differs from nominalization because the process stays a verb, something the listener does or undergoes.
entries.how_to: Use it when the exact route does not matter or when you cannot know what will work for this listener. Give the direction and leave the method to them: 'let go' instead of 'unclench your jaw'. When you need a particular physical or imagined act, name it specifically instead. Vague verbs combine well with permissive modals ('you can begin to change').
examples: You can simply let go now.
Something is beginning to change as you listen.
Allow yourself to experience this in your own way.
cues: process verbs with no manner or means: change, learn, experience, discover, understand, sense, become, allow, let go, drift, shift, settle
'in your own way', 'however it happens', 'somehow' following the verb
'begin to ...', 'allow yourself to ...', 'let yourself ...' plus a vague verb
no 'by ...' or 'with ...' phrase saying how the action is done

not_this.why: that turns the process into a noun; this keeps the verb and omits the manner
that states outright that the listener need not know how; this just leaves the how unsaid
deletion removes an object or topic from the sentence; here the verb itself is under-specified

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Listed in every Milton-model catalogue; its specific contribution to response has not been tested apart from permissive wording in general.

entries.name: Unspecified referent
entries.summary: Talk about 'people', 'a person' or 'that feeling' without saying who or which, so the listener applies it to themselves.
entries.definition: A noun phrase that does not pick out a specific person or thing: people, someone, one, a person, it, that feeling, certain things. Because the sentence is not about the listener by name, it draws no resistance, yet the listener is the only person present to apply it to. It differs from direct address, which says 'you', and from social proof, which cites others as evidence.
entries.how_to: Use it to offer a suggestion without directing it at the listener: say what 'a person can' do and let them take it up. It works best just before or after a 'you' statement on the same topic, so the transfer is easy. Demonstratives ('that feeling', 'this place') let the listener choose which feeling or place you mean. Overuse makes the script sound evasive.
examples: A person can relax more quickly than they expect.
One can listen and drift at the same time.
And that feeling can begin to spread.
cues: generic subject plus 'can' or 'may' plus a response verb: 'a person can', 'people can', 'one may', 'someone could'
'that feeling', 'this sensation', 'certain things', 'something' with no antecedent
'it' or 'this' with nothing earlier in the text to point to
a generic statement sitting between sentences addressed to 'you'
the sentence states a possibility, not a count or report of what others actually do

not_this.why: social proof reports what others actually do or feel ('most people find') as a reason to follow; here the generic subject is a stand-in for the listener and the sentence states a possibility
a truism is an undeniable general fact that asks for nothing ('everyone has felt tired'); this offers the wanted response under a generic subject ('a person can let go')
normalizing states that the response is ordinary and expected; this only leaves the subject open
that describes a specific third person responding in detail; this names no one

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: That listeners apply generic statements to themselves is plausible and consistent with self-reference research, but the pattern itself has not been tested as a hypnotic device.

entries.name: Comparative deletion
entries.summary: Make a comparison and leave out what it is compared with: more relaxed, deeper, better.
entries.definition: A comparative or superlative word with no stated standard. 'Deeper' does not say deeper than what, so any state at all can count as the baseline and any small change confirms the statement. It differs from the more-the-more form, which ties two increasing things to each other; here there is one quantity and a missing reference point.
entries.how_to: Use comparatives to suggest movement without claiming a level: 'more comfortable' is always safer than 'completely comfortable'. Repeat across a passage to build a sense of steady increase. Do not supply the standard unless you want it measured. It fits deepening passages and ratification ('that's better').
examples: You are becoming more relaxed.
And it feels better now.
This is the easiest way to rest.
cues: comparatives with no 'than' clause: deeper, more relaxed, easier, heavier, calmer, better, further
'more and more', 'even more', 'more deeply', 'less and less'
superlatives with no stated set: 'the best way', 'the deepest level'
'more' or '-er' adjective directly after become, feel, grow, get, go

not_this.why: that yokes two increases to each other; this is a single comparison with the standard missing

that is depth words restated across a passage; this is one comparative with no standard, on any quality. A run of 'deeper... deeper and deeper' takes the passage-level label, and a lone 'more comfortable' takes this one
'even more' and 'still deeper' also presuppose a prior amount; label that when the point is the assumed earlier state, this when the point is the open standard

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Ubiquitous in hypnotic scripts and plainly unfalsifiable by design; no study isolates its effect.

entries.name: Lost performative
entries.summary: State a value judgment as plain fact, without saying whose judgment it is.
entries.definition: An evaluation with the evaluator removed: 'it's good to let go' instead of 'I think it's good for you to let go'. With no judge named there is no one to disagree with, so the judgment reads as a general truth. It differs from a truism, which is verifiably true, and from authority, which names the source.
entries.how_to: Use it to give approval to a response without making it your personal opinion: 'it's good to...', 'it's important to...', 'the best thing is...'. Keep the judgment mild and easy to accept; a strong or contestable value stated this way invites the question 'says who?'. It works well just before a suggestion the listener may be holding back from. If you only mean that the response is allowed, that is permission, not a judgment.
examples: It's good to take this time for yourself.
And it's important to rest as deeply as you need.
The best thing to do with a busy mind is to leave it alone.
cues: 'it's good to', 'it's right to', 'it's important to', 'it's best to', 'it's wise to', 'it's wrong to'
evaluative adjective of worth or correctness (good, right, wrong, best, important, wise, natural) in an impersonal 'it is ... to/that' frame
'the best way to ...', 'the right thing is ...' with no one named as holding the view
no 'I think', 'for me', 'according to' attached to the judgment
the judged thing is a response or attitude the script wants, not a checkable fact

not_this.why: 'it's okay / all right / fine to' says the response is allowed and is permission-giving; label lost performative when the adjective asserts worth or correctness (good, right, best, important, wrong)
a free-standing 'that's right' or 'good' after a response confirms that it happened; a lost performative is a full sentence judging a response or attitude in general
a truism can be checked and is undeniable; this is an opinion presented as fact
normalizing says the response is common; this says it is good or right

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: The pattern is a real grammatical form; whether dropping the judge makes a value more readily accepted has not been tested in hypnosis.

entries.consent_note: Because the judge is hidden, the listener may take the writer's values as general fact; keep such judgments to ones the listener would endorse awake.

entries.name: Mind reading
entries.summary: State what the listener is thinking or feeling as though you know it.
entries.definition: A claim about the listener's inner experience with no stated basis: 'I know you're wondering', 'part of you is curious'. Kept general, it is likely to be true, and a correct guess makes the speaker seem attuned. It differs from pacing, which states what is outwardly verifiable (sitting, hearing, breathing), and from desire attribution, which specifically assigns the wish for the outcome.
entries.how_to: Claim only inner events that are near-universal in the situation: curiosity, wondering, some doubt, wanting to relax. Hedge the content, not the knowing ('you may be wondering just how...'). Use it early to build rapport and as a bridge into a suggestion. A specific wrong guess breaks rapport, so stay general or cover both sides.
examples: I know you're wondering how deep you can go.
Part of you is already curious about what comes next.
You may be thinking this is easier than you expected.
cues: 'I know you ...', 'I can tell you ...', 'I know that you ...' plus a mental verb
'you're wondering', 'you're thinking', 'you're curious', 'you're starting to feel'
'part of you ...' plus a thought or wish
second-person mental-state claim with no evidence given
'you might be asking yourself'

not_this.why: pacing states what the listener can verify externally right now; mind reading asserts unobservable thoughts or feelings
that attributes wanting the suggested outcome; mind reading covers any claimed thought or feeling
that names a likely objection in order to answer it; mind reading need not answer anything

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: People do rate general statements about themselves as accurate, which explains why it seems to work, but its effect on hypnotic response is untested.

entries.consent_note: Telling a listener what they think or want can replace their own report of it; do not use it to override a stated limit or doubt.

entries.name: Cause-effect link
entries.summary: Say that one thing causes another, usually something already happening causing the response you want.
entries.definition: An unsupported assertion that X produces Y: 'the sound of my voice makes you relax'. The stated cause is normally something present or certain, so the effect seems to follow from it. This entry is the explicit causal claim (makes, causes, because, so); the looser time-linked forms (as, while, when) are contingent suggestions. It differs from complex equivalence, which says X means Y, not X produces Y.
entries.how_to: Pick a cause the listener cannot deny is happening (breathing, hearing, sitting) and attach the response with a causal verb. The link does not need to be logical, but it lands better when it feels natural, such as breathing out and loosening. Start with weak links ('and', 'as') early in a script and move to strong ones ('makes', 'causes') once responses are coming.
examples: Each breath out makes your shoulders drop a little further.
Listening to these words causes your mind to grow quiet.
Because you are sitting still, calm comes easily.
cues: 'makes you', 'causes you to', 'forces', 'brings', 'sends you', 'takes you' linking a present event to a response
'because', 'so', 'and so', 'that is why' joining a present fact to an involuntary response, not to an instruction
'X will make Y happen' where X is the voice, breath, a sound or a count
a verifiable clause followed by a causal verb and an unverifiable response

not_this.why: that links by timing ('as', 'while', 'when', 'with every'); this asserts causation outright
that says X means or shows Y; this says X produces Y

there the 'because' clause gives grounds for doing or accepting what is asked; here a present event is said to produce a response that just happens. If the main clause is an instruction or a 'you can', it is reason-giving

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Stated causal expectations do shape response (expectancy research), but the specific NLP grading of weak to strong linkage is untested.

entries.name: Complex equivalence
entries.summary: Say that one thing means another: an observable sign is declared to be proof of the state you want.
entries.definition: An assertion that two different things are the same or that one is evidence of the other: 'your eyes closing means you're ready'. It gives an ordinary event a meaning chosen by the writer. It differs from a cause-effect link (X produces Y) and from reframing, which changes the meaning of something the listener already has a meaning for.
entries.how_to: Take something that is happening or about to happen and state what it means, using 'means', 'shows', 'is a sign that', or plain 'is'. Choose an X that is certain to be true, such as hearing the voice, sitting still or the room being quiet. Two common uses have their own entries: declaring relaxation signs to be evidence of trance (ratifying-trance-signs) and declaring the listener's actions to be proof of what they want (self-perception-proof).
examples: Being still means being safe.
Hearing my voice means it is time to rest.
A quiet room is a sign that nothing is needed from you.
cues: 'means', 'means that', 'which means'
'shows that', 'proves', 'tells you', 'is a sign that', 'is how you know'
'the fact that ... means ...'
'X is Y' or 'X-ing is Y-ing' where X is an observable event or condition and Y is a state, meaning or trait
two unlike things joined by 'is just another way of', 'is the same as', 'is what ... looks like'

not_this.why: that says X brings Y about; this says X is, or is evidence of, Y
when X is an ordinary bodily sign of relaxation and Y is trance, label that narrower entry; this is the general X-means-Y form
that is the narrower case of giving a felt body sensation a new cause or meaning; label it when X is a sensation being renamed
when X is something the listener voluntarily did and Y is what they want or are, label that; this covers the remaining X-means-Y claims

evidence.note: Interpreting ambiguous sensations as evidence of hypnosis is consistent with expectancy and misattribution research; the NLP pattern as such has no direct tests.

entries.consent_note: The listener is handed a meaning for their own reactions; avoid equivalences that turn hesitation or discomfort into agreement.

entries.name: Universal quantifier
entries.summary: Use all, every, always, never or nothing so the statement covers every case without exception.
entries.definition: A word that generalizes a statement to all instances, times or things: every breath, all of your attention, always, never, nothing, everyone. It removes exceptions, so a suggestion applies each time and to the whole of the listener. It differs from inevitability framing, which claims an outcome is certain, and from hyperbole, which exaggerates for effect and is not meant literally.
entries.how_to: Attach the quantifier to something recurring (each breath, every word, every time you hear this) to spread a suggestion across the session or across future occasions. Use 'all' and 'completely' for totality, 'never' and 'nothing' to rule out interference. One exception the listener notices breaks an absolute, so pair it with responses that are easy or self-confirming. Limit the scope of lasting suggestions explicitly.
examples: All of your attention rests here.
Nothing needs doing now.
Every part of you knows how to rest.
cues: all, every, each, any, always, never, none, nothing, no one, everyone, everything, everywhere
'every time', 'each and every', 'with every ...', 'all of your ...', 'every part of you'
'whenever', 'wherever', 'no matter what / where / when'
quantifier attached to a recurring event (breath, word, sound, count)

not_this.why: 'with every breath, ...' and 'each time ..., ...' are contingent suggestions (breath-deepener when tied to depth); label the quantifier separately only where no such linking form already covers it
that asserts the outcome cannot be avoided; a quantifier only removes exceptions from a statement
hyperbole is overstatement not meant literally; the quantifier is meant to hold in every case
a truism with 'everyone' is offered as plain fact to be agreed with; the quantifier label is for a suggestion made exceptionless
that specifically says any stimulus deepens trance; label that narrower device when the quantifier ranges over stimuli linked to deepening

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: A basic feature of language used throughout hypnotic scripts; no study isolates the effect of universal wording on response.

entries.consent_note: Words like always, never and everywhere extend a suggestion beyond the session; bound them with scope limits when the effect is meant to last.

entries.name: Modal operator
entries.summary: Choose can, may, will, must or can't to set whether the response is possible, permitted, certain or required.
entries.definition: A modal verb or equivalent that sets the status of an action: possibility (can, may, might, could, able to), certainty (will), necessity (must, have to, need to, should) or impossibility (can't, unable). The same suggestion changes force with the modal alone. Possibility modals are the working words of permissive suggestion; this entry is the word-level choice, whatever style it serves.
entries.how_to: Pick the modal to match how sure you are of the response and how far in the listener is. 'Can' and 'may' are almost never false and suit the start; 'will' commits you; 'must' and 'have to' suit an authoritarian style or a well-established response. A common build moves from possibility to certainty to necessity across a passage. 'Can't' is used for challenges and for removing an unwanted option.
examples: You can relax. You will relax. In a moment you must relax.
You have to let that breath go sooner or later.
You simply cannot hold on to that tension any longer.
cues: possibility: can, could, may, might, able to, it's possible to
necessity: must, have to, need to, should, got to, it's necessary
impossibility: can't, cannot, unable to, impossible to, won't be able to
'you' plus a modal plus a response verb
modals strengthening across a passage (can, then will, then must)

not_this.why: a suggestion offered with 'can', 'may' or 'might' is permissive-suggestion and needs no modal label; label the modal here only when it is one of necessity, certainty or impossibility, or when the passage shifts from one modal to another
that is a modal question ('can you...?') working as a request; this is a modal in a statement
that invites a test of a suggested inability; 'can't' alone, with no invited attempt, is just the modal
that asserts the outcome is certain as its whole point; a bare 'will' or 'must' inside another suggestion is the modal

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Permissive versus authoritarian wording has been compared in controlled studies with generally small or no differences in response; the NLP claims for particular modals go beyond that.

entries.name: Deletion
entries.summary: Leave out the object or topic of the sentence: ready for what, aware of what, curious about what.
entries.definition: A sentence with a required piece of information missing, usually the object of an adjective or verb: 'you are ready', 'you're becoming aware', 'you already know'. The listener completes it with whatever is on their mind. It differs from comparative deletion (a missing standard of comparison) and from an unfinished sentence, which is visibly broken off; a deletion is grammatically complete.
entries.how_to: Use state words that normally take a complement (ready, aware, curious, sure, open, willing) and stop before the complement. Place it where the context already points toward the response, so the listener's fill-in is the one you want. If the fill-in matters, such as what exactly they are agreeing to, state it instead.
examples: You are ready now.
And you're becoming aware.
You already know, don't you.
cues: ready, aware, curious, sure, willing, open, certain, prepared with no 'for', 'of', 'about' or 'to' phrase
know, understand, notice, remember, learn with no object
short 'you are / you feel' plus adjective sentence ending at the adjective
the question 'ready for what?' or 'know what?' has no answer in the surrounding sentences

not_this.why: that omits the standard of a comparison; this omits an object or topic
that breaks off mid-sentence so the gap is felt; a deletion sounds complete
there a noun is present but picks out no one in particular; here the element is absent altogether

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Listeners routinely fill missing arguments from context (a well-studied pragmatic fact); no evidence shows the deletion itself increases suggestibility.

entries.name: Sound-alike ambiguity
entries.summary: Use a word or phrase that sounds like a different word, so a second instruction is heard inside the sentence.
entries.definition: A homophone or near-homophone placed so that the spoken sentence carries a second reading: here/hear, know/no, your/you're, two/too/to, by now/buy now. The written sentence makes ordinary sense; the alternate reading exists only in sound. It differs from double meaning, where one word has two senses under the same spelling, and from circular wordplay, which piles sound-alikes up to confuse.
entries.how_to: Write the sentence so the surface meaning is natural and the sound-alike falls where the hidden reading forms a short command or statement. It needs audio; in text it only works if the reader sounds it out. The voice can mark it with a slight pause or drop in tone. Use one at a time; several in a row turn into confusion or comedy.
examples: Now, you can rest.
Here, you can let your shoulders settle.
Now, your breathing can slow.
cues: homophone pairs near a suggestion: here/hear, know/no, your/you're, to/two/too, by/buy, write/right, weight/wait, whole/hole
a deliberate 'misspelling' in a script that swaps one homophone for another
stage direction or emphasis mark on a homophone
the same sound repeated in both senses in one sentence ('you know... no need to')

not_this.why: that is one word with two senses; this is two different words that sound alike
that loops sound-alikes to overload sense-making; this is a single quiet second reading
an embedded command is plainly present in the wording; here the command exists only in the alternate hearing

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Both senses of an ambiguous word are briefly activated in comprehension, but there is no evidence that the unintended sense acts as an instruction.

entries.consent_note: It is meant to pass unnoticed; the hidden reading should say nothing the listener has not agreed to hear openly.

entries.name: Syntactic ambiguity
entries.summary: Write a phrase whose grammar can be parsed two ways, so who does what to whom stays open.
entries.definition: A phrase with two possible grammatical structures, classically an -ing word plus a noun: 'relaxing voices' can be voices that relax you or the act of relaxing them. The words are unambiguous; the roles are not. It differs from scope ambiguity, where the structure is clear but the reach of one modifier is not, and from double meaning, which rests on one word's two senses.
entries.how_to: Build it from a transitive verb in -ing form placed before a noun, or from a phrase that can attach to either of two parts of the sentence. Put it in a low-stakes descriptive line; the listener may take either reading and both should serve you. It is a decorative pattern: use rarely and never where the instruction must be clear.
examples: Relaxing muscles can be a pleasure.
Calming thoughts can be very easy.
You may enjoy quieting voices.
cues: transitive verb in -ing form directly before a plural noun ('relaxing muscles', 'calming thoughts', 'deepening feelings')
'-ing noun can be ...' as sentence subject
a phrase that could attach to either the subject or the object ('watching you relax with ease')
sentence gives two sensible answers to 'who is doing the -ing?'

not_this.why: there the parse is clear and only the reach of a modifier is open; here the grammatical roles themselves are open
that fuses two sentences on a shared word; this is one well-formed phrase with two parses
that depends on one word's two senses, not on grammar

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Structural ambiguity is well studied in psycholinguistics as a processing cost; no evidence supports a hypnotic effect.

entries.name: Scope ambiguity
entries.summary: Place a modifier where it is unclear how much of the sentence it covers.
entries.definition: A sentence in which an adjective, adverb or verb could apply to only the next item or to everything that follows. In 'your heavy arms and legs', heavy may cover only the arms or the legs too; in 'I wonder if you know that you are relaxing and going deeper', the going deeper may be inside the wondering or stated as fact. It differs from syntactic ambiguity because the grammatical roles are clear; only the reach is open.
entries.how_to: Put a modifier or a soft opening verb ('I wonder if', 'you may notice that') before a coordinated list joined by 'and'. The first item clearly falls under it; later items can be heard either as covered or as free-standing assertions. Use it to let a statement drift from tentative to factual, or to spread one quality across several things.
examples: Feel your heavy arms and legs.
I wonder if you know that you are relaxing and going deeper now.
Speaking to you as someone who relaxes easily and learns quickly.
cues: adjective or adverb before two or more nouns or verbs joined by 'and'
'I wonder if / I don't know whether / you may notice that' followed by clauses joined with 'and'
a long sentence where a late clause could be inside or outside an earlier hedge
'as' or 'when' clause followed by coordinated items

not_this.why: there the phrase has two different parses of who does what; here only the reach of a modifier is unclear
that joins a fact and a suggestion with 'and' to transfer acceptance; label scope ambiguity only when an earlier modifier may or may not cover the second part
'I wonder if' alone is an embedded question; this entry needs the trailing 'and' clause whose coverage is open

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume I, Meta Publications (1975)

evidence.note: A recognized linguistic phenomenon; its use as a hypnotic device is untested and it is the least used of the Milton-model ambiguities.

entries.name: Run-on ambiguity
entries.summary: Let the last word of one sentence also be the first word of the next, so the two run together.
entries.definition: Two sentences fused on a shared word or phrase with no break between them: 'you can feel your hand me the glass', 'notice how you can relax now is the time'. The pivot word belongs to both, so the listener cannot tell where one sentence ended. It differs from an unfinished sentence, which stops and leaves a gap, and from polysyndeton, which links complete clauses with conjunctions.
entries.how_to: Choose a pivot that ends the first thought and starts the second, often a word like 'now', 'deeply', 'relax' or a noun that doubles as a verb. Deliver or punctuate it with no pause at the join. The second sentence is usually the suggestion. Use sparingly; it produces a brief stumble, and repeated stumbles become confusion technique.
examples: You can begin to relax now is the time to let go.
Listening to my voice carries you down into comfort grows with every breath.
As you look at your watch how quickly your eyes grow tired.
cues: a sentence that is ungrammatical as a whole but splits into two good sentences sharing one word
'now', 'here', 'deeply', 'relax', 'down' sitting at a join with no punctuation
missing full stop or comma where a sentence boundary is expected
a noun that immediately serves as a verb (watch, hand, rest, feel, sink)
script note such as 'no pause' at a sentence boundary

not_this.why: that breaks off and leaves the thought hanging; this continues straight into a second sentence
that joins whole clauses with repeated conjunctions; here a shared word belongs to both sentences
that drops in an irrelevant statement; here the join, not the content, is what is odd

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume I, Meta Publications (1975)

evidence.note: Bandler and Grinder describe this overlapping-sentence technique in Erickson's speech; evidence that it makes the second clause more acceptable is lacking.

entries.name: Attributing feeling to things
entries.summary: Say that an object feels or does something only a person can, so the listener takes the statement as about themselves.
entries.definition: A sentence that gives an inanimate thing a human experience: 'the chair can relax', 'the room is growing sleepy'. Since objects cannot feel, the listener makes sense of the sentence by moving the feeling to the only available feeler, themselves. It is a single displaced predicate, not a sustained image; a thing given its own will or voice over a passage is personification, and a full parallel story is metaphor.
entries.how_to: Name something in the listener's surroundings or in the imagined scene and give it the state you want them to have. Keep it to a sentence or two and do not explain it. It suits indirect styles and listeners who push back on being told what they feel. Follow it with a statement about the listener so the transfer has somewhere to land.
examples: The chair beneath you knows how to rest completely.
Even the walls seem to be letting go of the day.
The lamp beside you feels no need to hurry.
cues: inanimate subject (chair, room, bed, tree, stone, candle) with a verb of feeling, knowing or intending
'the ... knows how to', 'the ... can relax', 'the ... feels', 'the ... is content to'
an object described with the target state shortly before 'you' is given the same state
one or two sentences only, with no developed story

not_this.why: personification gives the listener's own body parts or states a will ('your eyelids know'), or addresses the thing; label this entry when an outside object is given the feeling the listener is meant to have
a metaphor is a story or image with parallel structure; this is one predicate on the wrong kind of subject
that uses a generic human subject; this uses a non-human one

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Derived from Erickson's indirect work (for example speaking about a plant's comfort); the claimed mapping onto the self is plausible but untested.

entries.name: Double meaning
entries.summary: Use a word with two senses where both senses carry the suggestion.
entries.definition: A single word or phrase that has two established meanings, placed so each fits: 'going down', 'let it sink in', 'falling' asleep, 'light'. One sense belongs to the surface topic and the other to the trance or the suggestion. It differs from sound-alike ambiguity (two different words) and from metaphor (a developed comparison); the work is done by one word.
entries.how_to: Look for ordinary words that have both a literal and a state meaning: down, deep, drop, sink, fall, under, light, open, follow, absorbed. Put them in a sentence about the surface topic (stairs, water, a story) so the state meaning rides along. Works in text and audio. Too obvious a pun pulls the listener out to appreciate the joke.
examples: Let that idea sink in as you sink into the chair.
Step by step, you are going down.
It's so easy to follow where this voice leads.
cues: words with a literal and a trance sense: down, deep, under, drop, sink, fall, light, open, absorbed, follow, lost, blank
the same word used twice in one sentence in two senses
an idiom whose literal reading also fits the scene ('sink in', 'let go', 'drift off', 'fall for')
a direction or position word in a scene that matches a depth word in the trance

not_this.why: that uses two different words that sound the same; this uses one word with two senses
metaphor develops a parallel image or story; a double meaning rests on a single word
interspersal scatters suggestion words through unrelated narrative; label double meaning when one word is doing two jobs at once

evidence.note: Both senses of an ambiguous word are briefly active during comprehension, which is well established; that the second sense works as a suggestion is not.

entries.consent_note: The second sense is meant to pass without comment; it should carry nothing the listener has not agreed to hear said plainly.

entries.name: Pacing and utilization
aliases: meeting the listener where they are
entries.summary: Start from what is already true for the listener, and give whatever happens a job in the process.
entries.definition: This family groups devices that work by agreement with the listener's present reality instead of by instruction against it. Pacing devices describe what is already so (pacing, pacing trance signs, matching, normalizing, permission). Utilization devices take what the listener brings or what the setting throws up and assign it a role (utilization, incorporation of distractions, using the listener's own material). Pacing and leading is the bridge: it spends the credit that pacing earns. The family has no nested families; its nearest neighbours are the suggestion forms (truism, ratification, contingent suggestion) and resistance handling.
entries.how_to: Use pacing when you need agreement before you have earned it: the opening of a pretalk or induction. Use pacing and leading when you are ready to move the listener somewhere new. Use utilization and its variants when something could compete with the script: noise, restlessness, doubt, a wandering mind, the listener's own habits. Use normalizing and permission when the obstacle is worry about doing it wrong or shame about responding. Use pacing trance signs once the listener has had time to settle, so the signs you name are probably there. In a recording you cannot see the listener, so pace only what is true for nearly everyone, and write utilization as incorporation in advance.

not_this.why: that family is about how one suggestion is phrased; this one is about anchoring the script to the listener's actual situation
resistance handling deals with opposition specifically; utilization takes anything the listener brings, opposition included

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian and clinical hypnosis teaching; the general ideas fit expectancy and rapport research, but the family as a whole has not been tested against scripts that omit it.

entries.name: Pacing
entries.summary: State things the listener can check right now and find true.
entries.definition: Pacing is describing the listener's present experience in terms they can check at once: what they are doing, hearing, seeing or physically feeling at this moment. Each statement can be verified on the spot, so each one earns a small silent yes. It differs from a truism in that it is about this listener now, not a general fact about people; from mind reading in that it keeps to what can be checked and makes no claim about what the listener thinks or wants; and from pacing and leading in that it stops before any suggestion is added.
entries.how_to: Open with it, before you ask for anything. In a recording, pace only what is true for almost every listener: they are hearing a voice, breathing, sitting or lying somewhere, reading or listening to these words. Keep each statement plain and neutral; any adjective the listener could dispute ("comfortable", "relaxed") turns a pace into a lead. Vary the sense channel (hearing, sight, body) so the run does not read as a list. A statement about what the listener is thinking is a guess; it is mind reading, not a pace. One wrong pace costs more than several right ones gain, so hedge with "perhaps" when unsure.
examples: You're listening to the sound of my voice. You're breathing in, and breathing out.
You can feel the weight of your body where it rests, and the temperature of the air on your skin.
You've set this time aside. You're reading these words, one after another.
cues: second-person present-tense statements about the immediate situation: 'you are sitting', 'you can hear', 'you're breathing'
sensory verbs with neutral objects: hear the sounds, feel the chair, see the screen
references to the act of listening or reading itself: 'my voice', 'these words'
no evaluative or state words in the statement (no 'relaxed', 'deeper', 'calm')
typically at the opening of a script or section

not_this.why: a truism is a general undeniable fact ('everyone has drifted off in a lecture'); pacing describes this listener's experience right now
mind reading claims what the listener is thinking, wondering or wanting, which they cannot check against the senses; pacing names only what they can verify (sitting, hearing, breathing, reading)
pacing and leading adds a suggested statement after the verifiable ones; pacing alone suggests nothing
that entry paces specific signs and claims they mean trance; plain pacing attaches no meaning

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975)

evidence.note: Taught in most clinical and Ericksonian texts; that accurate statements build agreement is plausible and consistent with acquiescence research, but pacing as a hypnotic device has not been isolated in controlled studies.

entries.name: Pacing and leading
entries.summary: Give several statements the listener can verify, then one suggested statement that borrows their credibility.
entries.definition: A run of pacing statements is followed, in the same tone and grammar, by a statement that is not yet verifiable: the lead. The lead is delivered as if it were one more observation, so it tends to be accepted along with the rest. What marks it from plain pacing is the shift from fact to suggestion; what marks it from a yes set is that it is built from statements about present experience, not questions seeking an answer.
entries.how_to: Start with more paces than leads (three to one is the usual teaching ratio) and reverse the ratio as the session goes on. Join pace to lead with 'and', 'as' or 'which means' so there is no seam. Keep the first leads small and close to what is likely anyway (a slower breath, a little more comfort) so they come true and become paces for the next round. It fails when a pace is false for the listener or when the lead jumps too far from the paces.
examples: You're sitting there, hearing my voice, feeling the chair beneath you, and you can begin to feel a little more settled.
You're breathing in, and out. You're reading each word. Your shoulders are starting to soften.
You've closed your eyes. You can hear the room around you. You can feel your hands resting. And something in you is beginning to slow down.
cues: two or more verifiable present-tense statements followed by a state or change claim in the same sentence or the next
linkers between fact and suggestion: 'and', 'as', 'while', 'and that means'
final clause introduces a state word absent from the earlier clauses: relax, deeper, heavy, calm, drift
softeners on the last clause: 'you can begin to', 'you may notice'
ratio shifts over the passage: fewer verifiable statements per suggestion later on

not_this.why: a yes set seeks explicit or inner yes answers, often to questions and on any topic; pace and lead uses statements about present experience
compound suggestion is the single 'fact and suggestion' sentence form; pace and lead is the wider pattern of several paces and a shifting ratio
contingent suggestion makes the response depend on a specific event ('as X, then Y'); here the paces only lend credibility

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975)

evidence.note: The pattern is taught everywhere and is plausible on acquiescence and fluency grounds, but the specific claims (ratios, that accepted paces transfer to the lead) have not been tested in controlled hypnosis studies.

entries.consent_note: The lead is meant to pass as one more observation; use it for responses the listener has agreed to pursue.

entries.name: Utilization
entries.summary: Accept whatever the listener brings or does, and give it a role in the process.
entries.definition: Utilization treats any behavior, feeling, belief or event as usable: it is accepted as it is and then described as helping, or as the very route to the wanted response. Nothing is corrected or fought. It differs from reframing in that the thing is not only given a new meaning but put to work, and from resistance utilization in that it covers everything the listener brings, not only opposition.
entries.how_to: Name the thing as it is, without judgment, then link it to the direction you want: 'and that can...'. Live, you use what you observe. In a recording, write for the common cases: fidgeting, a busy mind, doubt, an itch, laughing, wanting to open the eyes. Keep the link plausible; restlessness can 'settle on its own once it has moved enough', but claiming it is relaxation will not be believed. Use it early, so the listener learns that nothing they do is wrong.
examples: If your mind is busy, good. Let it stay busy. A busy mind can keep itself occupied while the rest of you settles.
If you need to shift or scratch, go ahead, and notice how much easier it is to be still afterwards.
If you feel like smiling or laughing, let it happen. Each laugh lets a little more tension out, and you can settle further once it has passed.
cues: conditional naming of a listener behavior followed by acceptance: 'if you ... , that's fine', 'good', 'let it'
a behavior that would normally interfere (fidgeting, thinking, doubting, opening the eyes) described as useful
link phrases: 'and that can help you', 'use that', 'that is exactly what'
no instruction to stop or correct the behavior
'whatever you ... is right' followed by a specific use, not only reassurance

not_this.why: that entry covers the special case where the thing used is opposition or a contrary response
reframing only changes what something means; utilization assigns it a function in the procedure
no-fail framing declares every outcome a success; utilization takes one specific behavior and puts it to use

origin.source: Erickson, Further clinical techniques of hypnosis: Utilization techniques (1959)

evidence.note: A core principle of Ericksonian practice supported by case reports; there are no controlled comparisons showing that utilization raises responsiveness beyond standard procedures.

entries.name: Incorporation of distractions
entries.summary: Name likely interruptions in advance and make them part of the trance.
entries.definition: Incorporation is utilization applied to events in the environment: traffic, voices, a phone, a creak in the building. The script names them before or as they happen and says they belong to the experience, are unimportant, or help. It is narrower than utilization, which also covers what the listener does, feels and believes (a cough, an itch, a doubt), and it differs from 'everything deepens' in that its purpose is to stop a noise from breaking the state, not to turn all stimuli into deepeners.
entries.how_to: Place it early in the induction, before the first interruption is likely. Name the category ('any sounds around you'), not a specific noise that may not occur. Offer one of three treatments: the sound fades into the background, the sound is a sign that all is well, or the sound helps. Pair it with an emergency clause so real alarms still get through. One or two sentences is enough; repeating it draws attention to the noises.
examples: Any sounds you hear around you, a car, a door, a voice in another room, are just the ordinary sounds of the world carrying on, and they can help you settle.
If something makes a noise, you can notice it, let it go, and come back to my voice even more easily than before.
The hum in the room can become part of this, a steady background that lets you rest.
cues: 'any sounds', 'noises around you', 'outside sounds', 'whatever you hear'
a list of everyday interruptions: traffic, doors, phones, voices, a clock
outcome clauses: 'fade into the background', 'won't disturb you', 'only help you', 'part of the experience'
exception clause for emergencies nearby ('unless it needs your attention')
placed in the first minutes of an induction

not_this.why: that deepener declares every stimulus sends the listener deeper; incorporation only neutralizes or absorbs interruptions
narrowing attention makes everything but one thing fade; incorporation lets the distraction stay and gives it a place
the emergency clause that often follows is a separate safety device

evidence.note: Routine in clinical and recorded scripts; no controlled study isolates whether naming distractions in advance protects the state better than saying nothing.

entries.name: Using the listener's own material
entries.summary: Build the suggestion from the listener's own words, interests, habits or complaint.
entries.definition: This is utilization applied to content the listener supplied: their vocabulary for the state, their hobby, their job, their habitual way of doing things, or the problem itself. The suggestion is expressed in that material so that it reads as an extension of what they already think and do. It differs from matching, which copies style and tempo, in that it borrows subject matter and puts it to work as the vehicle of the suggestion.
entries.how_to: Collect the material first: an intake question, a custom-script brief, or a line in the script that asks the listener to supply it ('think of the thing you do that absorbs you completely'). Then use their terms unchanged; a paraphrase loses the effect. Map the wanted response onto a skill or pattern they already have (a runner already knows how to find a rhythm and stop thinking). For general-audience recordings, leave a slot the listener fills inwardly, or write for a named audience whose shared interests you know.
examples: You told me that when you paint, hours go by without your noticing. You already know how to do this. Let it be like that now.
Think of the word you would use for that settled feeling. Your word, not mine. Say it to yourself, and let it name what is happening.
You said you can't switch your mind off. So don't. Give that busy mind the job of counting each breath out, the way you would check a list.
cues: attribution to the listener: 'you told me', 'you said', 'as you described', 'your word for it'
a prompt for the listener to supply content, then reuse of it: 'think of a place you know... that place'
the listener's occupation, hobby or habit used as the model for the response ('the way you do when you ...')
quoted or unusual vocabulary repeated verbatim from an earlier listener statement
the presenting problem recast as a skill ('the same persistence that keeps you worrying')

not_this.why: matching mirrors tempo, breathing or sensory vocabulary for rapport; this entry builds the suggestion out of the listener's content
an analogy can use any familiar thing; here the comparison is taken from what this listener supplied
values linking ties a suggestion to what the listener cares about as a reason; this uses their material as the form of the suggestion

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Rests on Erickson's case reports and later clinical teaching; tailored messages and self-relevant material are better remembered in general research, but this hypnotic use has not been tested directly.

entries.name: Using resistance
entries.summary: Give the listener's resistance a task, so that resisting carries out the suggestion.
entries.definition: The writer accepts the resistance and assigns it a role whose performance is the wanted response: hold the eyes open (so they tire), keep the hand down (so the effort becomes the focus), stay alert (so the alertness is watched). It differs from reverse psychology, which instructs the opposite of what is wanted, and from resistance as participation, which only re-describes resistance without giving it work to do.
entries.how_to: Name the likely resistance without judgment, then hand it a specific job that ends in the response you want. Choose a job the listener can do fully, so success at resisting still lands in trance. Ratify whatever happens. It fails when the assigned task is something the listener can do indefinitely with no cost.
examples: Part of you wants to stay alert, and that part can keep watch, carefully, while the rest of you rests.
Go ahead and keep those eyes open as long as you can. Really work at keeping them open.
Hold on to that doubt tightly, so tightly that your hands begin to feel how much effort it takes.
cues: acknowledgment of resistance followed by a task for it ('that part can...', 'let it...')
'keep (doing X) as long as you can'
'part of you wants to... and that part can...'
instructions to try harder at the resisted behavior

not_this.why: reverse psychology tells the listener to do the opposite; using resistance assigns the resistance a task
resistance as participation re-describes resistance; using resistance gives it work
a reverse-set bind offers choices built for a contrary listener; using resistance needs no choice

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian clinical teaching; there are no controlled studies of resistance utilization as a separate technique.

entries.name: Normalizing
entries.summary: Describe the response as ordinary, natural and expected.
entries.definition: Normalizing tells the listener that what they are experiencing, or are about to experience, is common and unremarkable. It removes the worry that a response is strange, a failure or a loss of control. It differs from social proof in that it describes the response as natural to people in general without citing what specific others did, and from myth correction in that it reassures without arguing against a stated false belief.
entries.how_to: Place it in the pretalk and again wherever a response might alarm or embarrass: a wandering mind, twitching, tears, time slipping, not feeling much. State the experience, call it normal, and move on; one sentence is enough. Normalize a range ('some people feel heavy, some light, some notice very little at first') so no listener is left out.
