Do not use it to wave away real discomfort; that needs a safety or stop instruction, not reassurance.
examples: If your mind wanders, that's perfectly normal. Minds wander. It doesn't mean this isn't working.
It's natural for the body to twitch or shift a little as it lets go.
Some people feel heavy, some feel light, and some don't notice much the first time. All of that is ordinary.
cues: verdict words applied to a response: 'normal', 'natural', 'perfectly normal', 'ordinary', 'common', 'to be expected'
reassurance clause: 'it doesn't mean anything is wrong', 'it doesn't mean this isn't working', 'nothing unusual'
'it's natural to' or 'it's only natural that' followed by a response
a generic statement such as 'minds wander' followed by reassurance that this is ordinary or harmless
range statements ('some people ..., others ...') closed by a verdict that all of them are fine or ordinary

not_this.why: social proof reports what other people do or feel so the listener will expect or do the same ('most people find their hands get heavy first'); normalizing passes a verdict of normal, natural or nothing-wrong on something the listener might worry about. If the sentence carries that verdict, label normalizing even when it mentions other people; if it only reports what others do, label social proof
a truism is a bare undeniable fact used to build acceptance ('minds wander'); normalizing attaches the reassurance ('so it doesn't mean this isn't working')
myth correction names and rebuts a false belief about hypnosis; normalizing reassures about an experience
permission says the listener is allowed to respond; normalizing says the response is common

evidence.note: Standard in clinical pretalks; reducing fear and raising positive expectancy are known to improve response, and descriptive norms influence behavior, but normalizing phrases themselves have not been tested alone.

entries.name: Everyday trance
entries.summary: Liken trance to absorbed states the listener already knows, such as driving on autopilot or being lost in a book.
entries.definition: The writer names familiar absorbed states (driving a known route without remembering it, losing track of time in a film or book, daydreaming, the moment before sleep) and says trance is the same kind of thing. This normalizes trance specifically, and gives the listener a memory to work from. It is a variant of normalizing because the claim is 'you have already done this many times'.
entries.how_to: Use it in the pretalk or as the first move of a conversational induction. Give two or three examples so at least one fits; describe each with a concrete detail so the listener starts to recall it. Then draw the conclusion: this is the same, you already know how. If you go on to have the listener relive one example in detail, you have moved into revivification. Present it as a comparison, not as settled science; whether these states are the same as hypnosis is disputed.
examples: You've driven a familiar road and arrived with no memory of the last few miles. That was a kind of trance, and you did it without trying.
It's like being so caught up in a film that you forget the room around you. You already know how to do that.
You go through something like this every night in the moments before sleep. This is the same doorway, taken on purpose.
cues: stock examples: driving and missing the exit, lost in a book or film, daydreaming, staring out of a window, just before sleep
'you've done this before', 'you already know how', 'many times a day'
'it's just like', 'the same as', 'a kind of trance'
the phrases 'everyday trance', 'natural state', 'highway hypnosis'
past-experience framing with 'you have' or 'remember a time when' followed by an equation to trance

not_this.why: that induction has the listener relive a past absorbed state in detail until it returns; this only cites such states as a likeness
myth correction rebuts a false belief ('hypnosis is not sleep'); this offers a positive comparison
analogy is the general device of explaining by likeness; this is its specific use to make trance familiar

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: A standard pretalk move; trait absorption correlates modestly with hypnotizability, but whether everyday absorption is the same state as hypnosis is disputed, and the comparison works mainly by lowering fear and raising expectancy.

entries.name: Permission
entries.summary: Explicitly permit a response the listener may be holding back.
entries.definition: Permission addresses a response that is already available but inhibited by politeness, self-consciousness, duty or fear of doing it wrong: letting go, moving, feeling something, not paying attention, enjoying it. The writer says outright that it is allowed. It differs from a permissive suggestion, which is a soft phrasing for introducing a new response, in that permission removes a restraint on one the listener is already close to.
entries.how_to: Identify what this listener is likely to be holding back at this point, and name it plainly: 'it's okay to ...'. Place it just before the response is wanted, or right after normalizing it. Say who is granting it when that matters (the speaker, or the listener to themselves). Permission to do less (not listen, not try, not understand) is often the most useful. It fails when it permits something the listener has no pull toward; then it is only a weak suggestion.
examples: It's okay to stop paying attention to my words. You don't have to follow every one.
You have permission to let your shoulders drop. Nobody needs anything from you right now.
You're allowed to enjoy this. There's nothing you have to do to earn it.
cues: 'it's okay to', 'it's all right to', 'it's fine to'
'you're allowed to', 'you have permission to', 'I give you permission', 'give yourself permission'
an explicit option to release, rest, feel, move, or stop listening without disapproval
'you don't have to' when it grants a specific choice ('you don't have to keep your eyes closed; you can open them'); generic instructions to stop trying or doing belong to not-doing-not-knowing
often follows a normalizing statement

not_this.why: permissive suggestion is the 'you may / you can' phrasing used to offer any response; permission lifts a restraint on a response the listener is holding back
that form says no effort or knowledge is needed so the response feels automatic; permission says the response is allowed
there the listener asks the speaker for permission; here the speaker grants it unasked

evidence.note: Common in clinical and permissive-style scripts; it fits findings that autonomy-supportive wording reduces reactance, but explicit permission statements have not been tested as a separate hypnotic device.

entries.consent_note: Permission can release things the listener was holding back for good reason; permit only what falls inside what they agreed to.

entries.name: Binds and choices
entries.summary: Offer the listener a choice, or restrict the choices on the table, so that the options offered serve the wanted response.
entries.definition: Devices in this family work on the listener's sense of choosing. Either the writer offers alternatives that all contain the target response (double bind and its variants), or the writer claims that only two options exist (false dilemma), or the writer makes the listener pick from a closed list (forced choice). What separates the family from presupposition in general is that a choice is explicitly on the table. Citing a choice the listener already made as proof of wanting the result is a different move and is filed under compliance as you-chose-this.
entries.how_to: Use a double bind when every offered alternative includes the agreed response. Choose illusion of choice for an inconsequential concrete detail, time bind for when the response happens, conscious-unconscious bind when conscious alternatives leave the unconscious response fixed, reverse-set bind for a listener whose opposition is established, and non-sequitur bind for an illogical choice. Use forced choice to require a pick from substantively different options, and false dilemma to claim that only two paths exist. To draw a conclusion from a choice already made, use you-chose-this under compliance. Keep the options acceptable to the listener, and leave the real choice to refuse or stop clear. The family has no nested families.

not_this.why: presupposition builds a claim into any sentence; binds do it specifically through an offered or cited choice
compliance devices build agreement over a series of steps; a bind works within one offer

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975)

evidence.note: Binds are standard in Ericksonian texts and offering choice reduces reactance in experiments, but controlled studies have not shown that bind phrasing produces more hypnotic response than plain suggestion.

entries.consent_note: Binds give the feeling of choice without the substance, so the real choice (to take part at all, and to stop) must be offered plainly somewhere outside the bind.

entries.name: Double bind
entries.summary: Offer two or more alternatives that all lead to the wanted response, so choosing any of them is accepting it.
entries.definition: A double bind is an offer of alternatives in which the target response is common to every option. The listener's attention goes to choosing between the options, and the shared outcome is not put up for decision. Erickson and Rossi separated the bind (a choice between comparable alternatives that the listener makes consciously) from the double bind proper (where the response is assigned to something outside conscious choice); in common practitioner use, and here, the unit covers both and the variants carry the distinctions. It differs from an or-presupposition in that the alternatives are a real offer the listener is expected to take up, not just a clause in passing.
entries.how_to: Decide the response you want, then find a detail of it that does not matter to you: speed, timing, side, manner, which part of the mind does it. Offer that detail as the choice, with 'or' between the options, and make both options easy and pleasant. Place it where the listener is already cooperating, usually late induction through suggestion; early in a pre-talk it reads as a sales trick. Follow it by accepting whichever happens ('that's right') and do not stack several binds in a row, which makes the pattern obvious.
examples: You can drift down slowly, or you can let go all at once. I don't mind which.
Maybe the calm starts in your shoulders, or maybe in your hands. Find out which.
Your eyes may close by themselves, or you may decide to close them. Either is fine.
cues: 'X or Y' where both X and Y entail the same response
'either ... or ...', 'whether ... or ...'
'I don't know if ... or ...', 'I wonder whether ... or ...'
'which', 'which one', 'find out which' applied to a detail of the response
disclaimer of preference after the offer: 'it doesn't matter which', 'whichever you prefer'

not_this.why: a false dilemma offers two different outcomes and hides the others; a double bind offers alternatives that share the target outcome
that lists every possible response including none; a bind offers a short set that all include the target
forced choice requires a pick from substantively different options; a double bind offers alternatives that share the target outcome, whether or not the listener is asked to pick one

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian clinical texts; the presupposition it rests on is well studied, but the claim that binds outperform direct suggestion has no controlled support.

entries.consent_note: The listener is not offered the option of not responding, so use it only for responses they have already agreed to seek.

entries.name: Illusion of choice
entries.summary: Give a free, conscious choice between two concrete options that differ only in a detail that does not matter.
entries.definition: The plainest bind: the listener really does choose, and can say which they chose, but both options are versions of the same act. Erickson and Rossi called this a bind of comparable alternatives and treated it as the simple case, because the choice is made consciously and nothing is assigned to the unconscious. The salesperson's alternative-choice close has the same shape.
entries.how_to: Offer two options that are concrete, equally acceptable and visibly trivial: which hand, which chair, eyes open or closed, this breath or the next. Use it early, in pre-talk and the first lines of induction, where an easy real choice starts cooperation. It fails when one option is plainly worse, or when the listener wanted neither, so do not use it to slip in something they have not agreed to.
examples: Would you like to go into trance sitting up or lying back?
You can rest your hands in your lap or by your sides.
Pick a spot to look at: one on the wall, or one on the ceiling.
cues: 'would you like to ... or ...?', 'do you want to ... or ...?'
two concrete, physical or procedural options joined by 'or' (which hand, which chair, eyes open or closed)
'you can X or Y' where X and Y are both ways of doing the same thing
'whichever is more comfortable', 'whichever you prefer', 'your choice'
question about manner or position placed before the main instruction
nothing later in the script depends on which option was taken

not_this.why: forced choice demands a pick from options that differ in substance and uses the pick as commitment; here the options are equivalent
label time bind when the only thing that varies is when
that is an 'or' inside a sentence that moves on; here the listener is asked to actually choose

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975)

evidence.note: Providing even trivial choice raises motivation and lowers reactance in experiments; that the hypnotic form increases response to the underlying suggestion is untested.

entries.consent_note: The choice offered is real but small; it does not stand in for asking whether the listener wants the session.

entries.name: Conscious-unconscious double bind
entries.summary: Split the listener into conscious and unconscious mind and give each a job, so the response happens whatever the conscious mind does.
entries.definition: A double bind whose alternatives are assigned to two parts of the mind. Whatever the conscious mind does (listens, wanders, doubts, forgets) is allowed, and the response is given to the unconscious, which the listener cannot inspect or veto. Erickson and Rossi counted it among the double binds proper, because the response is placed outside conscious choice.
entries.how_to: Write two clauses, usually joined by 'while', 'and' or 'or': the first releases the conscious mind from any task, the second states what the unconscious does. Make the conscious half something the listener is probably doing anyway, so it works as pacing. Use it once the idea of an unconscious mind has been introduced, and keep the unconscious task simple and checkable later (a hand lifting, a feeling arriving). It falls flat for listeners who reject the conscious/unconscious model, so introduce that model first or use a time bind instead.
examples: Your conscious mind can listen to my words, or wander off somewhere else, while your unconscious mind takes in everything it needs.
Whether or not you consciously notice it happening, your unconscious has already begun to slow your breathing.
If your unconscious is ready to relax further, one hand will start to feel lighter. If it wants a little longer, the other one will.
cues: two or more options for the conscious mind joined by 'or' ('can listen, or wander') followed by a fixed statement about what the unconscious does
'whether or not you consciously ...' followed by a response assigned to the unconscious in either case
'you may or may not consciously notice/remember' followed by what the unconscious does regardless
paired 'if' branches in which the unconscious produces or directs a response in both branches
'it doesn't matter whether your conscious mind X or Y' followed by a fixed unconscious response

not_this.why: the split addresses the unconscious as a separate listener and offers no alternatives; label the bind only when the span states alternatives ('or', 'whether or not', paired 'if' branches) and the response is assigned to the unconscious in all of them. A plain 'your conscious mind can wander while your unconscious listens' is the split
that only releases the listener from effort; the bind also assigns the response to the unconscious
an implied directive adds a time clause and a signal that the inner response has happened; it can contain this bind

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975)

evidence.note: A staple of Ericksonian texts; the 'unconscious mind' it addresses is a working metaphor, and no controlled study shows the bind itself adds to response beyond the expectancy it sets.

entries.consent_note: It tells the listener the response is outside their conscious say, so pair it with a clear statement elsewhere that they can stop at any time.

entries.name: Time bind
entries.summary: Offer a choice only about when the response happens, never whether.
entries.definition: A double bind whose alternatives are points or spans of time. Every option is a time at which the response occurs, so the only open question is its timing. It is the easiest bind to write and the hardest to fail, because one of the offered times always arrives.
entries.how_to: Name two or three times for the response: now or in a moment, on this breath or the next, before I finish counting or after. Include a slow option so that a listener who has not responded yet is still inside the suggestion. It suits eye closure, deepening and posthypnotic responses. Keep the window short enough that the listener notices the response within it; 'today or sometime this week' is too loose to feel like anything.
examples: Your eyes can close now, or in a few more breaths.
I don't know whether you'll feel that calm settle in before I reach one, or just after.
You might notice the change tonight, or it might be tomorrow morning.
cues: 'now or in a moment', 'now or later', 'right away or in a little while'
'on this breath or the next'
'before ... or after ...' with the same response in both
'I don't know whether ... now or ...', 'I wonder if it will be ... or ...' naming two or more times
'today or tomorrow', 'tonight or in the morning' attached to a stated response
two or more named times or counts joined by 'or', with no option in which the response does not occur

not_this.why: a time clause ('before you go deeper') presupposes the response with no choice offered; a time bind offers alternative times
that hands over the timing of waking as a courtesy, not as a way to secure a response
label illusion of choice when the options differ in manner or place, not time

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson and Ernest L. Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1975)

evidence.note: Described in Ericksonian texts and widely used; no controlled comparison with a plain timed suggestion exists.

entries.consent_note: When the response is one that lasts past the session, the bind removes 'never' as an option, so the listener should have agreed to that response beforehand.

entries.name: Non-sequitur double bind
entries.summary: Offer alternatives that have no logical connection to each other or to the outcome, in the grammar of a real choice.
entries.definition: A double bind in which the options sound alike in content but do not follow from one another, or the link between option and outcome is absent. The sentence has the form of a choice or a conditional, so the listener starts working out the logic, finds none, and is left with the one thing both halves share: the response. It combines a bind with a small dose of confusion.
entries.how_to: Keep the grammar clean and the delivery matter-of-fact; the illogic must be in the content only. Both halves should mention or lead to the same response in similar words. Use it sparingly, with listeners who over-analyze or as a light confusion beat before a direct suggestion, and follow it at once with a plain instruction. Used on someone who is simply listening it is noise, and several in a row sound like a mistake.
examples: Do you want to settle into that chair before you relax, or relax while you settle into that chair?
You can go into trance with your eyes closed, or close your eyes as you go into trance.
Will your left hand feel lighter while the chair remembers your name, or will the chair remember your name while your left hand feels lighter? Now, notice that hand.
cues: 'or' joining two clauses that restate each other with the order of terms swapped
'either ... or ...' or 'would you rather ... or ...' where the second option shares words with the first but is not an alternative to it
same response word in both halves of an offered choice
question form that cannot be answered by picking a side
plain direct instruction immediately after an illogical choice

not_this.why: a non sequitur is any irrelevant statement used to confuse; label the bind only when it is framed as alternatives that share an outcome
confusion technique is sustained disorientation over a passage; this is a single choice-shaped sentence
chiasmus is the ABBA word order as style; here the reversal is offered as a choice between two things

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson and Ernest L. Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1975)

evidence.note: Named and illustrated by Erickson and Rossi from case material; it has not been studied on its own, and its effect cannot be separated from ordinary confusion.

entries.consent_note: It works by the listener failing to track the logic, so it belongs only in sessions where confusion methods were agreed to or are expected.

entries.name: Reverse-set double bind
entries.summary: Phrase the bind so that a listener who does the opposite of what is said ends up giving the wanted response.
entries.definition: A double bind built for a listener who is in the habit of opposing. The writer forbids, doubts or delays the wanted response, so that defying the writer means producing it, while obeying the writer is also acceptable (usually it just postpones it). In Erickson's version a run of statements first establishes the habit of contradicting, and the key statement is then delivered in reversed form.
entries.how_to: Use it only where opposition is real or expected: a listener who says 'that won't work on me', or a script that has invited resistance. State the wanted response as something they will not, cannot or should not do yet, and make the compliant reading harmless: 'you won't go under until you're ready' is fine whether they wait or not. Do not use it on a cooperative listener, who will simply do what the words say and hold back. It is weaker in recordings, where you cannot see whether the listener is opposing.
examples: You won't go all the way down until you're completely sure you want to.
You're not comfortable yet. You don't want to close your eyes. And you certainly can't go into trance sitting in that chair.
You probably can't let your eyes close yet, and that's fine. They can stay open and get heavier, or close anyway.
cues: 'you won't ... until ...' where the text also offers a route to the wanted response after the wait
a negated or doubted wanted response paired with explicit alternatives that both lead toward it: 'stay open and grow heavier, or close anyway'
'either way' after the two reactions, followed by the shared wanted response
a run of negative statements that visibly establishes the listener's contradiction before the wanted response is stated in reverse form
'I doubt you can ... yet' followed by an explicit account of what happens if the listener waits and if they prove the speaker wrong

not_this.why: a bare opposite instruction pays off if defied; label a reverse-set bind when the text establishes a pattern of the listener contradicting the speaker and then reverses the wanted response, or when it explicitly gives both compliance and defiance paths to the wanted response. An 'until' clause alone only postpones it
that names the response under a negation; it can co-occur, but negation alone does not establish opposition or a bind
a challenge invites an attempt expected to fail as proof; this uses established opposition or explicitly covers both reactions

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson and Ernest L. Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1975)

evidence.note: Rests on Erickson's case reports; reactance, the tendency it exploits, is well established, but the bind itself has not been tested and depends on correctly judging that the listener is opposing.

entries.consent_note: It turns the listener's refusal into the response, so it must not be used to override an actual wish to stop; a real 'no' ends the session.

entries.name: False dilemma
entries.summary: Present two options as the only ones, when others exist, so that rejecting one means taking the other.
entries.definition: A false dilemma narrows a situation to two outcomes that really are different, and leaves out the rest. Usually one option is made unattractive so the other wins by elimination. Unlike a double bind, the two options do not lead to the same place: the device works by what is hidden, not by what is shared.
entries.how_to: State the two options in strong, parallel terms and make the contrast feel complete: hold on or let go, think or feel, the old way or this one. Put it at a decision point, in pre-talk or just before a key suggestion, and let the listener reject the bad option themselves. It lands when the missing middle is not obvious and fails the moment the listener thinks of a third option, so it suits absorbed listeners and short passages. In copy it is an argument; say less and move on.
examples: You can keep carrying all that tension, or you can put it down. There isn't a third thing.
Either you're thinking, or you're relaxing. You can't do both.
There are two kinds of listeners: the ones who analyze every word, and the ones who let it work.
cues: 'either ... or ...' with two different outcomes, one clearly worse
'there are only two ...', 'two kinds of ...', 'you have two choices'
'you can't do both', 'there is no middle', 'no third option'
'if you're not X, you're Y'
'the only alternative is ...', 'it's this or ...'

not_this.why: in a double bind both options give the same outcome; here they differ and the other possibilities are hidden
antithesis sets two opposed ideas side by side for style without claiming they are the only options
forced choice asks the listener to pick; a false dilemma is a claim about what options exist and may ask for nothing

evidence.note: A long-catalogued informal fallacy; framing research shows that restricting the options offered shapes choices, but the figure as such is described, not measured.

entries.consent_note: It works by the listener not noticing the omitted options; do not use it to frame stopping or leaving as one of two bad choices.

entries.name: Forced choice
entries.summary: Make the listener pick one of a closed list of substantively different options the writer supplies, aloud or inwardly.
entries.definition: A forced choice is a demand to select one of a closed set of options, with a pause for the listener to do it. The options differ in substance, and the act of choosing is the point: the listener has done something and now owns the result. It differs from a double bind in that the options need not lead to the same place, and from a false dilemma in that the listener is made to answer.
entries.how_to: Give two or three clearly worded options, tell the listener to choose, and leave a real pause. Say how to answer: aloud, with a nod, or silently. Then refer back to the choice as theirs and carry on from it; in branching scripts each option leads to its own section, in linear ones the follow-up must fit any pick. It fails without the pause, with more than three options, or when the options are so alike that choosing means nothing. For a detail that does not matter, use illusion of choice instead.
examples: Choose now: do you want to go deeper, or stay right where you are? Say it in your mind.
Three doors. Rest, focus, or confidence. Pick one, and only one.
Calm or energy: which do you want from tonight? Nod once for calm, twice for energy. ... Good.
cues: imperatives of choosing: 'choose', 'pick', 'decide', 'select'
'which do you choose?', 'which is it?', 'which one?'
an enumerated or lettered list of options followed by a pause marker
'only one', 'you have to pick', 'you can't have both'
instruction on how to answer: 'say it aloud', 'nod', 'answer in your mind'

not_this.why: there the options are equivalent ways to do the same thing; here they differ in substance and the listener is required to select one
that is the later reference back to a choice as proof of wanting ('you chose this'); forced choice covers only the options and the demand to pick
that asks for a yes to one proposal; forced choice asks for a selection among several
a consent check offers stopping as a real, unpenalized option; a forced choice restricts the listener to the writer's list

evidence.note: Choosing among options reliably raises liking for and commitment to the chosen one in laboratory studies; whether a silent choice made while listening to a script has the same effect has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: If none of the listed options is acceptable the listener has no stated way out, so a session using it should offer a real exit elsewhere and must not treat a forced pick as consent.

entries.name: Confusion and overload
entries.summary: Devices that disrupt, saturate or starve orderly thinking so the next clear instruction is taken as relief.
entries.definition: A family of devices that interfere with the listener's running evaluation of what is said. Some break meaning (confusion technique, paradox, non sequitur), some break sequence (pattern interrupt, shock, unfinished sentence), some exceed capacity (cognitive overload, concurrent task, rapid delivery), and some under-feed attention until it lapses (monotony). What unites them is the second half: a plain, easy suggestion placed at the moment of disruption. Without that follow-up the listener is only confused or annoyed.
entries.how_to: Choose by what you want to disturb. To break meaning, use confusion-technique or one of its variants, paradox for a single contradiction, or semantic-satiation to wear one word down to sound; to break an expected sequence, use pattern-interrupt, shock-surprise or incomplete-sentence; to exceed or divert capacity, use cognitive-overload, dual-task, distraction-of-conscious-mind or fast-speech; to let vigilance run down, use boredom-monotony. Write the clear instruction that follows, and keep the disruption short enough that the listener can still follow it. The induction family holds the full-induction forms (confusion-induction, overload-induction, rapid-induction, double-induction); disrupt-then-reframe in the compliance family is the sales-research version.

not_this.why: vagueness leaves content open for the listener to fill in; this family blocks or overworks the filling-in
resistance handling addresses doubt by naming or using it; this family goes around evaluation without addressing it
absorption narrows attention onto one thing; this family splits, jams or drains it

origin.source: Erickson, 'The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964)

evidence.note: Distraction and disruption reduce counterarguing in persuasion experiments, but most hypnotic confusion methods rest on clinical report, and none has been shown to beat a plain induction.

entries.consent_note: These devices work by reducing the listener's ability to evaluate what follows, so what follows should be something the listener agreed to beforehand.

entries.name: Confusion technique
entries.summary: Say something grammatical but hard to resolve, then give one simple suggestion the listener can take as a way out.
entries.definition: Wording that sounds as if it should make sense but resists being worked out, followed at once by a clear, easy suggestion. The confusion can be a passage or a brief non sequitur. It is built from ordinary words and correct-seeming grammar, so the listener may keep trying to follow. It differs from cognitive overload, which adds more to track, and from paradox, which presents a contradiction: here the meaning keeps slipping.
entries.how_to: Start from true, simple statements so the listener commits to following, then tangle one dimension (time, direction, negation, sound-alikes) for two to five sentences. Deliver it seriously and at an even pace, as if it were perfectly clear. End with a short, plain suggestion in a different rhythm: this is the part that matters. It fails when it is so obviously nonsense that the listener stops trying, or when no clear suggestion follows.
examples: You can know that you don't know what you already knew before you knew you were relaxing, and you don't need to know. Just let go.
Part of you is listening to the part that isn't listening, and it doesn't matter which part is which. Close your eyes.
The thought you were about to think is not the thought you think it was, and as it slips away, you can simply rest.
cues: one word repeated in shifting senses within a sentence (know, think, part, right)
long sentence with nested clauses that does not resolve to a clear claim
short plain imperative directly after a dense passage
'it doesn't matter', 'you don't need to work it out', 'just let ...' closing the passage
mixed tenses, directions or negations in one sentence

not_this.why: overload is too much to track; confusion is content that will not resolve
that is a whole induction built on this device; this is the device wherever it appears
that is one odd phrase plus a reframe in a request; this is a sustained passage plus a suggestion

origin.source: Erickson, 'The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian texts and supported by case reports; controlled comparisons with plain inductions are few and do not show an advantage.

entries.consent_note: It works by making the following suggestion harder to weigh, so use it only to deliver what the listener came for.

entries.name: Time confusion
entries.summary: Tangle past, present and future references until the listener stops tracking when 'now' is.
entries.definition: A confusion passage built from time words: days, tenses and before/after relations are stacked so each clause is true but the whole cannot be held. It is the confusion technique with time as the tangled dimension. It differs from time distortion, which plainly suggests that time feels slow or fast, and from temporal presupposition, which uses one clear time clause.
entries.how_to: Begin with an obvious truth about today, then restate it from the viewpoint of yesterday and tomorrow, shifting tense each clause. Keep every clause defensible; the listener should feel that it would make sense with enough effort. Close with a present-tense suggestion, or use the loosened sense of time to lead into regression or future progression.
examples: Today is the tomorrow you thought about yesterday, and tomorrow, today will be the yesterday you can hardly remember. So right now is the only time to relax.
Before you had started, you had not yet finished what you will have begun later, and by then it won't matter when it was.
Last week's next week is this week, and next week this week will be last week, and all that time you can go on resting.
cues: 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' (or last/this/next) recombined in one sentence
three or more tense shifts in one sentence
future perfect and past perfect close together ('will have', 'had not yet')
'before ... after ... before' stacked
ends by resolving to 'now' or 'right now'

not_this.why: that states that time stretches or shrinks; this scrambles time references without claiming anything
one clear time clause that presupposes; nothing is tangled
regression sends the listener to a specific earlier time; time confusion may precede it but is only the scrambling

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson, The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964)

evidence.note: Described by Erickson as a lead-in to regression; known from case reports, not controlled tests.

entries.name: Left-right confusion
entries.summary: Tangle left and right, here and there, this and that until the listener stops tracking which is which.
entries.definition: A confusion passage built from direction and pointing words. It leans on the two meanings of 'right' and 'left' (direction; correct; remaining) and on words whose reference shifts with viewpoint. It is the confusion technique with space or the body as the tangled dimension, and it often feeds straight into a hand or arm suggestion.
entries.how_to: Direct attention to the hands first so the listener has something to track. Then swap the labels quickly, using 'right' as correct and 'left' as remaining alongside their directional senses. Finish with a simple physical suggestion (one hand lifts, both rest, eyes close). In audio the listener cannot re-read, so two or three sentences are enough; in text, readers can parse it, so keep it moving.
examples: Your right hand is the one that's left when the left hand isn't right, and that's right, isn't it? Let whichever one is left grow heavy.
What's here for you is there for me, and what's there is here once you go there, so wherever here is, settle into it.
This hand, not that hand, unless that one is this one, can start to feel lighter now.
cues: 'right' and 'left' several times in one sentence, in more than one sense
'here' and 'there', or 'this' and 'that', swapped within a sentence
'that's right' placed inside a left/right passage
'whichever', 'the one that's left', 'the other one'
followed by a hand, arm or eye suggestion

not_this.why: wordplay loops on any sound-alike; this is specifically direction and place words
that pairs two opposed experiences clearly (one rises, one sinks); here the labels are scrambled
a single pun that serves the suggestion, not a pile-up meant to confuse

evidence.note: A common worked example in Ericksonian and NLP training; no controlled tests of the variant itself.

entries.name: Stacked negation
entries.summary: Stack two or more negations in a sentence so the listener has to work out what is actually being said.
entries.definition: A sentence with two, three or more negatives whose net meaning takes effort to compute. The usual net meaning is the suggestion itself, so the listener either works it out and arrives at the suggestion or gives up and takes the named response. It differs from negative suggestion, which uses one negation to name a response.
entries.how_to: Decide the net meaning first, then wrap it in negatives: 'can't not', 'don't have to not', 'never fail to'. Two negatives read as emphasis; three or more start to confuse. Use one or two such sentences and follow with a positive, simple statement of the same suggestion. Check the arithmetic, because an odd count reverses the meaning.
examples: You can't not notice that you don't have to not relax.
There's no reason you shouldn't fail to stay tense, and nothing you need to not do about it. So let the shoulders drop.
You don't have to not listen, and you can't fail to not hold on. So let go.
cues: 'can't not', 'won't not', 'don't not'
three or more of not / n't / never / no / nothing / un- in one sentence
negated failure verbs: 'never fail to', 'not unable to', 'can't avoid not'
'no reason you shouldn't', 'nothing you need to not do'
plain positive restatement in the next sentence

not_this.why: one negation that names the response; meaning is clear
a clear instruction to do the opposite, not a meaning that must be computed
a clear statement that no effort is needed; negation is not stacked

evidence.note: Negated sentences are reliably slower to process and more error-prone; that this helps a suggestion land is practitioner claim.

entries.name: Non sequitur
entries.summary: Drop an irrelevant or illogical statement into the flow, delivered as if it belonged there.
entries.definition: A statement that has no connection to what came before, or that draws a conclusion that does not follow, spoken in the same tone as the rest. The listener searches for the link and finds none. It is a confusion device made of one sentence, where the main confusion technique is a sustained passage.
entries.how_to: Place it mid-passage, between two normal sentences, and do not mark it with a pause or a change of voice. Make it grammatical and concrete, not random word salad. Follow it immediately with a clear suggestion, while the listener is still looking for the connection. One per passage is usually enough; several in a row become comedy.
examples: Your breathing is slowing, and the chairs in a waiting room are always the same colour, so you can let your eyes close.
Because Tuesday comes after rain, your shoulders already know how to drop.
You're doing well. A door only has two sides. Now go deeper.
cues: sentence with no topical link to its neighbours
'so', 'because', 'which means' joining unrelated clauses
concrete everyday fact (weather, furniture, weekdays) inside a trance passage
imperative or suggestion directly after the odd sentence
no acknowledgement that anything odd was said

not_this.why: a bind offers two unlinked alternatives as a choice; this is a statement, not a choice
a causal link the listener can accept as plausible; a non sequitur is meant not to connect
shock relies on suddenness or intensity; a non sequitur is flat and only fails to follow

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson, The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964)

evidence.note: Erickson described out-of-context remarks as a core of his confusion method; the nearest controlled work is on disrupt-then-reframe, a sales setting.

entries.name: Circular wordplay
entries.summary: Loop the same word and its sound-alikes through a sentence until the listener loses track of which sense is meant.
entries.definition: A confusion passage built by repeating one word, its other senses and its homophones (know/no, here/hear, mind as noun and verb, right/write) in a circular sentence. The device is the pile-up: each use alone is clear. It differs from a single sound-alike ambiguity or pun, which carries a second meaning without trying to confuse.
entries.how_to: Pick a word that has a homophone or works as both noun and verb, and that suits the suggestion (know, mind, hear, feel, right). Write one or two sentences that return to it five or more times, changing sense each time. It is strongest heard, since spelling disambiguates homophones on the page. End on a short clear line.
examples: You know there's no need to know what you know, and no one knows that better than you. So let it go.
You can mind your mind, or never mind your mind, and your mind won't mind either way.
Hear what's here, and here is where you hear it, and you don't have to be anywhere but here.
cues: one word or homophone pair five or more times in one or two sentences
know/no, here/hear, right/write, mind (noun)/mind (verb), there/their
sentence that ends on the word it began with
same word as noun and verb in one clause
release line after the loop ('let it go', 'never mind')

not_this.why: when the looped words are direction or pointing words (right, left, here, there, this, that) used about the body or the room, label left-right confusion; label this for any other looped word
the same word in the same sense repeated back to back until it is only sound; here the word changes sense or spelling at each return and sits in a grammatical sentence
one sound-alike carrying a hidden instruction, not a loop built to confuse
a single pun where both senses serve the suggestion

evidence.note: Widely taught in Ericksonian and NLP training; no independent test of its effect.

entries.name: Pattern interrupt
entries.summary: Start an automatic sequence the listener knows by heart, break it midway, and give an instruction in the gap.
entries.definition: A familiar, automatic sequence (a handshake, a count, a stock phrase, a breathing rhythm the script has set up) is stopped before its expected next step. For a moment the listener has no prepared response, and a suggestion placed there meets less evaluation. It differs from shock, which needs no established pattern, and from an unfinished sentence, which is left hanging with no instruction replacing the missing part.
entries.how_to: The pattern must be automatic before you break it: use one the listener already has (counting, the alphabet, a common saying) or build one by repeating it several times in the script. Break it at the point of strongest expectation and put the instruction immediately after, with no pause to explain. In recorded audio the physical forms are unavailable, so interrupt counts, rhythms, refrains and sentence frames. It fails when the pattern was not established or when the instruction comes late.
examples: Five... four... three... sleep.
Breathe in... and out. In... and out. In... and hold it. Now drop.
A, B, C, D, and you've already stopped thinking about the next letter. Rest.
cues: a count, list or alphabet that stops before its end
a repeated frame or refrain broken on its fourth or later repetition
'sleep', 'drop', 'stop', 'now' at the break point
a stock saying cut off and replaced by an instruction
stage direction for a sudden stop or change mid-sequence

not_this.why: shock needs no prior pattern; an interrupt depends on one being under way
that leaves the gap open for the listener; here the gap is filled with an instruction
that is an induction that uses an interrupt plus a sleep command; this is the interrupt wherever it occurs

evidence.note: Unexpected events do capture attention and briefly halt ongoing action; that this opens a window of raised suggestibility is practitioner claim, not an established finding.

entries.consent_note: It is built to land an instruction before the listener can weigh it, so the instruction should be one they have already agreed to receive.

entries.name: Cognitive overload
entries.summary: Give the listener more things to track at once than they can hold, so they stop tracking and just follow.
entries.definition: Several simultaneous demands on attention: multiple sensations to monitor, a task to perform, more than one voice or stream. Each item is clear by itself; the quantity is what defeats tracking. It differs from the confusion technique, where a single stream will not make sense, and from sensory immersion, where many details build one coherent scene.
entries.how_to: Add items one at a time and tell the listener to keep all of them going: this breath, that hand, a sound, a count. Four or five concurrent items is usually past what people hold. Then offer the release, either by giving one simple thing to do or by permitting them to let everything go. Unlike confusion, this works on listeners who would dismiss nonsense, because every instruction is reasonable.
examples: Keep feeling your left foot, and the air at your nostrils, and count your breaths, and listen to the sounds outside the room, and notice your right thumb, all at once.
Hold the number in mind, keep following my voice, feel both hands, and watch the colour behind your eyelids. When it's too much, let all of it go.
Track the breath, the heartbeat, the weight of your legs and every third word I say. Or just stop keeping track.
cues: 'at the same time', 'all at once', 'while also', 'and keep ...'
list of four or more concurrent objects of attention
'keep track of', 'hold in mind', 'don't lose'
release line: 'let it all go', 'too much to follow', 'stop keeping track'
stage direction for two voices or streams at once

not_this.why: confusion is one stream that will not resolve; overload is many clear streams
that is a full induction built on overload; this is the device at any point in a script
dense detail that builds one scene to absorb the listener, not competing items to track

evidence.note: Working-memory limits and reduced counterarguing under load are well established; overload as a way to produce hypnotic response has not been independently tested, and Miller's 'seven plus or minus two' is routinely over-applied.

entries.consent_note: Suggestions given under load are harder for the listener to assess, so keep them within what was agreed.

entries.name: Shock / surprise
entries.summary: Insert one sudden, unexpected word, sound or claim, and place a suggestion right after it.
entries.definition: A single unexpected event: a sharp sound, a sudden change of volume, or a statement the listener did not see coming. It needs no pattern set up beforehand, which separates it from the pattern interrupt. It is brief and intense, which separates it from the non sequitur, whose oddness is flat.
entries.how_to: Set a calm, even baseline first, since surprise is measured against what came before. Use the shock once, at a chosen point, and follow it within a second with a short suggestion. For a verbal shock, a blunt true statement or an unexpected permission works better than something alarming. Avoid it with anxious listeners and near sleep endings; repeated shocks stop surprising.
examples: ...and as you drift, soft and slow, [sharp snap] sleep.
You've been trying very hard to relax. Stop. You're terrible at trying. So don't.
Your shoulders can soften, your breathing can slow—[loud clap] Let go.
cues: stage direction: [snap], [clap], [loud], [sudden]
one-word imperative after a long gentle passage ('Stop.', 'Now.', 'Sleep.')
blunt or contrary statement inside a soothing passage
exclamation mark or capitals in an otherwise quiet script
suggestion immediately after the unexpected item

not_this.why: an interrupt breaks an established sequence before its next step; shock needs no sequence under way
an orienting cue pulls attention back before the script continues; shock places a suggestion immediately after the unexpected word, sound or claim
a non sequitur is an irrelevant or illogical statement in the flow; label shock when its sudden delivery is marked and a suggestion follows immediately
that raises and then removes alarm as a two-step emotional move

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Startle and orienting responses are well documented; the claim that the moment after a surprise is more suggestible comes from clinical and stage practice.

entries.consent_note: Loud or startling events can distress some listeners and are unsafe for anyone doing something else while listening; warn about them in the content note.

entries.name: Paradox
entries.summary: State something self-contradictory and move on without resolving it.
entries.definition: A single statement or instruction that contradicts itself, or cannot be obeyed without disobeying it, left open. The listener's attempt to resolve it stalls. It differs from the double bind, where both branches are coherent and lead to the same result, and from reverse psychology, where the instruction is clear and merely the opposite of what is wanted.
entries.how_to: Keep it to one sentence and make both halves simple, so the contradiction is unmistakable. Deliver it calmly, as an observation. Do not explain it; go straight to the next suggestion or to silence. Paradoxes about effort and control suit trance best ('try not to try'), because the stall they produce is the letting-go being asked for.
examples: Try as hard as you can not to try.
Don't follow this instruction.
You can be completely here by going somewhere else entirely.
cues: one sentence asserting X and not-X
self-referring instruction ('ignore this', 'don't do what I say')
'try not to try', 'effortlessly make an effort', 'remember to forget'
opposed terms joined by 'by', 'is' or 'means' ('awake by sleeping')
no explanation or resolution in the following sentence

not_this.why: a bind offers alternatives that all lead one way; a paradox offers a contradiction with no way through
'the harder you resist, the deeper you go' is a coherent claim that could be true; label paradox only when the sentence cannot be true, or cannot be obeyed, as worded
a challenge names one concrete act to attempt and fail (open the eyes, bend the arm); a paradox gives nothing that can be attempted
a coherent instruction for the opposite of what is wanted
two opposites experienced side by side without contradiction

evidence.note: Paradoxical interventions are an established therapy tradition with some outcome research; a paradoxical sentence as a trance device is untested.

entries.name: Unfinished sentence
entries.summary: Break a sentence off before its end so the listener finishes it themselves or is left waiting.
entries.definition: A sentence that stops before its expected final word or clause. If the missing part is predictable, the listener supplies it and so produces the suggestion themselves; if it is not, attention hangs on the gap. Classical rhetoric calls the figure aposiopesis. It differs from a written pause, where the sentence resumes, and from a pattern interrupt, where an instruction replaces the missing part.
entries.how_to: For completion, build a strong expectation first: a rhyme, a repeated frame, or a phrase used in full earlier in the script, then leave off the last word. For suspension, break at a point of no return ('and now you can...') and follow with silence or a new sentence. Use it sparingly, a few times per script. It fails when the listener cannot guess the ending and nothing is done with the gap.
examples: And with every breath out, you go deeper and...
Down, and down, and all the way...
You already know what happens when I count to...
cues: sentence ending in an ellipsis or dash with the grammar incomplete
final word missing from a phrase given in full earlier
line ending on 'and', 'to', 'the', 'so', 'because', 'you can'
next sentence starts a new thought and does not resume
stage direction for a pause or silence after the break

not_this.why: a pause inside a sentence that then continues to its end
the break is filled at once with an instruction
an argument with a missing premise; the sentences themselves are complete
a complete promise or question whose answer is delayed for minutes, not a broken sentence

evidence.note: A classical figure; self-generated material is better remembered than supplied material, but the hypnotic use is untested and the Zeigarnik effect it is often credited to has a mixed replication record.

entries.name: Monotony
entries.summary: Keep the delivery deliberately flat, repetitive and uneventful until the listener stops watching for anything new.
entries.definition: A sustained stretch in which nothing new happens: same rhythm, same sentence shape, same small set of words, low stakes. With nothing to evaluate, vigilance lapses and attention drifts inward. It works by under-feeding attention where the rest of this family over-feeds or jams it. It differs from repetition used to drive in one suggestion, where the repeated content is the point.
entries.how_to: Write long runs of near-identical sentences about something neutral and true (breathing, the chair, the count), with no jokes, questions or new images. Ask for an even voice and steady pace. Let it run longer than feels comfortable to write; a few sentences are not monotony. Then place suggestions once responsiveness has dropped, or let it carry into a sleep ending. It fails with listeners who came for intensity and switch off.
examples: And the breath goes in. And the breath goes out. And the breath goes in. And the breath goes out. And nothing else needs to happen.
The next number is forty-one. Nothing happens on forty-one. The next number is forty. Nothing happens on forty.
[flat, even] The same chair. The same room. The same slow voice saying the same slow thing.
cues: five or more consecutive sentences with the same structure and near-identical words
neutral, low-information content (breath, counting, 'the same')
'nothing to do', 'nothing happens', 'nothing new'
stage directions: [monotone], [flat], [even], [droning]
long passage with no questions, images or new vocabulary

not_this.why: repeats one suggestion or mantra to absorb the listener; here the content is deliberately uneventful
repeats depth words to deepen trance, rather than keeping the delivery uneventful
repeats one word until it loses meaning; monotony uses sustained, uneventful phrasing or delivery
repeats a sentence shape while varying the content; monotony requires sustained sameness of content or delivery as well
outlasts active resistance by length; monotony keeps the material uneventful

evidence.note: Monotonous stimulation reliably lowers alertness and induces drowsiness; drowsiness is not the same as hypnotic responsiveness, and research finds relaxation is not required for hypnosis.

entries.name: Occupying the conscious mind
aliases: give the conscious mind a job
entries.summary: Hand the listener's analytical attention a harmless job and say that the rest of them can go on responding.
entries.definition: An explicit assignment of something for the 'conscious mind' to attend to or think about (watch a spot, follow the breath, wonder about a question, analyse the voice) so that it is not monitoring the suggestions. The job is a decoy and its content does not matter. It differs from the concurrent task in that the job need not be a procedure and is usually named as the conscious mind's share; it differs from the conscious/unconscious split, which only addresses the two separately.
entries.how_to: Name the job and give permission to do it fully: 'let your thinking mind keep busy with...'. Choose something mildly interesting and endless, not something that can be finished in ten seconds. Then address the suggestions elsewhere, to the body or 'the rest of you', without asking the listener to stop the job. It suits analytical listeners because it gives analysis a place to go without asking them to stop it.
examples: Let your thinking mind keep busy working out exactly how I'm doing this, while the rest of you gets on with relaxing.
Your conscious mind can follow the sounds in the room, every one of them, and it doesn't need to follow me.
Give the part of you that analyses a job: have it watch the breath and report nothing.
cues: 'your conscious mind can ...', 'let your thinking mind ...' followed by a named activity
'keep busy with', 'give it a job', 'occupy itself', 'something to do'
the assigned activity is open-ended attending or wondering (follow the sounds, watch the breath, work out how this is done)
'while the rest of you ...' directly after the assignment
the assigned focus is not mentioned again in the suggestions that follow

not_this.why: if the job is a procedure that can be done right or wrong (count by threes, spell backward, tap on a word), label the concurrent task; label this when the job is open-ended attending or thinking
label the split wherever the unconscious is addressed as a second listener; add this label only when the conscious mind is also given a named job, not merely told it may drift or need not attend
the bind offers the conscious mind alternatives ('listen or wander') and says the response happens either way; here one job is assigned and no alternatives are offered
suggests the critic relaxes or steps aside; here it is kept busy

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Distraction reduces counterarguing in persuasion experiments; the picture of a conscious mind kept busy while an unconscious mind receives suggestions is a clinical metaphor, not a demonstrated mechanism.

entries.consent_note: Its stated aim is that the listener stops monitoring what is suggested, so the content of the session should be disclosed and agreed before it starts.

entries.name: Concurrent task
entries.summary: Set a specific ongoing task, such as counting backward, and keep delivering suggestions while the listener does it.
entries.definition: Overload with exactly two streams: one explicit task the listener performs (counting down by sevens, spelling backward, tracking a sound) and the suggestions that continue over it. The task has a definite procedure and can be done right or wrong. That separates it from the looser instruction to occupy the conscious mind, which may only assign something to think about.
entries.how_to: Give a task that is effortful but possible: counting back from 300 by threes, saying the alphabet backward, pressing a finger on every exhale. State that the listener should keep going whatever else they hear. Deliver suggestions in the gaps or over the top. Decide how the task ends: say that losing the place is fine and is a sign of depth, otherwise failing at it becomes a worry.
examples: Start at three hundred and count backward by threes, silently. Keep counting while I talk. You don't need to listen to me at all.
Spell your street name backward, one letter per breath, and let my words pass by in the background.
Tap your finger each time I say the word 'down', and keep doing only that.
cues: 'count backward from', 'by threes', 'by sevens'
'keep counting', 'keep going while I talk', 'whatever else you hear'
'spell ... backward', 'every time you hear ... tap'
a task with a checkable procedure (a count, a spelling, a tally) set before a passage of suggestions
'if you lose your place, that's fine', 'start again from'

not_this.why: that names the purpose and may assign any occupation; this is a specific procedural task running under suggestions
there the counting is the target and is suggested away; here it is a side task that keeps attention busy
the writer counts and ties each number to depth; the listener is not given a competing task

origin.source: Festinger & Maccoby, 'On resistance to persuasive communications', Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology (1964)

evidence.note: A secondary task reduces counterarguing and raises acceptance of weak arguments in persuasion studies; whether it raises response to hypnotic suggestions is not established, and it lowers acceptance of strong arguments.

entries.consent_note: The task exists so that suggestions get less scrutiny; tell the listener beforehand what kind of suggestions the session contains.

entries.name: Semantic satiation
aliases: repeating a word until it is only sound
entries.summary: Repeat one word many times in a row, with nothing between, until it stops meaning anything and is heard as pure sound.
entries.definition: A single word is said, or given to the listener to say, in an unbroken run long enough that its meaning drops away and only the sound is left. The loss of meaning is the aim, and the script usually names it. That aim separates it from immediate repetition as a figure, which uses two to four repeats for emphasis and keeps the sense, and from a mantra, which is repeated so that its meaning sinks in. It disrupts meaning with one word in one sense, where circular wordplay does it by switching senses.
entries.how_to: Choose one short word: either a word whose hold you want to loosen (a worry word, 'think', 'try', 'should') or a neutral one used only to tire the meaning-making. Repeat it bare, at an even pace, for much longer than emphasis would need; lab studies use roughly fifteen to thirty seconds, and a handful of repeats will not do it. Having the listener repeat it, aloud or inwardly, works better than only hearing it. Name the change as it happens ('only a sound now'), then use the gap: give a plain suggestion, go into mind-blanking, or hand the emptied word a new meaning. It fails when other words are mixed into the run, since each one restores the sense.
examples: Say the word 'think' silently, over and over. Think, think, think, think, think, think, think, think, think, think, think, think. Notice it turning into a noise.
Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Worry. Just a sound now, with nothing behind it.
Keep repeating the word 'try' until it no longer sounds like a word at all. Then let it stop.
cues: one word repeated ten or more times consecutively with no other words between
'over and over', 'again and again', 'keep repeating the word' followed by a single quoted word
'until it loses its meaning', 'until it stops making sense', 'no longer sounds like a word'
'just a sound', 'only a noise', 'an empty sound' said of a word
a plain suggestion or a new definition of the same word directly after the run

not_this.why: a few repeats for emphasis, with the meaning kept and strengthened
a phrase repeated so its content is absorbed; satiation repeats to empty the content out
that loops one word through different senses and sound-alikes; this holds one word in one sense until the sense fades

origin.source: Wallace E. Lambert and Leon A. Jakobovits, Verbal Satiation and Changes in the Intensity of Meaning, Journal of Experimental Psychology (1960)

evidence.note: The brief loss of a word's felt meaning after rapid repetition is a replicated laboratory effect that fades within seconds to minutes; its use to open a gap for suggestion or to weaken a troubling word for good is practitioner claim with little direct testing.

entries.name: Attention and absorption
entries.summary: Devices that narrow the listener's attention onto one thing and keep it there.
entries.definition: This family covers the moves that select an object of attention (a voice, a sensation, a scene, a question, the listener's own name) and hold attention on it while everything else drops away. Absorption is the common ground of most accounts of hypnosis, so these devices appear in every stage, not only in the induction. They differ from the induction family in that they are single moves, usable anywhere, and do not by themselves claim that trance has begun. The family has no nested families.
entries.how_to: Choose by what you want attention to rest on. Use voice-focus or narrowing-attention to shut out the room; inward-focus to move from outside to inside; sensory-detail-immersion to hold attention inside a scene; curiosity-hook to hold it across time; direct-address and name-use to keep the listener personally engaged. Use novelty-orienting to recover attention that has drifted, and time-distortion once absorption is established, as a consequence and proof of it. Eye-contact-imagery is a fixation point for scripts with a strong speaker persona or a visual track. One or two of these at a time is enough; stacking all of them reads as noise.

not_this.why: inductions are procedures that start trance; these are single attention moves usable at any stage
that family disrupts attention to create a gap; this one gathers and holds it
deepeners intensify an existing trance; these devices direct where attention goes

evidence.note: Focused attention is part of standard descriptions of hypnosis and trait absorption correlates modestly with hypnotizability; the individual devices are mostly untested one by one.

entries.name: Voice focus
entries.summary: Tell the listener to attend to the speaker's voice and let it be the one thing they follow.
entries.definition: The speaker names their own voice as the object of attention. The voice becomes the fixation point, in the way a spot on the wall is for eye fixation, and it has the advantage of being present for the whole session. It is this entry when the instruction is about where attention goes; it is something else when the voice is said to cause depth or to become the listener's thoughts.
entries.how_to: Place it early, in the first lines of the induction, and return to it whenever the listener may have drifted. Give the voice a job: something to follow, rest on or be carried by. Do not demand effortful concentration; say that the listener need not listen carefully and that the voice will be there anyway. In written scripts, 'my words' takes the place of 'my voice'.
examples: Just listen to the sound of my voice. You don't have to do anything else.
Other sounds may come and go, and my voice stays with you, easy to follow.
Let my voice be the one thing you keep hold of as everything else settles.
cues: 'my voice' as the object of listen, focus, follow, attend
'the sound of my voice'
'only my voice', 'just my voice', 'nothing but my voice'
'my words' used the same way in text scripts
'follow my voice', 'stay with my voice'

not_this.why: there the voice is declared to send the listener deeper; here it is only what attention rests on
that entry claims the voice becomes the listener's own thoughts
that entry restricts a response to this voice and no other; it is about who can evoke the response, not where attention is

evidence.note: A standard element of scripted inductions, including research scales; its separate contribution has not been isolated.

entries.name: Narrowing attention
entries.summary: Suggest that everything except one chosen thing fades into the background.
entries.definition: The writer describes the field of awareness shrinking: the room, sounds, thoughts and concerns recede until one object remains. The defining feature is the subtraction. Other entries name what to attend to; this one says what is going away. It is neutral about whether the remaining object is outside (a voice, a light) or inside (a feeling).
entries.how_to: Name the things that fade, in order from far to near: the building, the room, the chair, stray thoughts. Use gradual verbs (fade, drift, soften, grow distant), not sudden ones. Always say what is left, or attention has nowhere to settle. Add that anything important will still get through, so the listener does not keep watch.
examples: The room around you grows less important, and the sounds outside drift away until only the sound of my voice remains.
Everything else fades to the edges, until there is only this breath and these words.
The street, the house, the chair beneath you all slip further off, and what is left is the one warm point of your own breathing.
cues: 'everything else' followed by fades, drifts away, disappears, falls away, doesn't matter
'nothing else matters', 'nothing but', 'only this'
'the rest of the world', 'the room around you' with a receding verb
'narrow', 'tunnel', 'shrinks down to', 'until there is only'
lists of things that become distant or unimportant

not_this.why: voice focus names the speaker's voice as the object; narrowing attention describes other things fading and can leave any object
mind-blanking suggests thoughts slowing or stopping; narrowing attention sends competing things, including thoughts, to the edge while naming what remains
incorporation keeps distractions and gives them a role; narrowing sends them away
setting doubt aside gives doubts or worries a stated place to wait until later; narrowing lets them recede with everything else

evidence.note: Narrowed attention is part of standard definitions of hypnosis, but suggesting the narrowing has not been tested as a separate ingredient.

entries.name: Turning attention inward
entries.summary: Direct the listener's attention away from the outside world and onto inner sensation, feeling or imagery.
entries.definition: A change of direction: from what is seen and heard in the room to what is felt, imagined or thought inside. It is the hinge between pacing the outer situation and working with inner experience. It is this entry when the text marks the shift itself; a passage that simply stays on one bodily sensation, or tours the body, belongs to other entries.
entries.how_to: Pace two or three outside things first, then turn: 'and as you notice those, you can begin to notice what is happening inside'. Eye closure is the natural moment for it. Give attention a first inner landing place, such as the breath or the weight of the hands, because 'go inside' with no target leaves many listeners unsure what to do. Keep the wording permissive.
examples: Let your attention turn inward now, away from the room and toward how your body feels.
You've been looking outward all day. For a while, you can look inside.
As your eyes close, your awareness comes home, to the quiet space behind them.
cues: 'inside', 'inward', 'within' as the destination of attention, awareness, focus or mind
'go inside', 'turn inward', 'drift inside', 'look inside'
an explicit contrast between outside or the room and inside or within
'away from' an outer thing paired with 'toward' or 'to' an inner one
'inner world', 'inner space' introduced as where attention now goes

not_this.why: that entry stays on one sensation and lets it spread as the induction; this is only the outward-to-inward turn
a body scan moves attention region by region; this is a single change of direction
dissociation places the listener outside their experience watching it; inward focus places them inside it

evidence.note: Standard in clinical and Ericksonian texts as a step in induction; no controlled test of the turn as a separate device.

entries.name: Sensory immersion
entries.summary: Describe a scene or sensation in dense detail across several senses so it takes over attention.
entries.definition: A passage of concentrated description that engages sight, sound, touch and often temperature, smell or taste in close succession. What makes it this entry is density and spread: several senses, several details each, in one stretch, with the purpose of displacing awareness of the real surroundings. A single sensory adjective is sensory language, not immersion.
entries.how_to: Use it where the listener must be somewhere else: the start of an imagery passage, or a deepener. Cover at least three senses, and prefer small specific details (the grain of a wooden rail under the hand) over general ones (a beautiful garden). Present tense and second person keep it close. Leave some details open ('whatever colour the light is for you') so the listener's own image is not contradicted, and stop before the passage becomes an inventory.
examples: Warm sand gives under your feet. You hear the long hush of each wave, and the air tastes faintly of salt.
The blanket is heavy and soft across your legs, the room dim and amber, and somewhere a clock ticks slowly.
Feel the cool rail under your palm, see the lamplight on each stair, hear your own steps, unhurried.
cues: three or more sensory modalities within a few sentences
runs of perception verbs: see, hear, feel, smell, taste
concrete nouns with texture, temperature, colour, weight or sound modifiers
second person, present tense description with little or no instruction
'notice the', 'feel the', 'hear the' repeated with different objects

not_this.why: sensory language is a concrete phrasing choice within a suggestion; immersion is a dense passage engaging several senses
sensory overlap leads from an active sense into another through a shared feature; immersion is a dense multi-sense passage, which may also contain that transition
guided imagery leads through an imagined scene step by step; immersion is the density of sensory description, with or without movement
story absorption depends on story events and characters; immersion needs no plot

evidence.note: Vivid multi-sense imagery is standard in clinical scripts and imagery vividness relates to absorption; the claim that more detail is always better is not supported, and over-specified detail can clash with the listener's own image.

entries.name: Curiosity hook
entries.summary: Raise a question or promise something early, then delay the answer so the listener keeps attending.
entries.definition: The writer points at a piece of information the listener does not yet have and withholds it. The gap between what is known and what has been promised holds attention until it is closed. It is one move: open and delay. When several stories are opened and closed in reverse order with suggestions in the middle, that is nested loops.
entries.how_to: Open it in the pre-talk or the first lines: say there is something to discover, without saying what. Make the gap specific enough to want ('one thing about how you breathe') and not so vague it can be ignored. Close it, and make the payoff worth the wait; an unpaid hook costs trust in the next script. In copy, the same move is the headline or subject line.
examples: In a few minutes I'll show you something about your own attention that most people never notice.
There's a reason your shoulders just dropped. I'll come back to that.
Before we finish, you'll find out why the third breath matters most.
cues: 'in a moment', 'soon', 'before we finish', 'later' with I'll tell you, I'll show you, you'll find out, you'll discover
'there's something', 'one thing', 'a secret' with the content withheld
'I'll come back to that', 'more on that later'
'you might be wondering' followed by deferral
a question posed and left unanswered for more than a paragraph

not_this.why: nested loops is a structure of several stories opened and closed in reverse; a hook is one opened gap
anticipation announces an experience or event and delays it; a hook withholds information
that breaks off inside a sentence; a hook is a complete statement that defers its content

origin.source: Loewenstein, The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation (1994)

evidence.note: Information gaps reliably raise the wish to know and the effort spent to find out; the claim that unfinished items are remembered better (Zeigarnik) has a mixed replication record, and nothing shows a hook raises suggestibility.

entries.name: Direct address
entries.summary: Speak to the listener as 'you' so every line is about them.
entries.definition: The speaker addresses the listener as 'you' and makes a point of it. Second person is the default of nearly all hypnosis scripts and is not labeled line by line. It is this entry where the address itself is put forward: the speaker says who they are talking to, singles the listener out, or turns to 'you' from a general, third-person or first-person passage. It needs no story, and it claims no relationship beyond speaker and listener.
entries.how_to: Write to one person, never to 'all of you' or 'listeners'. Keep 'you' as the grammatical subject of the lines that matter. Vary sentence openings so the page is not a column of 'You...'. Break the address on purpose only when you want distance: third person for a quoted or vicarious passage, first person for lines the listener is meant to say.
examples: I'm talking to you. Not to anyone else who might ever hear this. You.
Most people skim past this part. You're not most people right now; you're the one hearing it, and it is meant for you.
Yes, you. The one reading this line.
cues: statements about the address itself: 'I'm talking to you', 'this is for you', 'I mean you'
'you' set alone as a sentence or fragment: 'You.', 'Yes, you.'
a switch into 'you' right after a passage about 'people', 'most listeners', 'he', 'she' or 'I'
'you' contrasted with other hearers: 'not them, you', 'whoever else hears this'
'I ... you' pairings that state the speaker-listener channel: 'I speak, you listen'

not_this.why: that puts 'you' inside a story as its protagonist; direct address is the speaker talking to the listener
