that is written in the listener's own voice as 'I'
that simulates a personal relationship; direct address is only the grammatical choice it is built on

evidence.note: Self-relevant and second-person wording improves attention and recall in memory and message research; whether it adds anything to hypnotic response is untested, since almost every script uses it.

entries.name: Using the listener's name
entries.summary: Address the listener by their name, a pet name or a title, placed where attention should sharpen.
entries.definition: A vocative: a name or term of address inserted into the sentence. In live work it is the listener's own name; in recordings it is a pet name, a role title or a generic stand-in. It is a variant of direct address because it does the same job of singling the listener out, with a stronger pull on attention. It uses a term of address; giving the listener a new name is a different entry.
entries.how_to: Use it sparingly and place it just before or just after the line you most want heard. In live or personalised scripts, the real name works best at the start of the induction and with key suggestions. In recordings, pick a term that fits the agreed tone and keep it consistent. Overuse turns it into filler and it stops catching attention. A pet name carries a relationship and a tone with it, so check that the tone is one the listener signed up for.
examples: That's it, Sam. Just like that.
Listen closely now, my dear, because this part is for you.
You're doing so well, sleepyhead. Let the next breath be slower.
cues: a proper name or term of address used as a vocative, often set off by commas
a name template slot such as [NAME] or {name} in a position of address
endearments or titles used to address the listener: dear, love, pet, my friend
'good girl' or 'good boy' used to call or address the listener within another utterance, rather than to evaluate a response
a vocative placed directly next to an instruction or praise

not_this.why: renaming gives the listener a new name or identity; name-use addresses them by a term
'good girl' or 'good boy' evaluates a response when offered as approval; it is name-use when used as a vocative to call or address the listener, regardless of punctuation
a title that comes with expected behavior assigns a role; a term of address alone does not

evidence.note: In an early dichotic-listening experiment, about a third of listeners noticed their own name in an unattended channel. This does not establish that using a name increases hypnotic suggestibility or that pet names and titles have the same effect.

entries.consent_note: Pet names and titles that imply a relationship or rank should match what the listener agreed to; a repeated assigned title shades into renaming, which can persist.

entries.name: Time distortion
entries.summary: Suggest that time is stretching, shrinking, or no longer matters.
entries.definition: A suggestion about the felt passage of time: minutes that feel like hours, an hour that passes in a moment, or a sense that time has stopped counting. Losing track of time is a normal by-product of absorption, so the suggestion both describes and encourages it. It is this entry when the claim is about how time feels; moving the listener to another date or age belongs to the memory and time family.
entries.how_to: Use it after absorption is established, in deepening or just before the main suggestions. Keep it permissive and tie it to something already true: 'you may have lost track of how long you've been listening'. Choose the direction on purpose: stretching for rest and practice, shrinking for long or uncomfortable waits, timelessness for simple depth. Restore ordinary time sense in the emergence.
examples: Time can slow down here. Each second has room in it.
You may not know whether you've been listening for two minutes or twenty, and it doesn't matter.
There is no clock in this place. There is only now, and then the next now.
cues: 'time' with slows, stretches, stops, speeds up, flies, stands still, doesn't matter
'lose track of time', 'no sense of time', 'timeless'
mismatched durations: 'a minute feels like an hour', 'hours pass in a moment'
'no clock', 'no past or future', 'only now'
'how long has it been' asked without an answer

not_this.why: trance time expansion gives a stated clock interval, a longer suggested felt interval and a use for it; time distortion is the broader suggestion that time feels different
after-the-fact proof asks the listener to check elapsed time after waking as evidence, even if the instruction is given before emergence; time distortion suggests a change in felt time
time confusion tangles tense and date words; time distortion makes a plain claim about how time feels
future progression moves the listener to a future point; time distortion changes felt duration or the sense of time passing

origin.source: Cooper & Erickson, Time Distortion in Hypnosis (1954)

evidence.note: People commonly misjudge, usually underestimate, how long a hypnosis session lasted; whether suggested time expansion gives real extra thinking or practice time, as early reports claimed, is not established.

entries.consent_note: Altered time sense can outlast the session briefly; restore normal time orientation before the listener returns to anything time-critical.

entries.name: Trance time expansion
aliases: one minute feels like an hour
entries.summary: Give a short stretch of clock time and suggest it will feel much longer, to be used for rest, deepening or practice.
entries.definition: A specific application of time distortion: a stated clock interval (a minute, thirty seconds of silence) is paired with a stated experienced interval (an hour, a full night's sleep) and a use for it. It has three parts a labeler can find: the real duration, the felt duration, and the task. The general suggestion that time is stretching or ceasing to matter, with no interval and no task, is time-distortion.
entries.how_to: Announce both durations and the task, then give the silence or a music bed, then mark its end and ratify ('all the time you needed'). 'All the time you need' is safer than an exact ratio, since listeners rarely feel a literal hour. Good tasks are rest, sinking deeper, or mentally rehearsing something. Do not promise real extra learning or work done in the stretched time; suggest that it feels long and restful.
examples: I'm going to give you one minute of clock time. In trance, that minute will feel like an hour of deep, easy rest. Beginning now. [60s]
You have thirty seconds on the clock, and those seconds can feel like an hour, long enough to walk through the day ahead from start to finish. Starting now. [30s]
Those twenty seconds of silence may have felt like several minutes of rest.
cues: a clock interval set against a longer felt one: 'one minute ... like an hour'
'clock time', 'trance time', 'world time'
'all the time you need', 'plenty of time'
'beginning now' followed by a marked gap, then 'that's all the time needed'
'as if you had slept for hours'

not_this.why: the general suggestion that time stretches or stops mattering, with no stated interval or task
a framed gap for deepening with no claim about how long it feels; they often occur together
points at elapsed time after waking as evidence, a different moment and purpose

origin.source: Cooper & Erickson, Time Distortion in Hypnosis (1954)

evidence.note: People in hypnosis do misjudge elapsed time and suggestions can shift the estimate, but the original claim that useful extra mental work gets done in the expanded time was not supported by later controlled studies.

entries.name: Gaze capture
entries.summary: Use the speaker's eyes, imagined or shown on screen, as the point the listener's attention locks onto.
entries.definition: The fixation object is another person's gaze. In audio and text it is imagined; in video it is on screen; in person it is real eye contact. It differs from other fixation points in that eyes look back: the device carries a relationship, and usually a claim of authority, along with the fixation. The listener's own eyes may stay closed throughout.
entries.how_to: Establish the eyes with one or two concrete details, then tell the listener they cannot or need not look away. Let the pull grow by degrees. In audio, say plainly that the eyes are imagined so listeners with closed eyes can follow. It suits scripts with a defined speaker persona; in neutral relaxation work it can feel intrusive, and a spot on the wall does the same job with less charge.
examples: Imagine my eyes in front of you, steady and calm. Let your gaze rest in them.
Look into my eyes. The longer you look, the harder it is to look anywhere else.
Even with your own eyes closed you can feel mine on you, and your attention keeps returning to meet them.
cues: 'look into my eyes', 'meet my eyes', 'my gaze'
'my eyes' with hold, draw, pull, capture, fix
'can't look away', 'nowhere else to look'
descriptions of the speaker's eyes: deep, bright, glowing, steady
'imagine my eyes', 'picture my eyes' in audio or text

not_this.why: label by the target: a spot, light or object is eye fixation; a person's eyes, real, on screen or imagined, are gaze capture, even when tired eyes and closure follow
that fixes on an abstract moving visual with no person behind it
authority is the claim of entitlement to direct; gaze capture is the fixation move that often carries it

evidence.note: Direct gaze does capture attention in perception research, and gaze methods are old in stage and mesmeric practice; no evidence shows an imagined gaze induces better than any other fixation point.

entries.name: Attention call
entries.summary: Change something noticeable, or call for attention outright, to bring a drifting listener back.
entries.definition: A deliberate change in the stream (a new sound, a shift of voice or topic, a pause, a call such as 'now, listen') placed to trigger the automatic turn of attention toward anything new. Its purpose is recovery and emphasis: attention habituates to a steady voice, and this resets it just before something that matters. It is mild and brief. It does not aim to startle or to leave the listener without a next step.
entries.how_to: Place it immediately before a key suggestion, or at intervals in long passages where attention will have wandered. In text, use a marker word (now, listen, and here is the important part), a paragraph break, or a change of sentence length. In audio, script a change of tone, side, or a single sound. Keep it small enough not to lighten the trance, and use it rarely; a cue that repeats every minute stops being new.
examples: Now. Listen carefully to this next part.
[pause, then closer and quieter] And here is the thing I most want you to hear.
[single soft chime] Good. Stay with me here, because this next line matters.
cues: a one-word or two-word attention call set as its own sentence: 'Now.', 'Listen.', 'Listen closely.'
announcements of importance: 'this is important', 'pay attention to this', 'here is the part that matters'
stage directions for a change placed just before a key line: [pause], [tone shift], [bell], [closer]
an abrupt change of topic or sentence length followed at once by a key suggestion
'stay with me', 'are you still with me' with no object of attention named

not_this.why: shock or surprise presents a startling sound, word or claim; an orienting cue makes a mild change or explicitly calls for attention to the next line, though a startling cue can do both
a pattern interrupt breaks an automatic sequence midway; an orienting cue changes a steady stream to regain attention
tone shift is the marked delivery change; an orienting cue uses a change to draw attention back to the script
voice focus makes the speaker's voice the object of attention; an orienting cue calls attention to what follows without making the voice itself the focus

evidence.note: The orienting response to novel or changed stimuli, and its habituation with repetition, are well established; its use to strengthen the suggestion that follows is practitioner practice without direct tests.

entries.name: Imagery, metaphor and story
entries.summary: Devices that carry a suggestion in a picture, a comparison or a story instead of stating it outright.
entries.definition: This family groups the ways a script makes the listener simulate something: a scene to walk through, an image that stands for a state, a story to be absorbed in, a character to be, a future moment to rehearse. What they share is that the listener builds the experience themselves from the writer's description, and the suggestion rides on that experience. They differ in what is imagined (a place, a substance, a plot, a future act) and in whether the suggestion is stated openly or left to be inferred from the parallel. The family has no nested families.
entries.how_to: Pick by what the suggestion needs. To produce a state now, use guided imagery, or give the state a shape (state-as-substance, a container, a dial) or a cause (an imagined substance taken in). To deliver a change indirectly, use metaphor; to explain a response by likeness, analogy; to hide where the suggestion sits, nested loops. To make the listener live an event, use story absorption with character identification, usually in second person. To make a response show up later, use mental rehearsal or future pacing. To mark a change as done, use an imagined ritual. To make a response feel as if it comes by itself, personify the thing that responds. Always offer more than one sense and keep imagery permissive: vividness varies widely between listeners, and a few form no mental pictures at all.

not_this.why: that is imagery used specifically to start trance; this family covers imagery wherever it appears
that is density of description used to hold attention, not a picture or story carrying a suggestion
that is the session-scale choice to set the whole script inside a scene, not a device within it

evidence.note: Imagery and metaphor are standard in clinical hypnosis texts and mental imagery has measurable physiological and performance effects, but the children vary widely in how well each has been tested.

entries.name: Guided imagery
entries.summary: Lead the listener through an imagined scene step by step, telling them what to see, hear and feel there.
entries.definition: The writer narrates a scene in the second person and the listener builds it in imagination as it is described. The scene unfolds in order, one detail or movement at a time, and the wanted response is attached to features of the scene. It differs from metaphor in that nothing needs decoding: the listener is simply in the place, and the place does the work. It differs from story absorption in having no plot; things are there to be noticed, not events to be followed.
entries.how_to: Open with an invitation ('imagine', 'picture', 'find yourself') and then drop the invitation and narrate in present tense. Give one detail per sentence and move through at least two senses, starting with whichever is easiest to verify (temperature, weight, sound). Leave slots for the listener to fill ('a place you like', 'whatever colour seems right') so their own image is not contradicted. Tie each feature to the response you want ('the warmer the sand, the looser your legs'). It fails when it is too specific, too fast, or purely visual.
examples: Imagine a path through tall grass. You can feel the ground, firm and warm, under each step.
Picture a room you would like to rest in. Notice where the light comes from, and how quiet it is.
You're standing at the edge of a still lake. The air is cool on your face, and with every breath of it your shoulders settle.
cues: 'imagine', 'picture', 'see yourself', 'find yourself', 'in your mind's eye'
second-person present-tense description of a place the listener is not in
sequential movement words: 'as you walk', 'ahead of you', 'now you come to'
sense verbs applied to imagined things: 'feel the', 'hear the', 'notice the colour'
open slots: 'a place of your choosing', 'whatever it looks like to you'

not_this.why: same technique; label that only when the scene is the script's first trance-producing passage, with no completed induction before it, and guided-imagery for any later scene
that has events, other characters or a goal for 'you'; guided imagery has a place and things to notice, and nothing happens that changes the situation
a metaphor's scene stands for something else; guided imagery is taken at face value
story absorption needs events and stakes, not just a place to be in

evidence.note: Guided imagery has controlled trials for relaxation, pain and anxiety, with modest effects and variable study quality; vividness of imagery differs a great deal between people.

entries.name: Safe place
entries.summary: Have the listener build an imagined place where they are completely safe, and use it as a base to rest in or return to.
entries.definition: A guided-imagery scene whose defining feature is safety and whose content is chosen by the listener. Once built, it is kept: the script returns to it for rest, as a starting point for other work, and as somewhere to go if anything becomes uncomfortable. That reuse as a base is what separates it from any other pleasant scene.
entries.how_to: Let the listener choose the place, real or invented, and prompt for detail through the senses instead of supplying it. State that nothing and no one can come there without their invitation. Give it a way back in (a word, a breath, a door) and say they can return at any time, in or out of session. Build it early, before demanding work. Do not prescribe the scene: a beach or a forest is not safe for everyone.
examples: Let a place come to mind where you feel completely at ease. It can be real or imagined. Look around and notice what's there.
This place is yours. Nothing comes in unless you invite it.
Whenever you want to come back here, take one slow breath and picture the door.
cues: 'safe place', 'special place', 'sanctuary', 'a place where you feel completely safe'
listener choice of scene: 'real or imagined', 'wherever feels right to you'
ownership and protection statements: 'this place is yours', 'nothing can disturb you here'
return instructions: 'you can come back here any time'
later callbacks: 'go back to your special place'

not_this.why: that tells the listener directly that they are safe, with no imagined place
that is any scene used to start trance; label safe-place when safety and return are the point
that is an emergency-wake provision, not a scene

evidence.note: A standard stabilisation exercise in clinical hypnosis and trauma therapy; evidence comes mostly from treatment packages that include it, not from tests of it alone.

entries.consent_note: The way back in is a cue that outlasts the session. It should be the listener's own to use, and a later script should not bring anyone or anything into the place without their invitation.

entries.name: Metaphor
entries.summary: Tell a story or offer an image whose structure matches the change you want, and let the listener draw the parallel.
entries.definition: A metaphor describes something other than the listener (a garden, a river, a person learning to swim) whose parts and sequence map onto the listener's situation and the wanted outcome. The mapping is not stated; the listener makes it. That unstated mapping is what separates it from analogy, which says 'this is like that' out loud, and from guided imagery, where the scene means only itself. An isomorphic metaphor matches the problem element for element; a looser one shares only the direction of change.
entries.how_to: List the elements of the listener's situation (who, obstacle, resource, outcome) and build a story with one counterpart for each, ending in the resolution you want. Keep the surface topic far enough from the real one that it is not heard as a lecture, and close enough that the fit can be felt. Do not explain it afterwards; move on, or go straight into a direct suggestion that names the same outcome. It fails when the mapping is so loose nothing transfers, or so obvious it is argued with.
examples: A river doesn't push against the rock. It goes around, and in time the rock is the one that changes shape.
There was a gardener who stopped digging up the seeds to check on them. That was the spring they finally grew.
Learning to float, people discover the water was holding them the whole time. They only had to stop helping.
cues: a story or image about a third party or natural process, placed in a suggestion passage with no stated relevance
process vocabulary shared with the session goal: 'letting go', 'settling', 'opening', 'learning'
story openers mid-script: 'there was once', 'I knew someone who', 'a tree in winter'
the story's resolution matches the suggestion that follows or precedes it
no 'like' or 'just as' linking it to the listener

not_this.why: analogy states the comparison and its point; metaphor leaves the mapping to the listener
that shows a person performing the target response itself and what it earned them; a metaphor's subject does something else whose shape matches the change
that reports another person responding to hypnotic suggestions; a metaphor's story is about a different subject altogether
the listener is placed in the scene and it is not a stand-in for anything

origin.source: Gordon, Therapeutic Metaphors (1978)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian and clinical hypnosis texts; controlled comparisons have not shown metaphorical suggestions to outperform direct ones, and the claim that the unconscious decodes them is untested.

entries.consent_note: The suggestion is meant to pass without being recognised as one; the listener should have agreed beforehand to the goal the metaphor serves.

entries.name: Extended metaphor
entries.summary: Introduce one image early and return to it at every stage, so each new suggestion arrives as more of an image the listener has already accepted.
entries.definition: A single metaphor is set up near the start and then carried through the whole script: the induction, the deepening, the suggestions and the wake-up are all phrased in its terms. Each stage adds a new feature of the same image instead of a new image. What separates it from the parent is span and reuse: a metaphor can be told once and left, an extended metaphor is the thread the other passages hang on. The image stays a stand-in for the listener's change; if the listener is simply placed inside a scene for the whole session, that is a story frame.
entries.how_to: Pick an image with enough parts to cover every stage you need: a way in, a way further, something that changes, a way back. Introduce it plainly and early, when nothing is being asked. At each later stage, reuse the same nouns and add one feature that carries the new suggestion; do not switch to a second image halfway. Let the wake-up reverse or complete the image. It fails when the image is stretched to cover something it has no natural part for, or when its terms drift so the listener has to rebuild it.
examples: Early: Think of a lake at the end of the day, when the wind has dropped. Later: The last ripples reach the edge and are gone. Later still: And whatever I say now settles through that still water, all the way to the bottom.
You planted something a few minutes ago, when you first closed your eyes. Now the roots are finding their way down. By the time you wake, there will be a green shoot you can come back and tend.
The tide that carried your thoughts out earlier is turning now, and it brings back only what you want to keep.
cues: the same image nouns recurring in three or more separate sections ('the lake', 'the water', 'the surface')
back-references to the image: 'that same river', 'the garden from earlier', 'remember the lake'
each stage phrased as a further feature of one image (deeper water, the bottom, the surface again)
the emergence reverses or completes the opening image
suggestions stated in the image's terms instead of plainly ('let it settle to the bottom')

not_this.why: the parent covers any metaphor, including one told once; label this when one image is reused across stages
a story frame puts the listener inside a fictional scene for the whole session; an extended metaphor stays a stand-in for something else
a refrain repeats the same line; this repeats an image in new wording with a new feature each time
seeding mentions an idea once early so it is familiar later; this builds on the image at every stage

evidence.note: The extended metaphor or conceit is a classical figure and a common way to organize a hypnosis script; no study tests whether one sustained image works better than several separate ones.

entries.name: State-as-substance
entries.summary: Give the state a physical form, such as fog, warm liquid or light, that fills, coats or drains from the body.
entries.definition: An abstract state (relaxation, blankness, calm, focus) is described as a material with weight, temperature, colour and movement. The listener tracks the substance moving through the body, and wherever it goes the state goes. What makes it this entry is that the substance is the state: it is not a scene to stand in and not a control to operate.
entries.how_to: Choose a substance whose physical behaviour matches the state: thick and slow for heaviness, fog for blank thought, light for alertness or warmth. Give it an entry point and a route, and move it one body region at a time so it paces a relaxation pass. Use verbs of filling, pouring, soaking, spreading or draining. Let the listener choose colour or temperature. Avoid substances that can alarm (water over the face, anything that tightens or smothers) unless that is asked for.
examples: Relaxation pours in at the top of your head like warm honey, slow and heavy, and runs down behind your eyes.
A soft fog drifts through your thoughts. Wherever it settles, the thoughts go quiet.
With each breath out, the tension drains from your hands like water from a basin.
cues: substance nouns as the subject of a state: 'fog', 'mist', 'honey', 'syrup', 'warm water', 'light', 'static', 'haze'
flow verbs applied to the body or mind: 'fills', 'pours', 'spreads', 'soaks', 'seeps', 'drains', 'melts', 'coats'
a state noun joined to a material: 'liquid relaxation', 'a fog of calm', 'calm like warm honey'
region-by-region movement of a named material, not of a bare feeling
material properties given to the state: weight, thickness, colour, temperature

not_this.why: that moves a bare feeling (warmth, heaviness, 'a wave of relaxation') along a path; label this entry only when a material is named (fog, honey, light)
that is an agent taken in (drunk, breathed, injected) and credited with causing the state; here the material is the state itself and nothing is taken
a 'like' may introduce the material, but the material then moves through the body; an analogy names a familiar case and leaves it
that relaxes regions by instruction; the substance image is an optional vehicle for it

evidence.note: Common in clinical relaxation and pain scripts; no studies isolate the substance image from the relaxation suggestion it accompanies.

entries.name: Container imagery
entries.summary: Have the listener imagine a box, vault or other container and put a thought, worry or memory inside it.
entries.definition: A mental item is treated as an object that can be picked up and placed in an imagined container, which is then closed, locked, stored or sent away. The container gives the item a location that is not the listener's attention. It is this entry when the image is a vessel with an inside and a closure; the purpose (setting aside, protecting, hiding, keeping for later) varies.
entries.how_to: Name what goes in, describe the container in a few concrete details, then narrate the placing, the closing and where it is kept. State what happens to the contents: waiting until after the session, kept safe, or gone. Say who holds the key, because that decides whether the listener can retrieve it. For anything that matters outside the session, leave retrieval with the listener.
examples: Picture a sturdy wooden box. Put today's to-do list inside, close the lid, and leave it by the door for later.
Each worry goes into the vault, one at a time. Hear the door swing shut and the lock turn.
You can keep that confident feeling in a small jar on a shelf, where you can find it whenever you want it.
cues: container nouns: 'box', 'chest', 'vault', 'safe', 'drawer', 'jar', 'locker', 'bubble', 'balloon'
placing verbs with a mental object: 'put your worries in', 'place that thought inside', 'store', 'pack away'
closure words: 'close the lid', 'lock', 'seal', 'turn the key'
statement of where it is kept or who holds the key
'for later', 'until you come back for it'

not_this.why: that is the move of postponing doubt or resistance, with or without a container image; when doubt is put in a box, label both
that puts the item outside the self in any form; a container adds the vessel and the closure
that suggests forgetting directly; a locked box may serve it but is the image, not the suggestion

evidence.note: Containment imagery is a routine stabilisation exercise in clinical hypnosis and trauma therapy; it has little controlled testing as a separate component.

entries.consent_note: If the container is used to lock away memories, objections or the listener's own judgment beyond the session, say so beforehand and leave the key with the listener.

entries.name: Dial / switch imagery
entries.summary: Have the listener imagine a dial, switch or control panel that sets a sensation, thought level or feeling.
entries.definition: An inner quantity (discomfort, mental chatter, energy, confidence) is given an imagined control with settings, and changing the setting changes the quantity. It differs from other imagery in being an instrument with a current reading and a direction of adjustment. Who operates it matters: a listener-operated control is a self-regulation tool, a speaker-operated one is a statement of who is in charge.
entries.how_to: Establish the control and its present reading first ('notice where it is set now'), so the listener commits to a number. Then move it in small steps and describe the matching change after each step. Use dials for things that should vary by degree and switches for on/off. State who is turning it. If the listener is to use it later, rehearse them turning it both ways before the session ends.
examples: Imagine a dial numbered one to ten that sets how loud your thoughts are. See where it sits now, and turn it down one notch.
Somewhere in your mind is a control room. Find the switch marked 'tension' and flick it off.
As I turn the dial from six down to five, feel your shoulders drop to match.
cues: control nouns: 'dial', 'switch', 'knob', 'lever', 'slider', 'thermostat', 'control room', 'control panel', 'remote'
operation verbs: 'turn down', 'turn up', 'flick off', 'slide', 'set it to'
a numbered range tied to a feeling or sensation
'notice where it is set now'
a named operator: 'you turn', 'I turn', 'my hand on the dial'

not_this.why: that is a number or scale put on trance depth, with or without a control to operate; when an imagined dial sets depth, label both
a trigger is a cue that fires a set response; a dial is operated by degrees within imagery
that offers a number as a reference point for judgment, with no control to operate

evidence.note: Dial and control-room imagery is common in clinical pain and anxiety scripts, and hypnotic analgesia itself is well supported; the dial image has not been tested against plain suggestion.

entries.consent_note: When the speaker is given the controls, or a control is left in place after the session, that should be agreed beforehand and a way to reset it stated.

entries.name: Nested loops
entries.summary: Start several stories without finishing them, give the suggestions in the middle, then finish the stories in reverse order.
entries.definition: Story A is begun and broken off, story B is begun and broken off, sometimes a third; the direct suggestions are delivered at the centre; then the stories are closed innermost first. The shape is A B C [suggestions] C B A. What defines it is the bracket structure, not the content of the stories. The lore claim is that the unfinished stories hold attention and that the central material is less well remembered afterwards.
entries.how_to: Use two or three stories; more is hard to follow and hard to close cleanly. Break each one at a point of mild suspense with a pivot such as 'which reminds me'. Keep the centre short and plain. Close every loop, in reverse order, and briefly; an unclosed story is a loose end, not a technique. It works better spoken than read, because a reader can see the structure on the page.
examples: I was walking to the station one morning when I noticed a door I'd never seen. Which reminds me of a clockmaker I once knew...
...and while the clock sat unfinished on his bench, you can let your breathing slow, and let that ease stay with you. He fitted the last gear that evening.
And the door at the station? It opened onto a small garden, and I sat there for a while.
cues: a story interrupted before its outcome, followed at once by a new story
pivot phrases: 'which reminds me', 'but before I tell you', 'I'll come back to that'
direct second-person suggestions sandwiched between story openings and story endings
story endings appearing in the reverse of the order the stories began
return phrases: 'and as for the', 'you'll remember the'

not_this.why: that is a single open question or promise held open; nested loops is several stories bracketed around a centre
that brackets trance by resuming the pre-trance conversation; the amnesia claim is shared but no stories are stacked
that nests a second induction inside the first trance, not stories inside stories

steps.text: Begin story A and break it off before its outcome.
Begin story B, and optionally a third, breaking each off the same way.
Give the suggestions plainly and briefly at the centre.
Finish the innermost story first.
Finish the remaining stories in reverse order, ending with story A.

evidence.note: Taught in Ericksonian and NLP training as multiple embedded metaphor; the claims of amnesia for the centre and of heightened suggestibility there have no independent tests.

entries.consent_note: The form is meant to make the central suggestions hard to notice or recall; use it only for goals the listener has already agreed to.

entries.name: Story absorption
entries.summary: Tell a story with enough plot, character and concrete detail that the listener lives its events instead of judging them.
entries.definition: The writer uses narrative craft (a character who wants something, a sequence of events, sensory detail, uninterrupted flow) to pull attention fully into the story world. Transported listeners counter-argue less and shift their beliefs toward those the story implies. It differs from guided imagery in having events and stakes, and from metaphor in that the story need not stand for anything; the absorption itself is the tool.
entries.how_to: Give a point-of-view character, a want and something in the way within the first few lines. Narrate concrete events in order, in scene, with sensory detail, and do not step outside the story to comment or instruct. Put the beliefs or responses you want inside the story as things that happen or that the character finds true. Anything that reminds the listener they are being addressed (asides, technique talk, abrupt shifts of tense) breaks it.
examples: The lighthouse keeper climbed the last stair with the storm already on the glass, and the lamp was cold.
She had told herself she would only stay a minute. The fire was warm, the chair was deep, and the minute passed without her.
He had promised to be home before dark. Then the ferryman held out a hand, and the far bank looked nearer than the road back.
cues: sustained narration across many sentences with characters, events and a setting
plot markers: a goal, an obstacle, 'then', 'until', 'suddenly', a turning point
scene-level sensory detail and dialogue
absence of direct instruction to the listener for the length of the passage
one point of view held throughout, with no asides or comment from the narrator

not_this.why: that is labelled for the parallel between a story and the wanted change, at any length; this is labelled for sustained in-scene narration with events, whether or not it stands for anything. A long story with a parallel takes both
that marks the point of view ('you' as protagonist); this marks sustained plotted narration in any person. A long second-person story takes both
that is the session-level choice to set everything inside a scene; this is the absorbing narration itself
that is dense description without plot; it supports transportation but is not a story

origin.source: Green & Brock, The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives (2000)

evidence.note: Transportation reliably predicts story-consistent belief change in experiments and meta-analyses; effects are modest, and it has not been studied as a hypnotic procedure.

entries.consent_note: It works by reducing scrutiny of what the story implies; the listener should know the session uses story to carry suggestions.

entries.name: Character identification
entries.summary: Give the listener a character to be, or to feel with, so that the character's responses become the listener's own.
entries.definition: The script supplies a character and invites the listener to take that character's point of view: seeing through their eyes, sharing their goal, feeling what they feel. What the character then experiences is offered to the listener at one remove. It differs from My friend John in that the listener is asked to be the character, not to hear a report about them, and from role assignment, which tells the listener what they are without any story.
entries.how_to: Make the character easy to step into: few fixed traits, a situation and a starting feeling close to the listener's own, interior access to thoughts and sensations. Either invite the step directly ('be her for a moment') or simply narrate from inside. Have the character meet and resolve the doubt the listener is likely to have. Detailed looks, a name or a history the listener cannot share make identification harder.
examples: There's someone in this story who is just as tired as you are tonight. Step into their shoes for a while.
Be the traveller in this story for a while. What he notices, you notice; when his shoulders drop, yours do.
See the room through her eyes. Her breathing has already slowed; let yours match it.
cues: explicit invitations: 'be', 'become', 'step into', 'see through their eyes', 'you are playing', 'for now you are'
merge lines that yoke the character's experience to the listener's: 'what she feels, you feel', 'his hands are your hands'
a third-person story that switches to 'you' for the same character partway through
interior narration of a character's sensations and thoughts following one of the invitations above

not_this.why: that describes a third person being hypnotised for the listener to follow; no invitation to be that person
there the listener watches someone go under and follows from outside; label this entry only when the script invites the listener to take the character's viewpoint or merges the two
a model is watched performing the response and being rewarded; the listener is not asked to be them
that states the listener's role directly, outside any story
that installs a named alternate self to be switched in by cue after the story ends

origin.source: Cohen, Defining identification: a theoretical look at the identification of audiences with media characters (2001)

evidence.note: Identification with story characters predicts attitude and self-concept shifts in media experiments; its use as a carrier for hypnotic suggestion is practice, not tested.

entries.consent_note: Responses given to the character are meant to transfer to the listener; say so, and do not use the character to carry suggestions the listener would refuse if asked directly.

entries.name: Second-person narration
entries.summary: Tell the story with 'you' as the protagonist, narrating the listener's actions, perceptions and feelings as they happen.
entries.definition: The story's main character is addressed as 'you', so there is no separate character to identify with: the narration asserts what the listener does and feels inside the story world. It is the form of character identification with the distance removed. It is narrower than direct address, which is any speaking to 'you'; this requires story events with 'you' as their subject.
entries.how_to: Narrate in present tense and keep 'you' as the grammatical subject of actions and perceptions. Start with actions that are easy to accept (walking, looking, noticing) and move to feelings and decisions later, once the listener is going along. Leave appearance and backstory open. Each time the narration states a reaction the listener does not have, it costs credibility, so use 'you find', 'you notice' and permissive wording for inner states.
examples: You knock twice. The door opens before the second knock has landed, and a voice says they have been waiting for you.
You sit down by the fire, and before you've decided to, you're leaning back.
Someone hands you a cup. You notice your hands are steady as you take it.
cues: 'you' as subject of narrative action verbs in a fictional setting: 'you walk', 'you open', 'you turn'
other characters speaking to or acting on 'you'
events that change the situation: 'the door opens', 'then', 'suddenly', 'when you turn back'
a role, errand or goal given to 'you' inside the story: 'you have come to', 'you are the new apprentice'
decisions and reactions narrated as story facts: 'you decide', 'you find yourself answering'

not_this.why: that is any use of 'you'; this needs a story in which 'you' is the protagonist
that places 'you' in a scene to notice things; this has plot, other characters and events happening to 'you'
that marks sustained plotted narration in any person; this marks the point of view, and a long second-person story takes both
that tells the real listener what to do or feel now, outside any story world

evidence.note: Self-referent wording aids memory and second-person text can raise reported immersion in reading studies, but results are mixed and nothing tests it against third-person stories in hypnosis.

entries.name: Imagined ritual
entries.summary: Have the listener perform, in imagination, one symbolic act that stands for the change and marks it as done.
entries.definition: The listener imagines a discrete act with a clear before and after (signing a page, stepping through a doorway, setting down a weight, handing something over), and the script declares that the act is the change. It differs from metaphor in that the listener performs it in the first person and its meaning is stated. It differs from mental rehearsal in that the act is not the future behaviour itself; it is a sign for a decision or transition.
entries.how_to: Place it at the turning point of the suggestion section, after the reasons and before the sealing. Choose an act that already carries the meaning in ordinary life: signing for commitment, a threshold for transition, putting something down for release. Narrate the moment before, the act in physical detail, and the difference after. Say plainly what it means. One ritual per session carries more weight than several.
examples: In front of you is a doorway. On this side is the old habit. Step through, and hear the door close behind you.
Pick up the pen and sign your name under the promise you've just made to yourself.
Light the candle. As the flame catches, the decision is made, and it stays made.
cues: an imagined single act with ceremonial objects: 'door', 'threshold', 'bridge', 'pen', 'contract', 'key', 'candle', 'fire'
before/after language around the act: 'on this side', 'once you step through', 'from this moment'
stated meaning: 'this means', 'as you sign, you agree', 'that is you leaving it behind'
completion markers: 'it is done', 'the door closes behind you'
imperatives to perform the act in imagination: 'step', 'sign', 'hand it to', 'set it down'

not_this.why: that has the listener really state, write or sign something; this is done only in imagination
that turns an inner thing into an object that can be moved; label the ritual when the script says one act marks the change as done. A burden given a shape and then ceremonially set down takes both
that imagines the actual future behaviour; a ritual is a symbol for the change
that stores an item in a vessel; a ritual marks a transition and need not contain anything

evidence.note: Symbolic letting-go and commitment imagery is common in clinical scripts, and real commitments and rituals have experimental support; imagined ones have little direct testing.

entries.consent_note: An imagined vow or signing is meant to feel binding after the session; state its scope, and do not treat it as consent to anything not agreed while awake.

entries.name: Mental rehearsal
entries.summary: Have the listener imagine carrying out the wanted behaviour, step by step and in detail, as practice for doing it.
entries.definition: The listener runs through the actual future behaviour in imagination: the setting, each action, how it feels, how it ends. The imagined act is the same act they will later perform, which separates it from metaphor and ritual. It is practice of a behaviour in general; future pacing is the narrower form that ties an installed response to one specific upcoming cue.
entries.how_to: Place it after the suggestion is given, as its practice round. Use first-person viewpoint (seeing through their own eyes), present tense, and real-time sequence including the start of the action. Include the difficult moment and rehearse handling it, not only the success. Add how the body feels while doing it. Run it more than once, making it more concrete each time. Vague triumph imagery with no actions does little.
examples: See yourself walking to the front of the room. Feel your feet on the floor, and hear your first sentence come out clear and steady.
Run through it again, slower. Your hand on the door, the breath you take, the first words you say.
Imagine the moment you'd usually hesitate. This time you pause, breathe, and go on.
cues: 'imagine yourself doing', 'picture yourself', 'see yourself' followed by a real-world task
stepwise description of a task the listener will really perform: 'your hand on the door', 'the first words you say'
repetition markers: 'run through it again', 'once more', 'rehearse', 'practise it now'
the task named as the thing being practised: 'the presentation', 'the conversation', 'saying no'
inclusion of the difficult moment and its handling

not_this.why: label that when one named future occasion is imagined and an installed cue and response fire in it; rehearsal walks through the steps of a task the listener carries out deliberately
that has the listener observe their present self or body from outside; rehearsal runs a future task, whatever the viewpoint
that places the listener after the change, looking back on it as done
that fires and resets a real response repeatedly in session, not an imagined one

evidence.note: Mental practice improves performance in meta-analyses, more for cognitive than for strength tasks and less than physical practice; imagining the process helps more than imagining only the outcome.

entries.consent_note: It is meant to change behaviour after the session; rehearse only behaviour the listener has asked for.

entries.name: Future pacing
entries.summary: Walk the listener through a specific future moment in which the cue appears and the suggested response happens.
entries.definition: A short rehearsal aimed at one named future situation: the listener imagines the time and place, meets the cue, and experiences the installed response firing there. Its job is to connect work done in the session to the context where it must show up. It is narrower than mental rehearsal (one cue, one response, one moment) and differs from future progression, which stands the listener after the change looking back.
entries.how_to: Use it right after installing a trigger, anchor or posthypnotic suggestion and before emergence. Name a real, near, likely moment ('tomorrow morning when the alarm goes'). Narrate cue, then response, then the result, in present tense. Repeat with two or three different contexts so the response is not tied to a single one. Check the response is one the listener wants in that setting.
examples: Imagine tomorrow morning. You sit down at your desk, see the blank page, and feel that calm focus arrive.
Now go to the next time you hear your name called in a meeting. Notice the slow breath that comes before you speak.
Go to later this week. You close the front door behind you, and as it clicks, the day's tension drops away.
cues: specific future time markers: 'tomorrow', 'next time', 'later this week', 'the next time you'
an imagined future scene narrated in present tense
cue-then-response order: 'as you see ..., you feel ...'
reference to a trigger, anchor or suggestion installed earlier in the script
two or more future contexts run in succession

not_this.why: that states the future response; future pacing has the listener imagine living it
that orients the listener to a future where the change is already past and looks back
that fires the trigger for real in session; future pacing fires it in an imagined later scene

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Frogs into Princes (1979)

evidence.note: The NLP procedure itself is untested, but it resembles mental simulation and implementation intentions, both of which have experimental support for cue-linked behaviour.

entries.consent_note: It exists to make a response occur after the session; the listener should know which situations it has been attached to.

entries.name: Analogy
entries.summary: Explain or prompt the wanted response by stating outright that it is like something the listener already knows.
entries.definition: An explicit comparison between the target experience and a familiar one, with a marker such as 'like', 'just as' or 'the way'. The listener is told what maps onto what, so the familiar case lends both understanding and plausibility to the new one. It is this and not metaphor because the comparison is announced, and usually brief.
entries.how_to: Pick a source the listener has certainly lived (falling asleep, a warm bath, losing track of time in a book). State the likeness in one sentence and name the shared feature, then go straight to the suggestion. Use it in the pretalk to explain what will happen and in suggestions to borrow a known feeling. Keep it short; an analogy that needs explaining is the wrong analogy.
examples: It's like setting down a bag you've carried all day: you only notice the weight once it's gone.
Just as a muscle loosens in warm water, your thoughts can loosen now.
Your arm can feel the way it does when you've slept on it, heavy and not quite yours.
cues: comparison markers: 'like', 'just like', 'just as', 'the way', 'the same way', 'as if', 'similar to'
'it's a bit like', 'think of it as'
a familiar everyday experience named next to the target response
'just as ..., so ...' constructions
one or two sentences long, followed directly by a suggestion

not_this.why: metaphor leaves the mapping unstated and is usually longer; analogy says 'this is like that'
label that when the familiar case is an absorbed state (a film, a long drive, the edge of sleep) and the point is that trance is ordinary; analogy covers any other stated likeness
there the compared material goes on to move through the body and act on it; an analogy names the familiar case and leaves it
that asks the listener to suppose something is true and explore it, not to compare two things

origin.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric

evidence.note: Analogies aid comprehension and can shift judgments in learning and persuasion experiments; whether they strengthen hypnotic response beyond aiding understanding is not established.

entries.name: Personification
entries.summary: Describe a body part, a state or an object as having its own will, knowledge or voice.
entries.definition: A non-person (the eyelids, the breath, sleep, the chair, the trance itself) is made the subject of verbs of wanting, knowing, deciding or speaking, or is spoken to directly. The effect is to move agency away from the listener's deliberate effort: the thing does it. It is a figure of wording; it becomes parts work only when the personified thing is a part of the listener's psyche that is negotiated with.
entries.how_to: Make the thing the grammatical subject and give it an intention that matches the response: 'your eyelids want to close'. Use it where you want a response to feel like it comes by itself. You can also address the thing ('legs, you can rest now') to speak past the listener's effort. Keep the will you assign benign and consistent; an object with a hostile or controlling will is a different, heavier suggestion.
examples: Your eyelids know exactly how heavy they want to be.
Let the breath decide its own pace. It has been doing this all your life without your help.
Sleep has been waiting patiently at the edge of the room, and now it comes a little closer.
cues: body part, state or object as subject of mental verbs: 'wants', 'knows', 'decides', 'remembers', 'chooses', 'waits'
direct address to a non-person: 'hands, you can let go'
a state or object that speaks, whispers, calls or invites
'let your ... decide', 'your ... already knows how'
abstract nouns acting on the listener: 'trance takes your hand', 'calm finds you'

not_this.why: that gives an outside object the target feeling itself in a sentence or two ('the chair can relax') for the listener to take on; personification gives a thing will, knowledge or a voice and lets it act ('the chair wants to hold you', 'your eyelids know')
when the thing that knows or decides is 'your unconscious' or 'your deeper mind', label that entry; personification covers body parts, states and objects
that addresses or negotiates with a psychological part of the listener, as procedure and not as figure of speech
that says the response happens by itself, without giving the thing a will or voice

evidence.note: A classical figure; its use to make responses feel involuntary is standard practice but has not been tested on its own.

entries.name: Imagined substance
entries.summary: Describe an imaginary drug, gas, oil or drink entering the body, and credit it with causing the response you want.
entries.definition: The writer has the listener imagine taking in an agent: swallowing a drink, breathing a gas, feeling an oil rubbed in or an injection given. The response is then described as the agent's effect, with an onset, a spread and a strength, as a real drug would have. What makes it this entry is the causal credit: the substance does the work, so the listener has nothing to do but wait for it. It differs from state-as-substance, where the fog or honey is the state itself and no agent is taken in.
entries.how_to: Give the substance a route in (drink, breath, skin), one or two sensory properties (taste, warmth, colour, scent) and a stated effect before it is taken. Then narrate the taking, and follow the timeline a real dose would have: first sign, spreading, full effect. Tie more of it to more effect, with each sip or breath as a new dose. Borrow from what the listener knows: the numbness after a dentist's injection, the heaviness of a sedative, the warmth of a strong drink. Say in the script that it is imaginary and that it wears off completely at the end, and avoid drug imagery for listeners for whom real substances are a problem.
examples: Imagine a small glass of something warm and golden. As you drink it, the warmth spreads down through your chest, and everywhere it reaches lets go.
The air in this room carries a soft, sweet scent, and every breath of it makes your thoughts slower and your eyelids heavier.
A cool lotion is smoothed over the back of your hand. In a few seconds it begins to work, and the hand grows pleasantly numb.
cues: agent nouns: 'potion', 'elixir', 'drink', 'pill', 'gas', 'vapour', 'mist to breathe', 'oil', 'lotion', 'injection', 'serum', 'dose'
intake verbs with an imagined agent: 'drink', 'swallow', 'sip', 'breathe it in', 'inhale', 'absorbs into your skin'
pharmacological timeline: 'it begins to work', 'taking effect', 'kicks in', 'spreading through your bloodstream', 'wearing off'
the response credited to the agent: 'it makes you', 'the drink does it for you', 'that's the gas working'
dose language: 'each sip', 'another breath of it', 'a stronger dose', 'the more you breathe in'

not_this.why: there the substance is the state given a shape; here it is a separate agent taken in that causes the state
that suggests a feeling with no stated cause; this supplies an imagined cause and lets the feeling follow
that aims at perceiving an absent thing as present; here the tasting or smelling is only the vehicle for an effect

evidence.note: Imagined anaesthetic and imagined medicine are long-standing clinical suggestions, and expectancy and placebo effects on felt states are well established; no study isolates the imagined substance from the plain suggestion it carries.

entries.consent_note: Say that the substance is imaginary and that its effect ends with the session; do not use drug or intoxication imagery with listeners in recovery from substance use unless they have asked for it.

entries.name: Sensory overlap
entries.summary: Start in a sense the listener already has going and lead from it into another through something the two share.
entries.definition: The writer describes the scene first in the sense that comes easily to the listener, then names a feature that belongs to two senses at once (movement that can be seen and felt, a rhythm that can be heard and felt) and uses it to cross into the second sense. It is a lead with a direction: sense A, a bridge, sense B. That separates it from sense crossing, which describes one sense in the words of another inside a single phrase, and from plain sensory language, which simply uses each sense in turn.
entries.how_to: Find out, or guess from the listener's own words, which sense is easiest for them, and build the scene there first with two or three details. Then pick a bridge that naturally involves both senses: wind seen in the leaves and felt on the skin, waves seen and heard, footsteps heard and felt. Cross on the bridge and stay in the new sense for a few lines before crossing again. It is most used to give feeling or pictures to listeners who say they cannot get them. Do not jump senses with no bridge; that is just a list.
examples: See the leaves moving at the top of the tree. And as you watch them move, you can begin to feel the same breeze on your face.
Listen to the waves come in, one after another. Each one you hear, you can feel the rhythm of it, slow, in your own chest.
Feel the warmth of the cup in your hands. As the warmth spreads, notice the steam rising from it, and the colour of the light it rises through.
cues: a run of predicates in one sense followed by a switch to another within one passage (see... see... feel)
bridge clauses: 'as you watch X move, you can feel...', 'and as you hear it, notice how it looks'
one object given properties in two senses in sequence (waves heard, then felt; fire seen, then warm)
'the same breeze', 'that same rhythm' carrying across the switch
'you may not see it yet, but you can feel...' followed by a lead back toward seeing

not_this.why: sense crossing describes one sense in terms of another in a single figure; overlap leads step by step from one sense to the next
sensory language uses sight, sound and feeling words in any order; overlap needs a start sense, a bridge and a destination
pace-and-lead moves from verifiable statements to any suggestion; overlap is a lead between senses inside imagery
immersion is density of description across senses to crowd out the room, with no directed crossing

evidence.note: Taught in NLP as overlapping representational systems; the claim that people have a preferred sense system has failed controlled tests, and the lead itself has not been studied, though people do differ in how vivid their imagery is in each sense.

entries.name: Dissociation and parts
entries.summary: Separate the listener from part of their experience, or divide the self into parts that can be addressed one at a time.
entries.definition: This family covers suggestions that split experience: the watcher from the watched, the doer from the deed, the conscious mind from the unconscious, the self from a body part, a feeling or a named part. What unites the children is a line drawn inside the listener, with the suggestion addressed to one side of it; the line can be drawn in imagery, in a named part, or in the pronoun used for the listener. It differs from imagery, which adds a scene, and from identity work, which changes what the whole self is called. The family has no nested families.
entries.how_to: Choose by what is being split. To remove ownership of a response, use automaticity-framing. To move the listener's viewpoint, use dissociation-suggestion, or observer-self when a calm watching part should stay behind. To split the body from awareness, use body-dissociation. To address a second listener inside the person, use conscious-unconscious-split for the generic one and parts-work for a part picked out by its function; use positive-intention when that part is objecting and is credited with a good aim, and six-step-reframing for the full negotiation sequence. Use alter-persona only when the second self has a name and traits of its own. To put a thought or feeling outside the person as an object, use externalization. Every split made in a session, the observer included, should be closed before or during emergence.

not_this.why: imagery adds a scene; this family divides the listener's own experience
identity entries rename or redefine the whole self; these split it
the bind uses the split to make every option succeed; it is filed under binds

origin.source: Hilgard, Divided Consciousness (1977)

evidence.note: Reports of involuntariness and detachment under suggestion are well documented; whether they reflect a real division of control or an altered report about ordinary action is still disputed.

entries.consent_note: Splits can outlast the session; close them explicitly, and avoid them with listeners who report unwanted dissociation in daily life.

entries.name: Dissociation
entries.summary: Suggest that the listener watches their own body, thoughts or feelings from outside, at a distance.
entries.definition: The writer moves the listener's point of view away from what they are experiencing, so the experience continues but is observed instead of lived. The split is between viewpoint and content. It differs from body detachment, which changes how the body feels, and from externalization, which moves the content out and leaves the viewpoint where it was.
entries.how_to: Place it after some relaxation, when body feeling is already faint. Give a position (above, behind, across the room) and a distance, then describe what is seen from there in the third person or as 'that body'. Keep the tone calm and the distance modest; a far or abrupt separation can alarm. Use it to cool a strong feeling or to let responses run without interference, and bring the listener back into the body before waking.
examples: Imagine drifting up a little, and looking down at that body resting in the chair.
You can watch those thoughts go by from a distance, the way you would watch traffic from a window.
From over there, you see someone breathing slowly, perfectly at ease.
cues: 'watch yourself', 'see yourself', 'look down at'
'from a distance', 'from outside', 'from above', 'from over there' attached to a verb of seeing or watching
'that body', 'that person in the chair' as the thing being watched (with no seeing verb and no stated vantage point, 'that arm' or 'the body' is body-dissociation)
'floating above', 'stepping out of', 'drifting up out of your body'
shift from 'you feel' to 'you see yourself feeling'

not_this.why: that changes how the body feels (numb, distant, not yours) without moving the viewpoint
the variant names a lasting watcher part; the unit is any outside view
that moves a thought or feeling out; here the listener moves out

evidence.note: Standard in clinical hypnosis for pain and distress; distancing from a feeling has experimental support outside hypnosis, but the specific out-of-body wording has not been tested against alternatives.

entries.consent_note: Can be unpleasant for listeners prone to depersonalization; state the content in advance and return the listener to the body before the end.

entries.name: Observer self
entries.summary: Set up a calm part of the listener that only watches, while the rest of them responds.
entries.definition: A form of dissociation in which the outside view is given to a lasting part: a watcher that stays aware, safe and uninvolved. The rest of the listener is then free to respond fully. It differs from the parent in that the watcher is named and kept, not just a momentary viewpoint, and from general parts work in that this part's only job is to observe.
entries.how_to: Introduce the watcher early and give it a fixed position: at the back of the mind, at the edge of the room. Say what it does (watches, stays aware, notices) and what it does not do (interfere, judge). Refer back to it with the same words each time. It lets a cautious listener go further, because something of them stays awake. Do not dismiss the watcher mid-session, since its value is that it stays; at emergence, say that the watcher and the rest of the listener are one again. If the watcher is also said to reject unwanted suggestions, that promise is a separate device (objection-truce) and must be true of the script.
examples: A part of you can stay at the back of your mind, simply watching, knowing you are safe.
Let that quiet observer notice everything, without needing to do anything about it.
While the rest of you sinks down, the watcher stays exactly where it is, calm and awake.
cues: 'observer', 'watcher', 'witness' as a noun for part of the listener
'a part of you that just watches', 'simply observing'
'at the back of your mind', 'from the edge', 'from a safe distance'
'while the rest of you ...' paired with a watching part
'without interfering', 'without judging', 'only noticing'

not_this.why: there a part filters or rejects unwanted suggestions; the observer only watches, and both labels apply when it also filters
parts-work can address or negotiate with any functional part; observer-self specifically keeps a watching part aware while the rest responds
there the unconscious is addressed as a separate listener; here a watcher remains aware
that gives the analytical mind a decoy task so it stops monitoring; the observer continues to watch

origin.source: Hilgard, Divided Consciousness (1977)

evidence.note: Hilgard's hidden-observer reports were replicated, but later work showed their content follows the instructions given, so the observer may be a product of the suggestion and not a pre-existing part.

entries.consent_note: A promised watcher lowers the listener's guard; the promise that it keeps them safe should be true of the script.

entries.name: It happens by itself
entries.summary: Describe each response as happening on its own, so the listener experiences it as not done by them.
entries.definition: The writer words a response so that the listener is not its agent: the hand lifts, the eyes close, the thought fades. The feeling that a suggested response is involuntary is what hypnosis researchers call the classic suggestion effect, and this wording invites that feeling. It differs from not doing / not knowing, which removes effort and understanding, and from puppeteering, which names the speaker as the agent; here no agent is named.
entries.how_to: Make the body part or the state the grammatical subject, not 'you': 'the arm grows light', not 'lift your arm'. Add 'by itself', 'on its own' or 'without you doing anything', and invite the listener to watch with curiosity. It fails when the response is one the listener plainly has to perform, or when a direct command a line later contradicts it. Follow each visible response with ratification.
examples: That hand begins to lift, all by itself, and you can simply watch it happen.
The eyelids are closing on their own now. You are not doing it. It is just happening.
Relaxation spreads without any help from you.
cues: 'by itself', 'all on its own', 'automatically', 'of its own accord'
'without you doing anything', 'you are not doing it', 'without any help from you'
'it just happens', 'it is happening'
body part or state as subject of a verb of movement or change, with no command: 'the arm lifts', 'the eyes close'
'that hand', 'the eyelids' in place of 'your' as the subject of such a verb (with distance or ownership words and no movement, it is body-dissociation)
'just watch it happen', 'notice it happening' said of a response in progress

not_this.why: that tells the listener they need not try or know; this frames a particular response as happening without their effort
puppeteering presents the speaker or the speaker's device as moving the body, even when a later sentence leaves that agent unstated; automaticity-framing presents the response as happening on its own
personification gives a body part or state wants, knowledge or a voice; here it moves or changes without a will of its own
that uses a movement as the route into trance; this is wording that presents a response as unwilled

evidence.note: Felt involuntariness is a measured feature of hypnotic responding, and passive wording has been shown to raise involuntariness ratings; whether control is really altered or only its report is disputed.

entries.consent_note: It lowers the listener's sense of authorship over what they do; it should not be used to carry responses the listener has not agreed to.

entries.name: Conscious / unconscious split
entries.summary: Speak of the conscious and unconscious minds as two separate listeners, and address suggestions to the unconscious one.
entries.definition: The writer treats 'your unconscious' (or 'subconscious') as a second listener with its own hearing, knowledge and abilities, distinct from the conscious mind, and addresses it or credits it directly. The device is that claim and that address: a statement about what the unconscious hears, knows or will do. What is done with the conscious mind in the same passage is a different entry. If it is offered free alternatives so that the response follows whatever it does, that is the conscious-unconscious bind; if it is given a decoy job, that is occupying the conscious mind; if it is told to stand down, that is bypassing the critic.
entries.how_to: Introduce the two minds early, in the pre-talk or the induction, as a plain fact. Give each a different job in the same sentence: the conscious mind wanders, doubts or listens; the unconscious learns, hears or responds. After that, address the unconscious directly for anything the conscious mind might argue with. Use one term throughout; switching between 'unconscious', 'subconscious' and 'deeper mind' weakens the picture. It fails with listeners who reject the model, so keep the claims modest.
examples: I am speaking to your unconscious mind now, and it hears every word.
Your unconscious already knows how to relax. It has done it every night of your life.
Your unconscious has kept you breathing all day without any help from you, and it can take care of this too.
cues: 'your unconscious', 'your subconscious', 'your deeper mind' as the subject of a verb of hearing, knowing, learning or doing
'I am speaking to your unconscious now', 'your unconscious can hear me'
'your unconscious knows', 'already knows how', 'can learn', 'will take care of'
'unconscious mind' or 'subconscious mind' named as one of two minds, with no alternatives offered to the conscious one
the same term for the second mind repeated across the passage as the addressee

not_this.why: label the bind when the conscious mind is given free rein or alternatives ('can listen or wander', 'whether or not you consciously ...') and the response is assigned to the unconscious either way; a sentence that only addresses or credits the unconscious is the split, and where both readings fit, the bind takes the label
that assigns the conscious mind a decoy job; the split assigns it nothing and speaks to the other mind
that tells the analytical part to rest or step aside; the split says nothing about the critic standing down
a part is picked out by a function ('the part of you that worries') and can be one of many; the unconscious is the one generic second mind, called by that name

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: A standard Ericksonian teaching device; there is no evidence for an unconscious mind that hears and acts as a separate listener, and the wording has not been shown to beat direct suggestion.

entries.consent_note: It tells the listener their conscious attention is not needed, so say beforehand what the suggestions will cover.

entries.name: Parts
entries.summary: Address a part of the listener picked out by what it does, such as 'the part of you that worries', as if it were a separate person.
entries.definition: The writer picks out one function, wish or habit and speaks of it as a part with its own aims, then talks to it, thanks it, gives it a job or sets it against another part. The part is defined by what it does and has no name or personality of its own. It differs from the conscious / unconscious split, which has one fixed pair, and from a persona, which is a whole alternate self.
entries.how_to: Name the part by its function in the listener's terms, and grant it a good intention before asking anything of it. Then address it directly, or have the listener address it. Use parts to hold two attitudes at once: one part may doubt while another responds. Keep to one or two parts in a recorded script, since the listener cannot answer back, and end by stating that the parts belong to one person.
examples: I would like to speak to the part of you that puts things off. That part can listen closely now, because this is meant for it.
Let the part of you that already knows how to be calm come forward.
One part of you may still be wondering whether this is working, while another part has already let go.
cues: 'part of you', 'a part of you that', 'that part'
'one part ... another part'
direct address to a part: 'I am speaking to the part that'
'thank that part', 'that part can rest', 'give that part a new job'
'come forward', 'step back' said of a part
'the side of you', 'the voice in you that' with a function attached

not_this.why: that addresses the unconscious as the one generic second mind; parts are picked out by specific functions and can be numerous
a persona has a name and traits of its own; a part is picked out by its function
when an analysing or checking part is only told to rest or step aside, label the bypass; parts-work addresses or negotiates with a functional part
that assigns the analytical mind a decoy task to occupy it; parts-work addresses or negotiates with a function-specific part
personification gives a body part, state or object a will; a part is a division of the self

origin.source: Watkins & Watkins, Ego States: Theory and Therapy (1997)

evidence.note: Ego-state and related parts therapies are widely practised and have some outcome studies; the claim that parts are real separate entities is not established, and the wording itself is untested.

entries.consent_note: Do not use to sideline a part that is objecting to the session; reunite the parts before the end.

entries.name: Positive intention
aliases: what is this part trying to do for you
entries.summary: Treat the part that objects or causes the problem as well-meaning, and ask or state what it is trying to do for the listener.
entries.definition: A way of addressing a part: the writer separates what the part does (the worry, the habit, the holding back) from what it wants for the listener (safety, rest, respect), and presumes the second is good. The intention is either asked for or supplied, and the part is thanked for it. That turns an opponent into an ally whose aim can be met some other way. It is the parts form of reframing: the new meaning is given to the motive of a part, where plain reframing relabels an experience and resistance-as-participation relabels the resisting itself.
entries.how_to: Name the part by what it does, in the listener's words, and say outright that it has been trying to help. In live work, ask what it wants for the person and wait; in a recording, offer two or three likely intentions and let the listener pick ('to keep you safe, to keep you ready, or something else you know better than I do'). Thank it. Only then separate aim from method: the aim stays, the method can change. Do not use the move to overrule the part; if the intention is real, the script has to offer a way of meeting it, or the objection returns.
examples: The part of you that keeps you tense has been trying to protect you. It has worked hard, and it deserves thanks for that.
Ask that restless part what it wants for you. Perhaps to keep you ready, perhaps to keep you safe. Whatever the answer is, it is on your side.
That doubting voice is not your enemy. It only wants to be sure you are all right, and it can keep doing that while you rest.
cues: 'trying to protect you', 'trying to help you', 'trying to do for you' said of a part, habit or feeling
'what does that part want for you', 'what is it trying to do for you'
'means well', 'has a good reason', 'on your side', 'not your enemy' said of a part
'positive intention', 'good intention', 'its purpose'
'thank that part for' followed by a protective aim
aim split from method: 'it wants you safe; it has just been going about it the hard way'

not_this.why: that calls the resisting itself part of the process; this credits the resisting part with a good motive and leaves the resistance as it is
the recipe contains this as one step, between signalling the part and generating alternatives; label this entry when the step stands alone
plain reframing gives a new meaning to an experience or event; this one always works through a part and its motive

origin.source: Bandler & Grinder, Reframing: Neuro-Linguistic Programming and the Transformation of Meaning (1982)

evidence.note: A core NLP presupposition, shared in different words by ego-state and other parts therapies; the claim that every behaviour has a positive intention is an operating assumption, not a finding, and the wording has not been tested by itself.

entries.consent_note: An objecting part may be right; do not use the good-intention framing to argue the listener past a real reservation about the session.

entries.name: Body detachment
entries.summary: Suggest that a limb or the whole body feels distant, absent or as if it belongs to someone else.
