entries.definition: The writer separates awareness from the body: the body sleeps while the mind stays awake, a hand feels far away, an arm is 'that arm' and no longer quite the listener's. The split is between the self and the body or one part of it. It differs from numbness as a convincer, which removes feeling from an area as a test, and from heaviness and floating, which change how the body feels without separating it from the listener.
entries.how_to: Build it from ordinary relaxation: heaviness first, then stillness, then distance. Change 'your arm' to 'that arm' or 'the body' and describe it as resting somewhere apart from the listener's attention. For the whole body, pair 'the body sleeps' with 'the mind stays here with my voice'. Always reverse it explicitly, restoring full feeling and ownership, before waking.
examples: Your body can go to sleep now, while your mind stays awake and listening.
That arm feels very far away, as if it belonged to someone else resting nearby.
Your hands are resting somewhere down there, and you can no longer quite tell where.
cues: 'body asleep', 'the body sleeps while the mind'
'that arm', 'the body', 'those legs' replacing 'your', with a word of distance or ownership and no movement verb or outside vantage point
'far away', 'distant', 'as if it belonged to someone else', 'not yours'
'the body can rest without you', 'the body takes care of itself down there'
'you can no longer feel where your hands are', 'hard to tell where your legs end'
'only your mind remains', 'just a mind, just awareness'

not_this.why: that removes sensation from an area, usually to be tested; this removes ownership or nearness
that moves the viewpoint outside to watch; here the body recedes and the viewpoint stays
heavy or floating is still the listener's own body

evidence.note: Hypnotic analgesia has good controlled evidence and dissociative wording is one standard way to suggest it; 'body asleep, mind awake' as a distinct state is practitioner usage and unverified.

entries.consent_note: Lingering numbness or unreality is an unwanted after-effect; restore normal feeling explicitly, and do not mask pain that needs attention.

entries.name: Persona / alter
entries.summary: Define a named alternate self with its own traits, presented as separate from the everyday self and able to take its place.
entries.definition: The writer defines a second self: a name and a short list of traits and behaviours, presented as someone other than the everyday self, who steps aside while the persona is present. That presentation is the device. The cues that bring the persona forward and send it back are trigger installation and are labeled as that alongside this entry; a persona with no switch cue is still a persona. It differs from a part, which is one function with no name, and from role assignment, which gives the same self a role to play.
entries.how_to: Build it in order: name, three or four concrete traits, how it speaks or moves, then the switch-in cue, then the switch-out cue. Rehearse both switches in the session. State what the persona shares with the everyday self (memory, values, limits) and when the cue does not work. Keep traits behavioural; vague traits give the listener nothing to do. Always include the way back and a removal instruction.
examples: When you hear the words 'time for Sol', the calm, steady one called Sol steps forward and you rest behind them.
Sol speaks slowly, stands tall, and is never in a hurry. When I say 'thank you, Sol', you return, fully yourself.
She has her own name and her own way of smiling, and she is here only when invited.
cues: a proper name assigned to a self other than the listener's own
'steps forward', 'comes out', 'takes over', 'switches in'
'you step back', 'you rest behind', 'you watch from inside'
trait list attached to the name: 'X is ..., X always ...'
paired switch cues: 'when you hear ...' and 'when I say ... you return'
third-person talk about the persona, then direct address to it by name

not_this.why: a role is played by the same self; a persona is presented as a separate self that replaces it
renaming gives the one self a new name; here two selves each have a name
a part is a function without name, traits or switch cue

evidence.note: Suggested alternate identities can be role-enacted on cue, as sociocognitive studies of hypnosis show; durable separate personas are claimed by the community without independent validation.

entries.consent_note: It persists after the session and can be fired by cue; agree it in advance, state who may use the cue, and provide a switch-out and a removal.

entries.name: Externalization
entries.summary: Take a thought, feeling or the listener's will and place it outside them as an object or agent.
entries.definition: The writer turns an inner thing into an outer one: a worry becomes a stone in the hand, tension becomes a coat to take off, the will becomes something handed to the speaker. Once outside, it can be looked at, moved, left behind or given away. It differs from dissociation proper, where the listener moves away from the experience, and from container imagery, which is about what the thing is put into once it is out.
entries.how_to: Name the inner thing in the listener's words, then give it a form: a shape, colour, weight and location outside the body. Describe the moment it leaves, then do one thing with it: set it down, watch it shrink, hand it over. Say what the listener feels in the space it leaves. Use one object per feeling; a crowd of objects becomes a scene and loses the effect.
examples: Let that worry gather in your hand like a small grey stone, and set the stone down beside you.
The tension is not you. It is something you have been carrying, and you can put it down.
Picture your need to stay in charge as a set of keys, and place them on the table for now.
cues: 'outside you', 'out of you', 'in front of you' said of a thought or feeling
'give it a shape', 'a colour', 'a weight' followed by a location outside the listener
'set it down', 'put it down', 'hand it over', 'leave it there' said of an inner thing given physical form
'it is not you', 'something you have been carrying' when followed by placing it outside
an inner noun (worry, doubt, control) made into a physical object and placed outside the listener
'watch it drift away', 'watch it shrink' said of the object once it has a form outside the listener

not_this.why: that supplies the box or vault; externalization is the step of making the inner thing an outer object
there the state is a substance that fills, coats or drains through the body; label externalization when one discrete thing ends up outside the body and is set down, handed over or left
there the listener steps away from the experience; here the experience is taken out of the listener
personification gives a thing wants, knowledge or a voice; externalization is the move outside, and an externalized thing that then wants or speaks takes both labels

origin.source: White & Epston, Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends (1990)

evidence.note: Externalizing a problem is a core narrative-therapy practice and common in hypnotic imagery; outcome evidence is for the therapies as a whole, not for this wording alone.

entries.consent_note: When the thing handed over is the listener's will, judgment or control, state that it is returned at the end of the session.

entries.name: Six-step reframing
entries.summary: Contact the part behind an unwanted behavior by signal, find its purpose, have it pick new ways to meet it, check for objections, and rehearse the change.
entries.definition: A fixed NLP procedure for an unwanted habit or symptom. The behavior is attributed to a part of the listener, a yes/no signal is set up with that part, its purpose is separated from the behavior, new behaviors that serve the same purpose are generated and accepted, and other parts are asked whether they object. It is done without the listener needing to know consciously what the purpose or the new behaviors are. What makes it this recipe is the full sequence with its closing objection check; a single address to a part is parts work, and the purpose step alone is positive intention.
entries.how_to: Name the behavior neutrally and speak to the part with respect; it is treated as an ally doing a job badly, not as an enemy. Establish a signal the listener cannot easily fake, such as a change in a sensation, and calibrate it for yes and no before asking anything that matters. Ask for at least three alternatives, each as quick and reliable as the old behavior. Never skip the objection check: if another part objects, go back to generating alternatives with that part included. In a recording there is no one to read the signals, so write pauses and let the listener note their own.
examples: I'd like to speak to the part of you that runs the late-night snacking. If that part is willing to communicate, let it give a signal you can notice, perhaps a feeling in one hand.
That part has been doing this for a good reason. Let it show you, or simply know for itself, what it has been trying to get for you.
Now ask inside: does any other part of you object to these new choices? If the answer is no, imagine the next evening at home, and notice what you do instead.
cues: 'the part of you that...' or 'the part responsible for X' addressed directly
a signal being set up and calibrated: 'let that signal get stronger for yes, weaker for no'
'what is it trying to do for you' / 'positive intention' / 'separate the behavior from the purpose'
'your creative part' asked for 'three new ways' or 'other choices'
'does any other part object?' / 'ecology check'
an imagined next occasion at the end, with the new behavior in place

not_this.why: that is any address to or negotiation with a part; this is the whole fixed sequence ending in an objection check
that is the single move of crediting a part with a good purpose, which is step three here
a reframe gives an experience a new meaning in a sentence or two; this is a procedure that changes the behavior, not a statement

steps.text: Name the unwanted behavior and attribute it to a part of the listener, which is then addressed directly.
Ask the part to communicate, and settle on an involuntary signal for yes and for no.
Separate the behavior from its purpose: ask the part what it is trying to do for the listener, with or without telling the conscious mind.
Ask a creative part to produce new behaviors that serve the same purpose, and have the original part choose at least three it accepts, signalling yes for each.
Ask the part to take responsibility for using the new choices, and have the listener imagine the next occasion with one of them in place.
Ask whether any other part objects; if a signal comes, return to generating alternatives with that part.

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Frogs into Princes: Neuro Linguistic Programming, Real People Press (1979)

evidence.note: Widely taught in NLP training with no controlled trials of the procedure; the signals are real ideomotor or attentional effects, but nothing shows they report the views of separate inner parts.

entries.consent_note: The change is meant to persist after the session and may be negotiated without the listener consciously knowing its content, so agree beforehand which behavior is being worked on.

entries.name: Pronoun shift
entries.summary: Change the pronoun used for the listener partway through, so the grammar itself separates them from who they were a moment ago.
entries.definition: A deliberate change in how the listener is referred to inside the script: from 'you' to 'I' so the listener's inner voice takes over, to 'we' for merging with the speaker, or to 'it' for objectification. It is dissociation done in grammar: the new pronoun stands the listener somewhere else in relation to their own experience. The device is the switch point. It differs from first-person suggestion, which is in the first person throughout, and from third-person self-reference, which has the listener stop using 'I' for themselves.
entries.how_to: Establish one pronoun first, then switch at a marked moment (after a deepener, at a peak) and keep the new one consistently. Announce the switch or let it happen silently; silent switches are subtler but harder to follow. A switch that flips back and forth by accident reads as an error, not a device.
examples: You breathe slowly, you let go... and I breathe slowly, I let go.
You've been listening alone. Now we sink together, we rest together.
You are still. I am still. I am calm.
cues: second-person passage followed by the same content in first person
'you' replaced by 'we' mid-passage
listener referred to as 'it' after earlier 'you'
announced switch: 'now say it as I'

not_this.why: object language is the content; a shift to 'it' is one way of delivering it
second-person narration keeps 'you' as protagonist without a switch
first-person suggestion uses 'I' throughout, including an 'I' voice running at the same time as a 'you' lead; a pronoun shift needs a switch point

evidence.note: Widely used in community scripts; pronoun effects on self-reference are studied in psychology but not this device in hypnosis.

entries.consent_note: A shift to 'it' or a merged 'we' works below notice for many listeners and should be within what they agreed to.

entries.name: Third-person self-reference
entries.summary: Have the listener refer to themselves by an assigned term instead of 'I' and 'me'.
entries.definition: A pronoun shift carried into the listener's own speech: they say 'this one is calm' or use an assigned name rather than 'I'. It differs from the parent pronoun shift, which changes how the speaker refers to the listener, and from renaming, which assigns the term without requiring it in self-reference.
entries.how_to: Give the replacement term, give an example sentence, and ask the listener to repeat a few lines in that form. Correct or ratify slips in the script. It works best combined with repeat-after-me and an agreed scope; outside the session it should switch back.
examples: Say it the new way: 'This one is relaxed.'
No more 'I' for now. The Listener breathes. The Listener rests.
When you answer, answer as Seven: 'Seven is ready.'
cues: 'no more I' / 'don't say I'
'say it as ...' + third-person sentence
listener speech lines using a name or 'this one' instead of 'I'
correction of 'I' to an assigned term

not_this.why: renaming assigns the term; this requires the listener to use it for themselves
first-person suggestion has the listener say 'I'; this removes 'I'

evidence.note: Third-person self-talk is studied as a self-distancing tool that lowers emotional reactivity, but its community use for identity change is untested.

entries.consent_note: Removing 'I' targets self-concept and should be agreed and limited to the session.

entries.name: Conditioning
entries.summary: Build a lasting response by pairing cues with states, attaching consequences to behavior, and repeating until it runs without effort.
entries.definition: Conditioning covers every device that works by learning over repetitions, not by a single accepted suggestion. It has three nested families: classical conditioning (pairing a cue with a state), operant conditioning (following behavior with reward or cost), and triggers and anchors (installing, testing, bounding and removing cues). The rows that sit directly in this family are the practice devices that supply the repetitions: repeat listening, habit stacking, drill, mantra, affirmations and repeat after me. What separates the family from plain suggestion is that the text arranges repeated trials or schedules them.
entries.how_to: Decide first what must be learned. If a cue should evoke a feeling or state, use the classical conditioning children. If a behavior should become more or less frequent, use the operant children. If the cue must be named, tested, limited or removed, use triggers and anchors. Then add a practice device from this level to supply repetitions: drill inside the session, repeat listening across days, habit stacking to place the behavior in daily life, and mantra or repeat after me when the listener should produce the words themselves. State scope and a way to undo anything meant to last.

not_this.why: a single suggestion for a later response; conditioning is the repeated pairing or practice that builds it
repeating a suggestion's wording for emphasis, with no cue-response trials or schedule
works by commitment and consistency across escalating asks, not by association or consequence

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927); Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: Classical and operant conditioning are among the best-established findings in psychology, but whether spoken suggestion in a recording produces true conditioning, as opposed to expectancy and practiced compliance, has not been tested directly.

entries.consent_note: Conditioning is meant to outlast the session, so the listener should know beforehand what is being trained, where it applies, and how it can be undone.

entries.name: Repeat listening
entries.summary: Tell the listener how often and for how long to listen or practice.
entries.definition: The script, or its description, prescribes repetition across sessions: a frequency, a duration, or a condition for stopping. It is an instruction about using the recording, not a suggestion delivered inside it. It differs from drill, which repeats a response within one session, and from the craving frame, which describes relistening as a need instead of prescribing it.
entries.how_to: Put it in the pre-talk or description and repeat it just before or after waking. Give a concrete number and an end point: once a day for two weeks, then as needed. Spaced sessions hold better than several plays in one sitting, so prefer daily over back-to-back. State what to do if a day is missed, so one gap does not end the practice. It fails when the schedule is vague ('listen often') or open-ended with no review point.
examples: Listen once a day for the next fourteen days, at about the same time each day.
Play this recording every night this week. After seven nights, decide whether to carry on.
Three sessions a week is enough. If you miss one, simply pick it up at the next.
cues: frequency or timing phrases: 'once a day', 'every night', 'twice a week', 'come back tomorrow'
a stated course length or end point: 'for two weeks', 'until it feels automatic', 'then as needed'
a missed-day or review clause: 'if you miss a day', 'after a week, decide whether to continue'
appears in the description, pre-talk or the last lines before the wake-up

not_this.why: says future sessions will go faster and deeper ('each time you listen...'); a schedule says when and how often to listen and predicts nothing
assigns a separate action to carry out (an exercise, a report, an errand); a schedule only prescribes replaying or redoing the session itself
describes relistening as need or addiction; a schedule is a plain instruction
repeats the response many times inside one session, not across days

evidence.note: Daily self-hypnosis or recording practice is standard clinical advice and the spacing effect on learning is well replicated, but the best schedule for hypnotic suggestions has not been established.

entries.consent_note: A schedule multiplies exposure to everything else in the file, so say what repeated listening is expected to do and give an end point or review point.

entries.name: Habit stacking
entries.summary: Attach the new behavior to something the listener already does every day, in a when-then sentence.
entries.definition: The writer names a specific existing routine or situation and binds the new behavior to it: when X happens, you do Y. The plan is stated openly and the listener is expected to hold it deliberately; that is what separates it from an installed trigger, which is framed as automatic. Habit stacking in the strict sense uses an existing habit as the cue; the broader implementation intention accepts any specified situation.
entries.how_to: Pick a cue that already happens daily, has a clear end point, and occurs where the new behavior is possible. Write one cue and one small, concrete behavior in a single when-then sentence, then have the listener rehearse it in imagination once or twice. Having the listener say the plan in the first person helps. It fails with vague cues ('when you have time'), cues that vary from day to day, or behaviors too large to do on the spot.
examples: Whenever you finish brushing your teeth, you take three slow breaths before you leave the bathroom.
As soon as you sit down at your desk in the morning, you write the one task that matters most.
Say it to yourself now: when I put the kettle on, I stand tall and let my shoulders drop.
cues: 'whenever you [daily routine], you [behavior]'
'right after you ...', 'as soon as you ...', 'every time you finish ...'
first-person plan form: 'when I ..., I will ...', 'if ..., then I ...'
the cue is an ordinary routine: brushing teeth, pouring coffee, sitting down, getting into bed
the response is a deliberate action the listener performs, not a state that arrives by itself

not_this.why: also uses an everyday cue, but the response is framed as automatic and installed, not a plan the listener carries out
any suggestion for a later response; habit stacking is specifically an openly stated plan tied to an existing routine
links a response to something happening now in the session, not to a recurring cue in daily life

origin.source: James Clear, Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones, Avery (2018)

evidence.note: If-then plans have a large experimental literature showing better goal follow-through; 'habit stacking' is a self-help name for the special case of using an existing habit as the cue, and delivery under hypnosis has not been shown to add to the effect.

entries.consent_note: The behavior is meant to recur in daily life after the session, so the cue and the behavior should be ones the listener has chosen or agreed to.

entries.name: Drill
entries.summary: Fire the cue, get the response, reset, and do it again many times in one session.
entries.definition: A drill is a block of repeated cue-response-reset cycles inside a single session, continued past the point where the response first works. Its purpose is fluency: the response becomes faster and needs less effort. It differs from a trigger test, which fires the cue once or twice as proof, and from fractionation, where the cycling is used to deepen trance and not to train a specific response.
entries.how_to: Place it straight after the response has been installed and has worked once. Keep every cycle the same: cue, response, a short ratification, reset. Run at least five or six cycles and shorten the gaps or the wording as you go, so the response has to arrive faster. Announce the number of rounds so the block has an end. It fails when the reset is skipped, because then nothing is left to respond with, and it drags when no cycle differs in pace from the last.
examples: Say the word 'steady' and feel your shoulders drop. Good. Shake it off. And again: 'steady'. Good. Shake it off. Once more, faster this time.
We'll practice this ten times. Press your thumb and finger together, feel the calm arrive, then let go. That was one.
Again. Breathe in, say the word, feel your shoulders drop. And release. Again.
cues: 'again', 'once more', 'one more time', 'and again' repeated across a passage
three or more consecutive cue-response-reset cycles with near-identical wording
explicit practice language: 'let's practice', 'we'll do this ten times', 'another round'
numbered rounds: 'that was one', 'round three'
a reset instruction between firings: 'and come back up', 'open your eyes', 'let it go'
speed-up remarks: 'faster this time', 'quicker each time'

not_this.why: fires a cue once or twice as proof ('let's test that'); a drill is an extended block of cue-response-reset practice, often with counted rounds or 'again'
cycles between partial waking and renewed trance; a drill repeatedly fires and resets a named cue-response link. If both patterns are present, both labels can apply
repeats the suggestion's wording without firing and resetting the response each time

evidence.note: Practice continued past first success improves retention and speed in skill and verbal learning, with gains that fade without later practice; drilling hypnotic triggers specifically has not been tested in controlled studies.

entries.consent_note: A drilled response is built to fire quickly and to last, so pair the drill with stated trigger conditions and a way to remove the response.

entries.name: Mantra
entries.summary: Repeat one short fixed phrase, or a fixed set of a few short lines, many times, spoken by the voice, by the listener, or by both.
entries.definition: A mantra is a short phrase with fixed wording, or a fixed set of two to four short lines cycled in the same order, repeated in a sustained block or dense clusters, beyond a few repetitions for emphasis. The fixed phrase and its recurrence are the device; it can carry a suggestion or serve as an attention focus. A repeated phrase used to induce trance may also be a repetition induction. A refrain returns at wider intervals, while immediate repetition (epizeuxis) can be brief emphasis rather than a sustained block. Ordinary suggestion repetition may vary the wording and need not form a repeated phrase.
entries.how_to: Keep the phrase under about eight words, rhythmic, and easy to say on one breath. Fix the wording and do not vary it. Introduce it once, slowly, then repeat it in a block of at least five; later blocks can be longer or layered under other speech. Decide who voices it: if the listener is to join in, say so, and say whether aloud or silently. It fails when the phrase is long, changes between repetitions, or is repeated too few times to set a rhythm.
examples: Calm and clear. Calm and clear. Calm and clear. Let the words carry on by themselves. Calm and clear.
One step, then the next. One step, then the next. One step, then the next. One step, then the next.
Repeat it with me, silently, on every breath out: I listen, I relax. I listen, I relax. I listen, I relax. I listen, I relax.
cues: the same short fixed phrase, or the same few short lines in the same order, repeated as a sustained block, typically five or more times
one identical line recurring densely within a passage
'your mantra', 'chant', 'keep repeating', 'over and over'
repeated lines set as their own block or list
stage directions such as [mantra loops under voice] or [x10]

not_this.why: uses sustained repetition to lead into trance; label mantra as well when the same short fixed phrase forms a sustained repeated block
immediately repeats a word or short phrase, often just for emphasis; a mantra sustains a fixed phrase as a block, so a span can exhibit both
a line that returns at intervals through the script, not in a dense repeated block
repeats a suggestion a few times, often reworded; a mantra sustains fixed wording as a phrase
instructs the listener to say supplied words, even once; a mantra is the repeated phrase, whoever voices it, and both labels can apply

evidence.note: Repetition reliably raises familiarity and judged truth of a statement, and repeated-phrase meditation has relaxation studies, but lasting change in belief or behavior from a mantra inside a hypnosis script has not been shown.

entries.name: Repeat after me
entries.summary: Tell the listener to say the suggestion themselves, aloud or silently, in words the writer supplies.
entries.definition: The writer gives the exact words and instructs the listener to produce them, so the listener becomes the speaker of the suggestion. The defining feature is the instruction to voice it; the words can be said once or many times. It differs from first-person scripting, where the text is in the listener's voice but nobody tells them to say it, and from asking for a yes, where the listener only assents to the writer's statement.
entries.how_to: Give short lines, one clause each, in the first person. Leave a silence after each line that is long enough to say it; on a recording, about one and a half times the length of the line. Say whether to speak aloud or in the mind, and ratify after the gap. Start with lines that are easy to say and move toward the one that matters. It fails when lines are too long to hold in memory or the gap is too short to answer in.
examples: Repeat after me, out loud or in your mind: I am listening. ... Good. I am relaxing. ... That's right.
Say it with me now: I can do this.
In your own inner voice, tell yourself: every breath makes me calmer. ... And again.
cues: 'repeat after me', 'say it with me', 'say these words', 'tell yourself', each followed by the line to be said
'out loud or in your mind', 'in your own voice', 'silently'
a quoted or set-off first-person line followed by a written pause or [pause for response]
a second-person instruction immediately followed by a first-person line
ratification right after the gap: 'good', 'that's right', 'again'

not_this.why: writes the suggestion as 'I' without instructing the listener to say it
has the listener state, write or sign a commitment to future conduct; if the writer supplies a promise to repeat, both labels can apply
asks the listener to supply the words or reasons themselves ('tell me why'); repeat after me supplies the words
asks only for a yes or a nod, not for the listener to voice the supplied content
repeats a fixed phrase many times by any voice; repeat after me is the instruction to voice supplied words, even once, and both labels can apply

evidence.note: Laboratory work shows that self-generated material is remembered better and that stating a position can shift attitude toward it, but the script device itself has no controlled studies and the size of any lasting effect is unknown.

entries.consent_note: Words the listener says can later be cited back as their own commitment, so do not treat a line repeated on instruction as consent to anything.

entries.name: Classical conditioning
entries.summary: Devices that work by pairing: a cue is presented with a state often enough that the cue alone begins to evoke it.
entries.definition: Classical conditioning is learning by association between a cue and a response the listener does not choose, such as relaxation, arousal, calm or liking. The children of this family build an association (pairing and its variants), move it to a new cue (second-order conditioning), replace it (counterconditioning), widen it (generalization), narrow it (discrimination) or let it fade (extinction). It differs from operant conditioning, where a consequence follows something the listener does, and from triggers and anchors, which are the named cue-installation procedures hypnotists build on top of pairing.
entries.how_to: Start with pairing: decide the cue, decide the state, and make sure the state is actually present each time the cue appears. Use pleasure pairing or evaluative conditioning when the aim is how something feels or is valued, not a discrete response. Once a cue works, use second-order conditioning to hand it to a new cue, generalization to carry it into new settings, and discrimination to fence it in. Use counterconditioning to replace an unwanted reaction and extinction to retire a cue. If the script announces a cue word and its effect in so many words, label the announcement under triggers and anchors and the repeated cue-state passes under pairing.

not_this.why: there the listener does something and a consequence follows; here a cue and a state simply occur together
that family holds the explicit install, test and removal procedures; this one holds the pairing operations underneath them

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927)

evidence.note: Classical conditioning is among the best-established findings in psychology; how well a few verbal pairings in a recording produce lasting conditioned responses in adults is much less studied, and expectancy explains part of what scripts attribute to conditioning.

entries.consent_note: Conditioned responses are meant to outlast the session and can fire without the listener deciding; say what is being paired and give it limits and a way to undo it.

entries.name: Pairing
entries.summary: Present a cue together with a state, again and again, so that the cue alone begins to bring the state.
entries.definition: Pairing is the basic operation of classical conditioning: a neutral cue (a word, sound, image or touch) is made to occur at the same moment as a state the listener is already feeling. After enough repetitions the cue evokes some of that state alone. It is this and not trigger installation when the script simply makes the two co-occur without stating a rule, and not anchoring when no single peak moment is captured.
entries.how_to: Produce the state first, by deepening or suggestion, and check the script has given it time to build. Then deliver the cue while the state is at or near its strongest, slightly before the peak if you can. Repeat the cue-state pass several times in the session and across sessions, keeping the cue identical each time. It fails when the cue is said while the state is absent, when the cue is an everyday word that also occurs constantly without the state, or when there are only one or two passes.
examples: That calm is all through you now. 'Settle.' Let it spread a little further. 'Settle.' Warm, slow, easy. 'Settle.'
Feel that heavy, warm ease in your shoulders... [chime] Warm ease, right down your arms... [chime] And the ease in your hands... [chime]
Breathe out and feel yourself sink. 'Down.' Breathe out, sink. 'Down.' The word and the sinking are becoming one thing.
cues: the same cue word or sound recurring right next to the same state description, three or more times
the cue dropped in as a bare word or sound between state descriptions, with no sentence saying what it does
'the word and the feeling', 'linked', 'connected', 'associated', 'tied together', 'go together', 'becoming one thing'
cue set off in quotes, italics or caps and followed by a ratifying state phrase ('there it is', 'that feeling again')
stage directions placing a sound effect at the moment a state is described

not_this.why: that states the rule ('when I say X you will Y', 'each time you hear X'); pairing just makes cue and state co-occur repeatedly and never says what the cue does

anchoring is an explicit capture step: the script builds or recalls one state and tells the listener to apply a cue 'as it peaks' or 'at its strongest'; label pairing when the speaker simply delivers the cue beside state descriptions, pass after pass, with no capture instruction
there the pleasant event follows something the listener did; here nothing is required of the listener

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927)

evidence.note: Cue-outcome pairing is well established in animals and humans, but it is strongest when the cue comes just before the outcome; the usual script order, state first and cue delivered into it, is simultaneous or backward pairing, which conditions weakly in the laboratory. Whether pairing a word with a suggested (not physically produced) state yields a true conditioned response, as opposed to an expectancy-driven one, has not been separated in controlled work.

entries.consent_note: The association is meant to persist after the session; tell the listener which cue is being paired with what.

entries.name: Pleasure pairing
entries.summary: Pair a target word, act or idea with pleasure or arousal, so the target itself comes to feel good.
entries.definition: Pleasure pairing is pairing in which the state is pleasure, comfort or arousal and the cue is the thing the writer wants the listener to like or seek: a word, a behavior, an idea, the voice. The pleasure is present at the same time as the target, not handed out afterwards. That timing is what separates it from pleasure as reward, where pleasure is delivered because the listener complied.
entries.how_to: Build the pleasant state first and keep it running. Then name the target repeatedly while the feeling is present, and say outright that the two belong together. Keep the target wording fixed. It lands when the pleasure is real at that moment (physical comfort, relief, arousal the listener already has); it is weak when pleasure is only asserted. If the pleasure is made conditional on doing something, you have moved to reinforcement and should label that instead.
examples: Feel how good it is to let go... and as that good feeling spreads, think the word 'focus'. Focus. The word and the pleasure, together.
That warm, easy pleasure is here already, all through you. And in the middle of it, the idea of listening. Listening, and the warmth. Listening, and how good this feels.
Every slow breath is a small pleasure, and every slow breath carries the thought: I am calm and capable.
cues: 'X feels good', 'X is pleasure', 'it feels so good to X' repeated with the same X
pleasure or arousal words (good, warm, bliss, pleasure, tingle) adjacent to the target term in several consecutive sentences
equations of target and pleasure: 'obedience is pleasure', 'focus is bliss'
'X and the pleasure, together', 'that good feeling attaches to X', 'the feeling soaks into the word'
no condition on the pleasure (no 'when you do', 'because you', 'as a reward', 'you have earned')

not_this.why: reward arrives after and because of compliance; pairing has target and pleasure present together with no condition
that ties pleasure to trance depth; this ties pleasure to a target word, act or idea
that changes liking by pairing with already-valued things in general; this specifically uses a felt pleasure or arousal state

evidence.note: Appetitive and sexual conditioning are shown in laboratory studies with real stimuli, but the script practice of pairing a concept with suggested pleasure has no independent validation; community claims of durable rewiring outrun the evidence.

entries.consent_note: It aims to change what the listener finds pleasant beyond the session; name the target in the description and avoid pairing pleasure with things the listener has not agreed to want.

entries.name: Evaluative conditioning
entries.summary: Place a neutral thing next to things the listener already likes or dislikes, so it takes on their value.
entries.definition: Evaluative conditioning changes how much something is liked by pairing it with positively or negatively valued things. What changes is an attitude, not a reflex or a state: the target ends up feeling good, safe, dull or unpleasant. Unlike pleasure pairing it needs no bodily state at the moment of pairing; valued words, images, people or memories do the work.
entries.how_to: Pick the target and a small set of things the listener certainly values in the direction you want. Mention the target next to them, in the same sentence or image, many times, with varied companions. Do not argue for the link; simple adjacency is the device. To lower the value of a habit or thought, set it beside dull, stale or unappealing things. It works best for targets the listener has no strong prior opinion about, and it is weak against firm attitudes.
examples: Your desk in the morning. Clean light, fresh coffee, the quiet of a good start. Your desk, and that feeling of a day going well.
The old habit sits there with the stale air, the grey afternoon, the cold cup you forgot to finish.
Practice. Sunlight. Practice. A friend's laugh. Practice. The ease of something done well.
cues: a target term repeatedly placed beside strongly valenced words or images without any argument linking them
lists that alternate the target with liked (or disliked) items
the target described in the company of warmth, home, safety, success, or of staleness, grey, cold
no causal or reward language ('because', 'when you do', 'earn')
the same target with a different valued companion each time

not_this.why: that pairs the target with a pleasure state felt in the moment; this pairs it with valued things and changes liking

that takes a cue with a definite existing reaction and holds a felt state against it to replace the reaction; label this when the target is only placed among liked or disliked things, with no state built or maintained and no old reaction named
reframing states a new meaning outright; evaluative conditioning never asserts anything, it only places things side by side
seeding makes an idea familiar for later use; this changes its value by its company

origin.source: Levey & Martin, Classical conditioning of human 'evaluative' responses (1975)

evidence.note: The Hofmann et al. (2010) meta-analysis finds a reliable medium-sized effect on liking, larger when people notice the pairing; effects without awareness of the pairing are disputed, and durability outside the laboratory is less certain.

entries.consent_note: It is usually not announced and shifts attitudes that last beyond the session; the listener should know which likes or dislikes the script is built to move.

entries.name: Second-order conditioning
entries.summary: Pair a new cue with a cue that already works, so the response passes to the new cue.
entries.definition: Second-order conditioning builds a new cue from an old one. The established cue is fired to produce its response, and the new cue is presented with it; the original state is never produced directly. This differs from plain pairing, where the new cue meets the state itself, and from trigger chaining, where one response sets off a different trigger in sequence.
entries.how_to: Use it only with a cue that already works reliably, and fire that cue first so the response is present. Present the new cue with it several times, then test the new cue alone. Keep refreshing the original cue with its real state, because firing it over and over only as a carrier weakens it. Typical uses are moving a spoken trigger to a gesture or image the listener can use alone, or handing a response from the recording's voice to an everyday cue.
examples: You know what 'settle' does. Say it inwardly now, and as the calm arrives, press your thumb and finger together. Settle, and press. Soon the press alone is enough.
Each time the chime sends you down, see the colour blue. Chime, and blue. Before long, blue will do what the chime does.
'Focus.' There it is, that clear, narrow attention. Now close your hand around your pen. 'Focus', and the pen in your hand. Once more: 'focus', and the pen.
cues: an already-installed cue fired in the passage, with a new cue presented at the moment its response arrives
old cue and new cue alternating in close succession ('settle, and press', 'chime, and blue')
'will do what X does', 'works just like', 'takes on the same power', said while X is being fired
'soon Y alone will be enough', 'you won't need X any more'
the original state is not built again; only the old cue is used to bring it

not_this.why: pairing joins a cue to the state itself; this joins a cue to another cue
installation states what the new cue does, even when it says 'Y now works like X'; label this only when X is actually fired in the passage and Y is presented with its response
chaining makes one trigger's response fire a different trigger; here one response is copied onto a second cue
stacking adds more responses to one cue; this adds more cues to one response

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927)

evidence.note: Second-order conditioning is established in the laboratory but is weaker and less durable than first-order conditioning; its use to transfer hypnotic triggers is practitioner practice without direct study.

entries.consent_note: It adds cues that work after the session, sometimes everyday ones; state the new cue plainly and give it the same limits and removal as the original.

entries.name: Counterconditioning
entries.summary: Present a cue that brings an unwanted reaction while the listener is in an incompatible state, so the new reaction replaces the old.
entries.definition: Counterconditioning pairs a cue that already evokes one response, usually anxiety or aversion, with a state that cannot coexist with it, usually deep relaxation. With repetition the cue comes to evoke the new state. It differs from extinction, which presents the cue with nothing, and from collapsing anchors, which fires two installed anchors at once instead of meeting the real cue.
entries.how_to: Establish the incompatible state first and make it strong. Bring in the problem cue in imagination, starting with its mildest form, and hold it only while the calm holds. Return to the calm, then step up, in a graded list from least to most difficult. Do not raise the cue faster than the listener can manage; if overwhelmed, they may break off, and that escape can reinforce avoidance, with nobody present in a recording to guide them. The same form is used in reverse in aversion scripts, where a liked cue is paired with something unpleasant.
examples: Stay with that loose, easy calm. Now picture the lecture hall from far away, just the doors. Still calm. Still breathing slowly. Good. Let the picture go.
Bring the phone into view while your shoulders stay soft. The phone, and soft shoulders. The phone, and slow breath.
Now a step closer: the exam paper face down on the desk, and that same steady warmth in your chest. If the warmth thins, let the picture fade and rest. When it is back, look again.
cues: a feared or disliked cue introduced while a relaxed state is explicitly maintained
graded approach: 'from far away', 'a little closer', 'the next step', 'only as far as stays comfortable'
'still calm', 'stay relaxed as you picture ...', 'and the calm stays'
alternation between the difficult image and a return to relaxation or a safe place
'instead of the old feeling', 'where there used to be tension, now ...'

not_this.why: extinction shows the cue with no outcome and waits for fading; counterconditioning supplies an opposing response
that fires two installed anchors together; this brings the real problem cue into a prepared state
rehearsal has the listener imagine performing the future behavior; here the listener only holds the difficult image while a stated calm is kept, and the image is dropped when the calm slips
that only places a target among liked or disliked things; label counterconditioning when the cue has a named existing reaction and a felt state or sensation is held against it

origin.source: Wolpe, Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958)

evidence.note: Systematic desensitization has controlled trials for phobias and anxiety; later work suggests graded exposure does much of the work and that the relaxation component is not always necessary. Aversive counterconditioning has a poorer record and a history of harmful use.

entries.consent_note: It deliberately evokes distressing material and aims at lasting change; the listener should have chosen the target, be able to stop at any step, and aversive forms need explicit agreement.

entries.name: Generalization
entries.summary: Tell the listener the conditioned response also happens with similar cues, other voices or new settings.
entries.definition: Generalization is the spread of a conditioned response from the trained cue to cues that resemble it, and from the training setting to others. In a script it is the passage that widens a response on purpose: any voice, any room, written as well as spoken, alone as well as in session. It is the opposite of discrimination, which fences the response in.
entries.how_to: Place it after the response is established and tested. List the new cues or settings concretely and, where possible, rehearse each in imagination so the response is actually practised there. Vary the conditions of practice across sessions (time, place, posture); that does more than declaring it. Widen only as far as is useful and safe: a response that fires on any similar word, from anyone, anywhere, is hard to control and hard to remove.
examples: This calm is not only for this chair. It comes at your desk, on the train, in a crowded room, wherever you take that slow breath.
Whether you hear the word, read it, or simply think it, the same ease follows.
What you can do here with your eyes closed, you can do with your eyes open, standing, in the middle of an ordinary day.
cues: 'not only here', 'anywhere', 'wherever you are', 'in every part of your life'
'whether you hear it, read it or think it', 'in any voice', 'spoken or written'
lists of settings or cue forms each mapped to the same response
'just as well as', 'the same way', 'carries over', 'spreads into'
'eyes open as well as closed', 'awake as well as in trance'

not_this.why: discrimination narrows which cue fires the response; generalization widens it
that deliberately pairs one specific new cue with the old one; generalization extends to a class of similar cues or settings
a stated grant that a partner or other named people may fire a trigger is the shareable trigger; label generalization when the widening is over cue forms (heard, read, thought) or settings
future pacing rehearses one specific future moment; generalization asserts the range of cues and contexts
a bare 'always' or 'everywhere' is the quantifier; label generalization when it extends a conditioned response to new cues or settings

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927)

evidence.note: Generalization gradients are well established: the response weakens as the cue departs from the trained one. A newly conditioned response usually survives a change of setting fairly well, and it is extinction, not acquisition, that is strongly tied to context; practice in varied conditions helps transfer in skill learning. Whether telling a listener a response generalizes makes it do so has not been tested apart from expectancy.

entries.consent_note: It extends effects into daily life and to cues the listener does not control; say how far the response is meant to reach and exclude unsafe settings such as driving.

entries.name: Discrimination
entries.summary: Present a look-alike cue and let nothing happen, then present the true cue and let the response follow, so the response is trained to the exact cue.
entries.definition: Discrimination trains a response to occur to one cue and not to others that resemble it. The training is by contrast: a near miss (a similar word, the same word in casual use, the cue in the wrong tone) is presented and nothing happens, then the true cue is presented and the response follows. It is the opposite of generalization. A boundary that is only stated is not this entry: stated conditions on a named trigger are trigger conditions, and a stated limit on the session's suggestions as a whole is scope limits.
entries.how_to: State the working cue exactly, then name the near misses and say they have no effect. Where you can, demonstrate it: present a similar word or the same word in casual use, let nothing happen, then present the true cue and let the response follow. Choose cues that are distinctive enough to discriminate at all; a common word needs a qualifying condition such as a tone, a phrase or a speaker. A boundary that is only declared once is weaker than one that is rehearsed.
examples: Listen: 'we should settle the bill.' Nothing. Just a sentence. And now: 'settle now.' There. That is the one your body answers.
[soft bell, high] That one passes you by. [soft bell, low] And that one takes you down. High, nothing. Low, down.
If you hear 'drop' in conversation, nothing happens. When you hear it here, spoken slowly, like this... drop... you know the difference.
cues: a contrast pair in the passage: a similar cue presented with no response, then the true cue with the response
the cue word spoken inside an ordinary sentence and followed by 'nothing', 'just a word', 'passes you by'
'that one ... and this one', 'you know the difference', 'feel the difference', 'not that, this'
two near-identical words, tones or sounds presented in alternation with different stated outcomes
the true cue fired straight after a non-response and ratified ('there', 'that is the one')

not_this.why: a condition that is only stated for a named trigger ('only in my voice', 'in conversation it is just a word') is trigger conditions; label discrimination when the look-alike is actually presented with no response and the true cue then fired
a stated limit on where the session's suggestions apply is scope limits; discrimination is the contrast presentation of cues, whatever its motive
extinction presents the trained cue itself with nothing following until it fades; here a look-alike gets nothing and the trained cue still gets its response
generalization widens the range of cues and settings; discrimination narrows it

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927)

evidence.note: Discrimination learning through differential pairing is well established; in scripts the boundary is usually only stated, and how well a stated boundary holds has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: Usually protective, since it keeps a persistent response from firing on everyday look-alikes; tell the listener which cue is being kept and which are being trained out, and do not rely on it alone to keep a response out of unsafe settings.

entries.name: Extinction
entries.summary: Present the cue again and again with nothing following it, until the conditioned response fades.
entries.definition: Extinction weakens a conditioned response by presenting its cue without the state it was paired with. Nothing replaces the response; the cue simply stops predicting anything. That separates it from counterconditioning, which supplies an opposing response, and from trigger removal, which cancels a cue by direct statement. Extinction suppresses the association; it does not erase it.
entries.how_to: Present the cue repeatedly in a neutral, alert state and let nothing happen, saying so plainly each time. Use many passes and repeat them on later days and in different settings, because extinguished responses come back after a gap, in the original context, or after one fresh pairing. For retiring an installed trigger, combine it with an explicit removal statement. Writers also need it as a warning: firing a cue again and again without renewing the state wears the cue out.
examples: Hear the word now, wide awake: 'settle'. Nothing follows. 'Settle'. Just a sound. 'Settle'. Fainter each time, an ordinary word again.
The chime rings, and you stay exactly as you are. It rings again, and again nothing changes.
Each time you notice that old cue and simply carry on, it loses a little more of its pull.
cues: a known cue repeated with explicit non-response: 'nothing happens', 'nothing follows', 'you stay as you are'
'just a word', 'just a sound', 'an ordinary word again'
'fades', 'weaker each time', 'loses its pull', 'less and less'
the cue presented while alertness is stressed ('wide awake', 'eyes open')
a cue earlier followed by a state, now repeatedly presented while the passage marks its old response as absent

not_this.why: removal cancels the cue by declaration, and one later demonstration of non-response is still removal; label extinction when repeated presentations of the cue without its old response do the work
that pairs the cue with a new incompatible response; extinction presents it without its old outcome
satiation repeats a word until its meaning blurs; extinction repeatedly presents a previously effective cue without its old response
expiry sets an end time in advance; extinction is the repeated unpaired presentation itself

origin.source: Pavlov, Conditioned Reflexes (1927)

evidence.note: Extinction is well established, as are spontaneous recovery, renewal in the original context and rapid reacquisition, so a faded response should not be assumed gone; its use to retire hypnotic triggers has not been studied directly.

entries.consent_note: Tell the listener an extinguished response can return after a break or a new pairing, so they do not treat it as permanently removed.

entries.name: Operant conditioning
entries.summary: Devices that change how often the listener does something by controlling what follows it: reward, relief, cost, or nothing.
entries.definition: The operant family covers every device built on a contingency: if the listener does X, Y follows. It differs from classical conditioning, where a cue is paired with a state regardless of what the listener does. Here the listener's own response comes first and the consequence comes after. The family also holds the two operations that change how much a consequence is worth (deprivation and satiation) and the ways of arranging consequences over time (shaping, schedules, chains, tokens).
entries.how_to: First name the response you want and make sure the script can tell when it happens; in a recording you cannot see the listener, so reward responses you have just instructed or that are near-certain. To build a new response, use shaping with positive reinforcement and praise, a marker signal for precise timing, then thin to intermittent reinforcement so it lasts. To set up an exchange, use the earn-it contingency or points and tokens. To change how much a reward is worth, use deprivation and avoid satiation. Use negative reinforcement, punishment and response cost sparingly and only inside agreed limits. Pairing a cue with a state without any contingency belongs to classical-conditioning, and installed cues belong to triggers-anchors.

not_this.why: pairs a cue with a state regardless of what the listener does; no if-you-do-X contingency
installs a cue that evokes a response; the operant family manages what follows the response
builds agreement through commitment and consistency, not through consequences

origin.source: Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: The principles are among the best supported in psychology for observed behavior with real consequences; whether words in a one-way recording act as reinforcers for an unobserved listener has not been tested directly.

entries.consent_note: Contingencies meant to keep running after the session (points, penalties, earned permissions, denial) should be described up front and given an end condition.

entries.name: Positive reinforcement
entries.summary: Right after the listener does what you want, give them something they want, so they do it again.
entries.definition: Positive reinforcement is adding something wanted immediately after a response, which makes that response more likely in future. It is defined by the contingency and the order: response first, reward second, and the reward is given because of the response. A pleasant feeling that is handed out with no response required is pairing, not reinforcement. Strictly, something is a reinforcer only if the behavior goes up; in a script the writer can only arrange the contingency and state it.
entries.how_to: Place the reward in the sentence directly after the instructed response, not paragraphs later. Say what earned it ('because you let go'), so the listener knows which response to repeat. Pick rewards this listener values: approval, relief, pleasure, rest, permission, progress. In a recording, reward only responses that are close to certain (a breath, an exhale, continuing to listen), or the reward lands on nothing and reads as false. Reward every time while the response is new, then less often.
examples: Take one slow breath for me. Good. Feel that warm ease spread through your chest as your reward for doing exactly that.
Each time you let a thought go, you get a little more of that calm you came here for.
You followed that so well, and because you did, you can sink into the softest part of this now.
cues: instruction followed at once by a pleasant consequence
'because you ...', 'for doing that', 'as your reward'
'every time you ..., you get/feel ...'
'you've earned', 'that's what you get for'
reward wording that names the response it follows

not_this.why: pairing presents the good feeling alongside a cue whatever the listener does; reinforcement gives it only after a response

a contingent suggestion hangs the wanted response on something that is happening anyway ('as you breathe out, you relax'); in reinforcement the listener's own act is the condition and what follows is a payoff for it
ratification confirms that a response is happening and real; reinforcement adds a wanted consequence for it
negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant; positive reinforcement adds something wanted

origin.source: Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: Reinforcement of observed behavior is very well established; a recorded reward that cannot be made contingent on what the listener actually did is an approximation that has not been tested.

entries.name: Praise
entries.summary: Say a short word of approval the moment the listener does the wanted thing.
entries.definition: Praise is positive reinforcement delivered as verbal approval immediately after a wanted response. Praise evaluates the listener or the response, or states the speaker's approval ('well done', 'you did that perfectly', 'I'm pleased'). Ratification instead confirms that a response is occurring or has occurred ('there it is', 'that's right'). A bare 'good' can serve either function; use the surrounding wording and timing to decide.
entries.how_to: Put the praise in the beat right after the instruction, leaving just enough pause for the response. Keep it to one to three words so it does not interrupt the state. Tie it to a specific response at least some of the time ('good, just like that breath'). Praise is only worth something if the listener values the speaker's approval, so establish warmth or authority first, and do not praise so constantly that it turns into background noise.
examples: Let your shoulders drop. Good. That's exactly what I wanted.
Well done. You followed that perfectly.
Breathe out slowly... good... I'm so pleased with how you're doing this.
cues: evaluation of a completed response: 'well done', 'you did that perfectly', 'you're doing so well'
approval of the listener: 'good boy/girl', 'I'm proud of you', 'I'm pleased'
'good' or 'very good' extended with what was done well: 'good, just like that breath'
approval placed immediately after the wanted response

not_this.why: ratification confirms the response is happening; praise judges the listener as having done well
labeling assigns a standing trait to get matching behavior later; praise rewards one response just made
affection flooding is heavy approval given up front, not contingent on any response

evidence.note: Contingent praise raises rates of praised behavior in classroom and clinical studies; its effect depends on the listener valuing the source, and recorded praise for unobserved responses is untested.

entries.name: Pleasure as reward
entries.summary: Suggest a burst of pleasant feeling that arrives the moment the listener complies.
entries.definition: Pleasure as reward is positive reinforcement where the reward is a suggested bodily sensation: a wave of warmth, a tingle, a rush of calm or pleasure. The sensation is stated as the result of the response, not just described alongside it. That contingency separates it from pleasure pairing, where a word or idea is simply presented together with pleasure. It usually depends on a suggested sensation the listener can already produce.
entries.how_to: Establish the sensation earlier in the session so the listener can call it up, then deliver it in one short sentence right after the response. State the link plainly: you did this, so you get this. Keep each pulse brief and let it fade, so the next one is wanted. If the listener does not actually feel the sensation, the reward is empty, so use permissive wording the first few times and build on whatever they report or can be expected to feel.
examples: And because you let that thought go, a warm wave of pleasure rolls down through you. That is what letting go earns.
Each time you answer yes, feel a small pulse of bliss, like a reward dropped right into your chest.
You relaxed your hands when I asked. Here it comes: that soft, glowing feeling, just for doing as you were told.
cues: 'wave of pleasure', 'pulse', 'rush', 'glow' placed directly after a response
'because you ..., feel ...'
'every time you obey/follow/let go, it feels ...'
'your reward is', 'here it comes'
sensation wording that is conditional on an act, not free-standing description

not_this.why: pairing presents pleasure together with a word or idea, no response required; here pleasure is given for a response
the deepener ties pleasure to depth of trance, not to a specific act of compliance
a suggested sensation on its own is a phenomenon or proof; it becomes a reward only when made contingent on a response

evidence.note: Suggested sensations are a documented hypnotic response, but no controlled work shows that a suggested pleasure acts as a reinforcer for the behavior it follows.

entries.consent_note: When the reward is attached to obedience in general and suggested to continue after the session, say so in the description and give it a scope.

entries.name: Marker signal
entries.summary: Use one brief, distinct sound or word to mark the exact moment the listener gets it right, with the reward to follow.
entries.definition: A marker is a short, unmistakable signal that has first been paired with reward and is then given at the instant of the wanted response. It works as a conditioned reinforcer and as a bridge: it tells the listener which moment earned the reward even if the reward itself arrives a second later. It differs from praise in being a fixed, content-free signal used only for marking, and from a trigger in that it follows the response instead of calling for it.
entries.how_to: Choose a signal used for nothing else in the script: a click, a chime, a single clipped word. Charge it first by presenting it together with reward several times ('each time you hear this, a pulse of warmth'). Then give it at the exact moment of the response, once, and follow with the reward at least most of the time. Never use the marker to get attention or to command; one signal, one meaning. In text scripts, write it as a stage direction or a consistent marker word.
examples: [click] There. Each time you hear that sound it means: yes, exactly that, and the warm feeling follows.
Let the thought go... [click] ...and there is your reward.
When I say 'yes' in that one short way, you got it right. Breathe out... yes.
cues: stage directions: [click], [chime], [snap] placed immediately after a response
explanation of the signal: 'that sound means you did it right'
one fixed short word repeated after response moments, where the script has earlier defined it as a signal
an early passage pairing the signal with reward before it is used
the marked response precedes the signal; the reward may follow the signal

not_this.why: a sound trigger comes before the response and evokes it; a marker comes after the response and rewards it
praise carries approval in its meaning and varies in wording; a marker is one fixed signal whose value comes from pairing
ratification confirms a response in ordinary words; a marker is a trained signal backed by reward

origin.source: Karen Pryor, Don't Shoot the Dog!: The Art of Teaching and Training, Sunshine Books (1984)

evidence.note: Conditioned reinforcement is well established; animal studies comparing a clicker with prompt primary reward alone are mixed, and marker use in recorded hypnosis is practitioner lore.

entries.name: Negative reinforcement
entries.summary: Let the wanted response end something unpleasant, so the relief strengthens that response.
entries.definition: Negative reinforcement strengthens a response by removing or preventing something aversive when the response occurs. 'Negative' means something is taken away; the behavior still goes up, so it is not punishment. In scripts the aversive thing is usually already present or deliberately built: tension, effort, the strain of holding on, mental noise, an unmet urge. The device is the stated contingency that doing the wanted thing makes it stop.
entries.how_to: Name a discomfort the listener really has or that you have just built (held breath, clenched fist, the effort of thinking, waiting). Then state the exit: the moment you do X, it stops. Deliver the relief at once and describe it. The cleanest uses work with discomfort that is already there, such as the effort of resisting sleepiness. Building distress in order to sell the relief moves toward the coercive family and needs agreement.
examples: Hold that tension in your fists... and the moment you let your mind go quiet, all of it drains away.
It takes effort to keep thinking. As soon as you stop trying, that effort is gone.
That restless feeling eases every time you follow the next instruction. Follow, and it settles.
cues: 'the moment you ..., it stops/eases/drains away'
'as soon as you give in, the tension is gone'
'relief', 'release', 'let it stop', 'no more effort'
an unpleasant state described first, then ended by compliance
'it only gets easier when you ...'

not_this.why: punishment adds something unpleasant after an unwanted response to reduce it; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a wanted one
fear-then-relief uses the relieved moment to slip in a request; here relief is the consequence of the response itself
tense-and-release is a relaxation method using muscle contrast, with no contingency on compliance

origin.source: Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: Escape and avoidance learning are well established; relief that is only suggested in a recording has not been studied as a reinforcer.

entries.consent_note: If the script creates the discomfort it then relieves, the listener should have agreed to that in advance; a speaker who is the only source of relief is the dependency pattern.

entries.name: Punishment
entries.summary: Follow the unwanted response with something unpleasant, so the listener does it less.
entries.definition: Punishment is a consequence that reduces the response it follows. In its plain form something unpleasant is added: a suggested bad feeling, a scolding, an assigned chore, extra work. It is the mirror of reinforcement and is defined by its effect on behavior, not by how harsh it sounds. Taking away something the listener already holds is the response-cost variant; suspending access to rewards for a stated period is the time-out variant.
entries.how_to: State the rule before it can be broken: which response, what follows. Keep the consequence mild, brief and immediate, and always give the wanted alternative a reward, because punishment alone tells the listener what not to do and nothing about what to do. In a recording you cannot see the lapse, so punishment usually takes the form of a standing rule the listener applies to themselves. Punishment produces avoidance and resentment more reliably than it produces learning; most scripts do better with reinforcement of the alternative.
examples: Each time your attention wanders off, you feel a small, cold prickle of unease.
Speak before you are asked, and you write the rule out ten times before tomorrow.
Open your eyes before I say, and you will hear exactly how disappointed I am.
cues: 'if you ..., then' followed by an unpleasant consequence
'you will be corrected', 'there are consequences', 'you'll regret'
extra work added after a named lapse: 'do it again', assigned lines or chores (nothing the listener holds is taken away)
suggested unpleasant sensation tied to a named lapse
scolding after a lapse: 'no', 'bad', 'wrong', 'I'm disappointed'

not_this.why: negative reinforcement increases a response by ending something unpleasant; punishment decreases a response by adding it
there the unwanted response only goes unrewarded; punishment adds something unpleasant for it
humiliation uses shame as emotional charge and need not be contingent on any lapse
fear of leaving attaches dread to stopping the relationship or practice, not to one specified response

origin.source: Azrin & Holz, Punishment, in Honig (ed.), Operant Behavior: Areas of Research and Application (1966)

evidence.note: Punishment suppresses behavior in controlled studies, but with known side effects (avoidance, emotional responding, recovery when it stops); suggested or self-applied punishment from a script is unstudied.

entries.consent_note: Punishment should be agreed in advance, limited in scope and removable; rules that tell the listener to punish themselves after the session need an explicit end condition.

entries.name: Response cost
entries.summary: After the unwanted response, take away something the listener values.
entries.definition: Response cost is punishment by removal: a lapse costs the listener points, a privilege, a permission, progress or a pleasant state they already had. It differs from plain punishment in that nothing unpleasant is added; something good is subtracted. It needs the listener to hold something that can be taken, so it usually sits on top of a points system, a streak or an earned permission.
entries.how_to: Give the listener something first, then state what a lapse costs. Keep the cost small and proportionate, and make it recoverable, or the listener stops caring once everything is gone. Say how to earn it back. Pair it with rewards for the wanted response so the overall balance stays positive.
examples: If you speak before you are asked, you lose one of the points you earned tonight.
Skip a day and the streak goes back to zero.
Move before the count ends, and the permission you earned is withdrawn until tomorrow.
cues: 'you lose', 'I take away', 'is withdrawn', 'forfeit'
an accumulated total wiped: 'the streak goes back to zero', 'your points reset'
'minus', 'deduct', 'costs you'
privilege or permission revoked after a named lapse
the thing removed was given or earned earlier in the script or series

not_this.why: plain punishment adds something unpleasant or extra work; response cost removes something already held
time-out suspends the chance to earn or receive rewards for a stated period; response cost takes back a specific thing already earned
deprivation withholds in advance to raise a reward's value; response cost removes as a consequence of a lapse
extinction simply stops delivering the outcome; response cost takes back what was already given

origin.source: Weiner, Some effects of response cost upon human operant behavior, Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior (1962)

evidence.note: Response cost reduces target behavior in token-economy and classroom studies; nothing is known about self-applied penalties prescribed by a recording.

entries.consent_note: Penalties that run after the session, especially any involving money or real privileges, need prior agreement and a stated way to stop.

entries.name: Time-out
entries.summary: After the unwanted response, shut off the listener's access to rewards for a short, stated period.
entries.definition: Punishment by a fixed interval in which nothing good can be earned or received: no praise, no pleasant suggestion, no permission, no progress. Nothing unpleasant is added and nothing already earned is taken back; the listener is simply put outside the rewarding situation until the period ends. It only works if the time outside is plainly worse than the time inside, so it depends on a session or practice that is already rich in reward.
entries.how_to: State the rule before any lapse: which response triggers it and how long it lasts. Keep the period short and exact (a count, three breaths, a minute, the rest of this round), mark its end clearly, and return to full warmth at once without a lecture. In a recording the speaker cannot see the lapse, so write it as a standing rule the listener applies ('if that happens, you wait out the next ten breaths with nothing from me') or as a scripted pause after an instruction the listener is told they may have failed. Pair it with reward for the wanted response, and never leave the end open: an unbounded time-out is withdrawal of contact, not a consequence.
examples: If you open your eyes before I say, the pleasant feeling switches off for ten slow breaths. Then it comes back.
Speak out of turn and you sit out the next round. No praise, no points, until the round after.
When your attention drifts, I stop for a count of five. Nothing from me until five. Then we go on as before.
cues: 'for the next ten breaths / one minute / until I count to', attached to a named lapse
'no praise', 'no reward', 'nothing from me', 'you get nothing until'
'sit out', 'wait out', 'you wait', 'time-out'
'switches off', 'is paused', 'on hold' said of a pleasant state, with a stated return
'then it comes back', 'then we go on' closing the interval
a scripted silence framed as the consequence of a lapse

not_this.why: response cost takes back something already held (points, a streak); time-out removes the chance to receive anything for a period and takes nothing back
extinction stops rewarding one response with no end date and no announcement; time-out is a brief, bounded suspension of all reward after a lapse
deprivation withholds in advance to raise a reward's value; time-out withholds afterwards as a consequence
hot-and-cold withdraws warmth unpredictably to tighten attachment; time-out follows a stated rule, has a stated length and ends on schedule

evidence.note: Time-out from positive reinforcement reduces target behavior in controlled studies, mostly with children and when the surrounding setting is rewarding; a self-applied or scripted time-out in a recording is unstudied.

entries.consent_note: Agree it in advance, state its length, and end it on time; withdrawal of contact with no stated end, or carried into daily life, is the coercive hot-and-cold pattern and not a time-out.

entries.name: Shaping
entries.summary: Reward a small, easy version of the response first, then require a little more each time before rewarding.
entries.definition: Shaping builds a response the listener cannot yet produce by reinforcing successive approximations to it. The criterion for reward moves: what earned praise at the start no longer earns it later. That moving criterion is what separates shaping from simple repeated reinforcement. It also differs from a compliance ladder, which escalates what is asked through commitment; shaping escalates what is rewarded.
entries.how_to: Define the final response, then find a first step almost anyone already does (a slower breath, a moment of stillness). Reward it, repeat, then ask for slightly more and reward only that. Keep steps small enough that the listener nearly always succeeds; if a step is likely to fail, split it. Across a series, start each session one step back from where the last ended. In a recording you cannot check each step, so word steps permissively and reward effort as well as result early on.
examples: Just let your eyes blink a little slower. Good. Now let them stay closed a moment longer each time... good. And now let them rest closed.
Last time, three quiet breaths were enough. Today, hold that quiet for ten, and then you'll hear me say well done.
First only your fingers went loose, and that was right. Now the whole hand. Good. Now let it travel up the arm before I praise you again.
cues: 'a little more each time', 'this time, go further before ...'
'that was enough before; now ...'
