the same response requested in increasing size or duration, with reward after each
'first just ..., then ..., now ...' with praise between steps
explicit reference to an earlier, easier standard

not_this.why: the ladder relies on consistency with earlier agreements; shaping relies on a reward criterion that moves
graded escalation asks for more each time; shaping is the reinforcement of each approximation along the way
chaining links several different responses into a sequence; shaping refines one response

origin.source: Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: Shaping is a core, well-tested procedure when a trainer observes each approximation; a fixed script cannot adjust the criterion to the listener, and that version is untested.

entries.consent_note: Because each step is small, the listener may not notice how far the endpoint is from the start; state the endpoint of a shaped series up front.

entries.name: Intermittent reinforcement
entries.summary: Reward the response only some of the time, unpredictably, so it keeps going when rewards stop.
entries.definition: Intermittent reinforcement delivers the reward after some occurrences of the response and not others. Behavior maintained this way persists far longer without reward than behavior rewarded every time (the partial reinforcement extinction effect). Variable schedules, where the listener cannot predict which response pays, give the steadiest responding. It is a way of scheduling a reward, so it always sits on top of some reinforcer.
entries.how_to: Use continuous reward while the response is new, then thin it: reward most times, then about half, then occasionally, without a visible pattern. Do not thin so fast that the response dies. In a single recording the schedule is fixed, so repeat listeners learn it; to keep it unpredictable, vary across files or announce that the reward will come 'sometimes'. Say openly that not every response is rewarded, so a missed reward reads as part of the design and not as failure.
examples: Sometimes when you say the word, the warm wave comes. Sometimes it doesn't. You never know which time, so you keep saying it.
Breathe out. Nothing yet. Breathe out again. Nothing. And again... there. Good.
I won't praise you every time. Only now and then, when you least expect it.
cues: 'sometimes', 'now and then', 'not every time', 'you never know when'
'maybe this time', 'you'll have to keep going to find out'
repeated identical instruction where only some repetitions are followed by reward
praise or reward density that drops across a passage while the instruction continues
'unpredictable', 'at random', 'when you least expect'

not_this.why: hot-and-cold alternates warmth with coldness or hostility in a relationship; an intermittent schedule only omits some rewards
extinction stops the reward entirely so the response fades; an intermittent schedule keeps paying occasionally so it persists
anticipation announces something coming and delays it once; a schedule governs reward across many responses

origin.source: Ferster & Skinner, Schedules of Reinforcement (1957)

evidence.note: Schedule effects and resistance to extinction are robust in laboratory work; in a fixed recording the 'random' schedule is the same on every listen, and its effect there is untested.

entries.consent_note: This is the schedule behind gambling persistence and it makes a habit harder to drop; tell the listener it is in use, and do not combine it with relisten or dependency suggestions without agreement.

entries.name: Differential reinforcement
entries.summary: Reward one response and give nothing for the other, so the listener shifts toward the rewarded one.
entries.definition: Differential reinforcement puts two responses on different consequences: the wanted one earns reward, the unwanted one earns no reaction at all. Nothing unpleasant is added, which separates it from punishment. The standard forms reward an alternative response (DRA), an incompatible response (DRI), or any stretch of time without the unwanted response (DRO).
entries.how_to: Name both responses so the contrast is clear, and pick a wanted response that can replace the unwanted one in the same moment (quiet instead of analysing, stillness instead of fidgeting). Reward the wanted one warmly and at once. Give the unwanted one flat neutrality: no scolding, no attention, just the absence of reward. This is the first thing to try before punishment, because it teaches what to do.
examples: When a thought comes, nothing happens. When you let it pass and return to my voice, you feel that small warm glow.
I only answer stillness. Fidget, and I simply wait. Settle, and I tell you how well you are doing.
Every minute that goes by without checking the clock earns you a deeper breath of calm.
cues: paired contrast: 'when you A, nothing; when you B, you get ...'
'I only reward', 'only when you', 'nothing for ..., everything for ...'
'instead of X, do Y, and ...'
'every minute/moment without ... earns'
explicit ignoring of one response beside reward of another

not_this.why: punishment adds an unpleasant consequence for the unwanted response; here the unwanted response just goes unrewarded
extinction only withholds what used to follow; differential reinforcement withholds from one response and rewards another in the same passage
discrimination restricts a response to one cue or setting; differential reinforcement chooses between two responses
thought replacement instructs a swap directly; differential reinforcement arranges consequences so the swap pays

evidence.note: DRA, DRI and DRO are standard, well-tested procedures in applied behavior analysis with an observer delivering consequences; script-delivered versions are untested.

entries.name: Behavior chaining
entries.summary: Link several responses into a fixed sequence, so finishing each one is the signal to start the next.
entries.definition: A behavior chain is a sequence of distinct responses in which each completed step serves as the cue for the next and, by leading toward the final reward, as a small reward for the step before. Only the end of the chain needs an outside reward. It differs from shaping, which refines one response, and from chaining anchors, where installed cues fire each other. The chain is taught either from the first step forward or from the last step backward.
entries.how_to: List the steps and fix their order; do not vary it between rehearsals. State each link explicitly: when you have done A, that is your signal for B. Put the reward at the end of the whole sequence. To teach it backward, rehearse the last step with its reward first, then add the step before it, so the listener always moves toward a part they already know. Rehearse the full chain several times in session.
examples: You sit down, and sitting down is your signal to close your eyes. Eyes closed is your signal for one slow breath. And that breath out drops you all the way into calm.
Kneel, then palms on your thighs, then eyes down, then the words. Always in that order, each one leading into the next, and at the end you hear me say good.
Putting the headphones on tells you to lie back. Lying back tells you to press play. Pressing play tells you to close your eyes, and then you get the rest you came for.
cues: 'and that is your signal to', 'which leads into', 'tells you to'
three or more distinct acts given in a fixed order
'always in that order', 'each step leads to the next'
'then ... then ... then ...' ending in a single reward
a completed act named as the start condition for the next act

not_this.why: chaining anchors links installed cues and states; behavior chaining links the listener's own acts
habit stacking attaches a new behavior to an existing daily routine; behavior chaining links distinct acts so completion of each cues the next
a contingent suggestion ties one response to an ongoing or certain event; a behavior chain links successive acts
shaping moves the criterion on one response; chaining joins different responses end to end

evidence.note: Forward and backward chaining are established teaching procedures for observed behavior; chains installed by spoken description alone have not been studied.

entries.consent_note: A chain meant to run by itself after the session is a posthypnotic routine; describe it up front and say how to drop it.

entries.name: Earn-it contingency
entries.summary: Make something the listener wants to do available only after they do something they want less.
entries.definition: The earn-it contingency uses an activity as the reward: access to a preferred activity is granted only after a less preferred one is done. It differs from ordinary positive reinforcement in that the reward is a thing the listener gets to do, usually by permission, not a thing they receive. The wording is a first-then rule. Premack's finding was that a more probable behavior will reinforce a less probable one.
entries.how_to: Find the thing the listener already wants at that moment: to rest, to sink deeper, to open their eyes, to hear the next part. Put the wanted response in front of it as a plain first-then rule, and keep the first part short and doable. Then grant the permission clearly and at once. It fails if the listener can simply take the wanted activity anyway, so use it where the script controls access or where the listener has agreed to wait for permission.
examples: First, three slow breaths counted out for me. Then you may let yourself sink all the way down.
You can rest in that quiet place as soon as you have repeated the phrase five times.
Finish the task I gave you this morning, and tonight you are allowed to listen to the next file.
cues: 'first ..., then you may ...'
'once you have ..., you can ...'
'you're allowed to ... only after'
'earn', 'earned the right to', 'not until you'
permission to do something wanted, conditional on a completed act

not_this.why: that variant belongs to tease and denial and gates built-up release; the earn-it rule is the general first-then form with any wanted activity
an implied directive makes an inner response signal itself by a movement; no wanted activity is being earned
a contingent suggestion links a response to something already happening; here a wanted activity is withheld until a task is done

origin.source: David Premack, Toward Empirical Behavior Laws: I. Positive Reinforcement, Psychological Review (1959)

evidence.note: Activity reinforcement is well supported, though later work (response deprivation) shows what matters is restricting access below baseline, not simply which activity is preferred.

entries.consent_note: Rules that gate everyday activities on tasks outside the session should be agreed in advance and time-limited.

entries.name: Points and tokens
entries.summary: Give symbolic rewards (points, stars, a streak count) that add up toward something the listener wants.
entries.definition: A token is a symbol given right after the response that has value only because it can be exchanged for, or counts toward, a real reward. Tokens bridge the gap between a response now and a reward later, and they make progress countable. A system needs three parts: what earns a token, what tokens buy or unlock, and who keeps count. A streak is a token system where the token is an unbroken run of days.
entries.how_to: State the earning rule and the exchange rule in one or two sentences, and keep the numbers small. Award the token at the moment of the response, by name ('that's one'). In a recording the listener keeps the count, so make counting easy and tell them where to record it. Set a reachable first exchange so the tokens gain value early. Decide whether tokens can be lost; if they can, see response cost.
examples: Each full session you finish is one point. Five points, and you move up to the next level of this series.
That's one. Every time you drop on the word, add one to your count, and tell me the total at the end.
Seven days in a row earns the reward file. Mark each day on your calendar after you listen.
cues: 'point', 'points', 'score', 'star', 'token', 'credit'
'streak', 'days in a row', 'level up', 'unlock'
'that's one', 'add one to your count'
an exchange rule: 'N points earns ...'
instruction to keep or report a running total

not_this.why: a marker signal marks the moment and is not saved up; tokens accumulate and are exchanged
a depth scale puts a number on the state, not on rewards earned
the sunk-cost appeal cites past investment as a reason to continue; a token system is the counting itself

origin.source: Ayllon & Azrin, The Token Economy (1968)

evidence.note: Token economies change behavior reliably in supervised settings; effects often fade when the system is withdrawn, and self-counted points from a recording are untested.

entries.consent_note: A points system runs between sessions; explain it before trance, and never tie points to money or to real-world obligations without separate agreement.

entries.name: Deprivation
entries.summary: Hold back something the listener wants for a while, so it is worth more when you offer it as a reward.
entries.definition: Deprivation is a motivating operation: restricting access to a reward raises its value and raises the behavior that has earned it before. It is not a consequence of any response; it is done in advance, to set up a later reward. That separates it from response cost, which removes something because of a lapse. In scripts the withheld thing is usually praise, rest, the pleasant state, permission or release.
entries.how_to: Withhold one specific thing and say so, so the listener knows what they are waiting for. Keep the wait long enough to be felt and short enough that they stay engaged. Then make the withheld thing available through the response you want. Withholding with no way to earn it is just frustration. Outside the session, keep any abstinence instruction time-limited and safe to follow.
examples: I'm not going to tell you how well you're doing for a while. You'll have to wait for it.
You have had the same word of approval after every round. For the next few rounds, I will hold it back and give it again at the end.
Until our next session, save that quiet feeling. Don't reach for it on your own. It will be stronger for the wait.
cues: a named, previously available reward withheld for a period: 'I'm not going to give you that praise for a while'
'save it' or 'go without' tied to a specific reward the listener has already had
wording that says the withheld reward will become more wanted or effective after the wait
the reward is withheld before a task or contingency, rather than removed after a lapse
absence of language actively heightening desire for the approaching reward

not_this.why: tease and denial actively raises desire and then withholds satisfaction; deprivation is the withholding alone, with any reward
response cost takes something away because of a lapse; deprivation withholds in advance to raise value
anticipation announces and delays an event; deprivation restricts access to a reward the listener already knows

origin.source: Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: Deprivation reliably raises the reinforcing value of food, attention and activities in controlled studies; the effect of merely announcing that praise or a feeling is being withheld is untested.

entries.consent_note: Withholding that continues after the session should be agreed, time-limited and never applied to sleep, food, medical needs or contact with other people.

entries.name: Satiation
entries.summary: Give so much of a reward, or so much of a behavior, that the listener stops wanting it.
entries.definition: Satiation is the opposite motivating operation to deprivation: free or repeated access to a reward lowers its value, and the behavior it maintained drops. As a deliberate device it is used to reduce an unwanted pull by supplying it past the point of wanting. More often it shows up as a fault: praise or pleasure handed out so densely that it stops working as a reward.
entries.how_to: To use it on purpose, give the listener unrestricted access to the thing with no task attached, and keep going past the point where it is enjoyable, then name the loss of interest. To avoid it by accident, ration rewards: keep praise short, let reward pulses fade before the next, and thin the schedule once the response is steady. If a passage repeats the same reward in every sentence, expect it to go flat.
examples: Go ahead and worry as much as you like. Worry on purpose, all of it, more, until it is simply boring and there is nothing left to pick at.
Have all the reassurance you want. Good, good, good, as much as you can take, until you notice you don't need to hear it any more.
Check the time again. And again. Keep checking until checking is the dullest thing in the world.
cues: 'as much as you want', 'all of it', 'more than you need'
'until you've had enough', 'until it's boring', 'until you're tired of it'
instruction to repeat an urge or behavior on purpose, many times, with a stated end point of losing interest
'you don't need it any more', 'it's lost its pull'

not_this.why: reverse psychology instructs the opposite of the desired response in expectation of resistance; satiation calls for engaging in a behavior until its pull fades
semantic satiation repeats one word until it loses meaning; this repeats a reward or behavior until it loses value
extinction withholds what used to follow a response; satiation supplies an outcome until it loses value
wearing down outlasts the listener's opposition; satiation uses up the value of a reward or urge

origin.source: Skinner, Science and Human Behavior (1953)

evidence.note: Satiation lowering reinforcer value is well established, and stimulus satiation and negative practice have clinical reports of mixed quality; deliberate satiation delivered by script is untested.

entries.name: Self-administered reinforcement
entries.summary: Teach the listener to reward themselves each time they do the wanted behavior, so it continues without the speaker.
entries.definition: Self-administered reinforcement hands delivery of the reward to the listener: they notice their own response and give themselves the praise, the pleasant feeling or the treat. It solves the recording's main problem, that the speaker cannot see the response, because the listener is always present when it happens. It differs from a trigger, which evokes a response from a cue, and from affirmations, which are repeated regardless of behavior. The self-reward is contingent on having done the thing.
entries.how_to: Specify three things: the behavior that earns it, the reward, and the exact form of delivery (a phrase said inwardly, a breath with a suggested feeling, a mark on a chart). Rehearse it in session at least twice: do the behavior in imagination, give the reward, feel it. Keep the reward small and quick so it can be given every time. Make the behavior something the listener chose, or the self-reward will feel hollow.
examples: Each time you finish what you set out to do, you tell yourself, quietly, 'well done', and you let yourself feel it.
When you notice you stayed calm, take one slow breath and give yourself that warm glow. You know how to make it now.
After every practice, you are the one who says 'good'. You don't need to wait to hear it from me.
cues: 'tell yourself', 'say to yourself', 'give yourself'
'reward yourself', 'let yourself feel proud'
'each time you notice you have ..., you ...'
'you don't need me to say it'
reflexive pronoun plus reward wording, conditional on a behavior

not_this.why: affirmations are repeated on a schedule whatever the listener did; self-reward is given only after the behavior
self-policing has the listener watch for and report lapses; self-reinforcement has them reward successes
an internal-event trigger makes a thought or feeling the cue for a response; here the listener's response is followed by a self-given reward

evidence.note: Self-reward is a studied component of self-management programs with positive results, though behavior analysts dispute whether it is true reinforcement or works through self-monitoring and commitment.

entries.consent_note: This is designed to keep a behavior going after the session without the speaker; the behavior being maintained should be one the listener asked for.

entries.name: Group contingency
entries.summary: Make a reward or penalty depend on how other members of a group behave, so members watch and press one another.
entries.definition: A contingency in which the consequence for one person is set by the behavior of others: the whole group earns it together, loses it together, or gets it according to what one named member does. The enforcement moves from the speaker to the peers, who remind, praise and pressure each other. It differs from every other operant entry in whose behavior is counted: there the listener's own response earns the listener's own consequence.
entries.how_to: State the rule in one sentence: which group, what behavior is counted, what the group gets or loses. Use it only where a real group exists and can see the count, such as a live group session, a community challenge, a server or a partnered pair. Prefer a shared reward for a shared target; penalties for the whole group over one member's lapse turn the group on that member. Report progress back to the group so the contingency stays in view, and give members an allowed way to help each other.
examples: When everyone in the room has let their eyes close, and only then, we go on to the part you have all been waiting for.
This week's bonus session unlocks when the whole group has logged five days of practice. Check on each other.
If your partner finishes their breathing practice tonight, you both get tomorrow's reward. If not, neither of you does.
cues: 'when everyone has', 'once all of you', 'if the whole group', 'only when every one of you'
a reward or unlock stated for 'all of you', 'the group', 'the team', 'you both'
one person's outcome tied to another's act: 'if your partner ..., you ...'
a group total or shared goal: 'together you need', 'the group's count'
instructions to check on, remind or encourage other members
'don't let the others down', 'they are counting on you'

not_this.why: social proof reports what others do as a guide; a group contingency makes the listener's outcome depend on what others do
a token economy counts one listener's own responses toward that listener's own reward; here the count is across people
unity invokes shared identity with no consequence attached; a group contingency attaches a stated reward or cost

origin.source: Barrish, Saunders & Wolf, Good behavior game: Effects of individual contingencies for group consequences on disruptive behavior in a classroom (1969)

evidence.note: Group contingencies change behavior reliably in supervised classrooms and similar settings; their use in recordings or online communities, where nobody verifies the count, is untested.

entries.consent_note: It recruits peers as enforcers and keeps running between sessions, so every member should agree to the rule beforehand and be able to leave the group without penalty to themselves or the others.

entries.name: Triggers and anchors
entries.summary: Devices that set up a cue so that, later, the cue alone brings back a state or sets off an action.
entries.definition: This family covers the life of a cue: making it (anchoring, trigger installation and its cue-type variants), proving and strengthening it (trigger test, trigger strengthening), combining cues (stacking, chaining, collapsing), and bounding or ending it (trigger conditions, shareable trigger, removal, expiry). It sits under conditioning because the cue-response link is treated as a learned association, but most script triggers are built by stated rule and rehearsal, not by many pairings. It has no nested families.
entries.how_to: Choose by how the link is made: use anchoring when a state is present and you tie a cue to it as it peaks; use trigger installation when you state a rule ('when X, you Y'). Pick the cue variant by who will fire it and where: word or sound for a recording, touch for self-use, everyday or internal events when the listener's own day should fire it. Follow any install with a trigger test, and write trigger conditions, and a removal or expiry clause, in the same passage as the install. Use stacking, chaining and collapsing only after single cues work.

not_this.why: that family is about pairing as a learning process; this one is about the named cue a script sets up and manages
a suggestion form for any after-session response; a trigger is the cue-bound case with its own install, test and removal steps

evidence.note: Cue-bound posthypnotic responses are well documented in hypnotizable people; the NLP anchoring account and claims of strong, lasting, automatic triggers in general listeners are not independently validated.

entries.consent_note: Everything in this family is meant to work after the session, so the listener should know before listening what cue is installed, what it does, who can fire it and how it ends.

entries.name: Anchoring
entries.summary: Build or recall a state, and at its strongest moment attach a distinct cue so the cue can bring the state back.
entries.definition: Anchoring ties a cue to a state the listener is having right now. The state comes first and the cue is applied at its peak, usually more than once. It differs from trigger installation, which states a rule about a future response and does not need the state to be present.
entries.how_to: First get the state: recall a vivid memory of it or build it with suggestion. Tell the listener to apply the cue (a touch, a word, an image) just as the feeling is strongest and to release it before the feeling fades. Repeat two or three times, break the state, then test by firing the cue alone. It fails when the state is weak, the cue is one the listener already uses all day, or the cue is applied after the peak has passed.
examples: Remember a time you felt completely sure of yourself. Let it build. As it reaches its strongest, press your thumb and first finger together. Hold. Now release.
Feel that calm at its fullest right now, and as you do, say the word 'harbor' silently to yourself.
Each time that focus comes back this clearly, touch your left wrist, so the touch and the focus belong together.
cues: 'as that feeling peaks', 'at its strongest', 'when it is at its fullest' followed by a cue instruction
'press your thumb and finger together', 'touch your wrist', 'say the word ... to yourself' during a described state
the words 'anchor', 'anchored', 'anchor this feeling'
state elicitation ('remember a time when...') immediately before a gesture or word instruction
'hold... and release' timing around the cue

not_this.why: installation declares a cue-response rule in words ('whenever X, you Y'); anchoring has the cue applied while the state is live. A passage that does both gets both labels
that is a stated when-then rule whose cue is a touch or gesture; a touch applied at the peak of a live state with no rule stated is anchoring
pairing is the general repeated co-presentation of cue and state; anchoring is the specific peak-timed, usually listener-applied form
that is the judgment bias from a reference number, unrelated to state cues

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Frogs into Princes: Neuro Linguistic Programming, Real People Press (1979)

evidence.note: Cue-state association is real conditioning, but NLP's claim that one or a few peak-timed pairings give a reliable, lasting state switch has not been shown in controlled studies.

entries.consent_note: The anchor is meant to work after the session, so say plainly what state is being tied to what cue.

entries.name: Trigger installation
entries.summary: Tell the listener that a named cue will produce a named response from now on.
entries.definition: Trigger installation is a posthypnotic suggestion in rule form: it names one cue and the one response that follows it. The link is made by stating it, not by having the state present, though rehearsal usually follows. It is the parent of the cue-type variants (word, sound, touch, visual, everyday, internal).
entries.how_to: Place it in the suggestion section, once trance is established. State the cue exactly, state one concrete response, and say it will happen automatically. Repeat the rule in the same words at least three times, then rehearse it with a trigger test. Give its conditions and its end in the same passage. Vague cues, more than one response at first install, or a cue that is a common word all weaken it.
examples: From now on, whenever I say the words 'settle down', your shoulders drop and your breathing slows, all on their own.
Each time you hear that phrase from me, you return to this exact feeling of calm focus. The phrase, then the feeling. Every time.
When you sit at your desk and say 'begin' to yourself, your attention narrows to the task in front of you.
cues: 'whenever I say...', 'each time you hear...', 'every time you see...' followed by a response
'from now on', 'from this moment', 'in the future' before a cue-response rule
a quoted or capitalized word or phrase named as a cue
'automatically', 'instantly', 'without thinking', 'all on its own' attached to the response
the words 'trigger', 'cue', 'signal', 'keyword'
the same when-then rule restated several times in close succession

not_this.why: anchoring attaches the cue during a live peak state; installation states the rule in words

the broader form; label it alone when the later response has no discrete, reusable cue (a time, a general change). A cue set up only for use inside the session is installation without being posthypnotic

ties a response to something already going on in the session (the breath, the voice, a count) and names no cue for anyone to deliver later; installation names a discrete cue and says it will work from now on
also a when-then sentence, but the response is a deliberate act the listener plans to carry out; an installed response is worded as happening by itself

evidence.note: Cued posthypnotic responding is documented in laboratory and clinical work, mainly in highly hypnotizable subjects; how long it lasts and how well it works from recordings for ordinary listeners is not established.

entries.consent_note: It persists after the session; the listener should agree to the cue and response beforehand and be told how it is limited and removed.

entries.name: Trigger word / phrase
entries.summary: Install a spoken or written word or short phrase as the cue.
entries.definition: A trigger whose cue is language: a single word or a fixed short phrase. It is the commonest cue type in recordings because the speaker can deliver it with no props. What marks it is that the exact wording is fixed and named.
entries.how_to: Choose a word or phrase that is distinct and unlikely to come up by accident; an odd pairing of two ordinary words is safer than one common word. Say it the same way every time, and mark it in the script with quotes or capitals so the performer does too. State who has to say it and in what manner, or it will fire from television and conversation.
examples: The words are 'quiet water'. When I say 'quiet water', your mind goes still.
From now on the word 'FOCUS', said by me in this tone, brings your attention to a single point.
Whenever you say 'steady now' to yourself, your hands stop shaking and your voice evens out.
cues: a word or phrase set off in quotes, capitals or italics and then reused verbatim later
'the word...', 'the phrase...', 'when I say...', 'when you hear the words...'
'keyword', 'trigger word', 'command word', 'special word'
the same marked word appearing alone as a one-word line later in the script

not_this.why: a mantra is repeated for its effect while repeating; a trigger word is said once to set off a response
that is a trigger of any cue type whose response is specifically return to trance
non-verbal sound, not language
a cue recognized by its look (symbol, color, picture); a word is a trigger word whether it is heard, read on a screen or said inwardly

evidence.note: Verbal cues for posthypnotic responses are standard in the clinical and experimental literature; reliability outside highly responsive, practiced listeners is unmeasured.

entries.consent_note: Pick a word that will not fire by accident in daily life, and tell the listener what it is before the session.

entries.name: Sound trigger
entries.summary: Install a non-verbal sound, such as a snap, bell or tone, as the cue.
entries.definition: A trigger whose cue is a sound with no words. Because the sound carries no meaning of its own, the script must tell the listener what it does. In audio it depends on production: the sound has to be made or mixed in at the right moments.
entries.how_to: Name the sound and its response in words first, then let the listener hear it and respond. Use the identical sound each time; a different snap or a new chime sample weakens the link. Write the sound into the script as a stage direction at every firing. Avoid sounds common in the listener's day (phone alerts, doorbells) unless the script limits the trigger to this recording or this voice.
examples: From now on, each time you hear me snap my fingers, your shoulders drop and your breath slows. [snap]
That soft bell is your signal. When it rings, your thoughts go quiet. [bell]
Whenever you hear three slow clicks on this recording, your whole body lets go. [click] [click] [click]
cues: 'snap', 'click', 'bell', 'chime', 'tone', 'gong', 'clap' inside a when-then rule
bracketed or parenthesized sound directions: [snap], (bell), *click*
'when you hear the sound of...', 'that sound means...', 'each time it rings'
'on the snap', 'at the sound'

not_this.why: that is the production choice of using sounds; this is a sound given a stated response
a marker signal says 'that was right' after a response; a sound trigger comes before and causes the response
a continuous beat for pacing, not a discrete cue with a response

evidence.note: Sound cues are ordinary conditioned stimuli and a stage and recording staple, but no controlled work shows a snap or bell does more than a spoken cue.

entries.consent_note: Common sounds occur outside the session, so limit the trigger to the recording or the speaker and say so.

entries.name: Touch / gesture trigger
entries.summary: Install a touch, gesture, posture or worn object as the cue.
entries.definition: A trigger whose cue is felt in or done with the body: pressing two fingers together, a hand on the chest, kneeling, putting on a ring or collar. In recordings the listener applies it themselves; in person the hypnotist may. It is the usual cue type for self-use because the listener carries it everywhere.
entries.how_to: Pick a touch or gesture that is exact, repeatable and not something the listener does without thinking. Specify place, pressure and duration ('thumb and first finger of the left hand, firm, for one breath'). Worn objects fire continuously while worn, so write what wearing means and what taking it off does. For touch by another person, say who is allowed.
examples: Whenever you press your thumb and first finger together and take one slow breath, this calm returns.
When you place your hand flat on your chest, you feel steady, and your voice comes out clear.
Each time you fasten that bracelet, you step into this focused state, and when you take it off, you step back out.
cues: 'press', 'squeeze', 'touch', 'tap', 'place your hand' inside a when-then rule
a named body location with a gesture: 'thumb and finger', 'your wrist', 'your shoulder'
'when you wear', 'when you put on', 'while it is on' with an object (ring, bracelet, collar)
'when you kneel', 'when you sit in this position', 'each time you take this posture'
'when I touch your...', 'a tap on the...'

not_this.why: anchoring applies a touch at the peak of a live state without stating a rule; label this only when a when-then rule names the touch, gesture, posture or object as the cue. A passage that anchors and then states the rule gets both
a limb drop used once to deepen, with no standing cue for later
an imagined or one-time act that stands for the change, not a reusable cue

evidence.note: Self-applied cue gestures are used in clinical self-hypnosis and relaxation training, but the NLP claims for kinesthetic anchors have not been independently confirmed.

entries.consent_note: State who may apply the touch; a worn-object cue stays active for as long as it is worn, so the listener should know how to switch it off.

entries.name: Visual trigger
entries.summary: Install a seen image, color, symbol or shown object as the cue.
entries.definition: A trigger whose cue is recognized by its look, not its wording: a symbol, a color, a picture, a spiral, an object held up. It lets a response be fired by images and video without sound. A word shown on screen or typed in a message is a trigger word, because the fixed wording is what the listener responds to. It differs from an everyday-cue trigger in that the image is a specific chosen one that the author or the listener presents on purpose; a sight the day supplies without anyone deciding belongs to that entry.
entries.how_to: Describe the image precisely enough that the listener would pick it out from similar ones, or show it on screen while installing it. Pair the first installs with the image itself where the medium allows. Narrow it: 'this symbol', 'this shade when I show it to you', not a whole color, which would fire constantly.
examples: Whenever you see this blue circle on your screen, your breathing slows and your eyes soften.
When I hold up this silver coin, your eyes settle on it and your thoughts slow right down.
Each time you look at the small star you drew on your notebook, you remember exactly how focused you can be.
cues: 'whenever you see', 'when you look at', 'each time I show you' followed by a specific image, symbol or object and a response
named colors, shapes, symbols or pictures inside a when-then rule
'on your screen', 'this image', 'this symbol', 'the picture of'
'when I show you', 'when I hold up', 'when you display': someone deliberately presents the image

not_this.why: a word is a trigger word in any medium, including text on a screen; label this only when the cue is recognized by its look, not its wording
that uses sights the day supplies without anyone deciding ('every red light'); this is one chosen image that the author or listener presents on purpose
looking at a visual to induce trance, with no installed response for later
the production choice of showing visuals, not a rule tying one to a response

evidence.note: Visual stimuli condition like any other cue, and visual posthypnotic cues appear in experiments, but the image and text triggers used in online practice have not been studied.

entries.consent_note: Images and colors turn up uninvited, so tie the trigger to a specific image and sender and tell the listener what it is.

entries.name: Everyday-cue trigger
entries.summary: Use an ordinary event that recurs in the listener's day as the cue, so daily life fires the trigger without anyone present.
entries.definition: A trigger whose cue is something that will happen anyway: a door opening, a phone buzzing, a red light, the kettle boiling. Nobody has to deliver it, so it fires as often as the event occurs. That is what separates it from word, sound and visual triggers, which a person chooses to fire.
entries.how_to: Choose an event that happens at the wanted rate: several times a day for a brief reminder, once a day for something longer. Keep the response short and safe to have anywhere, since you cannot control where it fires. Future-pace one or two concrete occasions. Give it a scope and an expiry; an everyday cue has no off switch unless the script supplies one.
examples: Every time you walk through a doorway, your shoulders drop and you take one easy breath.
Whenever your phone buzzes, you remember, just for a second, how calm you felt here.
Each time you hear the kettle click off, your jaw unclenches and your breathing evens out.
cues: 'every time you', 'whenever you', 'each time you' followed by a routine event (open a door, hear your phone, see a clock, sit down)
'throughout your day', 'in your daily life', 'wherever you are'
'even when I'm not there', 'without anyone saying anything'
common objects or events named as cues: doorways, mirrors, traffic lights, notifications, water

not_this.why: habit stacking attaches a deliberate behavior to a routine; this attaches an automatic state or response
a specific chosen image shown on purpose, not whatever the day supplies
spreading an existing response to more cues, not installing a rule on a named everyday event

evidence.note: Tying a planned response to an everyday situation has solid support from implementation-intention research for deliberate actions; whether suggested automatic states fire this way from a recording is not tested.

entries.consent_note: It fires in daily life with no one choosing the moment, so keep the response harmless in any setting and give it a stated limit and end.

entries.name: Internal-event trigger
entries.summary: Use one of the listener's own thoughts, feelings or urges as the cue.
entries.definition: A trigger whose cue happens inside the listener: a thought, an emotion, a body feeling, an urge. No outside event is needed, and the listener's own mind fires it. It is a common form in clinical habit and anxiety work ('when you notice the urge, you...'). When the cue is a thought and the response is stopping that thought or swapping it for another, label thought replacement instead.
entries.how_to: Name the internal event in the listener's own terms and make it recognizable early: 'the first flutter in your stomach', not 'anxiety'. Attach a response that is quick and can be done anywhere. Rehearse it in trance by having the listener imagine the feeling starting and the response following. A cue that is too broad ('whenever you think') fires constantly and wears out.
examples: Whenever you feel that first tightness in your chest, you breathe out slowly, and the tightness loosens.
The moment you notice the thought 'I can't do this', your feet press into the floor and your shoulders come down.
Each time the urge to check your phone comes up, you notice it, smile, and return to what you were doing.
cues: 'whenever you feel', 'whenever you think', 'each time you notice', 'the moment you catch yourself'
an emotion, urge, sensation or quoted thought in the when-clause
'the first sign of', 'as soon as that feeling starts'
'the urge to', 'the thought of' followed by a response rule

not_this.why: the narrower case where a thought is stopped or swapped for another thought; here any response can follow
ties a response to a feeling present now in session, not a standing rule for later
the cue is an outside event, not a thought or feeling

evidence.note: Cueing a coping response to an internal signal is standard in clinical hypnosis and supported for deliberate plans by implementation-intention research; automatic firing from a recording is assumed, not shown.

entries.consent_note: The listener's own thoughts fire it and no one else can see it happen, so they should know exactly which thought or feeling is being linked to what.

entries.name: Thought replacement
aliases: whenever you think X, think Y
entries.summary: Suggest that a named unwanted thought stops, or is automatically swapped for a chosen one, whenever it appears.
entries.definition: A conditional suggestion whose cue is the listener's own thought and whose response is stopping it or replacing it with another. It differs from an internal-event trigger, which can fire any response from a feeling or urge, by targeting thought content specifically, and from mind-blanking, which empties thought in general rather than swapping one.
entries.how_to: Name the target thought in the listener's own words, give a clear replacement that can be said in a few words, and link them with 'whenever' or 'as soon as'. Rehearse the swap once or twice in session. Avoid long dwelling on the unwanted thought, which rehearses it.
examples: Whenever the thought 'I can't' comes, it turns into 'I'm learning', just like that.
That old worry starts, and stops, and where it was you hear one word: 'handled'.
As soon as you notice the doubt, you hear 'next step' instead.
cues: 'whenever you think ...' + replacement
'that thought turns into ...' / 'in its place'
'the thought stops'
quoted thought paired with a quoted replacement

not_this.why: an internal-event trigger can fire any response; this targets thought content and replaces it
mind-blanking quiets thought in general; this swaps a specific one
inner-voice suggestion changes whose voice thinks, not which thought

evidence.note: Thought stopping was a behavior-therapy technique, but suppression research shows trying to stop a thought can make it return more often; replacement with an alternative fares better than stopping alone.

entries.consent_note: Swaps that persist after the session should target thoughts the listener asked to change.

entries.name: Trigger test
entries.summary: Fire the trigger during the session so the listener feels it work.
entries.definition: A trigger test delivers the installed cue right after installation and describes or waits for the response. It does two jobs at once: it is practice for the link and it is proof to the listener that the link exists. It differs from a drill in number and purpose: a test is one or a few firings to show it works.
entries.how_to: Put it straight after the install. Reset first: bring the listener a little way out or change the subject, so the response has somewhere to come from. Announce the firing, fire it, leave a beat of silence, then ratify what happened. Make the first test easy, in deep trance with the response already half present, and make later tests harder (lighter trance, eyes open). A test that visibly fails can weaken the listener's belief in the trigger, so prepare the first one to succeed.
examples: Let's try it. Come up just a little... and now: 'quiet water'. There. Feel how quickly that happened.
In a moment I'll snap my fingers and you'll feel it for yourself. [snap] That's right. That's your signal working.
Open your eyes. Now press your thumb and finger together... and notice the calm arrive. Good.
cues: 'let's test that', 'let's try it', 'feel it for yourself', 'see how it works'
an installed cue fired within a few lines of its installation
'in a moment I'll say...' followed by the cue alone on its own line
ratification right after the cue: 'there', 'that's right', 'feel how fast that was'
a partial wake or reset between install and cue

not_this.why: a drill fires and resets many times for strength; a test fires once or twice to prove
any staged proof of trance; a trigger test proves one installed cue
wake-and-drop for depth, which may use a cue but aims at depth, not at showing the cue works
a trance cue fired as the way into trance, with no proof framing, is the re-induction trigger; any cue fired just after its install and followed by 'feel that work' is a test

evidence.note: Rehearsing and demonstrating a cued response is universal practice and consistent with expectancy research, but the added effect of an in-session test has not been isolated.

entries.name: Stacking anchors
entries.summary: Attach several states or responses to the same cue, so one firing brings all of them.
entries.definition: Stacking ties more than one separately built state or response to a single cue: either by eliciting several states in turn and applying the same cue to each, or by adding a new response to a trigger that already works. The cue stays the same; what it evokes grows. A single install whose response has several parts ('your shoulders drop and your breathing slows') is plain trigger installation. It differs from chaining, where each response is the cue for the next in sequence.
entries.how_to: Establish the cue with one response first and test it. Add the others one at a time, each with its own build-up, using the identical cue. Keep stacked states compatible if the aim is a coherent combined response. Keep the stack short enough that the listener can still say what the cue is for.
examples: You already know what pressing your fingers together does. Now add this: as well as calm, it brings a clear head. Calm and clear, on the same touch.
Remember a time you felt confident... press. Now a time you felt playful... same press. Now a time you felt completely safe... same press again.
That bell already quiets your thoughts. From today it also loosens your shoulders: the same bell, both together.
cues: 'as well as', 'on top of that', 'now add', 'and also' applied to an already named cue
the same cue instruction repeated after different state elicitations
a cue installed earlier named again with a new response attached: 'from today it also brings...'
'the same touch', 'the same word', 'that same signal'
'stack', 'layer', 'add to your anchor'

not_this.why: one rule whose response has several parts is still one install; stacking needs a response added to an existing cue, or several separately built states tied to it in turn
chaining is a sequence across several cues; stacking is several responses on one cue
strengthening makes the same response stronger; stacking adds different ones
that adds more cues to one response; stacking adds more responses to one cue
that declares suggestions strengthen each other, with no shared cue

evidence.note: A cue can be associated with more than one outcome, but the NLP claim that stacked anchors produce a stronger combined state is untested.

entries.consent_note: When adding to a trigger the listener already has, say what is being added; they agreed to the earlier response, not the new one.

entries.name: Chaining anchors
entries.summary: Set triggers up in sequence so that each one's response is the cue for the next.
entries.definition: Chaining anchors links several cue-response pairs in a fixed order, so firing the first runs the whole sequence. In NLP it is used to move from a stuck state to a distant wanted state through intermediate states. It differs from stacking in that the states occur one after another, not together.
entries.how_to: Use it when the gap between the starting state and the target is too large for one step. Choose two or three intermediate states, each a short distance from the last (stuck, then curious, then interested, then motivated). Install and test each link separately, then run the chain end to end several times. State each link explicitly: 'and as soon as you feel X, that feeling brings Y'.
examples: The word brings the calm. The calm, as soon as you feel it, brings the slow breath. And the slow breath opens the focus.
When you notice you are stuck, that noticing makes you curious. And the moment you are curious, you find you want to begin.
First touch: steady. Second touch: clear. Third touch: ready. One leads to the next, every time.
cues: 'which in turn', 'and that brings', 'leads to', 'sets off', 'and as soon as you feel that'
a response from one rule reappearing as the when-clause of the next
ordered sequence of states: 'first... then... then'
'chain', 'cascade', 'one after another', 'like dominoes'

not_this.why: a run of 'as you X, you Y' lines about what is happening now is contingent suggestion, however many links; label chaining only when the links are set up as a standing sequence that one cue will run later
behavior chaining links trained actions through reinforcement; this links installed cues and states by suggestion
stacking puts several responses on one cue at once
that transfers a response to a new cue; it does not build a sequence of different responses

evidence.note: Response chains are well established in behavior analysis for trained actions; the NLP procedure of chaining suggested states has no independent test.

entries.consent_note: The listener should know where the chain ends, since firing the first cue commits them to the whole sequence.

entries.name: Collapsing anchors
entries.summary: Fire the anchor for an unwanted state and the anchor for a stronger wanted state together, so the unwanted one loses its hold.
entries.definition: Collapsing anchors fires two anchors for opposed states at the same moment and holds them until the mixed feeling settles: one set for an unwanted state, one for a stronger resource state. The aim is that the old cue no longer brings the old state. The labelable move is the simultaneous firing; setting each anchor beforehand is anchoring. It resembles counterconditioning carried out through two installed cues.
entries.how_to: Anchor the wanted state first and make it clearly the stronger of the two, stacking if needed. Anchor the unwanted state lightly and briefly, on a different spot or cue. Fire both together, hold, then release the unwanted one first and the wanted one a few seconds later. Test by firing the old cue alone or by imagining the old situation. If the resource state is weaker, the result goes the wrong way.
examples: Left knee: that small flicker of nerves. Right knee: the full, strong confidence. Now press both at once, and hold, and let them mix until things settle.
Touch the spot for the old worry and the spot for the calm at the same moment. Keep both until the two feelings even out, then let go of the worry spot first.
Say your word for the tension and squeeze the hand that holds your steadiness, together, now. Stay with both until only one feeling is left.
cues: two cues set on two different places or signals for opposed states
'both at once', 'at the same time', 'together now', 'fire both'
'let them mix', 'blend', 'merge', 'cancel out', 'settle'
'release the first... then the second'
a re-test of the old situation right after: 'think of that now... what is different'

not_this.why: the general pairing of a cue with an incompatible response; collapsing is the specific two-anchor, fire-together procedure
removal cancels a trigger by stating it is gone; collapsing overrides a state by pitting another against it
a phrasing that sets opposites side by side, with no anchors

origin.source: Richard Bandler and John Grinder, Frogs into Princes: Neuro Linguistic Programming, Real People Press (1979)

evidence.note: Counterconditioning has experimental support, but this one-pass NLP procedure has not been validated and its claimed mechanism is unproven.

entries.consent_note: It deliberately calls up an unpleasant state; the listener should agree to that first, and it is not a substitute for treatment of serious distress.

entries.name: Trigger strengthening
entries.summary: Tell the listener the trigger gets stronger, faster or deeper every time it is used.
entries.definition: A suggestion about the trigger itself: that each firing increases its effect. It turns use into the source of strength, so the trigger needs no further sessions to grow. It is a stated claim, not a consequence delivered after the response, which is what separates it from reinforcement in the operant sense.
entries.how_to: Add it at the end of the install and again after each test. Use a the-more-the-more form tied to counting uses: 'each time', 'every time', 'twice as'. It also covers failure: a weak first response is framed as the start of a rising curve. Pair it with real repetition where possible; the claim alone does less than the claim plus practice.
examples: And every time you use it, it works a little faster and goes a little deeper.
Each time you hear that word, the response is stronger than the time before. It only ever grows.
The first time, you may notice only a little. By the tenth, it happens before you have time to think.
cues: 'every time', 'each time' with 'stronger', 'faster', 'more automatic', 'easier' said of the trigger or its response
'twice as fast', 'twice as strong' said of how the trigger will work on later uses, not of how deep one firing takes the listener
'the more you use it, the more...'
'it only grows', 'it never weakens', 'stronger with every use'
'than the time before', 'than last time'

not_this.why: there each firing adds a stated amount to the state ('each snap, twice as deep'); here the claim is that the trigger itself works better on later uses
that follows a response with a reward; this only asserts that strength increases
the same claim applied to future sessions and inductions, not to one trigger
a drill makes the trigger stronger by actually firing it many times

evidence.note: Repeated practice does strengthen cued responses and expectancy shapes them, but nothing shows that telling a listener the trigger strengthens itself adds to that.

entries.consent_note: It tells the listener the effect will grow beyond what they have felt so far, so they should have agreed to a trigger that escalates.

entries.name: Trigger conditions
entries.summary: State who can fire the trigger, where and when it works, and when it does nothing.
entries.definition: A clause attached to a trigger that sets its conditions of use: which person or voice, which settings, which states of the listener. It is discrimination written as a rule, applied to one trigger. It differs from the general scope-limits entry in that it bounds a specific cue, not the session's suggestions as a whole.
entries.how_to: Write it in the same passage as the install, not at the end of the script. Cover three things: who (only this voice, only you, only a named person), where and when (only when sitting or lying somewhere safe, never while driving or working), and the listener's veto (only when you want it to). State the negative case too: 'at any other time it is just a word'.
examples: This works only when you hear it in my voice, and only when you are somewhere safe to close your eyes.
If anyone else says it, or if you are driving or busy, it is just an ordinary word and nothing happens.
It works when you want it to, and only then.
cues: 'only when', 'only if', 'only while', 'only in my voice', 'only from me'
'never while driving', 'never when it would be unsafe', 'not at work'
'if anyone else says it', 'from anyone else it is just a word'
'when it is safe and appropriate', 'when you choose', 'if you want it to'
'nothing happens', 'has no effect' in a stated exception

not_this.why: a stated condition on a named installed trigger is trigger conditions; discrimination presents a look-alike cue with no response and then the true cue with its response
bounds the session's suggestions in general; this bounds one named trigger
expiry sets when the trigger ends in time; conditions set who and where while it lasts
tells the listener when not to play the recording; this says when an installed trigger does nothing

evidence.note: Limiting a posthypnotic cue to stated persons and settings is standard safe practice, and posthypnotic responses are known to be context-sensitive; how reliably a written condition holds is not measured.

entries.consent_note: This is the clause that keeps a persistent trigger within what was agreed; leaving it out is a safety gap, and widening it later needs fresh agreement.

entries.name: Shareable trigger
entries.summary: Write the trigger so that people other than the author can fire it.
entries.definition: A trigger condition that widens the 'who': a partner, a named person, anyone the listener chooses, or anyone at all. It is the opposite setting to 'only my voice'. Recordings use it so that a listener's partner can use what the file installs.
entries.how_to: Say exactly who is included, and prefer a route that runs through the listener's choice ('anyone you tell the word to', 'the person you give this to') over an open grant. Keep the where-and-when limits even when the who is widened. An unlimited 'anyone, anywhere' grant removes the listener's control and should not be written without that being the explicit, agreed point.
examples: This word works for me, and for anyone you decide to share it with, and for no one else.
When your partner says it, in private, with your agreement, it works exactly as it does here.
You can hand this signal to someone you trust, and you can take it back whenever you choose.
cues: 'anyone you choose', 'anyone you share it with', 'someone you trust'
'your partner', 'your hypnotist', a role named as allowed to use the cue
'works for', 'will work when ... says it', 'in anyone's voice'
'give', 'hand over', 'share', 'pass on' applied to the trigger
'and you can take it back'

not_this.why: widens a response across similar cues, settings or media; this widens only who may fire one named trigger. 'It works in any room' is generalization; 'it works when your partner says it' is this
the parent covers any condition; use this label when the clause adds people who may fire the trigger
asks the listener to bring others in to the content, not to let others fire a cue

evidence.note: Clinical texts describe transferring rapport or cues to another operator, but whether a recorded trigger works for a third party has not been studied.

entries.consent_note: It gives other people a way to affect the listener, so the listener must choose who, and must be able to withdraw it.

entries.name: Trigger removal
entries.summary: Tell the listener, in plain words, that a named trigger or suggestion no longer has any effect.
entries.definition: Removal is the explicit cancellation of something installed earlier: the cue is named and declared to be ordinary again. It is done by direct suggestion, in or out of trance. It differs from expiry, which is written at install time and acts later by itself, and from extinction, which works by unrewarded exposure, not by statement.
entries.how_to: Name the trigger exactly as it was installed, say it is cancelled, and say what the cue now is ('just a word'). Do it in trance if the install was in trance, and repeat it as carefully as the install was repeated. Then fire the cue once and ratify that nothing happens. Writers of persistent triggers should also say at install how removal works, or supply a removal passage or file.
examples: The word 'quiet water' is now just two ordinary words. It has no special effect on you, from me or from anyone.
Every trigger and suggestion from this session is cancelled and cleared. Your responses are entirely your own again.
I'll say it once more: 'quiet water'. And notice that nothing happens at all.
cues: 'no longer', 'from now on has no effect', 'is just a word', 'ordinary again'
'cancel', 'remove', 'clear', 'erase', 'lift', 'undo', 'release' applied to a trigger or suggestion
'all suggestions from this session are...' followed by a cancellation
an earlier-installed cue named again together with a negation of its response
a cue fired followed by 'nothing happens'

not_this.why: expiry is a time limit set at install; removal is an act of cancelling done later
fades the response by presenting the cue with no outcome, without saying it is cancelled
forgetting the trigger hides it and leaves it active; removal ends it

evidence.note: Cancelling suggestions before the end of a session is standard procedure in clinical practice and in standardized hypnosis scales; it is assumed to work as other direct suggestions do and is rarely tested on its own.

entries.consent_note: A listener can ask for removal at any time and should be told beforehand how it is done; a script that says a trigger can never be removed is making a permanence claim, not stating a fact.

entries.name: Expiry clause
entries.summary: State, when installing, the time or event after which the trigger or suggestion stops working.
entries.definition: An expiry clause builds the end into the install: a date, a duration, a number of uses, or a condition such as 'unless you listen again'. The trigger then lapses with no further action. It differs from removal, which is a separate later act, and from trigger conditions, which limit who and where but not for how long.
entries.how_to: Put it directly after the install and its conditions. Give a limit the listener can check: 'until you wake tomorrow', 'for seven days', 'for the next three times'. Say what the cue becomes afterwards and, where renewal is intended, how it is renewed. Short defaults that the listener extends by relistening are safer than long ones.
examples: This lasts until you fall asleep tonight. Tomorrow it is just a word again.
The effect fades over the next seven days and is gone completely, unless you choose to listen again.
It will work three times. After the third, it quietly switches itself off.
cues: 'until', 'for the next ... days / hours', 'for one week', 'by tomorrow'
'fades', 'wears off', 'switches off', 'expires', 'lapses'
'unless you listen again', 'unless renewed', 'each listen renews it'
a count limit: 'three times', 'once only'
'after that it is just a word', 'and then it is gone'

not_this.why: removal cancels by a later statement; expiry is a limit written in from the start
conditions cover who, where and when it may fire; expiry covers how long it exists
the opposite move: asserting the effect never ends

evidence.note: Posthypnotic responses tend to weaken over time without renewal, but whether a stated expiry makes a suggestion end on schedule has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: It is a safeguard for persistent suggestions; do not rely on it alone, and offer removal as well.

entries.name: Compliance and commitment
entries.summary: Build agreement in small steps, then use the listener's own words and actions as the reason to go further.
entries.definition: This family covers devices that work through the order of requests and through the listener's own record of having agreed. Most come from social-psychology research on compliance; a few come from hypnosis and sales practice. They differ from suggestion forms, which concern how one sentence is phrased, and from social influence, which appeals to other people. Here the lever is the listener's earlier yes, earlier act or stated identity. The family has no nested families.
entries.how_to: Choose by what you already have. If the listener has given nothing yet, start a compliance ladder (yes set for verbal agreement, small physical tasks for acts, foot in the door for one small request before a larger one), or ask for a trial period so that agreeing now costs little. If they have already agreed or acted, point back at it: commitment and consistency, stated commitment, your actions prove it, labeling, sunk-cost appeal. If you expect a refusal, use door in the face, but you are free, or disrupt then reframe; if they are still weighing an offer, use that's not all. Use task assignment, asking permission, asking for a yes and self-persuasion when you want the listener to produce the response themselves. Low-ball hides the full cost and sunk-cost appeal argues from a known bias; keep both out of anything that is not agreed fantasy.

not_this.why: appeals to what other people do or say, not to the listener's own prior agreement
works through the shape of an offered choice, not through a sequence of agreements
changes behavior by what follows it, not by consistency with what came before

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: Several members have controlled studies and meta-analyses, mostly on one-off requests between strangers; how well they transfer to recorded hypnosis scripts has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: Several members work best when the listener does not notice the sequence; state the destination up front when the content is consequential.

entries.name: Compliance ladder
entries.summary: Ask for a series of small agreements or acts, ordered easy to hard, so each one makes the next easier.
entries.definition: A graded sequence of requests in which the early ones are almost impossible to refuse and the later ones are the real targets. The device is the ordering, not any single request. Its variants differ in what the rungs are made of: answers (yes set), one small request (foot in the door), physical acts (small physical tasks), or whole sessions (graded escalation).
entries.how_to: List what you want the listener to do, sort it from easiest to hardest, and add two or three trivial steps at the bottom. Keep each step only slightly larger than the last and acknowledge each one before asking for the next. Do not skip rungs: a jump that the listener refuses breaks the run and gives them a no to stay consistent with. Place the ladder early, in the pre-talk or induction, so the suggestion section inherits the habit of following.
examples: Take a breath in. Good. Let it out slowly. Good. Now let your shoulders drop. And now let your eyes close.
Listen for one breath. Good. Follow my count for three breaths. Good. Now keep following it with your eyes closed.
First just notice your hands. Now let them rest. Now let them grow heavy. Now let that heaviness move up your arms.
cues: three or more requests in a row that increase in size or intimacy
short confirmation after each step ('good', 'that's right') before the next request
'now' or 'and now' opening successive instructions
early requests are trivial (breathe, sit back, listen) and later ones are the session's real aims
'just', 'only', 'for a moment' minimizing the early steps

not_this.why: pacing states verifiable facts and then one suggestion; a ladder asks for a rising series of responses
shaping reinforces approximations to one final behavior; a ladder orders separate requests by size
chaining makes each response the cue for the next, without any increase in size

evidence.note: Ordering suggestions from easy to hard is standard in clinical texts and in suggestibility scales, and the foot-in-the-door effect is experimentally supported, but long multi-step ladders in scripts have not been tested as such.

entries.consent_note: The listener should know where the ladder leads before the first rung; a ladder toward an undisclosed end is manipulation.

entries.name: Yes set
entries.summary: Give a run of statements or questions the listener will answer yes to, then make the one that matters.
entries.definition: A compliance ladder whose rungs are agreements, spoken or inward. Three or more items that are plainly true or plainly acceptable come first; the target suggestion follows in the same rhythm. It differs from pacing and leading in that it seeks an answer of yes to each item, usually through questions or tag questions, where pacing only states what is observable.
entries.how_to: Use three or four items, each one the listener can confirm without thought. Keep them short and in the same sentence shape so the final item sounds like one more of the same. Make the target a modest step, not a leap. If an item could get a no or a maybe, cut it; one doubtful item spoils the set.
examples: You're sitting comfortably, aren't you? You can hear my voice. You chose to be here. And you can let yourself relax now.
You want to feel calmer. You've felt calm before. You know what it's like. So you can let that feeling come back.
It's been a long day, hasn't it? You've earned some rest. And it would be good to let go for a while, wouldn't it?
cues: three or more consecutive undeniable statements or easy yes/no questions
tag questions: 'isn't it?', 'aren't you?', 'haven't you?', 'wouldn't it?'
final item introduced with 'and', 'so' or 'which means' and not itself verifiable
parallel sentence shape across the run
explicit prompts such as 'yes?' or 'right?' after each item

not_this.why: a yes set strings together easy-to-agree items to build assent to a target, including plain statements; pacing and leading uses verifiable present experience to lend credibility to a suggested state, and a span may fit both
a truism is one undeniable statement; the yes set is the run of them plus the target
that asks outright for one yes at a chosen moment, with no run-up of easy items

origin.source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976)

evidence.note: Standard in Ericksonian and sales teaching; a few experiments on agreement momentum support a small effect, but the claim that three yeses reliably carry a fourth is not established.

entries.name: Foot in the door
entries.summary: Get a small request granted first, then make the larger related request you wanted all along.
entries.definition: The two-step form of the compliance ladder: one small request that is granted and actually carried out, then a larger request of the same kind. The listener who did the first comes to see themselves as someone who does such things. It differs from the low-ball, where the request stays the same and its cost rises, and from door in the face, which runs large to small.
entries.how_to: Make the first request small enough that nearly everyone does it, but real enough that doing it means something. Let it be completed and acknowledged before the second request appears. Keep the second request in the same domain as the first; an unrelated second request gains little. Do not pay or pressure for the first act, or the listener will attribute it to the pressure and not to themselves.
examples: For now, just close your eyes for one breath. Good. Since that was easy, let them stay closed for the rest of this session.
Try this recording for two minutes. That's all I ask. ... You've done two minutes. Stay with me for the next twenty.
Write down one thing you'd like to change. Done? Then write down what you'll do about it tomorrow.
cues: a minimized first request ('just', 'only', 'for one breath', 'that's all I ask')
explicit completion check or acknowledgment before the next request
second request larger and in the same domain as the first
bridging phrases: 'since you did that', 'now that you have', 'that was easy, so'
exactly two request steps, small then large

not_this.why: low-ball keeps one request and raises its cost after agreement; FITD makes a second, larger request
opposite order: a large request refused, then a smaller one
that is many trivial acts to build a habit of following, not one meaningful small request before a target

origin.source: Freedman & Fraser, Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique (1966)

evidence.note: Replicated many times; meta-analyses find a real but small average effect that depends on the first request being performed, unpaid and related to the second.

entries.consent_note: Used honestly when the larger request is foreseeable; used to draw someone toward a request they would have refused outright, it works by their not noticing.

entries.name: Small physical tasks
entries.summary: Give trivial physical instructions (breathe, nod, uncross your legs) so the listener starts following before anything important is asked.
entries.definition: A compliance ladder whose rungs are small bodily acts with no stake. Each act is something the listener would do anyway or has no reason to refuse; what is being built is the habit of doing what the voice says. It differs from the yes set, which collects agreement, and from task assignment, where the task itself matters.
entries.how_to: Open with three to five instructions that cost nothing: adjust position, take a breath, let the hands rest. Give one at a time and leave room for it to be done. Acknowledge each briefly. Adding 'for me' turns the act from self-care into following, which suits dominant scripts and is out of place in clinical ones. Stop once the pattern is set; a long run of pointless instructions reads as filler.
examples: Uncross your legs. Rest your hands in your lap. Take one deep breath for me. Good.
Roll your shoulders back. Let your jaw loosen. Nod once when you've done that.
Wiggle your fingers. Now let them go still. Easy, isn't it, just to follow along.
cues: short imperatives for trivial body actions (breathe, nod, sit back, uncross, swallow, blink)
'for me' appended to an instruction
several such imperatives in a row near the start of the script
brief acknowledgment after each ('good', 'that's it')
comment on how easy following is ('see how easy that was')

not_this.why: an assigned task has its own purpose or duration; these acts are trivial and exist only to start the following
pacing describes what the listener is already doing; this instructs them to do it
breath focus used as the route into trance, not as a token act of following

evidence.note: Common in stage, street and recorded erotic hypnosis; it is consistent with foot-in-the-door research but has not been tested as a separate technique.

entries.name: Graded escalation
entries.summary: Make each section or session ask slightly more than the one before it.
entries.definition: A compliance ladder stretched over sections of one script or over a series of files. The step size is small relative to what has already been accepted, so no single step looks like a decision. It differs from shaping, which reinforces closer approximations to one behavior; escalation raises the size of the ask itself.
entries.how_to: Plan the end point first and divide the distance into steps that each feel like a small addition. Open each step by recalling the last one as done and comfortable, then add the increment. In a series, say at the start how far the series goes, so the listener chooses the whole path and not just the next step. Hold or step back when a level has not settled; pushing on turns escalation into wearing down.
examples: Last time you relaxed your body. Today we go one step further and let the mind go quiet too.
You've held that focus for one minute. This time, two. Just a little further than before.
In part one you followed my voice. In part two you'll follow it with your eyes open. One small step more than before.
cues: 'a little further', 'one step more', 'more than last time', 'this time' attached to a request
reference to an earlier level as already achieved before a larger ask
numbered levels, stages or parts with rising demands
the same kind of request repeated across sections or files with a larger amount each time (one minute, then two)
increments stated as small ('just a bit more', 'only slightly')

not_this.why: shaping rewards successive approximations of one target behavior; escalation enlarges the request
that predicts future trance will come faster and deeper; escalation raises what the listener is asked to do
the series is the container of ordered files; escalation is the rising ask inside it
that persists at the same ask until refusal tires; escalation increases the ask across sections or sessions

evidence.note: Gradual commitment is well documented in social psychology as a phenomenon, but stepwise escalation across recorded sessions is community practice without direct tests.

entries.consent_note: Because each step looks small, the listener may never weigh the total; disclose the end point of a series before it begins.

entries.name: Door in the face
entries.summary: Ask for something large that will be refused, then retreat to the smaller request you actually wanted.
entries.definition: A two-step request running large to small. The first request is big enough to be turned down; the second, made at once by the same speaker, looks like a concession and invites one in return. It differs from the contrast principle alone in that a refusal and a retreat are part of the move, and from foot in the door, which runs the other way.
entries.how_to: Make the first request large but not absurd; an absurd opener is dismissed and earns no concession. Follow it immediately with the real request, framed as backing down ('all right, then just').
