In a recording the listener cannot refuse aloud, so write the refusal in: name the reluctance, accept it, and retreat. The second request must come from the same voice and concern the same thing.
examples: Give me a full hour of perfect stillness. No? Too much. All right, then give me the next five minutes.
Let go of everything, all at once, right now. Too much to ask? All right. Then just let your shoulders go.
Listen to this every day for a month. No? Fair enough. Then once more this week, that's all.
cues: a large request followed by a smaller one of the same kind
scripted refusal or reluctance between the two requests ('No?', 'too much?', 'you'd rather not?')
retreat markers after the refusal: 'all right, then just', 'fair enough', 'at least', 'how about only'
explicit framing of the second request as a concession ('I'll settle for', 'that's all I'll ask')
the first request is actually made before the speaker retreats to the smaller one

not_this.why: runs small to large and depends on the first request being granted, not refused

contrast only mentions a larger thing beside the target ('I could ask for an hour. I won't.'); label door in the face only when a refusal or reluctance is voiced between the two requests and the speaker backs down
that improves one offer before any answer; this replaces a refused request with a smaller one

origin.source: Cialdini et al., Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique (1975)

evidence.note: Replicated with a small-to-moderate average effect in live requests; whether a scripted, one-sided version with an imagined refusal works is untested.

entries.name: Low-ball
entries.summary: Get agreement to a request, then reveal the rest of what it costs.
entries.definition: Agreement is secured on incomplete terms; the full cost is disclosed only after the listener has said yes. The request stays the same and only its price changes, which separates it from foot in the door, where a second and larger request is made. People tend to stand by the decision even though the reason for it has changed.
entries.how_to: State the request in its light form and get a clear yes. Then add the condition or cost as a detail of what was already agreed, not as a new question. The pull depends on the listener having committed freely and actively before the reveal. In consensual scripts, treat it as a fantasy device only if the real terms were given outside the fiction; otherwise leave it out.
examples: You agreed to follow my voice. Good. Following my voice means following it all the way down, with no stopping to think.
You said yes to a short exercise. It works best if you repeat it every night this week.
You've decided to relax with me. Of course, that includes letting me decide when you wake.
cues: reference to a yes already given, followed by a new condition on the same request
'of course, that means', 'that includes', 'what that involves is', 'one more thing'
cost or duration stated only after the agreement point
added terms presented as detail, not as a fresh question
'you agreed', 'you said yes' immediately before the larger terms

not_this.why: FITD makes a second, separate request; low-ball changes the price of the one already accepted
advance agreement is openly content-blind; low-ball hides part of a specific request
that asks for an act that is plainly an instance of what was agreed; label low-ball when the line adds a cost, duration or condition the agreement did not mention

origin.source: Cialdini, Cacioppo, Bassett & Miller, Low-ball procedure for producing compliance: Commitment then cost (1978)

evidence.note: Supported by controlled studies and meta-analysis for live requests; no studies cover its use in hypnosis scripts.

entries.consent_note: It works by withholding the terms until after agreement, which defeats informed consent; use only as agreed fantasy with the real terms disclosed beforehand.

entries.name: That's not all
entries.summary: State the offer, then improve it with a bonus or a lower cost before the listener has answered.
entries.definition: An offer is made and, without a pause for a reply, made better: something is added or the price drops. The first version serves as the reference point against which the improved one is judged. It differs from door in the face in that nothing is refused; the improvement comes unprompted.
entries.how_to: Give the base offer in one sentence and let it stand for a beat. Then add the bonus as something extra, not as part of the original. Keep the first offer plausible; if it is plainly inflated the sweetener reads as a trick. It fits pre-talk and description copy, where the listener is still deciding whether to take part, better than it fits trance text.
examples: This session will leave you relaxed. And that's not all: you'll keep a cue that brings the calm back whenever you want it.
Twenty minutes of rest. And because you came back today, you'll sleep more easily tonight as well.
You get the feeling of calm, and on top of that, the calm gets easier to find each time.
cues: 'and that's not all', 'on top of that', 'as well', 'plus', 'what's more'
a benefit stated, then a further benefit added before any response is invited
'and because you ..., you also get'
a cost reduced unprompted ('not an hour, just ten minutes')
stacked benefits in pre-talk or description copy

not_this.why: DITF needs a refusal and a retreat to a smaller request; here the same offer is improved unasked
reciprocity gives first and asks later; the bonus here is part of the offer being made
contrast compares the target with something else; this compares the offer with its own earlier version

origin.source: Burger, Increasing compliance by improving the deal: The that's-not-all technique (1986)

evidence.note: Supported in sales-style experiments; the effect weakens or reverses when the first offer is too large, and it has not been studied for suggestions.

entries.name: Commitment and consistency
entries.summary: Point to something the listener already said or agreed to and ask for behavior that matches it.
entries.definition: The writer cites the listener's earlier commitment, in the session or before it, and frames the new response as what follows from it. The lever is the wish to be, and appear, consistent with one's own word. It differs from your-actions-prove-it, which draws a conclusion about what the listener is or wants; this one asks for the next act.
entries.how_to: Obtain or locate a real commitment first: a stated goal, a yes, the decision to press play. Quote it back accurately, then connect the request to it with 'so' or 'which means'. The link must be one the listener would accept; stretching a small commitment to cover a large demand invites reactance. Commitments the listener stated actively and freely carry the most weight.
examples: You told yourself you wanted to feel calmer. So this is the moment to do what you said, and let the tension go.
You agreed to follow along. Following along means letting this next breath take you deeper.
Earlier you said yes. Stay true to that now.
cues: 'you said', 'you agreed', 'you promised', 'you decided', 'you told me'
'so', 'which means', 'that's why' linking the earlier commitment to a present request
appeals to keeping one's word or being consistent ('stay true to that', 'as you said you would')
a quoted or paraphrased earlier statement by the listener
reference to the stated reason for listening, followed by an instruction

not_this.why: that infers a trait or desire from what the listener did; this requests the next behavior from what they said
low-ball adds a previously undisclosed cost or condition to an agreed request; this cites a prior commitment to support matching behavior
sunk cost cites effort already spent, not a promise made
that treats the choice to be here as proof of wanting the result; this cites a specific commitment and asks for follow-through

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: The pull toward consistency with active, freely made commitments is well supported; its strength varies between people and it is weaker for commitments felt as coerced.

entries.consent_note: Cite only commitments the listener actually made; attributing an agreement they never gave shades into gaslighting.

entries.name: Stated commitment
entries.summary: Have the listener state, write or sign a commitment so there is a definite act to stay consistent with.
entries.definition: The form of commitment and consistency in which the commitment is created on the spot and made explicit: said aloud, written, signed, or declared to someone. Active and witnessed commitments bind more than private intentions. It differs from repeat-after-me, where the listener voices a suggestion; here the listener voices a promise about future conduct.
entries.how_to: Word the commitment in the first person, specific and short enough to say in one breath. Ask for an overt act: speak it, write it down, sign it, tell someone. Place it after the listener has reason to want the outcome and before the work that depends on it. For lasting effect make it concrete (what, when), and remember that a pledge extracted under pressure binds weakly and can backfire.
examples: Say it out loud now: 'I will practice this every evening this week.'
Take a pen and write one sentence: what you commit to doing tomorrow. Sign your name under it.
Before we finish, tell one person you trust what you have promised to do, and by when.
cues: 'say it out loud', 'write it down', 'sign', 'promise me', 'I want to hear you say'
first-person future statements the listener is told to utter ('I will ...', 'I promise ...')
words such as pledge, vow, oath, contract, agreement
instruction to tell another person or post the commitment
later reference back to 'what you promised' or 'what you signed'

entries.name: Labeling
aliases: you're the kind of person who
entries.summary: Tell the listener they are a certain kind of person, then ask for behavior that fits the label.
entries.definition: The writer assigns a trait ('you're someone who responds easily') and then makes a request that a person with that trait would grant. The label comes first and the request leans on it. It differs from a bare identity statement, which is the suggested change itself, and from act-to-trait generalization, which derives the label from something the listener did.
entries.how_to: Pick a label the listener would be glad to accept and that is at least plausible. State it as an observation, not flattery, and give a small piece of support if you have one. Follow within a sentence or two with the request the label implies. A label that contradicts the listener's self-view is rejected, and the request with it.
examples: You're the kind of person who can focus when it matters. So focus now, on just this one point.
People with a good imagination go into trance easily, and you clearly have one. Let it work for you.
You're a careful listener. A careful listener follows each word, all the way down.
cues: 'you're the kind of person who', 'you're someone who', 'people like you'
'you are a(n) [adjective] [noun]' followed by an instruction that fits it

'as a [label], you ...'
generic statement about a type ('good subjects always ...') after placing the listener in that type

not_this.why: that states what the listener is as the suggestion itself; labeling uses the trait as a lever for a request
that builds the trait out of a specific act; labeling assigns it outright
praise follows a response as a reward; a label precedes the request it supports

origin.source: Richard L. Miller, Philip Brickman and Diana Bolen, Attribution versus Persuasion as a Means for Modifying Behavior, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1975)

evidence.note: Trait labels have raised label-consistent behavior in several experiments, mostly short-term; durable identity change from a spoken label is not shown.

entries.consent_note: A label can outlast the session; keep to labels the listener would accept when alert, and avoid demeaning ones outside agreed play.

entries.name: Your actions prove it
entries.summary: Point at something the listener has done or is doing and present it as evidence of what they want or are.
entries.definition: The writer names an observable act (still listening, eyes closed, came back again) and draws a conclusion from it about the listener's desire, state or nature. The act is real; the inference is supplied. It differs from commitment and consistency, which asks for the next behavior, and from pacing trance signs, which reads involuntary signs as trance; here a voluntary act is read as proof of wanting.
entries.how_to: Choose an act that is certainly true of anyone hearing the line: they are listening, they have not stopped, they followed the last instruction. State it flatly, then state what it shows. Keep the inference one step from the act; a long leap gets checked. It works best after a few acts have accumulated, so place it past the opening.
examples: You're still listening. That tells you something: part of you wants this.
You closed your eyes when I asked, and you kept them closed through the count. That shows how ready you are.
You've followed each instruction so far. That shows how willing you are to keep going.
cues: 'you're still listening', 'you haven't stopped', 'you did that the moment I asked', 'you followed every word'
'that means', 'that shows', 'that proves', 'which tells you' after a described act
past or present action of the listener in one clause, a present want, readiness or state in the next
'you followed that instruction' paired with 'that shows you're ready'
no stress on the act having been freely chosen (if 'you chose', 'nobody made you' or 'you could have stopped' appears, label the variant you-chose-this)

not_this.why: the variant for lines that name a choice or stress that the act was free ('you chose', 'nobody made you', 'you could have stopped'); use this parent label when an act is cited without that stress
that reads bodily signs as proof of trance; this reads voluntary acts as proof of wanting or being
that turns one act into a standing trait; this may conclude only a present want or readiness

evidence.note: Self-perception theory has experimental support, but telling a listener what their behavior proves is a script convention that has not been tested as a device.

entries.consent_note: The inference is the writer's, not the listener's; do not use continued listening as proof of consent to content that was not disclosed.

entries.name: You chose this
entries.summary: Point at a choice the listener made (to start, to stay, to continue) and present it as proof they want what follows.
entries.definition: The writer names a real, observable choice and draws a conclusion from it about the listener's will: you chose to be here, so this is what you want. The anchor is a specific act of choosing, which separates it from general claims about the listener's desires. It converts the freedom the listener did exercise into responsibility for content they may not have foreseen.
entries.how_to: Cite a choice that is true and that the listener will recognize: pressing play, lying down, coming back for another session, not stopping when offered the chance. Place it after such a choice, most often at the end of pre-talk, after a consent check, or at a point of escalation. Keep the inference modest; 'you chose to listen, so part of you is curious' is accepted, 'you chose to listen, so you agreed to everything' is heard as a trick. It is strongest straight after a real opportunity to stop.
examples: Nobody made you press play. You chose this, and you chose it for a reason.
You could have stopped a minute ago. You stayed. That tells you something.
You came back tonight. That was your decision, and it was a good one.
cues: 'you chose', 'your choice', 'you decided', 'your decision' in past tense about being here
'nobody made you', 'no one forced you', 'you didn't have to'
'you pressed play', 'you clicked', 'you came back' paired with a word of choosing or freedom (without one, label the parent)
'you could have stopped ... but you didn't'
'so' / 'which means' / 'that tells you' linking the choice to wanting the result

not_this.why: that asserts what the listener wants without citing a choice; label this entry when a specific act of choosing is the evidence
the parent cites any voluntary act as proof; label this variant only when the line names a choice or decision or stresses that the act was free
that cites an earlier promise and asks for matching behavior; this cites a choice and infers a wish

evidence.note: People do infer their attitudes from choices they believe were free, and perceived choice strengthens that inference in laboratory studies, but the scripted line itself is untested and can backfire when the listener notices the inference is larger than the choice.

entries.consent_note: Choosing to start is not agreement to everything that follows; never use this line to argue that the listener has given up the right to stop or has consented to content they were not told about.

entries.name: From act to trait
aliases: you did X so you are X
entries.summary: Take one thing the listener just did and declare it proof of a standing trait.
entries.definition: The script points at a single act and states the trait it supposedly reveals: 'you closed your eyes so easily, you are a natural'. The move is the explicit inference from one act to a lasting quality. It differs from your-actions-prove-it, which uses behavior as evidence of a present wish or state, and from labeling, which assigns a trait without requiring an act first.
entries.how_to: Wait for a real, observable response (eyes closing, breath slowing, following an instruction), name it, then name the trait in 'so you are' or 'that shows you are' form. Keep the act fresh and specific. Generalizing from an act the listener did not feel themselves do will not land.
examples: You let your eyes close the moment I asked. You are someone who follows easily.
That breath went all the way down. That shows what a natural you are at this.
You've stayed this still for this long, so you are, plainly, a calm person.
cues: observed act + 'so you are ...'
'that shows you are ...' / 'that proves you're ...'
'someone who can do that is ...'
'you're a natural' / 'you're good at this' directly after a named act

not_this.why: your-actions-prove-it treats the act as evidence of a present want or state, not a lasting trait
labeling assigns the trait without needing an act and then asks for behavior
ratification confirms the response is happening without generalizing it

evidence.note: Attributing a trait to someone after a behavior increases later trait-consistent behavior in controlled studies; its effect inside hypnosis is untested.

entries.name: Task assignment
entries.summary: Give the listener a specific action to carry out, during the session or afterward.
entries.definition: An instruction to perform a concrete, checkable action that has its own purpose: practice, a report, an errand, a change in routine. Carrying it out is both the behavior wanted and an act of commitment that later devices can point to. It differs from small physical tasks, which are trivial by design, and from a posthypnotic suggestion, which is meant to fire by itself on a cue.
entries.how_to: State what, when, how much and how the listener will know it is done. Size the task so it will actually be completed; an unfinished task teaches not following. Give it late in the session, repeat it once before waking, and refer to it at the start of the next file. In dominant scripts, keep tasks inside what was negotiated and give them an end.
examples: Your task for this week: each evening before bed, sit for three minutes and breathe the way we practiced.
When this recording ends, write down three things you noticed. Do it before you do anything else.
Before you go to sleep tonight, tidy one drawer. Next time, tell me how it felt to finish it.
cues: 'your task', 'your homework', 'your assignment', 'your orders', 'I want you to'
a concrete action with a time or count ('each evening', 'three times', 'before bed')
instructions placed just before or after the wake-up that concern later behavior
request for a report or record ('write down', 'tell me next time')
reference in a later session to whether the task was done

not_this.why: a posthypnotic response is suggested to happen automatically on a cue; a task is done deliberately
trivial in-session acts that exist only to start the habit of following
that attaches a behavior to an existing recurring cue; a task explicitly assigns an action, often with a count, deadline or report, and one line can use both
that prescribes re-listening or repetition of the session itself, not a separate action

evidence.note: Between-session assignments are standard in clinical hypnosis and behavior therapy, and homework completion is linked to better therapy outcomes; tasks given as obedience exercises have not been studied.

entries.consent_note: Tasks carry the session into daily life; keep them safe, bounded in time, within agreed limits, and free of money, disclosure or other people's involvement unless negotiated.

entries.name: Money ask
entries.summary: Instruct the listener to pay, tip or send money to the speaker, inside the script.
entries.definition: A direct instruction or suggestion to spend money on the speaker, often framed as devotion, proof or relief. The device is the ask itself; what makes it coercive is pairing with other devices in this family, such as dependency, fear of leaving or a trigger tied to paying. A plain tip request in a pre-talk is the same device without the coercive load.
entries.how_to: State the action plainly (send, tip, pay), name the speaker as the recipient, and attach a meaning to it: proof, gratitude, release. Placement inside trance, especially right after pleasure or tied to a trigger, is what makes it manipulative. It fails if the amount or pressure outpaces the listener's investment. Keep any real money ask outside trance, in the pre-talk or description, with no conditioning attached.
examples: When you wake, you'll want to show your gratitude. You know how. Send it.
Every time you hear the word, your hand reaches for your wallet, and it feels good to give.
Paying is how you prove this is real for you.
cues: 'send', 'tip', 'pay', 'tribute', 'wallet', 'give'
money framed as proof, gratitude or devotion
a pay instruction inside trance or tied to a trigger
the act of paying described as pleasurable

not_this.why: a task assignment can be any act; a money ask is specifically a payment to the speaker
reciprocity creates a felt debt from a gift; a money ask directly instructs payment
recruiting asks for other people; a money ask asks for money

evidence.note: Common in commercial erotic hypnosis and financial-domination content and documented in cult finance; there is no study of scripted money asks.

entries.consent_note: A money instruction inside trance or tied to a trigger bypasses ordinary financial judgment; it requires the listener's explicit prior agreement and should never persist past the session.

entries.name: Recruiting others
entries.summary: Instruct the listener to bring other people to the speaker, share the files, or introduce others to the experience.
entries.definition: A direct instruction to recruit: share, recommend, play the file for someone, or bring a partner or friend in. In high-control groups recruitment both grows the group and deepens the recruiter's own commitment. It differs from social proof, which reports that others already take part, and from a shareable trigger, which designs a trigger others can use without instructing anyone to recruit.
entries.how_to: Name the action (share, send, play for someone) and frame it as generosity, duty or a sign of devotion. Placed inside trance or attached to a trigger, it becomes manipulative; placed as an open request in a description, it is ordinary promotion. It fails if it names specific people. Never instruct listeners to play files to people who have not agreed.
examples: Someone you know needs this too. When you wake, you'll want to share it with them.
Every new listener you bring makes your own connection deeper.
Good followers spread the word. You'll find the right person to tell.
cues: 'share', 'send it to', 'bring a friend', 'tell someone', 'spread'
sharing framed as duty, generosity or a sign of devotion
recruitment linked to the listener's own reward or depth
a share instruction inside trance or as a posthypnotic suggestion

not_this.why: social proof reports others' participation; recruiting instructs the listener to add more people
a shareable trigger can be used by others; recruiting instructs bringing them in
a money ask requests payment; recruiting requests other people

evidence.note: Recruitment duties are documented in high-control groups and multi-level marketing, and public advocacy is known to strengthen commitment, but scripted recruitment asks have not been studied.

entries.consent_note: Recruitment instructions extend influence to people who never agreed; never instruct listeners to expose others without their informed consent.

entries.name: Asking permission
entries.summary: Have the listener ask for the thing they want before they are given it.
entries.definition: The script makes the listener the one who requests: to go deeper, to rest, to receive the next step. Asking puts the wanting in their own words and places the granting with the speaker. It is the reverse of permission-giving, where the speaker offers leave unasked.
entries.how_to: Build some wanting first, then withhold the next step until it is asked for. Supply the wording, leave a pause for the listener to say it aloud or inwardly, and then grant it promptly. Granting after the first sincere ask keeps it warm; requiring repeated or more abject asking moves it toward tease and denial or humiliation, which should be a deliberate choice.
examples: If you'd like to go deeper, ask me. Just think the words: 'please take me deeper.' ... Good. Then down you go.
Before I count you down, I want you to ask for it. Say 'may I?' ... Yes. You may.
Ask nicely, and I'll let you rest.
cues: 'ask me', 'ask for it', 'say please', 'beg', 'ask nicely'
scripted lines for the listener beginning 'may I', 'please'
a pause or beat marked after the instruction to ask
granting formula following the ask ('yes, you may', 'since you asked')
'if you want X, you have to ask'

not_this.why: there the speaker grants leave unasked; here the listener must request it
that collects a yes to the speaker's proposal; this has the listener originate the request
recitation of a suggestion, with nothing being requested or granted

evidence.note: A convention of dominance-themed scripts; it plausibly draws on commitment and self-perception effects, but it has not been studied.

entries.consent_note: A scripted 'please' inside trance is part of the scene, not evidence of consent to the content; consent is settled before the session.

entries.name: But you are free
entries.summary: Make the request and say plainly that the listener is free to refuse.
entries.definition: A request with a statement of the listener's freedom attached: 'but you are free to say no'. Affirming the freedom reduces the urge to push back and tends to raise compliance. It differs from a consent check, which is a real stopping point with a way out, and from permission to resist, which invites resistance as part of the play.
entries.how_to: Put the freedom statement directly beside the request, in the same breath. Say it once, plainly, and mean it; a freedom the script then contradicts is a false reassurance. It suits the pre-talk and the start of any larger ask. The exact wording matters little as long as the freedom to decline is unmistakable.
examples: I'd like you to close your eyes now. Of course, you're free not to.
Give me your full attention for the next ten minutes. You don't have to, of course; it's your call.
Let this next part take you deeper, or don't. It's up to you.
cues: 'but you are free to', 'you're free not to', 'feel free to say no'
'it's up to you', 'it's your choice', 'you decide', 'only if you want to'
'you can stop any time', 'you don't have to'
a freedom statement adjacent to a direct request
'no obligation', 'no pressure'

not_this.why: a consent check is an actual exit point with a pause; BYAF is a phrase attached to a request

origin.source: Nicolas Guéguen and Alexandre Pascual, Evocation of Freedom and Compliance: The ‘But You Are Free of...’ Technique, Current Research in Social Psychology (2000)

evidence.note: Meta-analysis of dozens of studies finds a reliable effect for face-to-face requests acted on at once; it is weaker when the request is remote or the response is delayed, which is the situation of a recording.

entries.consent_note: Only say it when it is true: the listener must really be able to stop, and nothing later in the script should deny it.

entries.name: Disrupt then reframe
entries.summary: Phrase one detail of the request oddly, then immediately follow with a simple reason to say yes.
entries.definition: A small, harmless oddity in the wording of a request (an unusual unit, a reversed phrase) briefly interrupts the listener's routine evaluation; a short positive reframe is delivered in that gap. Both parts and their order are required. It is the brief, sales-scale relative of the confusion technique, which uses sustained confusion and ends in a suggestion, not a reframe of the offer.
entries.how_to: State the request with one unexpected element, such as time in seconds or a quantity in unusual units. Follow at once, with no pause, with a plain reframe: 'it's a bargain', 'it's nothing at all'. Keep the disruption mild; a real puzzle makes the listener stop and analyze. Reversing the order, or leaving out either part, removes the effect.
examples: Stay with me for nine hundred seconds. That's fifteen minutes. It's hardly any time at all.
Give me three hundred breaths of your attention. That's about twenty minutes, and it's a small price for a quiet mind.
Stay with me for one hundred and twenty heartbeats. That's about two minutes. It's nothing at all.
cues: a quantity in an unusual unit followed by its ordinary equivalent ('that's ...')
a short evaluative reframe directly after ('it's a bargain', 'it's nothing', 'it's easy')
odd word order or an unexpected term inside an otherwise routine request
disruption and reframe within two adjacent sentences
the reframe always after the oddity, never before

not_this.why: sustained confusing language resolved by a suggestion; DTR is one mild oddity plus a reframe of a request
the interrupt alone, with no reframe required
a new meaning given without any preceding disruption

origin.source: Davis & Knowles, A disrupt-then-reframe technique of social influence (1999)

evidence.note: Supported by the original studies and a later meta-analysis, mainly in sales and donation requests; untested in hypnosis scripts.

entries.consent_note: It works by interrupting evaluation of the request; do not use it on the points where the listener's considered agreement is needed.

entries.name: Sunk-cost appeal
entries.summary: Cite the time or effort the listener has already put in as the reason to keep going.
entries.definition: The writer points to what has already been spent (minutes, sessions, effort) and treats stopping as wasting it. The reason offered looks backward at cost, not forward at benefit. It differs from commitment and consistency, which cites a promise, and from your-actions-prove-it, which reads past behavior as evidence of desire.
entries.how_to: Name the investment concretely: how long, how many times, how far down. Then frame continuing as the way to make it count. It belongs at points where attention may flag: mid-deepener, before a harder section, late in a series. Use it sparingly and only to carry the listener through something they chose; as the main reason to continue it is a weak and manipulative argument.
examples: You've come this far. It would be a shame to stop now, with the best part so close.
Ten minutes of letting go already. Don't waste them. Let the next minute build on all of it.
Five sessions in. Stopping now would throw all of that away, so stay with it.
cues: 'you've come this far', 'you've already', 'after all this', 'so far'
'don't waste', 'it would be a shame to stop', 'too late to turn back'
a stated amount of time, sessions or effort followed by a reason to continue
'no point stopping now', 'might as well'
framing stopping as loss of what has been built

not_this.why: that cites what the listener said they would do; sunk cost cites what they have spent
that reads past acts as proof of wanting; this argues from the cost of abandoning them
that attaches dread to stopping; sunk cost argues only from waste

origin.source: Arkes & Blumer, The psychology of sunk cost (1985)

evidence.note: The sunk-cost effect on decisions is well replicated; whether reminding someone of their investment increases persistence in a session has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: It discourages stopping by appeal to a known bias; never place it against a consent check, a safeword or the listener's stated wish to end.

entries.name: Asking for a yes
entries.summary: At a chosen moment, ask the listener outright to say or nod yes.
entries.definition: A direct prompt for an overt yes: spoken, whispered, thought or nodded. The yes is an act, and it becomes a commitment that later lines can cite. It differs from the yes set, where agreement is collected implicitly across a run of easy items, and from a consent check, whose purpose is to let the listener stop.
entries.how_to: Ask a single clear question whose answer you can count on, and tell the listener how to answer: 'say yes', 'nod'. Leave a real pause. Acknowledge the answer, then build on it. Place it just before a step up, or just after a response the listener enjoyed. Do not present a yes obtained in trance as consent to something new.
examples: Does that feel good? Nod for me. ... Good.
Are you ready to go deeper? Say yes, out loud or just in your mind. ... Then let's go.
You'd like more of this calm, wouldn't you? Tell me yes.
cues: 'say yes', 'nod', 'nod for me', 'tell me yes', 'answer me'
a yes/no question followed by an instruction on how to answer
a marked pause after the question
scripted 'yes' line for the listener
acknowledgment of the answer ('good', 'that's what I thought') followed by a new request

not_this.why: a run of easy items that gather implicit yeses before a target; this is one explicit request for a yes
a consent check offers a real exit; this prompts an expected yes to build commitment
an ideomotor nod is suggested to happen by itself; here the listener nods or speaks on purpose

evidence.note: Common in live and recorded hypnosis and in sales; active commitment effects are documented, but a prompted yes inside a script has not been tested for added effect.

entries.consent_note: A prompted yes in trance is a compliance device, not consent; the alias 'consent harvest' should not be read as meaning it secures consent.

entries.name: Self-persuasion
aliases: tell me why you want this
entries.summary: Have the listener produce the reasons or the content themselves, so it is owned as their own.
entries.definition: The writer supplies a prompt and a gap, and the listener supplies the argument: why they want the change, what it will give them, what the scene looks like. The speaker never states the reasons, so there is no outside claim to argue with. It differs from repeat-after-me, where the words are supplied, and from asking for a yes, where the listener only assents; here the content itself comes from the listener.
entries.how_to: Ask an open question whose honest answers all point the way you want ('what would be better if this were easier?'), then leave a real pause for the answer. Ask for the listener's own reasons, in their own words, and for more than one. Do not correct or replace what they come up with; acknowledge it and build on it without restating it for them. Asking 'why not lower?' after a self-rating draws out reasons for, while asking 'why not higher?' draws out reasons against. It fails when the question is leading enough that the answer is plainly yours, or when the pause is too short to think.
examples: Think of one reason you want to feel calmer this week. Your own reason. Take a moment and find it... Now find a second.
You gave your focus a four out of ten, not a one. Tell me, silently, why it is not lower.
I won't describe the place. You know better than I do what makes a place feel safe, so build it yourself, one detail at a time.
cues: open 'why' or 'what' questions about the listener's own motives: 'why do you want', 'what would it give you'
'your own reason', 'in your own words', 'only you know', 'you tell me'
'think of one reason', 'find three reasons', 'list for yourself'
a marked pause or [pause] after the prompt, with no answer supplied by the script
a self-rating followed by 'why not lower?'
the script declines to supply content: 'I won't tell you what it is', 'you decide what that looks like'

not_this.why: repeat-after-me gives the exact words to say; self-persuasion gives a question and takes whatever the listener generates
asking for a yes collects assent to the speaker's statement; here the listener authors the statement
desire attribution tells the listener what they want; self-persuasion asks them and waits
a question as suggestion is answered by having the response; this question is answered by producing reasons or content

evidence.note: Arguments people generate themselves change their attitudes more, and for longer, than the same arguments heard from someone else; this is shown for live role-play and writing tasks, not for a silent pause in a recording.

entries.name: Trial period
entries.summary: Ask for the thing only as a short, fixed, reversible trial, so agreeing now is not agreeing for good.
entries.definition: The request is cut down in time and in finality: do it for a stated period, then decide. Three parts mark it: a time limit, a promise that it can be undone, and a deferred decision. It differs from foot in the door, where the first request is smaller in kind and a second, larger request follows; here the request is the full thing, made temporary, and the hope is that the listener simply keeps it.
entries.how_to: State the length exactly and keep it short: one session, three days, a week. Say what happens at the end, and make that a real decision point with stopping as a named option. Remove the cost of trying: nothing to sign, nothing lost by going back. Then let the trial do the work; do not argue for the permanent version during it. It fails when the period is vague ('for a while'), or when the listener suspects the way back is not real.
examples: You don't have to decide anything today. Just try the evening practice for seven days, and on the eighth day you choose whether to keep it.
For the length of this recording only, let my voice do the thinking. When it ends, everything goes back exactly as it was.
Wear the idea for an hour, the way you would try on a coat. If it doesn't fit, you take it off.
cues: 'just try', 'try it for', 'give it a week', 'for now', 'for today only'
an exact, short duration attached to the request: 'for seven days', 'for the next ten minutes', 'just this once'
a reversal promise: 'you can always go back', 'everything returns to normal', 'nothing is permanent'
a deferred decision: 'then decide', 'you don't have to decide now', 'see how it feels'
'no commitment', 'nothing to lose', 'if you don't like it, stop'
trying-on comparisons: 'like trying on', 'test drive', 'sample'

entries.consent_note: The promise of reversal must be true: the trial has to end when stated, stopping must cost nothing, and extending it requires a fresh yes; a 'trial' that later turns out to be permanent is a low-ball.

entries.name: Social influence
entries.summary: Appeals that get a suggestion accepted because of other people: what they do, who the speaker is, and what the listener owes or shares.
entries.definition: This family groups appeals based on what other people do, the speaker's standing, or a bond with the listener, along with modeling and perceptual contrast. It includes six of Cialdini's seven principles: social proof, authority, liking, reciprocity, scarcity, and unity. Commitment and consistency sits in the compliance family because it draws on the listener's own past acts.
entries.how_to: Pick by what the listener is unsure about. If they doubt the response is normal, use social proof or a testimonial. If they doubt the speaker, use authority or liking. If they need a reason to act now, use scarcity or exclusivity; if they need a reason to give something back, use reciprocity. Unity and in-group language suit series and communities where a shared identity already exists. Most of these belong in the pre-talk or the description; inside trance they should be short and should not invite evaluation.

not_this.why: compliance devices work from the listener's own earlier acts and agreements, not from other people
framing sets how the experience is interpreted without appealing to people or relationships
coercive patterns cut off alternatives and exits; these appeals leave the listener free to weigh them

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: Each principle has controlled studies in sales and compliance settings; almost none has been tested inside a hypnosis script, so effect sizes there are unknown.

entries.consent_note: These appeals are honest only when the claims behind them are true; invented crowds, credentials or shortages are deception.

entries.name: Social proof
entries.summary: Tell the listener what other people do or feel in this situation, so they treat it as the right response.
entries.definition: Social proof cites the behavior or experience of other people as a guide to what the listener should do or expect. It names or implies a reference group: most people, other listeners, people like you. It differs from normalizing, which calls a response natural without pointing at anyone, and from authority, which rests on one expert source instead of many peers.
entries.how_to: Use it where the listener is unsure what counts as a correct response, usually the pre-talk or just before a new phenomenon. Make the reference group as close to the listener as possible: 'people who listen to this for the first time' beats 'people'. State what the others do, then leave the listener to follow; do not add a command on top. It fails when the claim is implausibly universal or when the listener sees themselves as unlike the group.
examples: Most people notice their breathing slow down somewhere around here.
Thousands of listeners have sat exactly where you are and found this easier than they expected.
People who are good at focusing usually find their hands get heavy first.
cues: 'most people', 'many people', 'everyone', 'thousands of listeners'
'people like you', 'others who', 'listeners often'
a statistic or count about other people's responses
third-person plural subject followed by the response the script wants
'you're not alone', 'just like everyone else who'

not_this.why: normalizing reassures that a response the listener has, or fears having, is ordinary ('that's normal', 'nothing is wrong'); social proof reports what others do or feel so the listener does the same. If the line predicts or invites a response, label social proof; if it excuses one, label normalizing
modeling shows one person performing the response and what it earned them; social proof reports what many do, with no scene and no reward
'people can relax' states a possibility about a vague subject; social proof reports what others actually do
authority rests on one expert or powerful source, not on the number of peers

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: Conformity and descriptive-norm effects are well replicated; whether a line of social proof inside a recording changes hypnotic response has not been tested directly.

entries.consent_note: Claims about what others do should be true or clearly generic; invented numbers are deception.

entries.name: Testimonial
entries.summary: Report what a particular earlier listener experienced, in enough detail that the new listener expects the same.
entries.definition: A testimonial is social proof carried by one specific case instead of a count. It describes, or quotes, an individual who went through the process and what happened to them. The single vivid case is what separates it from general social proof; the fact that the person is presented as real and reporting separates it from My friend John, where the third person is a vehicle for live suggestions.
entries.how_to: Place it in the pre-talk or the description. Give one or two concrete details of the person's doubt before and their experience after; the doubt is what lets a skeptical listener identify. Keep it short and specific, and let the reported experience match what the script will suggest next. It fails when it reads as advertising or when the reported result is too large to believe.
examples: One listener wrote to say she was sure it wouldn't work on her. She says she lost track of the room about four minutes in.
Someone told me last week that the first thing he noticed was his shoulders, and then nothing else for quite a while.
A man who had tried three other recordings told me afterwards, 'I didn't think I was under until I tried to move.'
cues: 'one listener', 'someone told me', 'a client of mine', 'a woman who wrote to me'
reported speech or a quoted remark from one past listener
before-and-after story about a third person ('she was sure it wouldn't work... then')
'they said', 'he described it as', 'she reported', 'told me afterwards'
past-tense report of a finished session, not a scene narrated as it happens

not_this.why: modeling shows someone performing a response and its consequence; a testimonial reports an earlier person's completed experience as evidence, whether quoted or described by the speaker
My friend John delivers live suggestions through the third person; a testimonial reports a finished result
vicarious deepening narrates someone going under in the present for the listener to follow
borrowed authority cites an expert or science, not a peer's experience

evidence.note: Single cases can shift judgment, and base rates are often underused, but studies comparing narrative with statistical evidence give mixed results; no controlled work shows testimonials inside a script raise hypnotic response.

entries.consent_note: Invented testimonials presented as real are deception; composite or illustrative cases should be worded as such.

entries.name: Manufactured consensus
entries.summary: Stage the appearance of many people agreeing, using extra voices, crowd sound or characters who all respond the same way.
entries.definition: Manufactured consensus is social proof that is shown instead of claimed. The script or production supplies the crowd: a chorus repeating the line, background voices saying yes, a scene where every character complies. It differs from plain social proof, which only asserts what others do, and from layered voices, which is the audio technique and need not carry agreement.
entries.how_to: Write the agreeing voices as stage directions or as characters in the scene, and have them respond just before the listener is asked to. Keep the chorus lines short and identical so they read as unanimity. It works best inside a fiction frame, where the listener knows the crowd is part of the scene. It fails when one dissenting or awkward voice breaks the unanimity, or when the staging is so heavy it draws attention to itself.
examples: [Several voices, together:] Yes. We listen. We relax.
All around you the others have already closed their eyes. Every one of them. You can hear them breathing slowly.
[Background murmur of agreement] And everyone in the room nods, so you nod too.
cues: stage directions for a chorus, crowd, murmur or multiple voices saying the same line
'we' lines spoken by a group voice that is not the main speaker
scene description in which every other character has already complied
'all of them', 'every one of them', 'the whole room'
the same short line repeated by different named or numbered voices

not_this.why: plain social proof asserts what others do; this stages the others so the listener seems to witness it
layered voices is the audio technique of overlapping tracks, whatever they say
vicarious deepening follows one person going under; this shows a unanimous group

evidence.note: Conformity to a unanimous group and effects of staged audience reactions are established in the lab; their use in recorded hypnosis is untested practice.

entries.consent_note: Outside an acknowledged fiction frame the crowd is fake evidence; do not present staged voices or invented agreement as real listeners.

entries.name: Authority
entries.summary: Establish the speaker as expert, experienced or entitled to direct, so instructions are followed with less checking.
entries.definition: Authority is any statement or stance that sets up the speaker's standing: training, experience, track record, role or plain assurance. The claim is about the speaker, not about the technique or the recording. That separates it from the potency claim, which praises the method, and from borrowed authority, where the standing belongs to someone else.
entries.how_to: Establish it early, in the pre-talk, in one or two factual lines; then show it through certainty and plain instructions instead of repeating the claim. Experience stated as numbers or years is more credible than adjectives. Match the kind of authority to the script: clinical competence for self-help, command and role for dominance. It fails when it is overclaimed, defended at length, or contradicted by hesitant wording later.
examples: I've guided people into trance for fifteen years, and I'll tell you exactly what to do at each step.
You don't need to work anything out. That's my job. Yours is to follow.
I know how this goes. I've watched it happen many hundreds of times.
cues: first-person statements of training, years, numbers of clients or sessions
'trust me', 'I know', 'leave that to me', 'that's my job'
titles or roles the speaker claims (doctor, hypnotist, teacher, a dominant title)
explicit division of roles: 'I lead, you follow'
unhedged declaratives about what will happen, attributed to the speaker's experience

not_this.why: borrowed authority cites an outside source; authority is the speaker's own standing
the potency claim is about how strong the recording or technique is, not who the speaker is
role assignment tells the listener what they are and how that role behaves; authority states the speaker's standing or right to direct. 'I lead' is authority; 'you are my student' is role assignment
a direct suggestion is the command itself; authority is the standing that makes commands acceptable

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: Obedience to authority and source-credibility effects are well documented; perceived prestige of the hypnotist raises expectancy, but its separate effect on hypnotic response is modest and mixed.

entries.consent_note: False credentials are deception, and claimed clinical authority carries a duty of care the script must be able to meet.

entries.name: Borrowed authority
entries.summary: Cite science, tradition or a respected expert as backing for what the script says will happen.
entries.definition: Borrowed authority supports a claim by pointing to a source outside the speaker: research, medicine, an old practice, a named figure. The source does the persuading; the speaker only reports it. It differs from authority, where the standing is the speaker's own, and from giving a reason, where any 'because' clause will do whether or not a source is named.
entries.how_to: Use one citation, in the pre-talk, attached to the specific response you are about to ask for. Be accurate and proportionate: 'relaxation slows the heart rate' can be said plainly; claims about the unconscious mind cannot. A vague 'studies show' is weaker than a concrete, true statement and is easy for a skeptical listener to dismiss. Avoid it in deep trance, where citations invite analysis.
examples: Slow breathing like this is known to lower your heart rate. That part is just physiology.
People have used a steady point of focus to quiet the mind for centuries. You're doing something very old.
Researchers who study attention say it narrows when you give it one thing to hold. So give it my voice.
cues: 'studies show', 'research shows', 'science tells us', 'it's been proven'
'doctors', 'psychologists', 'researchers', 'experts' as the subject of a claim
'for centuries', 'ancient', 'traditional', 'monks have long'
a named expert, school or institution cited in support
technical vocabulary (brainwaves, neurons, the nervous system) used as backing

not_this.why: authority is the speaker's own expertise or role, not an outside source
reason-giving attaches any 'because'; borrowed authority needs a cited source
social proof cites many ordinary peers, not an expert or a body of knowledge

evidence.note: Credible sources raise acceptance of a message in persuasion research; many 'science says' lines in hypnosis scripts cite findings that do not exist or do not say what is claimed.

entries.consent_note: Citing science or experts that do not support the claim is deception; cite only what is true.

entries.name: Liking
entries.summary: Make the listener like the speaker, through warmth, shared ground and sincere compliments, before asking for anything.
entries.definition: Liking covers what the speaker says to be liked: friendliness, stated similarity, compliments, humor, care for the listener. People agree more readily with those they like. It differs from praise, which rewards a specific response just made, and from matching, which copies the listener's tempo or language instead of expressing warmth.
entries.how_to: Open with it and keep it going in small doses. State a real point of common ground, compliment something the listener actually did (showing up, making time), and speak as one person to another. Keep compliments specific and modest; flattery that the listener cannot believe lowers trust. Warmth in the pre-talk also makes later firm instructions easier to take.
examples: I'm glad you made time for this. It's not easy to stop in the middle of a day.
I'm the same way. My mind takes a while to quiet down too, so we'll go at an easy pace.
I like people who are curious enough to try something like this. I think we'll get on well.
cues: 'I'm glad you're here', 'it's good to have you', greetings with warmth
'I'm like that too', 'just like you, I' - stated similarity
compliments not tied to a response just performed
'I like', 'I enjoy', 'I care about' with the listener as object
light humor shared with the listener
a personal admission by the speaker (label the self-disclosure variant, which also counts as liking)

not_this.why: praise follows a specific response as its reward; liking builds affection before or apart from any response
matching mirrors the listener's pace or words; liking is expressed warmth and similarity
affection flooding is intense, sustained and out of proportion; liking is ordinary warmth

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: Similarity, compliments and familiarity reliably raise liking and compliance; rapport is held essential in clinical hypnosis but its measured contribution to hypnotic response is small.

entries.name: Parasocial intimacy
entries.summary: Speak as if in a private, ongoing, one-to-one relationship with the listener, though the recording goes to many.
entries.definition: Parasocial intimacy simulates a personal relationship in a one-way medium. The speaker talks as if alone with this listener, remembers them, missed them, and is paying attention only to them. It differs from ordinary liking in claiming a relationship, not just showing warmth, and from direct address, which is only the use of 'you'.
entries.how_to: Write as to one person in a private room: refer to shared history ('last time'), to the present moment between you, and to your attention being on them. Keep details general enough to fit any listener. Close-mic or whispered delivery supports it. Be clear in the description that this is a recording and a role; it fails, and can hurt, when a listener takes the relationship as real and it is not answered.
examples: It's just you and me now. Nobody else is here, and I'm not going anywhere.
I was hoping you'd come back tonight. I remember how well you settled last time.
I'm right here with you, paying attention to you and nothing else.
cues: 'just us', 'just you and me', 'nobody else', 'alone together'
'I missed you', 'I was thinking about you', 'I'm glad you came back'
references to shared history: 'last time', 'like we always do'
'I'm right here', 'I'm watching you', 'I can see you' in a recording
pet names and terms of endearment
stage directions for whispering or close-mic delivery

not_this.why: liking shows warmth and similarity; parasocial intimacy claims a private ongoing relationship
isolation runs down or replaces the listener's other people ('they wouldn't understand'); intimacy says only that speaker and listener are alone together now, with no claim about anyone else
affection flooding is overwhelming approval used to bind; this is the simulated one-to-one frame at any intensity
direct address is second-person wording; intimacy adds the claim of closeness
mind reading claims to know the listener's inner state; this claims presence and relationship

origin.source: Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl, Mass Communication and Para-Social Interaction: Observations on Intimacy at a Distance, Psychiatry (1956)

evidence.note: Parasocial relationships are well documented and can raise a source's persuasive pull; nothing shows they raise hypnotic response, and effects on lonely listeners are a known concern.

entries.consent_note: The closeness is simulated and one-way; say so outside the session, and do not use it to build dependency or to press for money or more listening.

entries.name: Self-disclosure
entries.summary: The speaker reveals a small personal feeling, flaw or difficulty of their own, which makes them more likeable and easier to trust.
entries.definition: A first-person statement about the speaker's own inner life or imperfection that is not needed to carry out the session: a nervousness, a habit, a mistake, what they enjoy about this work. It is the form of liking that works by showing something of oneself, as opposed to complimenting the listener or claiming similarity. In a persona-driven script it often appears as a brief step out of role, where the speaker drops the character's voice to say something as themselves.
entries.how_to: Keep it small, relevant and brief: one or two sentences, then return to the listener. Place it in the pre-talk, or at a turn where trust matters, such as just before asking for something harder or just after intense content. A minor flaw from a speaker who is otherwise competent raises liking; a large one, or one that bears on their ability to run the session, lowers confidence. Do not let it become the subject: disclosure that asks the listener to look after the speaker reverses the roles. If the disclosure is written for a character, it should still be true of the person voicing it or be clearly inside the fiction.
examples: I'll admit I still get a little nervous before recording these. I want it to be good for you.
My own mind is a noisy one. It took me a long time to learn to do what I'm about to show you.
Let me step out of the role for a moment. I enjoy this part more than I probably should.
cues: 'I'll admit', 'I have to confess', 'to be honest with you', 'between us' followed by a statement about the speaker
first-person feeling or flaw statements: 'I get nervous', 'I used to struggle with', 'I'm not good at'
'stepping out of character', 'speaking as myself for a moment', 'out of role'
a short passage whose subject is 'I' in a script otherwise addressed to 'you'
the speaker naming their own enjoyment, doubt or mistake

not_this.why: confession has the listener disclose private material to the speaker; here the speaker discloses to the listener
that claims a private ongoing relationship with the listener; a disclosure is one revealed fact about the speaker and claims no relationship
naming the technique tells the listener what is being done to them; self-disclosure tells them something about the speaker

origin.source: Collins & Miller, 'Self-disclosure and liking: a meta-analytic review' (1994)

evidence.note: Disclosure raises liking for the discloser and invites disclosure in return in controlled studies, and a small blunder can make a competent person more likeable; the scripted, one-way version in a recording has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: A disclosure invented to win trust works only while the listener takes it as real; do not fabricate vulnerability, and do not use a real one to draw a matching disclosure the listener would not otherwise give.

entries.name: Reciprocity
entries.summary: Give the listener something first, name it as given, then ask for something in return.
entries.definition: Reciprocity uses the felt obligation to repay. The script provides a benefit (rest, pleasure, attention, a free session), marks it as a gift from the speaker, and then makes a request. Both halves must be present: the gift and the ask. It differs from positive reinforcement, where the reward comes after the response, and from door in the face, where the 'gift' is a concession on a refused request.
entries.how_to: Deliver something the listener actually feels before the ask: a good stretch of relaxation is enough. Name it briefly as something you gave, then ask once, for something proportionate. The closer the ask follows the gift, the stronger the pull. It fails when the gift is not felt, and it sours when the debt is pressed or when the return asked is far larger than what was given.
examples: I've given you this quiet, and all this time to rest. Now do one small thing for me: listen again tomorrow.
That calm is my gift to you. In return, give me your full attention for the next few minutes.
I took care of you just now. So let me ask something of you.
cues: 'I gave you', 'my gift to you', 'I've done this for you'
'in return', 'in exchange', 'now do something for me'
'you owe', 'the least you can do', 'it's only fair'
a benefit described as coming from the speaker, followed within a few lines by a request
'free', 'at no cost' attached to the session, followed by an ask

not_this.why: reinforcement rewards after the response; reciprocity gives before the ask
door in the face trades a concession on a refused large request, not a prior gift
thanking has the listener express gratitude; reciprocity asks for repayment
that's-not-all adds extras to an offer still on the table, before any answer

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: An unrequested favor raises later compliance in controlled studies; the effect of a 'gift' that is itself only suggested has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: Using a felt debt to extract money, escalation or continued listening the listener did not sign up for is manipulative; keep the ask proportionate and refusable.

entries.name: Scarcity
entries.summary: Present the experience or offer as limited in time, quantity or access, so the listener values it more and acts now.
entries.definition: Scarcity states that the opportunity is rare, short-lived or about to be lost. Things that are harder to get are judged more valuable, and a possible loss moves people more than an equal gain. It concerns the availability of the offer; the exclusivity variant narrows it to who is allowed. It differs from deprivation, which actually withholds something to raise its value, where scarcity only describes the limit.
entries.how_to: State the limit concretely: this session, this moment, these few minutes. Put it where a decision is needed, typically the description, the pre-talk or the point of commitment. One clear limit works better than repeated urgency. False limits are quickly discounted on a recording that can be replayed, so prefer limits that are true: a state that will pass, a moment of depth that will not last unless used.
examples: You won't get many moments in a day as quiet as this one. Use it.
This depth doesn't last long. While it's here, take in what I say next.
There are only a few minutes left in this session, and they are the ones that matter.
cues: 'limited', 'rare', 'just this once', 'only a few' applied to the session, the moment or the offer
'while it lasts', 'before it's gone', 'this moment won't come again'
deadlines and counts: 'only a few minutes left', 'the last chance'
'don't miss', 'don't waste', loss wording attached to the present opportunity
'now or never', 'it won't be here later'

not_this.why: deprivation actually withholds something; scarcity describes the offer as limited
loss framing recasts an outcome as an avoided loss without claiming limited supply
a warning-as-lure forbids or cautions; scarcity says supply or time is short

origin.source: Cialdini, Influence (1984)

evidence.note: Scarce items are rated more valuable in controlled studies, with effect size depending on context; no evidence shows scarcity wording changes hypnotic response.

entries.consent_note: Invented deadlines or shortages are deception and pressure the listener to skip their own judgment.

entries.name: Exclusivity
entries.summary: Tell the listener they have been singled out, or that this is offered only to a few people like them.
entries.definition: Exclusivity is scarcity of access: what is limited is who may have it. The listener is told they were chosen, qualify, or are among the few who can do this. It differs from plain scarcity, which limits time or quantity for everyone, and from labeling, which assigns a trait in order to ask for behavior that fits it.
entries.how_to: Give a reason the listener qualifies, tied to something true of them: they came back, they listened this far, they respond well. Then describe what follows as reserved for people who did that. One statement is enough. On a public recording an unqualified 'only for you' is plainly false, so tie it to a condition the listener has met.
examples: Not everyone gets this far. This next part is only for the ones who do.
I don't say this to most people. I'm saying it to you because you kept listening.
This is for the few who can stay this still. You're one of them.
cues: 'only for you', 'just for you', 'not for everyone', 'not everyone can'
'chosen', 'selected', 'singled out', 'special'
'the few who', 'most people never', 'I don't tell most people'
access wording: 'reserved', 'invitation', 'members only', 'you've earned'
a qualifying condition followed by privileged content

not_this.why: plain scarcity limits time or supply for everyone; exclusivity limits who is allowed
unity says speaker and listener share an identity ('we', 'one of us'); exclusivity says the listener was admitted to something others are not, and needs no shared 'we'
labeling assigns a trait to get matching behavior; exclusivity raises the value of what is offered
isolation devalues everyone outside the speaker; exclusivity flatters the listener's selection without running anyone down
parasocial intimacy simulates a one-to-one relationship; exclusivity only says the listener was selected

evidence.note: It follows from scarcity research and is standard in sales copy, but being 'chosen' by a mass recording has no direct test.

entries.consent_note: Telling every listener they alone were chosen is a false claim; tie it to a condition the listener really met.

entries.name: Unity
entries.summary: Tell the listener that they and the speaker belong to the same group, so the suggestion comes from one of their own.
entries.definition: Unity invokes a shared identity: speaker and listener, or listener and a community, are 'we'. The appeal is membership, not resemblance: liking says 'I am like you', unity says 'we are the same kind'. It differs from social proof, which reports what a group does, by placing the listener inside the group.
entries.how_to: Name the group and what makes the listener part of it, then phrase what follows with 'we' and 'us'. Use an identity the listener already holds or has just earned (people who practice, those who have listened before). It suits series and communities more than a single cold recording. It fails when the group is one the listener does not recognize, or when 'we' appears with nothing behind it.
examples: We're the kind of people who take the time to do this properly, you and I.
You're one of us now. Everyone who has done this session shares what you're feeling.
This is what we do. We slow down, we listen, and we let go together.
cues: 'one of us', 'you belong', 'part of', 'our kind'
a named group or collective noun the listener is placed in
'we' or 'us' as subject of a statement about what the group is or does ('we're the kind of people who', 'this is what we do'), not 'we' for a shared task
family or kin terms used for a non-family group
'people like us' followed by a norm of the group

not_this.why: liking is similarity and warmth between two individuals; unity is membership in one group
social proof cites what others do; unity makes the listener one of them
labeling gives the listener alone a trait and then asks for behavior that fits; unity puts speaker and listener, or listener and a group, in one category
exclusivity says the listener was let in to something restricted; unity says the listener and the speaker are the same kind
pronoun shift is the change of pronoun as a device; unity is the membership claim, whatever the pronoun

origin.source: Cialdini, Pre-Suasion (2016)

evidence.note: In-group favoritism and greater influence from in-group sources are well established; unity as a distinct principle is Cialdini's later synthesis and is untested in hypnosis.

entries.consent_note: Belonging offered on condition of compliance, or set against outsiders, shades into the coercive family.

entries.name: In-group language
entries.summary: Use special words that members of the group know, so that understanding and using them marks the listener as one of them.
entries.definition: In-group language is unity carried by vocabulary. The script uses terms of art, nicknames for states, or set phrases that an outsider would not know and a member would. Recognizing the term signals belonging. It differs from loaded language, where the special terms carry a built-in judgment and close down thought; in-group terms only mark membership.
entries.how_to: Introduce a term once with a plain gloss, then use it without explanation so the listener has the experience of knowing it. Keep the set small and consistent across a series. Words for states the listener has just felt work best, since the term then names a shared experience. It fails when too many terms arrive at once, or when a new listener is left unable to follow.
examples: Those of us who do this call it 'the hush', that moment when the room goes quiet inside. You know the one.
You've reached what regulars here call the floor. Rest on it.
Welcome back. You already know what we mean when we say 'settle'.
cues: 'we call it', 'what we call', 'regulars call', 'those of us who'
a coined or capitalized term for a state or practice, used without explanation
scare quotes or italics around a term presented as the group's word
'you know what that means', 'you know the one'
the same coined term recurring across files in a series

not_this.why: loaded language builds a verdict into the term and narrows thought; in-group terms only mark membership
naming the state tells the listener what a state is called; in-group language presents the name as the group's own
a trigger word is installed to produce a response; an in-group term only signals belonging

evidence.note: Shared vocabulary as a marker of group membership is documented in sociolinguistics; its effect on acceptance of suggestions has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: A private vocabulary that outsiders cannot follow can make the listener harder to reach for people outside the group; keep terms explainable in plain words.

entries.name: Modeling
entries.summary: Show or describe someone else doing the wanted response and being rewarded for it, without telling the listener to copy them.
entries.definition: The script presents a model: one person who performs the response, and what they get for it. The listener is given no instruction; they watch, and the shown consequence does the persuading. It differs from social proof, which reports that many people do something, in showing one performance and its outcome. It differs from My friend John, where the third person is a channel for live suggestions the listener carries out as they are given. Modeling here is the social-learning sense; the NLP use of the word, copying an expert's strategy, is a different thing.
entries.how_to: Choose a model the listener can see themselves in, close to them in age, doubts and starting point. Show the response in concrete steps, including a moment of hesitation that the model gets past, then show the reward clearly and at once. Leave out 'and you will too'; the comparison is the listener's to make. A model who succeeds too easily or is too unlike the listener is dismissed. In video or live work the model is an actual demonstration; in a script it is a described person. The modeled response can be a sound: a sigh, a moan or a whimper placed right after a line supplies the reaction the listener is meant to have.
examples: The woman before you sat in that same chair, sure it wouldn't work for her. She let her shoulders drop anyway, and I watched the worry leave her face.
He answered without stopping to think, and she smiled at him. 'That's it,' she said. 'That's exactly right.' He had not felt that pleased with himself in weeks.
Watch how she does it. One slow breath, her hands open, and she is already calmer than she was a moment ago.
cues: a third person (he, she, a named character, 'the last person who sat here') performing the target response
the model's reward stated right after the act: praise received, relief, pleasure, approval
'watch how...', 'notice what happens when she...', 'I once worked with someone who...'
no imperative addressed to the listener within the passage
the model's initial doubt or hesitation described, then overcome
a reaction sound placed right after a line by stage direction: [sigh], [whimper]

not_this.why: social proof reports what many people do as a norm; modeling shows one person doing it and what it earned them

entries.name: Expectation and framing
entries.summary: Devices that set, before and during the session, what the listener expects and how they interpret what happens.
entries.definition: Framing devices do not ask for a response directly; they shape the expectation or meaning that a response will be read through. Some act before the experience (expectation setting, seeding, title priming, myth correction), some reinterpret it as it happens or after (reframing and its variants, naming the state, redefinition). The family is distinct from presupposition, which builds a claim into sentence grammar, and from suggestion forms, which phrase the request itself.
entries.how_to: Choose by timing and target. Before the experience, use expectation setting, seeding, myth correction, objection preemption or title priming to decide what the listener will look for. During it, use naming the state, reframing or no-fail framing to decide what what they notice means. Use gain/loss framing, reference points and redefinition when the job is to change how a single outcome or word is judged; use inevitability or the as-if frame when the job is to change how certain or how real the outcome feels. Fiction frame and naming the technique set the overall contract with the listener and should be chosen early, since they change how everything after is evaluated.

not_this.why: presupposition hides the claim inside sentence grammar; framing states or shapes the interpretation openly

evidence.note: Expectancy effects on hypnotic response and framing effects on judgment are both well studied; individual named devices in the family range from experimental to practitioner-lore.

entries.name: Contrast
entries.summary: Put the thing you want judged next to something more extreme, so it seems smaller, easier or better by comparison.
entries.definition: Contrast sets up a comparison whose only job is to shift how the next item is judged. A large effort is described first so the actual request feels small; tension is described so the calm feels deeper. It differs from antithesis, which is a balanced phrasing of opposites for style, and from the numeric reference point, which sets a number that later estimates adjust from.
entries.how_to: Give the extreme comparison first, briefly, then the real item straight after. The two must be on the same dimension (effort, time, intensity). Use it before a request that might seem large or before a state you want felt as strong. It fails when the comparison is so far-fetched it is ignored, or when too much time passes between the two.
examples: You spent the whole day holding everything together. All I'm asking for is ten minutes of doing nothing.
Compared with how tight your shoulders were when you sat down, notice how loose they feel now.
I could ask you to clear your whole mind. I won't. Just let go of one thought.

entries.name: Expectation setting
entries.summary: Tell the listener in advance what they will experience, so they look for it and read what happens as that.
entries.definition: A plain forward-looking statement of what the session will feel like or do. It works by giving the listener a template to match their experience against. It differs from seeding, which mentions an idea casually without announcing it as the plan, and from direct suggestion, which asks for the response now.
entries.how_to: Put it in the pre-talk or at the start of each section. Describe likely, achievable experiences in concrete sensory terms (heaviness, a slowing breath, sounds becoming distant). Set ranges, not single outcomes, so that whatever happens fits. Overpromising dramatic effects backfires when they do not arrive.
examples: In a few minutes you will probably notice your arms getting heavier, and your breathing slowing on its own.
Some people feel a pleasant tingling, some feel very still. You will find out which it is for you.
First your breathing will slow, then your body will start to feel heavy, and after that your thoughts will get quiet.
