evidence.note: Expectancy reliably predicts hypnotic response in controlled studies, though it explains only part of the variance in suggestibility.

entries.name: Potency claim
entries.summary: Assert in advance that the recording or technique is unusually strong or effective.
entries.definition: Expectation setting aimed at magnitude rather than content: the listener is told the effect will be strong, fast or hard to resist. It raises expectancy without describing what will be felt. It is distinct from authority, which builds the speaker's standing, though the two often appear together.
entries.how_to: Place it in the title, description or opening lines. A short, specific claim (this file is designed to work quickly) lands better than piled superlatives. If the claim far outruns what the listener then feels, it turns into evidence that the file failed, so pair it with a no-fail frame.

evidence.note: Labelling a procedure as hypnosis or as powerful raises response in studies of expectancy, but the gain is modest and depends on the claim being believed.

entries.name: Warning as lure
entries.summary: Issue a warning about the file's effects that reads as an invitation to listen.
entries.definition: A caution phrased to raise curiosity and appeal rather than to inform. It combines a potency claim with a touch of prohibition, so listening becomes a dare. It differs from a content note, whose aim is informed choice, and from reverse psychology, which instructs the opposite of the wanted act within the session.
entries.how_to: Put it at the top of the description or pre-talk. Name an effect and tell the listener not to proceed unless they want it. It works on listeners who enjoy defying a limit; it can read as a gimmick to others. If the warning is also meant to protect, keep a separate, plain content note.
examples: Do not listen to this file unless you are ready to stop thinking for a while.

entries.name: Seeding
entries.summary: Mention an idea early and in passing so it is already familiar when the real suggestion arrives later.
entries.definition: An early, low-key reference to a later target response, made without asking for it. The later suggestion then lands on prepared ground. It differs from interspersal, which scatters suggestion words through the same passage, and from expectation setting, which openly announces what will happen.
entries.how_to: Put the seed in the pre-talk or induction, well before the target. Mention the idea in an unrelated context (a remark about how hands sometimes feel light on a warm day before an arm levitation). Keep it casual; a seed that is stressed reads as a suggestion and loses its point. Make the later suggestion echo the seed's words so the link is felt.
examples: Funny how on a warm afternoon your hands can feel almost weightless resting in your lap.
Some mornings you wake before the alarm and have no idea how long you have been lying there.
I once watched a cat fall asleep in a sunbeam, completely still, without deciding to.

entries.name: Reframing
entries.summary: Give an experience, behavior or sensation a different meaning so the listener responds to the new meaning.
entries.definition: The facts stay the same; what they mean is changed. A meaning reframe says what X really signifies; a context reframe names a setting where X is useful. It differs from redefinition, which changes the meaning of a word, and from complex equivalence, which is the grammatical form 'X means Y' that a reframe often uses.
entries.how_to: Start from something the listener is actually experiencing or doing, ideally something they see as a problem. Offer the new meaning as a plain statement, then build on it at once so it is used rather than argued. A reframe lands when it fits the facts at least as well as the old meaning; a reframe the listener can easily refute invites counterargument.
examples: That restlessness is just your body using up the last of the day's energy before it settles.
A wandering mind is not a problem here. It means you have stopped forcing things.
Being stubborn is exactly what you want once you have decided to stay relaxed no matter what.

entries.name: Relabeling sensation
entries.summary: Tell the listener that a body sensation they already feel has a specific cause or meaning other than the one they would assume.
entries.definition: A reframe applied to a physical sensation the listener already has: a tingle, warmth, heartbeat or flutter is given a specific new cause or meaning, such as the speaker's influence, a particular suggestion taking hold, or a different emotion. Name the sensation, then attach the meaning in the same sentence. Keep the meaning tied to the suggestion's goal. It is weak if the listener does not have the sensation, so hedge with 'if you notice'.
examples: That flutter in your stomach isn't nerves. It's your body getting ready to enjoy this.

entries.name: No-fail framing
entries.summary: Declare in advance or after the fact that whatever the listener experiences, including apparent failure, counts as success.
entries.definition: A reframe that removes failure as a category: not going deep, staying alert or not feeling anything is defined as correct or as part of the process. entries.name: Surrender as freedom
entries.summary: Present letting go of control, or following instructions, as relief and liberation rather than loss.

entries.name: Resistance as participation
entries.summary: Describe the listener's resistance as one more way of taking part in the process.

entries.name: Doubt as a sign

entries.name: Fiction frame
entries.summary: Present the content as fiction, play or pretend, which lowers how strictly the listener evaluates it.

entries.name: Myth correction

entries.name: Gain / loss framing

entries.definition: The speaker declares what a word truly means (real strength is letting go; relaxing is a skill) and then relies on the new sense. The listener's positive or negative feeling about the word carries over to the new content. It differs from reframing, which changes the meaning of an experience, and from loaded language, which is a group's whole stock of judgment-laden terms.
entries.how_to: Pick a word the listener already values or fears. State the new definition as a plain truth, then use the word several times in its new sense so it sticks. It works best when the new sense is a plausible stretch of the old one; a definition that is obviously false invites pushback.
examples: Real focus isn't straining. Real focus is letting everything else go quiet.
Control doesn't mean holding on. Control means choosing where your attention goes.
cues: real ... is
true ... means
what ... really means
... is just another word for
a valued word followed by 'is' and an unusual definition

not_this.why: reframing changes what an experience means, not what a word means
in complex equivalence X is an event or behavior that is said to show Y; in redefinition X is a word or value term (often marked 'real', 'true', 'really') whose sense is being replaced
loaded language is a group's whole vocabulary of judgment-laden terms

origin.source: Stevenson, Persuasive definitions (1938)

evidence.note: Persuasive definition is a long-recognized rhetorical and argumentation figure; its persuasive effect is not directly measured.

entries.name: Inevitability
entries.summary: Present the outcome as certain, so the only open question is when or how it happens.
entries.definition: Open assertion that the response will happen whatever the listener does. It removes the question of whether. It differs from presupposition (already-happened framing), which builds the outcome into the grammar rather than asserting it, and from the permanence claim, which concerns how long the change lasts.
entries.how_to: Use calm, certain language: will, is going to, sooner or later. Pair with a time or manner choice so the listener has something to do with the certainty. Delivered as threat it raises reactance; delivered as a quiet fact it lowers effort.
examples: Sooner or later your eyes are going to close. It might be now, it might be in a minute.
You can't stop the relaxation from spreading. You can only notice where it goes next.
cues: sooner or later
it's only a matter of time
you can't help
you can't stop
inevitably
no matter what you do

not_this.why: a plain 'you will' states the response; label inevitability only when the wording says it will happen whatever the listener does
'it happens by itself' is about who is doing it; inevitability is about whether it can fail to happen
already-happened framing treats the result as done via grammar instead of asserting it will come
a time bind offers a choice of when; inevitability may stand without any choice

evidence.note: Confident framing raises expectancy, which predicts response, but strong inevitability language can also trigger reactance; no direct study.

entries.consent_note: Inevitability language aimed at outcomes after the session should be balanced by a stated way to stop or undo them.

entries.name: As-if frame
aliases: what would it be like if
entries.summary: Ask the listener to suppose the outcome is already true and explore what that is like.
entries.definition: An invitation to imagine a hypothetical as real and to elaborate it from the inside. The listener generates the details, which makes the outcome feel more possible and more their own. It differs from the fiction frame, which declares the whole content to be play, and from mental rehearsal, which runs a specific future behavior step by step.
entries.how_to: Phrase it as a question or a 'suppose': what would it be like if...? Then give room (a pause, follow-up questions) for the listener to fill it in. It works best on outcomes the listener wants but doubts. Follow it with a suggestion that some of what they imagined can stay.
examples: Suppose, just for a moment, that you were already completely calm. What would you notice first?
What would it be like if your mind were quiet right now? How would your breathing change?
cues: suppose the outcome had already happened
what would it be like if
imagine that you already
just for a moment, pretend that you
act as though you already
a hypothetical outcome followed by a question about what the listener notices

not_this.why: the fiction frame declares the whole content to be play
mental rehearsal walks through a specific future behavior
the pretend induction asks the listener to act hypnotized as the route into trance

evidence.note: Imagining an outcome raises its judged likelihood and can inflate belief that it happened; the NLP 'as if frame' itself is not independently tested.

entries.name: Title and description priming
entries.summary: Use the title, tags, cover text and description to set the listener's expectations before the audio starts.
entries.definition: Framing carried in the material around the script rather than in it: the file name, summary, tags, listed effects and length. It decides what the listener comes in expecting and so what they look for. It differs from expectation setting, which happens inside the session, and from a content note, whose aim is informed choice.
entries.how_to: Write the title and description as part of the script. Name the experience and the main effect clearly; tags and effect lists act as a promise. Keep claims consistent with what the file delivers, or the gap becomes evidence of failure. Put safety and content information here too, separately from the hook.
examples: Title: Heavy and Still. Description: A slow, gentle induction for deep physical rest. Effects: relaxation, heavy limbs, easy sleep.
Tags: induction, deepener, sleep, no wakener.
cues: Title:
Description:
Tags:
Effects:
text outside the spoken script that names effects or style

not_this.why: expectation setting is spoken inside the session
a content note states what the file contains so the listener can decide; it may share the description but has a different job
a potency claim may appear in a title but asserts strength, not content

evidence.note: Prior labels shape expectancy and experience in placebo and expectancy studies; the effect of file paratext on hypnosis audio is untested.

entries.name: Convincers and tests
entries.summary: Suggested experiences staged so the listener notices something unusual happening and takes it as proof of trance or of the speaker's influence.
entries.definition: This family holds the phenomena a script suggests in order to be noticed: locked eyelids, a rigid arm, numbness, a hallucinated sound, a forgotten number, a finger that lifts by itself. What unites them is purpose, not mechanism: each one gives the listener a felt experience they did not consciously produce, and the script then treats that experience as evidence. It differs from ratification, which comments on what already happened, and from the convincer section, which is the place in the script where these devices sit.
entries.how_to: Pick by what the listener can check alone with a recording. Body challenges (eyelid lock, rigid arm, stuck hand, freeze) give a clear pass or fail and suit a first session; sensation and numbness are gentler and almost always succeed partly; hallucinations and amnesia are harder and should come after easier items have worked. Use a suggestibility test before the induction, a convincer after deepening, and an after-the-fact proof after waking. Always ratify the result whatever it was, and prefer items that cannot visibly fail when you cannot see the listener.

not_this.why: the section is the place in the script; the family is the set of devices used there
ratification interprets a response as proof; a convincer is the suggestion that produces the response
the challenge is the 'try and you can't' wording; convincers are the phenomena it is often attached to

evidence.note: Most of these phenomena are items on standardized susceptibility scales and respond reliably in high scorers; that passing one deepens trance or strengthens later suggestions is practitioner belief, not an established finding.

entries.consent_note: Convincers can be used to persuade a listener they are under more control than they are; a script should not use them to imply the listener cannot stop or leave.

entries.name: Convincer
entries.summary: Suggest an effect, have the listener check it, and treat the result as proof of trance or of the speaker's influence.
entries.definition: A convincer is a suggested effect staged to be checked: the script names an effect, usually an inability, has the listener test it, and treats the result as proof of trance or of the speaker's influence. Its point is the check, not the effect. Label the whole passage, from build-up to release, with the named variant where one fits (eyelid lock, rigid arm, stuck, freeze, speech lock, name or number amnesia) and with this generic label only where none does, such as a limb too heavy to lift. The 'try and you can't' sentence inside the passage is also a challenge suggestion, and the comment that follows the result is ratification.
entries.how_to: Place it after induction and some deepening, when the listener is settled. Build the effect first with several sentences of direct suggestion, then give a short, permissive test ('try, and notice'), then stop the test quickly and release the effect explicitly. Ratify the outcome either way: a pass is proof, a partial pass is 'already beginning'. Do not run a long test, which gives effort time to win.
examples: Your right arm is so heavy it will not lift from your lap; try lifting it, then notice how that shows the suggestion took hold.
That word has slipped from your mind; try saying it now, and notice how the gap shows something has changed.
Feel your left hand grow lighter than your right; lift both and compare them, then notice the difference as proof that you responded.
cues: 'try to ...' after a run of suggestions about the same body part
'and you can't', 'it won't', 'the harder you try the more'
'stop trying', 'let it go now', 'back to normal' right after the test
'that's how you know', 'proof', 'see how deep you are'

not_this.why: the challenge is the single 'try and you can't' sentence; the convincer is the whole staged passage from build-up to release. Label the sentence as the challenge and the passage as the convincer; both apply
ratification is the short comment on a result ('that's right'); the convincer is the suggestion and test that produce the result
a suggestibility test is run awake before the induction and framed as imagination; a convincer is run in trance and framed as proof
a trigger test fires an installed cue to show the cue works; a convincer checks an effect suggested just now

evidence.note: Challenge items behave reliably on susceptibility scales, but the clinical claim that a passed convincer deepens trance or improves outcomes has not been tested directly.

entries.consent_note: A convincer persuades by producing an experience the listener did not choose; release every inability explicitly before the session ends.

entries.name: Eyelid lock
entries.summary: Suggest the eyelids are so relaxed or stuck that they will not open, then invite the listener to try.
entries.definition: The eyelid form of the convincer: suggest that the eyes cannot open and invite the listener to try opening them. Practitioners often use it as an early challenge. It differs from eye closure, which asks only that the eyes close, by the added attempt to open them.
entries.how_to: Use it once the eyes are closed and the listener has relaxed the small muscles around them. Frame the lock as relaxation ('so relaxed they won't work') rather than force, which makes trying feel like breaking the relaxation. Keep the test to a second or two, then tell them to stop trying and relax further. In self-hypnosis or recordings, phrase it so trying is optional.
examples: Relax the muscles around your eyes so completely that they just won't work.
When you're sure they won't open, test them. Try. That's right, stop trying now and go deeper.
cues: 'eyelids', 'eyes' with 'glued', 'stuck', 'sealed', 'locked', 'won't open'
'relax them so much they won't work'
'test them', 'try to open them' after eye-closure suggestions
'stop testing', 'stop trying' immediately after

not_this.why: closure only asks the eyes to close; the lock adds a test of opening
eye-roll uses the eyes as a fixation start; the lock tests them after closure

evidence.note: Eye catalepsy is an item on standard group and individual scales and is passed by roughly half of participants in normative samples; its use as a gateway to deeper trance is clinical convention.

entries.name: Rigid arm
entries.summary: Suggest an outstretched arm becomes rigid like a bar and will not bend, then invite the listener to try bending it.
entries.definition: The arm form of the convincer: an outstretched arm is suggested to be stiff and unbendable, and the listener is invited to try bending it. It differs from a stuck convincer, where the limb is fixed to something, and from arm levitation, where the arm moves instead of locking. The listener tenses the arm under the suggestion, so the effect is partly genuine effort reframed as involuntary. 'Arm catalepsy' in Ericksonian writing also means a lifted arm that simply stays where it is put, with no stiffness; label that here only when the script goes on to test it.
entries.how_to: Have the listener extend an arm and make a fist first. Build rigidity with imagery (steel, a bar, a board) and with time, then invite one bend attempt. Release it clearly, arm loose and resting, before moving on. Skip it for listeners who may have shoulder problems or who are lying down with nowhere to hold the arm.
examples: Stretch your arm out in front of you and make a fist. Feel it becoming straight and stiff, like a bar of steel.
So stiff that it won't bend. Try to bend it, and find it stays straight.
Now let it go loose, and rest it down.
cues: 'arm' with 'stiff', 'rigid', 'steel', 'bar', 'board', 'locked'
'stretch your arm out', 'make a fist' before the lock
'try to bend it'
'let it go loose', 'soft again' afterward

not_this.why: stuck fixes a part to a surface; rigid arm fixes the joint itself
levitation produces movement; rigidity prevents it
freeze locks the whole body, not one limb

evidence.note: Arm rigidity is a standard item on susceptibility scales; it is also one of the items most easily produced by plain voluntary tension.

entries.name: Stuck
entries.summary: Suggest a hand, foot or the body is stuck to a surface and cannot be lifted, then invite a try.
entries.definition: A convincer that fixes a body part to something outside it: hand to the table, hands clasped together, back to the chair, feet to the floor. The fixation is to a surface or another body part, which separates it from rigid arm (a joint locks) and freeze (the whole body stops).
entries.how_to: Name the surface concretely and give it a property: glue, a magnet, cement. Pressing down first helps, since the listener's own pressure becomes the 'stick'. Test once, briefly. Release with an equally concrete unsticking ('the glue dissolves') so nothing is left ambiguous after the session.
examples: Press your hand flat on your leg. Feel it sticking there, as if glued.
The more you try to lift it, the more firmly it stays.
Now the glue melts away, and your hand lifts easily.
cues: 'stuck to', 'glued to', 'stuck fast', 'magnet'
'hands locked together', 'fingers interlocked and stuck'
'try to lift', 'try to pull apart', 'try to stand'
'the glue dissolves', 'unstuck', 'free again'

not_this.why: rigid arm locks the joint; stuck fixes the limb to a surface or to another body part
freeze stops all movement; stuck fixes one contact point
a hand clasp done awake before the induction and framed as imagination is a suggestibility test; the same lock in trance, framed as proof, is this
magnetic hands suggests the hands come together; stuck suggests they cannot come apart

evidence.note: Hand-lock and hands-stuck-together items appear on standard scales; stage forms (stuck to the chair) are stage practice without separate study.

entries.name: Name / number amnesia
entries.summary: Suggest that one familiar item, such as a number or the listener's name, is gone, then ask them to count or say it to find it missing.
entries.definition: A convincer that tests memory instead of muscle: one well-known item is suggested away, and a routine task (counting fingers, saying their name) reveals the gap. It differs from amnesia suggestion in its narrow target and built-in test, and from speech lock, where the word is known but cannot be said.
entries.how_to: Choose one item the listener uses without thinking, often a number between one and ten. Suggest it fades, is removed, or is simply not there, then give a quick task that passes through it. Treat hesitation as success. Restore the item explicitly and test that it is back before moving on or waking.
examples: The number seven is drifting away now, out of your mind, gone.
Count your fingers for me. One, two, three... and notice what happens.
Now the number comes back, exactly where it belongs.
cues: 'forget the number', 'the number ... is gone'
'you can't remember your name', 'your name slips away'
'count your fingers', 'tell me your name' right after
'it comes back now', 'remember it again'

not_this.why: amnesia suggestion targets events or content of the session; this removes one known item and checks at once that it is missing
in losing the numbers the listener counts down a long run and all the numbers fade as a route to depth; here one item is removed and a short task shows the gap
speech lock blocks saying a word that is still known ('you can't say it'); here the item is suggested as unknown ('it's gone', 'you can't remember it')

evidence.note: A stage and clinical staple; suggested amnesia in general is well studied, but the single-number form is not studied separately and responses vary widely.

entries.consent_note: Always restore the item explicitly and check it before the session ends.

entries.name: Speech lock
entries.summary: Suggest the listener cannot speak, or can say only one fixed word or phrase, then invite them to try.
entries.definition: A convincer that blocks or narrows speech. The listener keeps knowing what they want to say; the suggestion targets the saying. A narrowed form allows only a chosen word, often used in erotic and stage scripts. It differs from name amnesia, which removes the knowledge itself.
entries.how_to: Build the effect on the throat, jaw or voice ('your voice is resting'), then invite a single attempt, such as trying to say their name. In the narrowed form, name the one allowed word and invite them to try any other. Release with a clear statement that full speech is back, and never leave it running when the listener might need to call for help.
examples: Your voice is resting now, so quiet that no words come out. Try to say your name.
The only word you can say is 'yes'. Try to say anything else.
Your voice comes back now, clear and easy.
cues: 'can't speak', 'can't say', 'no words come out'
'the only word you can say is'
'voice is resting', 'throat is quiet', 'mouth won't open'
'your voice comes back'

not_this.why: amnesia removes the item from memory; speech lock blocks saying it
freeze locks the whole body; speech lock targets the voice
repeat-after-me asks for speech; a one-word lock forbids everything else

evidence.note: Verbal inhibition is a recognized challenge item in hypnosis testing and stage work; it has not been studied as a separate effect.

entries.consent_note: A speech lock can stop a listener using a safeword; keep it short, never cover the safeword, and release it explicitly.

entries.name: Freeze
entries.summary: Suggest the whole body is locked in place and cannot move until released, then invite a try.
entries.definition: The whole-body form of the convincer: every limb stops at once. Scripts use it as a dramatic proof and, in dominance contexts, as a show of control. It differs from stuck and rigid arm by scope, and from relaxation deepeners that describe heaviness without testing movement.
entries.how_to: Lead up through a part (eyes, then arms) before claiming the whole body. Keep breathing and blinking explicitly free. Test with one small, named movement, release fully and promptly, and invite a stretch afterward to confirm the release. Avoid it in files meant for sleep, where the release may be missed.
examples: Your whole body is still now, like a statue. Only your breath moves.
Try to move a finger, and find everything stays exactly as it is.
And now you're free. Stretch, and feel everything moving easily.
cues: 'can't move', 'frozen', 'statue', 'paralysed', 'locked in place'
'whole body', 'every muscle' with an inability
'try to move' after a body-wide stillness suggestion
'free to move again', 'stretch' as a release

not_this.why: stuck fixes one contact point; freeze stops the whole body
heaviness describes weight without testing movement
a deepener uses the body to go deeper; freeze stages a test of control

evidence.note: A stage and community staple; full-body immobility is not a standard scale item and has not been studied apart from single-limb challenges.

entries.consent_note: A freeze implies the listener cannot act; keep it short, leave breathing and safewords free, and release it clearly.

entries.name: Ideomotor signal
entries.summary: Ask the unconscious to answer by lifting a chosen finger or moving the head, so the movement feels like it happened on its own.
entries.definition: A small movement assigned a meaning (yes, no, ready) and requested from 'the unconscious' rather than the listener. Because it often comes slowly and jerkily, the listener experiences it as involuntary, which makes it both an answer and a convincer. It differs from a deliberate response request in that the script frames the movement as not chosen, and from ideomotor induction, where movement is used to deepen rather than to answer.
entries.how_to: Set the signals first: name which finger means yes and which means no, and ask for them to be tested. Then ask questions and wait, describing the finger as lifting 'by itself'. Accept any movement, even a twitch. In recorded scripts, where no one can see the answer, use the signal as a self-check ('when you are ready, your finger lifts') rather than as a question needing a reply.
examples: Let your unconscious answer yes by lifting your index finger; is this the right time to continue? Wait for that finger to move.
Let one finger mean yes and another mean no; ask whether you are ready to go deeper, and allow one finger to answer.
Let a small nod mean yes; ask your unconscious whether it wants to pause, and notice whether the nod comes.
cues: 'yes finger', 'no finger', 'I don't know finger'
a movement assigned a meaning: 'this finger means yes', 'a nod for yes'
'let your unconscious answer', 'let the finger answer'
a yes/no question followed by a pause or a wait for movement
'lift on its own', 'by itself' said of the assigned finger or the head

not_this.why: the implied directive is the sentence 'when X has happened inside, your finger will lift'; the signal is a movement given a meaning and used to answer. Label setting up the signal and asking it questions here; label a 'when ..., your finger lifts' sentence as the implied directive, and add this label only if the finger was set up as a signal
ideomotor induction uses a movement as the route into trance; the signal uses it to answer
automaticity framing words any response as happening by itself; the signal is one movement assigned a meaning
the split is the address to 'your unconscious' as a separate listener; the signal is the channel it is asked to answer through

origin.source: Cheek & LeCron, Clinical Hypnotherapy (1968)

evidence.note: The ideomotor effect itself is well established; the clinical claim that finger signals give reliable access to unconscious knowledge is not supported and risks producing false answers.

entries.consent_note: Do not treat finger answers as revealing hidden facts, especially about memories; they follow expectation.

entries.name: Suggested sensation
entries.summary: Suggest a felt sensation (warmth, tingling, pressure, touch) in a named place with no physical cause.
entries.definition: A suggestion for something felt in the body that nothing outside is causing. It is the gentlest convincer, since attention alone produces mild tingling or warmth in most people, and the script can claim it. It differs from positive hallucination, which covers sight, sound, taste and smell, and from sensation relabeling, which renames a feeling already there.
entries.how_to: Name a body part and one sensation, and describe it in small specific terms: where it starts, how it spreads. Choose sensations attention tends to produce (tingling in fingertips, warmth in the hands) for early convincers, and harder ones (cold, a touch on the shoulder) later. Pace any real sensation first. Ask the listener to notice it rather than to feel it, so a faint response counts.
examples: Notice a gentle tingling starting in the tips of your fingers.
A warmth gathering in the palm of your right hand, spreading slowly to the wrist.
Perhaps a light pressure on your shoulder, like a hand resting there.
cues: 'tingling', 'warmth', 'coolness', 'pressure', 'buzzing' tied to a named body part
'notice a sensation', 'you may begin to feel'
'as if a hand', 'like a touch', 'a breath on your skin'
a sensation stated with no outside cause and no instruction to imagine a scene

not_this.why: positive hallucination is perception of an absent sight, sound, smell or taste; suggested sensation is a feeling in the body
relabeling renames a feeling already there; this creates one
heaviness or floating is a whole-body weight feeling tied to depth; this is a local feeling in a named place with no depth claim
a sensation stated as the result of the listener's response is a reward; one simply suggested is this
sensory language describes a scene in sense terms; a suggested sensation tells the listener they feel it in their own body now

evidence.note: Suggested warmth and tingling are routine in clinical scripts and autogenic training; attention alone produces mild versions, so success says little about trance.

entries.name: Numbness
entries.summary: Suggest a body area grows numb and cannot feel, often a hand first, then test with a pinch or pressure.
entries.definition: A suggested loss of feeling in a named area. Glove anesthesia, the classic form, numbs one hand so it can be tested and later transferred. It is the most studied convincer: suggested analgesia reduces reported pain in controlled studies. It differs from negative hallucination, which removes an outside perception, and from body dissociation, which separates the listener from the body rather than numbing it.
entries.how_to: Start with cold or heaviness, which are easier, and build toward numbness: 'like wearing a thick glove', 'like after the dentist'. Name the borders of the area. Test with something mild the listener can do alone, such as pinching the back of the hand, and compare it with the other hand. Restore normal feeling explicitly before the session ends, unless the numbness is a clinical goal.
examples: Your right hand is growing cool, then numb, as if it were wrapped in a thick winter glove.
Pinch the back of that hand gently, then the other, and notice the difference.
Now feeling returns to your hand, normal and comfortable.
cues: 'numb', 'no feeling', 'can't feel', 'like the dentist'
'glove', 'wrapped', 'wooden', 'cold' leading into numbness
'pinch', 'press' as a test, 'compare with the other hand'
'feeling returns', 'normal sensation' as a release

not_this.why: negative hallucination blocks an outside percept; numbness blocks body feeling
dissociation detaches from the body; numbness removes feeling in it
transfer moves an established numbness; this creates it

origin.source: Hilgard & Hilgard, Hypnosis in the Relief of Pain (1975)

evidence.note: Suggested analgesia reliably reduces reported pain in controlled laboratory and clinical studies, more so in high scorers. That evidence concerns pain relief; the use of a numb hand as proof of trance has not been studied separately.

entries.consent_note: Restore normal feeling explicitly unless pain relief is the agreed goal; numbness can hide injury.

entries.name: Sensation transfer
entries.summary: Tell the listener that a sensation already established in one place moves to another place, usually by touching it there.
entries.definition: A variant that moves an existing suggested sensation instead of building a new one. The classic form transfers glove anesthesia from the hand to the face or another area by touch. It differs from numbness or suggested sensation by depending on one that has already worked, which lets the script reuse a proven response.
entries.how_to: Only use it after the first sensation has been tested and ratified. Give a physical carrier: touching the target area, stroking, or imagery of the feeling flowing. Say the source area returns to normal as the feeling leaves, so nothing is left behind. Test the new area the same way as the old one, then restore it.
examples: Now place that numb hand on your cheek, and let the numbness pass from your hand into your cheek.
Press your warm palm against your other hand and feel the warmth move from the palm into the other hand.
Touch your knee with the warm hand, and feel the warmth pass into the knee as the hand cools to normal.
cues: 'let the feeling flow into', 'transfer', 'move the numbness to'
'place your hand on' after a sensation in that hand
'as it leaves your hand, your hand returns to normal'
earlier established sensation named again with a new location

not_this.why: a travelling sensation is described moving through successive body regions; transfer moves an established sensation from one named area to another
numbness suggests a loss of feeling; transfer moves an established feeling from one area to another
linkage ties a stimulus or response to going deeper; transfer moves an established sensation to a new place

evidence.note: Glove anesthesia transfer is standard in clinical pain-control scripts; the transfer step itself has not been studied apart from hypnotic analgesia in general.

entries.consent_note: Restore normal feeling to every area that received the transfer before the session ends.

entries.name: Travelling sensation
entries.summary: Describe one suggested sensation moving through the body region by region, stating what it brings wherever it goes.
entries.definition: The form of suggested sensation in which a single feeling (warmth, heaviness, tingling, a wave) is given a starting point, a path and an effect: it begins in one place, moves through named regions in order, and changes each one as it arrives. The moving sensation, not an instruction, does the work in each region. It differs from progressive relaxation, which tells each region to relax, and from sensation transfer, which declares an established sensation to have jumped from one place to another.
entries.how_to: Pick one sensation and stay with it; start it where it is easiest to feel, usually the hands, feet or the top of the head. Name the regions in anatomical order and give the sensation a motion verb at each one (spreads, flows, rises, rolls). Say at least once what it does on arrival ('and everything it touches lets go'), then let later regions inherit that. Pace it slowly enough to follow, and end with the whole body or with the place you want the effect to settle. Skipping around the body, or changing the sensation midway, breaks the track.
examples: A warmth begins in the palms of your hands. It moves up through the wrists, into the forearms, and everything it reaches grows loose and heavy.
Feel a slow wave start at the top of your head. It rolls down over your face, your neck, your shoulders, and wherever it passes, the muscles let go.
That tingling in your fingertips starts to travel. Up the arms. Across the chest. Down the spine. And it leaves quiet behind it.
cues: one sensation noun as the subject of motion verbs: 'spreads', 'flows', 'moves', 'travels', 'rolls', 'rises', 'washes'
'a wave of ...' followed by body regions
body regions named in order with path prepositions: 'up through', 'down into', 'across', 'all the way to'
a start point: 'begins in', 'starting at'
an arrival effect: 'wherever it goes', 'everything it touches', 'as it reaches', 'it leaves ... behind'
the same sensation carried through three or more regions

not_this.why: progressive relaxation instructs each region in turn to relax; here a sensation travels and the regions change because it arrives
transfer declares an established sensation moved from one area to another, usually by touch; a travelling sensation is described moving continuously along a path
state-as-substance describes the state itself as a material (fog, honey, light); a travelling sensation is a literal bodily feeling with no substance image

evidence.note: Spreading warmth and waves of relaxation are routine in clinical relaxation scripts; attention to a body part produces mild sensation in most people, and no study separates the travelling form from plain region-by-region relaxation.

entries.name: Positive hallucination
entries.summary: Suggest the listener sees, hears, smells or tastes something that is not present, often as a test.
entries.definition: A suggestion to perceive an absent thing with the outer senses: a sound in the room, a scent, a taste, a colour on a real object. It differs from guided imagery, which asks the listener to imagine and knows it is imagining, by claiming the thing is actually perceived; and from suggested sensation, which covers body feeling.
entries.how_to: Pick a sense and an object the listener knows well, often a smell or taste for audio work. Build it by detail and lead in from imagery ('imagine, and then notice it becoming real'). Ask for noticing, not certainty, and ratify faint responses. End by removing it explicitly. Full visual hallucination with open eyes is rare; do not stake the session on it.
examples: Notice now the smell of fresh coffee, faint at first, then clearer.
There's a taste of lemon on your tongue, sharp and bright.
And you can hear a soft hum somewhere in the room.
cues: 'you can smell', 'you can taste', 'you can hear' with an absent source
'now you notice', 'becoming real', 'really there'
named smells and tastes (coffee, lemon, flowers) without a scene to imagine
'and now it fades' as a removal

not_this.why: imagery asks the listener to picture; hallucination claims they perceive
body feeling belongs there; this covers sight, sound, smell and taste
imagined substance is a fictional object whose effects are suggested; here the percept itself is the proof

origin.source: Weitzenhoffer & Hilgard, Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (1962)

evidence.note: Hallucination items are on standard scales and pass mainly in high scorers; imaging studies show suggested colour changes alter brain activity, but most listeners report vivid imagery rather than true perception.

entries.name: Negative hallucination
entries.summary: Suggest the listener cannot see, hear or otherwise perceive something that is present.
entries.definition: A suggestion to not perceive a real object, sound or person. It is one of the harder phenomena and mainly a stage and test item. It differs from numbness, which removes body feeling, and from attention-narrowing, which tells the listener to ignore things rather than claiming they are not there.
entries.how_to: Pick one specific target the listener can check: a sound in the recording, an object in the room, a smell. State that it is gone or invisible, then invite them to look or listen. In recordings, use a planned sound you can name and remove, since you cannot know what is in the room. Restore perception explicitly.
examples: In a moment the ticking you hear will fade until there is no ticking at all.
Open your eyes and look at the chair across from you. Notice the empty space where it was.
Now everything is back exactly as it should be.
cues: 'you can't see', 'you can't hear', 'invisible', 'not there'
'fades until there is no', 'disappears from your awareness'
'look at ... and notice it's gone'
'it's back now', 'you can see it again'

not_this.why: adds a percept; negative removes one
narrowing says ignore; negative hallucination says it is not there
numbness removes body feeling, not outside percepts

origin.source: Weitzenhoffer & Hilgard, Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (1962)

evidence.note: Negative hallucination items are among the hardest on standard scales and pass in a minority of participants; studies show changes in report and some brain response, not true blindness.

entries.consent_note: Do not suggest that a person or something the listener needs to see for safety is invisible, and restore perception before waking.

entries.name: Suggestibility test
entries.summary: Before the induction, run a short imagination exercise that produces a small automatic response the listener can notice.
entries.definition: A brief exercise done awake, before formal trance, to show the listener they respond to words. Typical forms: imagined lemon making the mouth water, swaying backward, magnet fingers drawing together, a pendulum swinging in the hand. It differs from a convincer by placement and stakes: it comes before the induction and is framed as a game about imagination, not proof of trance.
entries.how_to: Present it as a test of imagination, never of whether they can be hypnotized. Choose one that nearly everyone passes (lemon, finger magnets) for recordings. Give clear setup, thirty seconds of vivid suggestion, then ask what they noticed. Ratify any response as the skill the session will use, and move straight into the induction while expectancy is high.
examples: Hold your hands together with the two index fingers apart, and imagine magnets in the tips pulling them closer.
Picture a cut lemon. Bring it to your mouth and bite into it.
Whatever you noticed, that's the same ability we'll use in a moment.
cues: 'imagine a lemon', 'bite into it'
'fingers' with 'magnets', 'pulling together'
'sway', 'falling backward', 'pendulum'
'this is just a test of imagination', 'before we begin'

not_this.why: a convincer is run in trance and framed as proof; a suggestibility test is run awake before the induction and framed as imagination
the same magnet exercise is an induction when contact is tied to closing the eyes or going under; with no trance claim at contact it is this test
book and balloon is one named form of this test; use its label when the two-arm weight and balloon exercise appears
expectation-setting tells the listener what will happen; the test has them do an exercise and notice a response

evidence.note: Responses to such tests correlate with formal hypnotizability scores, and the waking items share much with nonhypnotic suggestibility; that a pass improves later trance is assumed rather than shown.

entries.name: Book and balloon
entries.summary: Have both arms out, suggest one carries a heavy weight and the other is lifted by a balloon, then let the listener open their eyes to see the gap.
entries.definition: A convincer built from two opposite imagined sensations at once, ending with the listener seeing the result. Unlike other convincers it does not test an inability; it makes movement the listener can measure, so even a small response produces visible proof. It is used mostly before or at the start of an induction as a suggestibility screen.
entries.how_to: Have the listener hold both arms straight out, palms opposite ways, eyes closed. Build the heavy side and the light side in alternation with vivid detail, adding weight and adding balloons, for thirty seconds or more. Then ask them to open their eyes and look at their hands. Treat any gap as success and say so; do not mention a lack of gap.
examples: Hold both arms out in front of you. In your right hand, a heavy book. Tied to your left wrist, a big balloon.
Another book on top, heavier, pulling down. More balloons, lifting up, up.
Open your eyes and look at where your hands are now.
cues: 'one arm' / 'the other arm' with 'heavy' and 'light' in alternation
'book', 'bucket', 'dictionary', 'weight' paired with 'balloon', 'helium'
'open your eyes and look at your hands'
'notice the distance between them'

not_this.why: apposition pairs opposite experiences in a sentence; book and balloon is the two-arm exercise ending with a visible comparison, and both labels may apply to their respective spans
heaviness-lightness suggests a weight feeling as a depth cue; book and balloon contrasts the two arms and asks the listener to see the gap
levitation ties one arm's rise to induction or depth; here the two arms diverge and the gap is shown as a test
suggestibility test is the general waking exercise before induction; use book and balloon for this named two-arm form, whether it occurs before or after induction

evidence.note: Widely used in stage and clinical pre-talks; the related hand-lowering and hands-moving items are validated scale items, but this particular test has not been studied on its own.

entries.name: Puppeteering
entries.summary: Suggest the speaker's words move parts of the listener's body without the listener choosing to move them.
entries.definition: A suggestion that the speaker directs specific movements (a hand lifts, the head nods, fingers curl) while the listener only watches. It differs from ideomotor signal, where the unconscious answers through movement, and from obedience task, where the listener chooses to act on a command; here the framing is that the body moves without them.
entries.how_to: Begin with movements the body makes easily and slowly (a finger lifting, a hand drifting) and describe them in present progressive as already happening. Use strings, wires or a remote as an image if wanted. Give the listener an observer frame ('just watch it'). Return control explicitly at the end of the segment.
examples: Watch your right hand. I'm lifting it now, as if I held a string tied to your wrist.
Now I turn your head slowly to the left. You are only watching it happen.
I draw your hand toward your shoulder with my words; when I release it, control returns to you.
cues: first-person verb with the listener's body part as object: 'I lift your', 'I'm moving your', 'I turn your'
'puppet', 'pulling the strings', 'my strings', 'remote control'
'my words move you', 'your body follows my voice, not you'
'just watch it move' paired with the speaker as the cause
'control returns to you', 'I give your body back'

not_this.why: automaticity framing says the movement happens by itself and names no mover; puppeteering names the speaker as the one moving the body
the signal is a movement given a meaning and used as an answer; puppeteering is a movement the speaker claims to drive
a task asks the listener to choose to act on an instruction; here the movement is framed as not chosen
levitation suggests lightness and ties trance to the hand's rise; puppeteering claims the speaker is moving the limb as a show of control

evidence.note: Built on the established ideomotor effect; as a named device it comes from stage and community practice and has no separate study.

entries.consent_note: Framing the body as controlled by the speaker works by the listener not owning the action; agree to it beforehand and return control explicitly.

entries.name: Suggested arousal / orgasm
entries.summary: Suggest a build of arousal and a peak without touch, usually released on a word or count.
entries.definition: A suggested bodily response of arousal and release, built in steps and tied to a cue. It is used both as a convincer (proof of the speaker's influence) and as the goal of a file. It differs from suggested sensation by its build-and-release shape and cue, and from pleasure pairing, which attaches a feeling to something else rather than producing a peak.
entries.how_to: Build gradually with sensation language, a rising count and reinforcement of each increase, and name the cue for release well before giving it. Hold and release only on the cue. Ratify any response, including a partial one, so the listener does not read a weaker response as failure. Keep the build and cue separate from triggers meant to fire outside sessions unless that is agreed.
examples: With every number the warmth builds a little more. One. Two.
Hold it there, right at the edge, until you hear the word.
Now. Let it all go.
cues: 'on my count', 'when I say the word', 'not until I say'
rising count paired with 'building', 'higher', 'closer', 'edge'
'hands-free', 'without touching'
'let go', 'release', 'now' as a single-word cue after a hold

not_this.why: the finale is the session-level shape of ending on a counted release of any kind; this is the suggested build and climax itself. Label the section as the finale and the build-and-release passage as this
tease-and-denial withholds the peak; this delivers it on a cue
a plain sensation has no build, hold or release cue
pairing attaches pleasure to a word or idea; this produces the peak itself

evidence.note: Orgasm from imagery alone, without touch, has been recorded physiologically in a small laboratory sample of women (Whipple, Ogden & Komisaruk, 1992). No controlled study of the suggested, cue-released form used in hypnosis is known, and success rates claimed online are anecdotal.

entries.consent_note: Sexual content needs explicit adult consent before the session; a release cue meant to work after the session is a persistent trigger and must be disclosed.

entries.name: After-the-fact proof
entries.summary: After waking, point the listener to evidence that something happened: more time gone than it felt like, a lingering heaviness, parts they cannot recall.
entries.definition: A convincer placed after emergence. The script asks the listener to check something they can verify on waking, usually the clock, and interprets the result as proof of trance. It differs from time distortion, which suggests the altered sense of time, and from ratification during trance, which comments on responses as they happen.
entries.how_to: Set it up earlier if possible: suggest during trance that time will feel shorter, then after waking ask them to check the clock. Other checks: a hand still slightly heavy, a gap in what they remember. Phrase it as noticing ('you may be surprised'), not a claim, since you cannot know the result. Keep it brief so the wake stays clean.
examples: Before you do anything else, check the time, and notice how much longer you were away than it felt.
You may find your hands still feel a little heavy for a minute or two.
Try to remember everything I said in the middle, and notice what's simply not there.
cues: 'check the time', 'look at the clock'
'longer than it felt', 'where did the time go'
'still a little heavy', 'lingering' after the count-up
'try to remember' after waking

not_this.why: time distortion is the suggestion that time feels different, given during trance; this is the check of the clock after waking
amnesia on waking suggests the forgetting; this invites the listener, once awake, to look for the gap
ratification confirms a response at the moment it happens in the session; this comes after the wake and points at something the listener can check for themselves
that cites a voluntary act (still listening, came back) as proof of wanting; this cites after-effects of the session as proof of trance

evidence.note: Time underestimation after hypnosis is commonly reported and was observed in early studies, but expectation explains much of it; as a deliberate script device it is practitioner convention.

entries.name: Memory and time
entries.summary: Suggestions that change what the listener remembers or forgets, or where in time they place themselves and their traits.
entries.definition: Devices that act on memory or on the listener's sense of when they are: forgetting, unusually clear remembering, returning to the past, stepping into the future, recasting a new trait as old, suggesting events that did not happen, and seeding later dreams. They differ from time distortion (attention-absorption), which changes how long the session feels, not which time the listener is in or what they recall.
entries.how_to: Pick by what the suggestion should do to memory or time. To make material fade, use amnesia suggestion or one of its variants: on waking (tied to the exit), structured (bracketing the trance with one resumed topic), source (the idea stays, its origin goes) or distraction (an abrupt change of subject). To recover a resource or state from the past, use revivification; to suggest the listener is a younger age, use age regression. To make a change feel finished, use future progression; to make it feel like it was always there, use 'it was always so'. Suggested memory adds an event that did not happen and needs the strongest consent framing. Dream suggestion carries content into sleep; memory enhancement suggests clearer recall of named material. Related devices live elsewhere: name amnesia (convincers), losing the numbers (deepening), time distortion and trance time expansion (felt duration), time confusion (confusion), future pacing (imagery-story) and revivification induction (induction).

not_this.why: changes felt duration of the session, not which time the listener is in or what they remember

evidence.note: Hypnotic amnesia and suggested false memories have controlled studies; age regression and hypnotic recall enhancement are standard in clinical texts but studies show they do not produce genuine childhood states or more accurate memory.

entries.consent_note: Devices in this family can leave effects the listener does not notice or that persist after the session; say in the pretalk what will be forgotten, revisited or suggested about the past.

entries.name: Amnesia suggestion
entries.summary: Tell the listener that some part of the session, or a specific detail, will be forgotten or hard to recall.
entries.definition: A suggestion whose content is forgetting: of the whole session, of one section, or of a word, number or event. It is often permissive ('you may find it easy to forget') so that remembering does not count as failure. Label this unit itself only where forgetting is stated in the text. Its variants narrow it: amnesia on waking ties the forgetting to the exit, and source amnesia keeps the content and removes its origin. Structured amnesia and amnesia by distraction aim at forgetting by arrangement, with nothing about forgetting said; they are separate devices, not forms of this one. It differs from name amnesia, a short in-trance convincer with a built-in test, and from losing the numbers, where the fading of a count is the route to depth.
entries.how_to: Say what will be forgotten and when, ideally tied to emergence or to a cue. Permissive or ambiguous wording ('you might remember, or you might simply let it drift away') lands better than a flat command, because partial recall still fits the suggestion. Pair it with a reason (it is not needed, the unconscious keeps it) and avoid asking the listener to check whether they remember, which brings the material back. It fails when it is stated once with no frame and the listener is invited to recall right after.
examples: That last part can slip to the back of your mind now, the way a stranger's name does a minute after you hear it.
You don't need to remember any of this. Your unconscious keeps what matters, and the rest can simply go.
Whether you forget all of it or only most of it doesn't matter at all.
cues: forget / forgetting / forgotten
you don't need to remember
drift away / fade like a dream
remember to forget
whether you remember or forget
the harder you try to remember

not_this.why: a brief in-trance convincer: one familiar item is suggested away and tested at once so the listener notices the gap
the listener's own count is relaxed away as a deepener; the fading is the route to depth, not a suggestion about recalling the session
suppresses perception of something present, not memory of something past
changes the ability to remember in general ('your memory gets foggy'); amnesia names particular material to be forgotten
gets forgetting from how the session is arranged; no forgetting is stated in the text

evidence.note: Posthypnotic amnesia is a standard item on hypnotic susceptibility scales and is reliably produced in highly suggestible people, but it is usually partial and reversible on a cue.

entries.consent_note: Forgetting removes the listener's ability to review what was suggested; tell them beforehand what kind of material will be forgotten and keep it reversible.

entries.name: Amnesia on waking
entries.summary: As part of the wake-up, suggest that some or all of the session will not be remembered once the listener is awake.
entries.definition: An amnesia suggestion delivered at the exit and tied to the moment of waking: the higher the count or the wider the eyes, the less is recalled. It may cover the whole session, the wording only, or named parts, and often leaves the effects in place while removing the memory of their source. It is the general amnesia suggestion specialized by position and by its link to the wake.
entries.how_to: State the scope exactly: what is forgotten, what is kept, and whether effects remain. Tie the forgetting to the wake steps or to a familiar model of forgetting such as a dream fading on waking. Follow the wake with a change of subject, which helps more than insisting. Expect partial results; most listeners keep a gist. Include a reversal condition (a cue, a time, or 'you can remember whenever you need to') and say in the description that the file suggests forgetting.
examples: As I count you up, the words of this session slip away like a dream on waking. The calm stays.
By five, you remember feeling relaxed and very little else, and that is fine.
You can leave the details here, and recall them later whenever you need to.
cues: 'forget', 'won't remember', 'slips away', 'fades', 'out of reach' inside or just before the wake passage
'when you wake', 'as you wake', 'once your eyes open' governing a forgetting clause
'like a dream', 'the harder you try to remember'
contrast of memory and effect ('the words fade, the feeling stays')
a release clause ('until I say', 'you will remember when')

not_this.why: the general device, usable anywhere; this row is its use tied to the wake
that keeps the idea and removes only where it came from
that gets forgetting from an abrupt topic change, with no forgetting suggestion in the text

origin.source: Weitzenhoffer & Hilgard, Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (1962)

evidence.note: Suggested posthypnotic amnesia is a standard, measured scale item: it is a temporary recall failure that reverses on a cue, occurs fully in a minority of highly responsive people, and does not erase the memory.

entries.consent_note: It works against the listener's later ability to review what was suggested, so it must be disclosed beforehand and paired with a way to recover the memory.

entries.name: Structured amnesia
entries.summary: After trance, pick up exactly where the conversation stopped before trance, so the middle drops out of memory.
entries.definition: An amnesia move done by structure, not by instruction. The speaker stops mid-sentence or mid-topic before the induction and resumes that same sentence or topic immediately after emergence, so the trance sits between two halves of one continuous thread and tends to be skipped in recall. No forgetting is suggested aloud.
entries.how_to: Before the induction, start a concrete, mundane sentence or topic and break off at a clear point. After emergence, resume with the exact words or the same topic, as if nothing happened. Keep the resumed line identical or close to identical; any comment on the trance ('how was that?') breaks the bracket. In audio scripts it works best when the opening topic is distinctive and the emergence is short.
examples: [Pretalk] ...and the thing about rainy afternoons is that the light goes soft and grey and— well, let's begin. [Emergence] ...the light goes soft and grey, and everything slows down.
[Before induction] So, as I was saying about the train timetable— [After waking] —about the train timetable, the 8:15 is always late.
cues: a sentence broken off just before the induction and resumed word for word after emergence
as I was saying (directly after emergence)
same topic in the last pretalk line and the first post-emergence line
no mention of the trance between the resumed lines

not_this.why: changes to a new subject after the material; structured amnesia returns to the old one
states the forgetting aloud; structured amnesia never mentions it
opens and closes stories inside the session around the suggestions; structured amnesia brackets the whole trance with one piece of ordinary talk begun before the induction and resumed after the wake
breaks a sentence off and never resumes it; here the same sentence is picked up again after emergence

origin.source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of hypnotic amnesia, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1974)

evidence.note: Described in Ericksonian clinical literature and consistent with event-boundary effects on memory; no controlled test of the scripted form.

entries.consent_note: Works without the listener noticing; disclose in advance if the script uses it.

entries.name: Forgetting where it came from
aliases: it feels like your own idea
entries.summary: Suggest the listener keeps the idea or change but forgets that it was suggested, so it feels self-generated.
entries.definition: A suggestion about where a suggested idea will seem to have come from. The content stays and its origin is removed, in one of two ways a labeler can see: the script says the listener will not remember where the idea came from, or it says the idea, urge or behavior will later feel like their own decision. Both forms point forward from a suggestion just given. It differs from plain amnesia suggestion, which removes the content; from retroactive framing, which says the trait was always there; and from 'it's what you want', which claims a wish the listener has now and makes no statement about how a suggested idea will be experienced later.
entries.how_to: State the content first, then attach the source-forgetting: 'you'll simply find yourself ... and it will feel like your own idea'. Phrase it around ownership and naturalness, not concealment. It is stronger when the change is small and plausible. Do not combine it with checking questions that remind the listener of the session.
examples: Tomorrow you'll reach for water instead of coffee, and it will just feel like something you decided.
You won't remember where this idea came from. It will simply be yours.
Later, the thought will arrive on its own, as if you'd always meant to think it.
cues: 'feel like your own idea', 'your own choice', 'your own thought' said of a suggestion just given
'you won't remember where the idea came from', 'you won't remember being told it'
'as if you decided it yourself' said of a decision the script has just suggested
a prediction that the listener will later attribute the suggested thought or action to themselves rather than to the speaker

not_this.why: says the trait was always there; source amnesia says a newly suggested idea will lose its origin or seem self-made
removes the content itself, not only its source
claims the listener wants the response now or already; source amnesia predicts how a suggested idea will be experienced later
cites a choice the listener has already made as proof of wanting; source amnesia makes no appeal to a past choice
suggests the speaker's voice becomes the listener's thinking voice from now on; source amnesia concerns the origin of one suggested idea

origin.source: Frederick J. Evans and William A. Thorn, Two Types of Posthypnotic Amnesia: Recall Amnesia and Source Amnesia, International Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hypnosis (1966)

evidence.note: Posthypnotic source amnesia for facts learned during hypnosis has been demonstrated experimentally. That does not establish that a scripted suggestion can make a newly suggested idea feel self-generated.

entries.consent_note: Designed to hide its own influence; the listener should know beforehand that suggestions may later feel self-generated.

entries.name: Distraction amnesia
entries.summary: Right after the material to be forgotten, switch abruptly to an unrelated topic so it never gets rehearsed.
entries.definition: Amnesia produced by denying rehearsal: the speaker moves attention away immediately after the key material, usually at emergence, with an unrelated question, task or topic. Nothing about forgetting is said. It differs from structured amnesia, which returns to a pre-trance topic, and from a pattern interrupt, which breaks a state rather than following key content.
entries.how_to: Place the shift directly after the suggestion or the emergence count, with no pause and no recap. Use something concrete and attention-grabbing (a simple question, a small task, a sensory detail in the room). Avoid summarizing the session afterwards; that undoes it.
examples: ...three, two, one, eyes open. Now, quick question: what did you have for breakfast today?
...and that's settled. By the way, did you ever find out who left that umbrella by the door?
cues: unrelated question or task immediately after emergence
abrupt topic change after a key suggestion
quick question / by the way (right after waking)
no recap or reference to the session after waking

not_this.why: returns to the pre-trance topic rather than switching to a new one
directs attention to body feeling, the room, or alertness after trance; distraction amnesia switches to unrelated content to draw attention away from the preceding material
uses a change of sound, voice, or topic to capture attention; distraction amnesia uses a topic switch after material to reduce rehearsal of it
breaks an ongoing sequence rather than shifting away from material after it has ended

origin.source: Milton H. Erickson and Ernest L. Rossi, Varieties of Hypnotic Amnesia, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1974)

evidence.note: Used in Ericksonian practice; consistent with research showing interference after encoding reduces later recall, but the scripted technique itself is not separately tested.

entries.consent_note: Works without the listener noticing; disclose in advance if the script uses it.

entries.name: Age regression
entries.summary: Suggest the listener goes back to an earlier age or time and experiences it as if they were there now.
entries.definition: A suggestion that moves the listener's sense of self to an earlier age, often by counting back through years or walking back through rooms or calendars. It covers both 'remembering as an adult' and 'being younger now'. It differs from revivification, which relives one specific memory and its state, and from suggested memory, which adds events that did not happen.
entries.how_to: Give a clear path back (counting years down, pages turning, a corridor of doors) and a clear target age or period. Use present tense once arrived, and ask open sensory questions rather than supplying details. Always provide a matching return path and reorient to the present age before emergence. It fails or harms when the script supplies emotionally loaded details the listener may take as real memory.
examples: With each number I count, you go back one year younger... ten... nine... eight... and now you're small again.
Notice how big the table looks from down here. What do you see?
And now, coming back up through the years, all the way to today, your own age, here, now.
cues: 'younger and younger', 'smaller', 'going back through the years'
counting backwards through years, ages, birthdays or school grades
a stated age or period as the present: 'you are seven now', 'it is your first day of school'
child's-eye details: furniture looking big, small hands, a childhood room
return passage naming the present age or date: 'back up to today', 'your own age'

not_this.why: the listener stays their present self and recalls one memory for its feeling; label age regression only when the text states or implies a different age, body or date
supplies events that did not happen; regression moves the listener back without itself adding events
moves forward to a future time, not back
scrambles days and tenses without sending the listener to any particular time; it may lead into regression but is only the scrambling

origin.source: Nash, What, if anything, is regressed about hypnotic age regression? (1987)

evidence.note: Listeners report vivid regression, but controlled studies find adult, not child-like, cognition and no special accuracy of recovered details.

entries.consent_note: Can surface distressing material and produce confident but inaccurate memories; tell the listener beforehand, give a clear return path and do not treat what emerges as fact.

entries.name: Revivification
entries.summary: Have the listener recall one past experience in enough sensory detail that its feeling or state returns now.
entries.definition: A recall device aimed at re-entering a state: the listener picks or is led to a real memory and walks through its sights, sounds and body sensations until the feeling comes back. The target is the state (calm, confidence, absorption), and the listener stays their present self. This is the Ericksonian and NLP sense of the word; older hypnosis texts use 'revivification' for the complete form of age regression, in which the earlier time is relived as the present, and that sense is covered here by age regression. Label age regression when the text changes the listener's age or date, and revivification induction when the recalled memory is of trance and the passage is the induction.
entries.how_to: Let the listener choose the memory ('a time when you felt completely calm') rather than supplying one. Move through senses one by one in present tense, then name the state as it returns. Often followed by anchoring the state. It fails when the memory is rushed or narrated in past tense from outside.
examples: Remember a time you felt completely sure of yourself. Be there now. What do you see around you?
Notice the temperature of the air, the sounds nearby, and that feeling of being sure, coming back now.
Go back to the last time you were truly rested, and let your body remember it.
cues: remember a time when
go back to that moment / be there now
what do you see / hear / feel there
past memory narrated in present tense
that feeling coming back now

not_this.why: moves the listener's felt age back; revivification only re-enters one memory's state
uses a memory of past trance to induce trance; revivification targets any resource state
builds an imagined scene rather than recalling a lived one

evidence.note: Standard in clinical hypnosis for accessing resource states; affect returns with vivid recall in ordinary memory research, but the hypnotic version is not separately validated.

entries.name: Future progression
entries.summary: Place the listener at a future date where the change has already happened, and have them look back on how it went.
entries.definition: A time-orientation suggestion: the listener is told it is now a later date, the goal is achieved, and they recall how they got there. The defining feature is looking back on the change as finished. It differs from future pacing, which rehearses using a change in a future situation from the present, and from retroactive framing, which places the trait in the past rather than the listener in the future.
entries.how_to: Name a concrete future point (next month, a year from now), then switch to past tense for the change: 'you remember how it started to get easier'. Ask the listener what helped, so they supply the path. Bring them back to the present before emergence. It is weaker if the script stays in future tense, which makes it ordinary rehearsal.
examples: It's a year from now. Look back at this past year and notice how easily the change happened.
From here, six months on, you can remember the first day it got easier. What did you do differently?
Now come back to today, bringing that finished feeling with you.
cues: a later date asserted as now: 'it's a year from now', 'it is next spring'
'look back on', 'looking back from here'
past tense about events that are still in the future
'you remember how it changed', 'remember the day it got easier'
questions about the path from the future side: 'what did you do differently?'
return passage: 'come back to today'

not_this.why: rehearses a future cue or response as it happens; progression places the listener after the change and looks back on it
runs through the future behavior itself; progression looks back on it as completed
asks the listener to suppose an outcome is true; a hypothetical future scene can also be future progression when it places them at a later time looking back on a completed change
places a new trait in the listener's past; progression places the listener at a future time
presupposes finished change without moving the listener to a later time

origin.source: Erickson, Pseudo-orientation in time as a hypnotherapeutic procedure (1954)

evidence.note: A standard clinical technique since Erickson; no controlled studies show it beats ordinary goal imagery.

entries.name: It was always so
entries.summary: Describe a newly suggested trait or response as something the listener has always had.
entries.definition: A framing move that backdates the suggestion: instead of 'you will become calm', the script says 'you've always been calm underneath'. The new trait is presented as rediscovered, not installed. It differs from an identity statement, which asserts the trait in the present with no claim about the past, and from suggested memory, which supplies specific false events.
entries.how_to: Use perfect tense and continuity words: always, all along, never really stopped, remember. Present the session as noticing rather than changing. Works best with traits that plausibly have some past evidence, which the listener can then supply. Overreaching ('you have always obeyed') against clear contrary memory breaks belief.
examples: You've always been calmer than you thought. You're only noticing it now.
This focus isn't new. It's been there all along, waiting to be used.
Some part of you has always known how to rest like this.
cues: always / all along / always have been
you've always (been / known / wanted)
it was never new
you're only noticing / remembering it now
deep down you always

not_this.why: asserts the trait now, with no claim it was always there
claims a wish the listener has now; label retroactive framing when a backdating word (always, all along, never new) is present, and both when a wish is backdated ('you've always wanted this')
supplies specific past events rather than a timeless trait
presupposes a change has happened; retroactive framing denies there was a change
tells the listener their own memory or perception is wrong; retroactive framing adds a claim about the past without disputing what the listener recalls

evidence.note: Common in practitioner and community scripts; it relies on presupposition and self-perception, which are studied, but the device itself is not.

entries.consent_note: Rewrites how the listener understands their own past and can persist after the session; the listener should know the script presents new traits as always present.

entries.name: Suggested memory
entries.summary: Suggest that the listener remembers a specific event that did not happen.
entries.definition: A suggestion that supplies the content of a memory: an event, a conversation, a scene, presented as something the listener now recalls. It differs from retroactive framing, which backdates a trait without specific events, from revivification, which recalls a real memory, and from age regression, which moves the listener back without itself adding events.
entries.how_to: Frame it explicitly as play or fiction in the pretalk if it is not meant to be believed. Inside the script, invite remembering rather than asserting ('you might remember the time...') and add sensory detail; detail and repetition make the image feel more like memory. Close by marking it as a story or a suggestion so the listener can file it correctly. Never use it on real-world history the listener cares about.
examples: You might remember the afternoon you first learned to float, the water holding you up, the sky so wide.
Remember the first time you heard this voice, years ago, on a train, and how you leaned in to listen.
And you can recall what you said that evening on the porch, the exact words, and how easy they were to say.
cues: 'you remember the time when' followed by a specific event the speaker introduces as the listener's memory
'remember when you ...' followed by a specific scene supplied by the speaker
past time or place details introduced as the listener's own recollection, without an established memory to elaborate
vividness instructions attached to a scene supplied as the listener's past experience
detailed past-tense scene presented as the listener's own recollection

not_this.why: invites recall of an experience the listener supplies; suggested memory supplies the event
backdates a trait without supplying a specific event
