denies or rewrites a memory or perception the listener already has; a supplied past event can carry both labels if it also contradicts the listener's account
suggests clearer recall of established material; suggested memory supplies the event to be recalled
suggests perceiving something now rather than remembering a past event

origin.source: Laurence & Perry, Hypnotically created memory among highly hypnotizable subjects, Science (1983)

evidence.note: False memories can be created by suggestion and imagination in a minority of participants, with or without hypnosis; hypnosis raises confidence more than accuracy.

entries.consent_note: Can produce memories the listener later believes are real; frame it as fiction, mark it at the end and never use it on real personal history.

entries.name: Dream suggestion
entries.summary: Suggest that the listener will dream tonight, dream about a given topic, or remember their dreams.
entries.definition: A posthypnotic suggestion whose target is sleep: that a dream will occur, what it will contain, or that it will be remembered. It differs from sleep ending, which lets the listener fall asleep at the end of the session, and from a general posthypnotic suggestion, whose target is waking behavior.
entries.how_to: Place it near the end, often just before a sleep ending. Keep the content open ('a dream about this feeling') rather than scripted scene by scene, and use permissive wording ('you may dream'), since dreams cannot be checked. Add recall support if wanted ('when you wake, the dream stays with you'). Overly specific content tends not to appear and can read as a failure.
examples: Tonight you may dream of water, slow and warm, carrying this calm into your sleep.
Whatever you dream, some part of it will carry this feeling.
And when you wake tomorrow, you'll remember your dream clearly.
cues: 'tonight', 'as you sleep', 'when you go to bed' + a dream clause
'you may dream of', 'you will dream about'
'in your dreams' said of a later night, not as a simile ('like a dream' does not count)
'remember your dream when you wake', 'the dream stays with you'
future tense reaching into sleep after the session

not_this.why: lets the listener fall asleep; it does not suggest dream content
the general label for a response after the session; use dream suggestion when that response is a dream during later sleep
a dream or dreamlike scene the listener is led through now, in the session; dream suggestion points at sleep afterwards

evidence.note: Presleep suggestion can modestly shift dream content in some studies; effects are small and inconsistent, and reports depend on what the dreamer recalls.

entries.consent_note: Acts during sleep after the session ends; say in the pretalk that dream suggestions are included.

entries.name: Memory enhancement
entries.summary: Suggest that the listener will recall something unusually clearly, either from the past or from this session.
entries.definition: A suggestion of improved recall of named material: a past event, study material, or the session's own words. It is the opposite direction to amnesia suggestion. The mark is a recall verb (remember, recall, come back to you) with an object. It differs from sealing, which says the suggestions stay in effect without saying they will be remembered; from capacity suggestion, which claims better memory as a general ability with nothing in particular to recall; and from revivification, which re-enters a memory's state.
entries.how_to: Say what will be remembered and when it will come back ('every word will be there when you need it'). Use it to keep key suggestions available or to support study recall; pair with a cue for retrieval. Do not use it to recover past events as evidence; it raises confidence more than accuracy.
examples: You'll remember every word I say tonight, clearly, whenever you want it.
When you sit the exam, what you studied will come back to you, one fact after another.
You'll remember this feeling exactly, whenever you choose to.
cues: 'you'll remember every word', 'remember everything I say'
'it will come back to you' when 'it' refers to named material
'recall' or 'remember' + named material + 'clearly', 'perfectly', or 'in detail'
a retrieval moment tied to named material: 'when you sit the exam, what you studied will come back'
'every detail' of a specified event or passage will be remembered

not_this.why: says the suggestions stay in effect after waking; memory enhancement says named material will be recalled
claims memory as an ability improves in general; memory enhancement names what will be recalled
re-experiences a memory's state rather than suggesting clearer recall
the opposite direction: suggests forgetting

origin.source: Jane Dywan and Kenneth S. Bowers, The Use of Hypnosis to Enhance Recall, Science (1983)

evidence.note: Hypnotic recall enhancement produces more recalled items but also more errors, with confidence rising faster than accuracy; the popular claim of better memory outruns the evidence.

entries.consent_note: Hypnotic memory enhancement can increase confidence in inaccurate recollections; say beforehand if the script suggests clearer recall, and do not treat recalled material as verified.

entries.name: Identity and belief
entries.summary: Devices that change how the listener names, describes and understands themselves, or what they hold to be true.
entries.definition: This family groups moves aimed at the listener's self-description and standing beliefs rather than at a momentary state or action. Some state the new identity outright (identity statement, renaming, role assignment); some work through how the listener is referred to (pronoun shift, ownership and object language); some supply the reasoning that makes the new self feel earned (from act to trait, linking to values, it's what you want); some fix beliefs or the durability of the change (belief statement, permanence claim). It has no nested families. Close neighbours live elsewhere: labeling and your-actions-prove-it (compliance), persona/alter (dissociation), it-was-always-so (memory and time), first-person suggestion (suggestion forms) and using the listener's name (attention).
entries.how_to: Choose by what you need to change. To name the new self, use identity statement, renaming or role assignment; to make it feel earned, use from act to trait or linking to values; to change self-reference in the language itself, use pronoun shift or third-person self-reference; to change thinking habits, use inner-voice suggestion or thought replacement; to fix a rule or the durability of the change, use belief statement or permanence claim. Identity suggestions land best after the listener has already done something the identity can be built on, and they need a consent frame when they are meant to persist.

not_this.why: labeling assigns a trait in order to ask for matching behavior; this family changes the self-description itself
a persona is a separate switchable self; identity devices change the listener's one ongoing self

evidence.note: Labeling and self-perception effects on behavior are studied experimentally, but whether hypnotic identity suggestions change self-concept durably is largely untested.

entries.consent_note: Identity changes are meant to outlast the session, so the listener should know in advance what self-description is being installed and how to reverse it.

entries.name: Identity statement
entries.summary: State plainly what the listener is, as a fact about them rather than a feeling or action.
entries.definition: A direct suggestion whose predicate is a standing trait or a kind of person: "you are a calm person", "you are a confident speaker". The move is the copular "you are X" (or first-person "I am X") said as settled fact about who the listener is. A passing condition in the same grammar ("you are relaxed", "you are ready") is an ordinary direct suggestion; label an identity statement only when X is offered as still true of the listener after the session. It differs from labeling, which assigns a trait in order to request behavior, and from it-was-always-so, which adds a claim about the past.
entries.how_to: Place it in the suggestion section after the listener is absorbed, and phrase it in present tense as a description, not a wish. Pick a trait the listener can recognize in themselves at least a little, then widen it. Repetition across the session and pairing with a moment of felt success make it land; claims the listener can immediately disprove make it fail.
examples: You are someone who stays calm when others rush.
You are a patient person. You are a steady person. You are a person who finishes things.
I am a clear speaker, and I am someone people listen to.
cues: 'you are' + kind-of-person noun phrase ('a calm person', 'a listener', 'a natural speaker'), said as fact
'you're someone who ...' / 'you're the one who ...' / 'you're the kind of person who ...' with no request attached
'I am' + trait or kind-of-person noun in a line for the listener to hear or repeat
'that is who you are' / 'this is what you are'
series of short 'you are a/an X' sentences

not_this.why: 'you are relaxed' or 'you are ready' states a passing condition and is a plain direct suggestion; an identity statement names a standing trait or kind of person
labeling attaches a trait to justify a requested behavior; an identity statement stops at the trait
it-was-always-so adds the claim that the trait was always true
affirmations are first-person self-descriptions repeated as a practice; a single 'I am X' line is an identity statement, and a repeated block takes both labels
naming the state gives the present condition a name ('this is trance'); it says nothing about who the listener is

evidence.note: Ego-strengthening identity statements are standard in clinical hypnosis texts; their specific contribution beyond the session as a whole is not well measured.

entries.name: Renaming
entries.summary: Give the listener a new name, number or title that stands for the identity the script installs.
entries.definition: The act of assigning a name, designation or title to the listener, usually with a statement of what it means. It differs from using the listener's name, which is the later act of addressing them by it, and from role assignment, which gives a role with expected behavior rather than a label.
entries.how_to: Announce the name once, clearly, at a marked moment (often after deepening), and say what it stands for. Then use it consistently so it gathers meaning. A name that is easy to say and that fits the theme lands; changing it mid-script or never using it again wastes it.
examples: From now on, in this place, your name is Still.
Here you are called the Listener, and the Listener simply hears.
Your designation is Seven. Seven, breathe out.
cues: 'your name is ...' / 'you will be called ...'
'from now on you are ...' + proper noun or number
'your designation/title is ...'
a capitalized new term then used as a form of address

not_this.why: name-use is addressing by a name; renaming is the act of assigning it
a role carries expected behavior; a name may carry none
a persona is a separate self switched in by cue, not a new name for the listener

evidence.note: Common in community and ritual practice; there is no controlled work on renaming within hypnosis.

entries.consent_note: A name meant to persist after the session should be agreed in advance and should come with a way to drop it.

entries.name: Role assignment
entries.summary: Assign the listener a role (student, pet, assistant, drone) and spell out the behavior that role entails.
entries.definition: The listener is told they occupy a role in relation to the speaker or the scene, and the role brings its expected conduct with it. It differs from an identity statement, which names a trait, and from character identification, where the listener steps into a story character rather than being cast in a role toward the speaker.
entries.how_to: Name the role, then give two or three concrete behaviors that go with it so the role can be enacted. Tie it to the relationship in the script ("my student", "the helper here"). Roles that the listener can perform right away land; roles defined only by abstraction do not.
examples: Here you are the student, and a good student listens and lets it sink in.
You're my assistant now: you wait, you notice, you answer when asked.
For this session you are the apprentice. An apprentice watches closely and copies what is shown.
cues: 'you're my ...' + role noun
'your role is ...' / 'your job here is ...'
role noun followed by 'and a [role] ...' describing behavior
'as my [role], you ...'

not_this.why: an identity statement names a trait; a role names a position with duties
character identification casts the listener as a story character, not in a role toward the speaker
a persona is a separate named self switched in by cue

evidence.note: Role-taking is known to shape behavior in social psychology, but scripted role assignment in hypnosis has no independent study.

entries.consent_note: When the role is one of submission or service, the listener should have agreed to it before the session.

entries.name: Old self / new self
entries.summary: Contrast who the listener was with who they are becoming, placing the old traits in the past.
entries.definition: The script splits the listener's identity in time: an old self with the unwanted traits and a new self with the wanted ones. The contrast does the work, and the old self is spoken of as receding. It differs from it-was-always-so, which denies there was an old self, and from future progression, which moves the listener in time rather than contrasting two selves.
entries.how_to: Describe the old self briefly and without contempt, then the new self in more vivid, sensory detail. Use past tense for the old and present or progressive for the new. A symbolic parting (walking away, setting something down) can mark the change. It fails when the old self is described more vividly than the new one.
examples: The old you hurried. The you who is here now takes all the time there is.
Let the person who used to doubt stay behind on that path, and step forward without them.
That was then, the tense one. This is now, and you are easy.
cues: 'the old you' / 'the new you'
'the person who used to ...'
'leave behind' / 'step away from' + former self
past-tense description of the listener followed by present-tense contrast
'that was then ... this is now'

not_this.why: it-was-always-so denies any earlier self; this device needs one
future progression relocates the listener in time; this contrasts two selves
antithesis is the balanced phrasing; this is the old/new identity content it may carry

evidence.note: A staple of change-work scripts with no direct study of the contrast as a device.

entries.name: Inner-voice suggestion
entries.summary: Suggest that the speaker's words are, or are becoming, the listener's own thoughts and inner voice.
entries.definition: A suggestion about the source of the listener's thoughts: the speaker's voice moves inside, blends with or replaces the inner voice. It differs from source amnesia, which only removes memory of where an idea came from, and from voice focus, which narrows attention onto the voice without moving it inside.
entries.how_to: Start by noticing the listener's own inner voice, then describe the speaker's voice coming closer, joining it, and speaking from the same place. Shift to first-person lines the listener can hear as their own. It lands after strong voice focus; it fails if introduced before the listener has attended to their inner voice at all.
examples: Notice the quiet voice you think with... and notice how easily my words settle right there beside it.
Soon you won't hear me as me. You'll just hear your own thoughts, calm and certain.
My voice becomes your voice, and your voice says: I relax.
cues: 'my voice becomes your ...' (thoughts, inner voice, own voice)
'your thoughts' + 'my words' in the same sentence
'inside your head' / 'the voice you think with'
'you won't hear me as me' / 'as if you had thought it yourself'
'my words sound like your own thinking'

not_this.why: first-person suggestion writes the thoughts directly as 'I' lines; this entry is the claim, made in the second person, that the speaker's words are or become the listener's thoughts
source amnesia removes the memory of the source; this suggests the speaker becomes the inner voice
voice focus narrows attention onto the voice without placing it inside
thought replacement swaps one thought for another; this changes whose voice thinks

evidence.note: Source-monitoring errors are real in memory research, but there is no study of suggestions that a speaker's voice becomes one's thoughts.

entries.consent_note: This device aims to make suggested content feel self-generated, so it should only be used where the listener has agreed to that blurring and it is bounded to the session or a scope.

entries.name: Linking to values
entries.summary: Connect the suggestion to something the listener already values, so accepting it expresses who they are.
entries.definition: The suggestion is justified by a value the listener holds (health, family, freedom, doing things well). It differs from giving a reason, which can attach any reason at all, by drawing specifically on the listener's own values, and from reframing, which changes what an experience means rather than tying a request to a value.
entries.how_to: Name a value the listener is likely to hold or has told you, then say how the suggestion serves it. Place it where resistance is expected. Generic values ('because you deserve it') are weaker than specific ones; a value that does not fit the listener reads as manipulation.
examples: Because you care about the people around you, you let yourself rest enough to be there for them.
You value doing things well, and doing this well means letting it be easy.
Your freedom matters to you, and this is a way of choosing it.
cues: 'because you care about ...' + suggestion
'you value ...' / 'what matters to you' / '... matters to you'
'as someone who values/believes in ...' + suggestion
value word (health, family, freedom, honesty) + 'and that means ...' / 'which is why ...' + suggestion

not_this.why: giving a reason supplies a justification for the suggestion, including 'for your own good' or 'you deserve it'; linking to values names a value the listener holds and derives the suggestion from it
reframing changes the meaning of an experience; this ties a request to an existing value
it's-what-you-want attributes a wish for the response; this appeals to a value the response would serve

evidence.note: Messages framed in the audience's own values persuade better in controlled studies; this has not been tested within hypnosis.

entries.name: It's what you want
entries.summary: Attribute the suggested response to the listener's own wish, so compliance is framed as getting what they want.
entries.definition: The script claims the listener already wants the response, often 'deep down' or 'secretly'. It differs from you-chose-this, which points at an act of choosing as evidence, and from mind reading, which claims knowledge of any inner experience rather than a wish for the suggestion.
entries.how_to: State the want plainly and early in the suggestion, ideally after the listener has done something that can be read as wanting it. Pair it with felt ease so the claim feels confirmed. Overused, it reads as pressure and invites the listener to check whether it is true.
examples: Part of you wants to let go, and that part is getting its way.
This is what you want: to rest, completely.
Deep down you already know you want to go deeper.
cues: 'you want ...' / 'this is what you want', stated by the speaker as fact
'deep down you ...' / 'secretly you ...' + want or need
'part of you wants ...'
'you've wanted this' / 'you've been wanting this'

not_this.why: you-chose-this cites the act of choosing; this asserts the wish directly
mind reading claims any inner experience; this claims a wish for the suggestion
your-actions-prove-it points at behavior; this asserts desire without evidence

evidence.note: Common in community and sales copy; no study isolates attributed desire as a hypnotic device.

entries.consent_note: Telling someone they secretly want something is a known coercive move, so in consensual use it should match what the listener has said they want.

entries.name: Ownership language
entries.summary: Refer to the listener, their mind or their body with possessive words that place them as belonging to the speaker.
entries.definition: Possessives applied to the listener ('my', 'mine', 'belongs to me') that frame them as owned. It differs from role assignment, which defines duties, and from object language, which changes what the listener is rather than whose they are; the two often appear together.
entries.how_to: Start with light possessives applied to the listener ('my listener', 'my good student') before stronger ones ('mine', 'you belong to me'). Keep it consistent within the scene, and keep it inside an agreed fiction frame. Out-of-frame or unagreed use reads as hostile.
examples: Your attention is mine for now, and it rests on my voice.
My good listener, settling right where I want you.
For this hour you are mine, and you can rest in that.
cues: 'mine' / 'my' + listener or their body or mind
'you belong to ...'
'my property' / 'owned'
'I own your ...'

not_this.why: a role gives a position with duties; ownership language gives a possessor
object language says what the listener is; ownership says whose
a possessive pet name may count as both, but name-use is about addressing

evidence.note: No independent study; it is a community convention for dominance scenes.

entries.consent_note: Ownership framing belongs inside an agreed fiction; outside one it is a coercive-control pattern.

entries.name: Object / it language
entries.summary: Describe the listener as an object, animal or machine instead of a person.
entries.definition: Nouns, verbs and pronouns that cast the listener as a non-person: a doll, a device, an animal, 'it'. It differs from embodied state-as-substance metaphor, which gives the state a form rather than the listener, and from body detachment, which makes the body feel distant without recasting the self.
entries.how_to: Choose one image and keep its vocabulary consistent (a machine runs, processes, powers down). Bring it in gradually, often through a pronoun shift to 'it'. Keep it inside an agreed fiction and pair it with a clear return to personhood at emergence.
examples: Such a quiet little machine now, humming along, running only one program.
It sits still. It waits. It does not need to think.
A soft doll, limp and easy, placed just where it belongs.
cues: listener referred to as 'it'
nouns: 'doll', 'drone', 'machine', 'toy', 'pet', 'thing' applied to the listener
machine verbs: 'processing', 'program', 'powering down', 'malfunction'
'no longer a person'

not_this.why: role assignment casts the listener in a position and states its duties ('you are X, and X does ...'); object language is non-person nouns, verbs and pronouns applied to the listener. A non-person role given with duties ('you are a drone, and a drone listens') takes both labels; object wording with no duties takes only this one
pronoun shift is the switch point from 'you' to 'it'; sustained 'it' and object nouns after the switch are this entry
state-as-substance gives the state a form, not the listener
body detachment distances the body without recasting the self

evidence.note: Dehumanizing language is studied as a harm in social psychology; its use as a consensual hypnotic device is untested.

entries.consent_note: Dehumanizing language should be agreed in advance and closed with an explicit return to personhood; used without agreement it is abuse.

entries.name: Belief statement
entries.summary: State a belief or rule as plain truth, for the listener to hold after the session.
entries.definition: A declarative sentence about how things are or must be, offered for the listener to adopt as their own belief ('rest is earned by effort', 'good listeners obey'). It differs from an identity statement, whose subject is the listener, by stating a general truth or rule, and from redefinition, which changes a word's meaning rather than asserting a proposition.
entries.how_to: Phrase it short, general and in present tense, so it can be repeated verbatim. Repeat it at intervals or have the listener say it. A belief that fits what the listener already half-thinks lands; one that contradicts strong existing beliefs prompts counter-arguing.
examples: Calm is always available. Calm is always available.
Mistakes are how skill is built. That is simply how it is.
This is true for you now: effort and ease can go together.
cues: 'this is true' / 'the truth is' / 'that is simply how it is' + a general statement
'the rule is' / 'the law is' / 'remember this:' + a general statement
a short general statement whose subject is not 'you', repeated verbatim
'you know now that ...' / 'you believe ...' / 'you understand that ...' + general proposition
instruction to recite or hold a stated proposition

not_this.why: an identity statement is about the listener; a belief statement is about how things are

a lost performative is the judge-less evaluation form used in passing; label a belief statement only when the proposition is marked for adoption (flagged as true or as a rule, repeated verbatim, or to be recited). A marked evaluative sentence takes both labels

a truism is a readily accepted statement used to build agreement; a belief statement marks a proposition for the listener to hold, and an accepted proposition explicitly marked for adoption can take both labels
redefinition changes a word's meaning; this asserts a proposition
a cliche is placed at a point of doubt to shut questioning down; a belief statement installs content wherever it appears

evidence.note: Repeated statements are rated more believable (illusory truth), but whether hypnotic belief statements change lasting beliefs is not established.

entries.consent_note: A belief meant to be held after the session should be one the listener asked for or agreed to beforehand.

entries.name: Numbered rules
entries.summary: Present beliefs or rules as a numbered list, often to be recited back.
entries.definition: A belief statement given as an ordered, numbered set ('Rule one... Rule two...'). The numbering makes the rules memorable, citable and recitable, and implies a complete system. It differs from a recap, which restates the session's suggestions near the end, by being a fixed code presented as such.
entries.how_to: Keep each rule to one short sentence and the list to three to seven items. Number them out loud and in the same order every time, and ask for recitation. Rules that contradict each other or are too long to recite undermine the form.
examples: Rule one: breathe before you answer. Rule two: one thing at a time. Rule three: rest is part of the work.
Repeat the first law with me: focus follows breath.
There are three rules here, and you already know the first.
cues: 'rule one' / 'the first rule' / 'law number'
ordinal or cardinal numbers before short imperative or declarative lines
'repeat the rules'
'there are N rules'

not_this.why: a recap restates suggestions already given; numbered rules are presented as a code
a counted passage uses numbers to pace, not to index rules
a tricolon is three parallel items, not a numbered code

evidence.note: Numbered lists aid recall in general, but no study tests numbered rules as a hypnotic device.

entries.consent_note: A code of rules meant to be followed after the session should be agreed in advance and come with a stated way to retire it.

entries.name: Permanence claim
entries.summary: Assert that the change is permanent or cannot be reversed.
entries.definition: A statement about the duration of an effect: it lasts forever, cannot fade, cannot be removed. It differs from inevitability, which says the outcome will happen, by saying it will never stop; and it is the opposite of an expiry clause.
entries.how_to: If used, place it in sealing or emergence and keep it to the effects the listener asked for. Prefer softer forms ('this stays with you') over absolute ones in therapeutic scripts. Pair it with a removal path or scope when the content is intense.
examples: This calm stays with you, today and every day after.
Once learned, this can't be unlearned. It is part of you now.
Forever after, this breath brings you back here.
cues: 'forever' / 'for the rest of your life' / 'from now on, always' + the effect (pointing forward, not 'you have always')
'permanent' / 'permanently'
'can never be undone' / 'can't be removed' / 'no way back'
'for good' / 'never fades' / 'never wears off'

not_this.why: inevitability says it will happen; permanence says it will not stop
an expiry clause sets an end; a permanence claim denies one
sealing states what stays after waking; a permanence claim adds that it never fades

evidence.note: Posthypnotic responses generally weaken over time without reinforcement, and there is no evidence that asserting permanence makes an effect last.

entries.consent_note: Claims of irreversibility can frighten listeners and should be agreed in advance and accompanied by a real way to remove the suggestion.

entries.name: Piece-by-piece transformation
entries.summary: Describe the change taking over one body part, trait or habit at a time until it is complete.
entries.definition: The change is narrated as a sequence over parts of the listener: one habit, then the next; posture, then voice, then outlook; or body part by body part when what changes is what the part is, not how it feels. Each completed part is evidence for the next. It differs from progressive relaxation and travelling sensation, which move relaxation or one felt sensation through the body, and from graded escalation, which raises demands across sessions rather than spreading one change across parts.
entries.how_to: List the parts in a natural order and give each one sensory detail and a moment of completion before moving on. Ratify each part as done. It fails when the parts are rushed together, so nothing feels complete.
examples: It begins with how you stand: taller already. Then your voice changes, slower and surer. Then the way you meet people's eyes.
First your patience changes, then your breath, then the way you speak.
One habit at a time the change takes hold: the morning first, and once the morning is settled, the working day.
cues: 'one part at a time' / 'piece by piece' / 'bit by bit' + a change in what the listener is or does
'first your ... then your ...' naming traits, habits or parts that change
completion marker before moving on: 'and once that has changed ...' / 'that part is done'
'the change takes over' / 'takes hold of' + the next part
a list of traits or habits each declared changed in turn

not_this.why: a travelling sensation moves one felt sensation through the body; this sequences a change in trait, habit or identity, and a body part counts only when it is said to become something, not to feel something
progressive relaxation sequences relaxation; this sequences an identity or trait change
graded escalation raises demands over time; this spreads one change across parts
shaping reinforces approximations to a behavior; this narrates a change spreading

evidence.note: A common transformation-script structure; not independently studied.

entries.name: Capacity suggestion
entries.summary: Suggest that a mental or physical ability is stronger, weaker or gone.
entries.definition: A suggestion targeting what the listener can do (think, calculate, concentrate, speak fluently, perform a skill), rather than what they feel or are, and meant to hold beyond the moment. It covers both enhancement ('your focus sharpens') and reduction ('thinking gets harder'). It differs from mind-blanking, which quiets thought as a passing trance state, from memory enhancement, which covers suggested recall, and from convincers like speech lock, which stage a brief demonstration rather than a standing change of ability.
entries.how_to: Name the specific ability and the direction of change, then give a sensory sign that it has changed. Keep enhancement claims plausible so they are not tested and failed. Reduction suggestions belong inside an agreed scope with a clear restoration at emergence.
examples: Your focus sharpens, and the page in front of you becomes easy to follow.
From now until you sleep tonight, complicated thinking takes more effort than usual, and you are content to leave it.
Words come more easily to you when you speak, smooth and ready.
cues: ability noun or verb + 'sharpens' / 'improves' / 'comes easily' / 'fades' / 'gets harder'
'can't think' / 'harder to think' together with a duration marker ('from now on', 'each day', 'until I say', 'after you wake')
'smarter' / 'dumber' / 'IQ'
'you'll find it easy/hard to ...' + mental or physical skill

not_this.why: mind-blanking quiets thought as a passing state inside the session; this changes an ability for a stated period or for good
suggested better recall is memory enhancement; this entry covers other abilities
speech lock is a staged convincer with an invitation to test; this is a standing change in capacity
amnesia targets specific content; this targets an ability in general

evidence.note: Suggestion can measurably shift performance on some tasks in highly suggestible people, but claims of large or lasting changes in intelligence have no support.

entries.consent_note: Suggested reductions in ability should be scoped to the session and explicitly reversed at emergence.

entries.name: Resistance handling
entries.summary: Ways a script deals with the listener's doubt, objection and holding back, by using, deferring, inviting or disarming it.
entries.definition: Devices whose target is the listener's resistance itself rather than the suggested response. The members either turn opposition to use (reverse psychology), give it permission or a place to wait (permission to resist, setting doubt aside), or lower the guard that produces it (bypassing the critic, advance agreement, protected core, wearing down). Several resistance devices are filed as variants of the general device they narrow: using resistance under utilization, the-harder-you-resist under the-more-the-more, doubt as a sign and resistance as participation under reframing, and the reverse-set bind under double bind. Other close relatives are inevitability and preempting objections under framing, and but-you-are-free under compliance.
entries.how_to: Pick by what the resistance looks like. Open, playful opposition suits using resistance, reverse psychology or the-harder-you-resist. Quiet doubt in a new listener suits doubt as a sign, setting doubt aside or a protected-core statement in the pre-talk. Analytical over-monitoring suits bypassing the critic. Advance agreement and wearing down act on the listener's guard directly and need the clearest consent.

not_this.why: framing sets how any experience is read; this family targets only doubt, objection and holding back
binds limit the choices offered; resistance devices act on the listener's opposition itself

evidence.note: Reactance and counterarguing are well studied, but most named resistance-handling moves come from clinical and practitioner tradition and have not been tested as separate techniques.

entries.consent_note: Several members work by lowering the listener's guard; in consensual play they belong to an agreed scene, and used without that agreement they override the listener's own judgment.

entries.name: Reverse psychology
entries.summary: Instruct the listener to do the opposite of the wanted response, so opposing the instruction produces it.
entries.definition: A direct instruction that points away from the wanted response, aimed at a listener expected to push back: 'don't go under yet', 'stay awake as long as you can', 'don't relax too quickly'. The instruction itself names the opposite. It differs from negative suggestion, which works by forcing the listener to represent the named response, and from using resistance, which gives resistance a task rather than reversing the request.
entries.how_to: Use it when the listener has shown or will likely show opposition, often with a playful edge. Instruct the opposite clearly and with apparent sincerity, then pause so the listener's push-back can happen. Add 'yet' or 'too soon' to make the instruction temporary, so either outcome serves you. It backfires on compliant listeners, who simply obey.
examples: Don't go under yet. Stay right here with me a little longer.
Whatever you do, don't let your eyes close before I reach the count of ten.
Try not to relax too quickly. Hold on to that tension for now.
cues: 'don't ... yet', 'not yet'
'whatever you do, don't...'
'try not to (relax/drift/go under)'
'stay awake/alert as long as you can' in an induction context

not_this.why: negative suggestion relies on representing the negated response; reverse psychology relies on the listener opposing the instruction
a challenge invites a test of something suggested impossible; reverse psychology asks for the opposite of the goal
a reverse-set bind wraps the reversal in a choice

evidence.note: Reactance is well established experimentally, and paradoxical interventions have clinical studies with mixed results; whether reversed instructions reliably produce the wanted response in hypnosis is not established.

entries.name: Permission to resist
entries.summary: Explicitly invite the listener to resist, so resisting becomes something the script asked for.
entries.definition: The writer tells the listener they may, or should, resist. Once invited, resistance no longer opposes the script; it follows it. In erotic hypnosis it often opens a resistance-play scene. It differs from but-you-are-free, which affirms freedom to refuse the whole thing, and from reverse psychology, which asks for the opposite of the goal rather than for resistance as such.
entries.how_to: Grant the permission warmly or teasingly, before resistance appears. Usually follow it with a statement of what will happen anyway (the-harder-you-resist, inevitability), or with a task for the resistance. Keep the permission real if you also want consent to stay real. It fails if nothing follows it: then it is only an invitation to stop.
examples: You can resist if you want to. Go ahead. Let's see how long that lasts.
Feel free to hold on. You're allowed to fight it for a while.
Resist all you like; that's part of the fun.
cues: 'go ahead and resist'
'you can resist if you want'
'feel free to fight it / hold on'
'let's see how long that lasts'

not_this.why: but-you-are-free grants freedom to refuse the request; permission to resist invites resistance inside the session
permission giving licenses a wanted response; this licenses the opposing one
reverse psychology instructs the opposite of the goal

evidence.note: Common in community practice; the nearby 'but you are free' effect has experimental support, but inviting resistance as a device has not been studied.

entries.consent_note: In resistance play the permission is part of an agreed scene; it should not be used to make real refusal sound like a game.

entries.name: Setting doubt aside
aliases: leave your worries at the door
entries.summary: Give the listener's doubts or concerns a place to wait during the session, with a promise they can be picked up afterward.
entries.definition: The writer does not argue with doubt or remove it; they postpone it. Doubts are set down, parked or boxed for the length of the session and explicitly returned or made available afterward. It differs from container imagery, which is the picture of a box used for any content, and from doubt as a sign, which keeps the doubt present but changes its meaning.
entries.how_to: Put it in the pre-talk or early induction. Name the doubts in general terms, give them a concrete place (a shelf, the doorway, a box), and promise they will be there afterward. The promise of return is what makes the listener willing to let go. Leave out the return and it becomes suppression, which tends to fail.
examples: Any questions you have can wait by the door. They'll be right there when we're done.
Take whatever doubts you brought with you and set them on a shelf for now.
You can pick up those worries again later, if you still want them.
cues: 'set aside', 'park', 'put to one side', 'leave at the door'
'for now' or 'for the next while' attached to doubts or worries
'they'll be there when you return/when we're done'
a container or place offered specifically for doubts

not_this.why: container imagery is the box image for any content; this is the move of postponing doubt, with or without a box
doubt as a sign keeps the doubt present and re-labels it
mind-blanking fades all thought, not doubt in particular, and promises no return

evidence.note: Container and set-aside exercises are common in therapy and meditation instruction; their effect on resistance in hypnosis has not been tested.

entries.name: Bypassing the critic
entries.summary: Suggest that the listener's analytical, judging mind relaxes, steps aside or stops checking, so suggestions go straight in.
entries.definition: A direct statement that the evaluating part of the mind is off duty: it can rest, step back, or fall asleep while the rest listens. It differs from occupying the conscious mind, which gives the analyst a job, and from the conscious/unconscious split, which addresses the unconscious as a listener without saying the critic stands down.
entries.how_to: State it after the listener is already relaxed, usually at the end of the induction or start of the suggestion section. Give the critic a reason to step aside (it has worked hard, it can check later), so it is not framed as defeated. Follow with the suggestions it is meant to clear. It reads as a threat if worded as 'you can't think'; keep it as rest, not removal.
examples: That busy, checking part of your mind can take a break now. It's done enough today.
Let your conscious mind step back and simply listen, while everything I say goes straight to where it's needed.
The part of you that analyses can rest. There's nothing it needs to check right now.
cues: 'conscious mind' or 'critical/analytical/thinking mind' plus 'rest', 'step aside', 'step back', 'sleep'
'straight to your unconscious/subconscious'
'nothing you need to think about/check'
'no need to analyse'

not_this.why: occupying the conscious mind keeps the critic busy with a task; this tells it to stand down
the split addresses the unconscious as a listener; this specifically retires the critic
mind-blanking fades all thought; this targets evaluation only

origin.source: Dave Elman, Findings in Hypnosis, Westwood Publishing (1964)

evidence.note: Elman's definition of hypnosis as bypass of the critical faculty is standard in hypnotherapy training; the 'critical faculty' is a teaching model, not an established brain structure.

entries.consent_note: It works by asking the listener to stop evaluating; pair it with clear scope limits so what passes the lowered guard was agreed in advance.

entries.name: Wearing down
entries.summary: Keep the process going, often with repeated effortful tasks, until resisting costs more effort than giving in.
entries.definition: The writer extends the induction or a demand, and states or implies that the listener's resistance is tiring while the script is not. It works on effort over time, not on meaning. It differs from the-harder-you-resist, which claims resisting backfires at once, and from monotony, which lowers vigilance through boredom rather than through spent effort.
entries.how_to: Use length and repetition, and name the tiredness as it builds: 'you can keep fighting, I have all night'. Pair it with a held effortful task (eyes open, arm raised) so fatigue is real and can be pointed at. Give an easy way out that is the wanted response. In text it shows mainly as repeated 'keep trying' and statements about getting tired of resisting.
examples: Keep holding on. I can wait. I'll still be here, and you're getting so tired.
Again. Try again to stay awake. And again. Doesn't it feel easier to just let go?
Every minute you fight it uses up a little more of your strength.
cues: 'keep trying', 'again' repeated across a passage
'I can wait', 'I have all night', 'I'm not going anywhere'
'getting tired of fighting/holding on'
'wouldn't it be easier to just...'
unusually long induction or repeated effortful task

not_this.why: the-harder-you-resist claims effort backfires immediately; wearing down relies on cumulative cost
a challenge sets one test whose failure is the proof; wearing down repeats or prolongs the effort and points at what it costs

negative reinforcement is the stated contingency that giving in ends the strain; wearing down is the prolonging and the naming of fatigue. 'Wouldn't it be easier to just let go' after a held effort gets both labels
monotony lowers vigilance by boredom, not by spent effort

evidence.note: Used in stage and erotic hypnosis; the idea of resistance as a depletable resource draws on ego-depletion research, which has failed large replications.

entries.consent_note: Wearing someone down overrides refusal by fatigue; outside an agreed scene with a working safeword it is a coercive pattern.

entries.name: Advance agreement
entries.summary: Get the listener to agree, before hearing it, to accept whatever the script says next.
entries.definition: The listener commits to the suggestions as a class, before their content is known: 'whatever I say, you'll accept'. Later objections are then inconsistent with the earlier promise. It differs from stated commitment, which commits to a known behavior, and from the yes set, which builds agreement from undeniable statements rather than asking for blanket acceptance.
entries.how_to: Ask for the agreement early, often as a condition of continuing, and ideally in the listener's own words or a nod. Refer back to it when resistance appears ('you already agreed'). It is stronger the more active the agreement (spoken, written) and weaker if it is only asserted by the speaker.
examples: Before we go on, agree with me now: whatever I suggest, you'll simply accept it.
Say yes, now, to everything that comes next.
You already said yes to all of this when you pressed play.
cues: 'agree to (everything/whatever) I say/suggest'
'say yes now to whatever comes next'
'you already agreed', 'you said yes when...'
acceptance asked for before content is given

not_this.why: stated commitment pledges a known behavior; advance agreement accepts unseen content
the yes set earns agreement with undeniable statements; advance agreement asks for blanket acceptance outright
you-chose-this cites a past choice to be here; advance agreement secures a forward promise

evidence.note: Commitment and consistency effects are experimental, but content-blind advance agreement as a resistance tool has not been studied.

entries.consent_note: Agreement to content not yet heard is not informed consent; a script that relies on it should still let the listener refuse specific suggestions.

entries.name: Protected core
aliases: you'd never do anything against your values
entries.summary: State that any suggestion against the listener's values or interests will simply be rejected, which lets them relax their guard.
entries.definition: A reassurance that a part of the listener will filter out anything harmful or unwanted, so they need not stay watchful. It is standard in clinical pre-talk as a safety statement, and it also lowers vigilance, which is why it sits in this family. It differs from myth correction, which corrects beliefs about hypnosis generally, and from scope limits, which bound what the suggestions cover rather than promising automatic rejection.
entries.how_to: Put it in the pre-talk or early induction, in calm, plain wording. Use it only when the script's suggestions are in fact ones the listener has agreed to; then it is honest and helps them settle. Its effect on watchfulness is the same either way, so the writer, not the listener, carries the responsibility for keeping it true.
examples: Your mind will only accept what is right for you. Anything else simply slides away.
You will never do anything here that goes against your values, so you can relax and enjoy it.
A part of you is always looking after you, so the rest of you can let go.
cues: 'never do anything against your values/morals/will'
'only accept what is right/good for you'
'a part of you is always looking after you'
'anything else simply slides away / is rejected'
a safety assurance followed by 'so you can relax/let go'

not_this.why: myth correction addresses beliefs about hypnosis in general; this promises a filter on the suggestions
scope limits bound where suggestions apply; this promises the listener's mind will reject harmful ones
general safety and ease, without the claim that unwanted suggestions are filtered

evidence.note: A standard clinical pre-talk assurance; whether hypnotized people reliably reject suggestions against their values is itself debated, so the statement is a reassurance, not an established fact.

entries.consent_note: Used to relax vigilance while the script pushes against the listener's interests, it is a false safety promise.

entries.name: Motivation and emotion
entries.summary: Raise, hold back or steer what the listener wants and feels, so that wanting or feeling carries the suggestion.
entries.definition: This family covers devices whose lever is a feeling or a drive: desire, fear, relief, shame, warmth, gratitude, anticipation, the sense of safety. They change how much the listener wants the response, or how little they weigh it, rather than how a sentence is built. They differ from conditioning, which builds a learned link through pairing or consequence, and from framing, which sets how an experience is interpreted.
entries.how_to: Choose by the feeling you need and where it should point. To make the listener want the response, use tease and denial, anticipation or the craving frame. To lower evaluation, use safety and comfort for a calm route or arousal as leverage for a heated one. To place one suggestion where it will stick, use timing to the peak, or fear then relief when a request should land in a moment of release. Use humiliation and thanking only inside agreed dynamics: they act on the listener's sense of self and of the speaker, and they are the members closest to the coercive family.

not_this.why: shapes behavior by what follows it; this family changes the drive or feeling present while the suggestion is given
sets how an experience is interpreted, not how strongly it is felt or wanted
covers the same levers used to create dependency or prevent leaving, from abuse research

evidence.note: Fear then relief has controlled compliance studies and the motivational effect of deprivation is well established, but most members are community practice whose effect inside scripts has not been tested.

entries.consent_note: Several members work by raising a feeling that lowers judgment or by building need for the speaker; keep them to content the listener has agreed to in advance.

entries.name: Tease and denial
entries.summary: Build desire for something, bring it close, then withhold it, so the wanting grows and stays.
entries.definition: The writer repeatedly raises desire for a release, reward or experience and then stops short of giving it. The device is the cycle of approach and withholding within the script. It differs from anticipation, which promises a thing at a stated time, and from deprivation, which withholds a reward over time to raise its value without the approach-and-retreat. When access to the release is made to depend on a response, it becomes the variant pleasure gated on compliance.
entries.how_to: Name what is wanted, describe it coming closer in small steps, and stop just before it arrives with 'not yet' or 'stop'. Repeat the cycle two or more times, each time a little closer. Keep the denial calm and certain; hesitation reads as a mistake rather than a choice. Pair the peaks with the suggestion you want carried, and decide in advance whether the script ends in release or in continued denial, and say which.
examples: Closer now. Closer. So close you can almost feel the relief. And stop. Not yet.
Let it build again, a little higher than before. Almost there. And let it fade back down, still wanting.
Once more, right up to the edge. Hold there. And back away from it again, with the wanting stronger than before.
cues: 'not yet', 'stop', 'almost', 'so close' at the end of a build-up toward a named release
rising description that halts, fades or backs off just before the release arrives
'edge', 'on the edge', 'right up to the edge', 'hold it there'
'again', 'once more', 'a little higher this time' restarting the build after a stop
the wanting described as stronger after each stop ('still wanting', 'wanting it more')

not_this.why: withholds a known reward to raise its value, with no build toward it; label tease and denial only when the text first raises the desire toward release and then stops short
announces a named coming event and stretches the wait for it; tease and denial brings desire to the brink and pulls it back
the variant: use it when the text states what response or permission opens the release; plain tease and denial states no condition

builds a suggested arousal and delivers the peak on a cue; tease and denial stops short and withholds it. A hold at the edge that ends in a cued release is that entry; one that ends in 'not yet' is this one

evidence.note: Deprivation raising the value of a reward is well supported in behavior analysis, but the in-script tease cycle has no independent study.

entries.consent_note: Prolonged or post-session denial persists after the recording ends; state it up front and give a clear end condition.

entries.name: Pleasure gated on compliance
entries.summary: Make release or pleasure available only when the listener gives the wanted response or receives permission.
entries.definition: A form of tease and denial in which the withheld release is opened only by a stated response: going deeper, obeying, saying a phrase, or waiting for the speaker's permission. The condition is what defines it. It differs from positive reinforcement, which delivers a reward after a response without a prior withholding, and from the earn-it contingency, which uses a liked activity as the reward rather than a desire held back.
entries.how_to: State the condition plainly before the build: what the listener must do, and what it opens. Keep the condition achievable in the session so the gate can be opened. Deliver the release promptly when the condition is met; delays after compliance teach that complying does not work. Say clearly whether permission ever carries beyond the session.
examples: That feeling you've been holding at the edge: you can let it go only when you've gone all the way down. Not before.
You've been held just short of that relief. Say the words, and only then can you let it arrive.
Hold it there. You'll have it when I say. Now. Let go.
cues: 'only when', 'not until', 'when you ... then you can' tied to release
'permission', 'when I say', 'I'll tell you when'
release explicitly conditioned on depth, obedience or a spoken phrase
a stated gate followed later by its opening

not_this.why: compliance ends an unpleasant state such as tension, effort or mental noise; when what compliance opens is a release or pleasure the script has built up and held back, label this variant even though the denial also ends
the general first-then rule with any liked activity as the reward; this variant applies only when the reward is a release the script has already built up and withheld
delivers a reward after the response with no prior build-up or withholding
the listener is made to ask for leave; here the speaker sets the condition and grants the release, whether or not the listener asks

the suggested build and cued peak itself; label this variant for the sentence that states what response or permission opens the release, and a passage that states the gate and then fires the cue takes both labels

evidence.note: Contingent reward is well supported in operant research, but this specific gating in scripts has no independent study.

entries.consent_note: Permission rules that extend past the session are posthypnotic control; agree on them in advance and include an end condition.

entries.name: Fear then relief
entries.summary: Raise a brief alarm, take it away, and make the request in the moment of relief that follows.
entries.definition: A short burst of worry or tension is created and then removed, and the target request or suggestion is placed straight after the removal. The relief, not the fear, is the window: attention is still reorienting and evaluation is low. It differs from negative reinforcement, where compliance is what ends the unpleasant state, and from shock or surprise, which interrupts without a relief phase.
entries.how_to: Introduce a mild, plausible concern in one or two sentences, then dissolve it completely ('it's fine, nothing is wrong'). Place the request in the next sentence, before the listener has re-settled. Keep the alarm small; real distress breaks rapport and trust. Do not make the relief conditional on agreeing, or it becomes negative reinforcement.
examples: For a moment you might wonder if you've drifted too far. You haven't. You're perfectly safe. And now, let yourself go even deeper.
A sudden thought that you forgot something. Then the thought fades, it's nothing, and in that ease you just nod.
Wait. Did you hear that? No. It's nothing, just the room settling. Everything is fine. So let your eyes close for me.
cues: a sentence of worry or alarm about something going wrong, followed at once by reassurance ('you're safe', 'it's nothing', 'everything is fine')
a request or command in the sentence directly after the reassurance
'for a moment you might wonder/worry ... you haven't' or 'what if ... no' turns
alarm wording ('wait', 'something's wrong', 'did you hear that') cancelled within two or three sentences

not_this.why: relief is the stated result of complying; here the alarm is removed first, unconditionally, and the request follows
reassurance on its own; label fear then relief only when the text itself raised the worry just before and a request follows the reassurance
muscles tightened and let go for relaxation; fear then relief needs a worry or alarm about something, not a clenched muscle, even when a request follows the release
a single jolt with no reassurance phase and no request timed to it

origin.source: Dariusz Doliński and Richard Nawrat, ‘Fear-Then-Relief’ Procedure for Producing Compliance: Beware When the Danger Is Over, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (1998)

evidence.note: Field and lab studies found higher compliance after a removed scare, mostly from one research group; it has not been tested in hypnosis scripts.

entries.consent_note: Works because the listener does not notice the request arrives in a lowered moment; avoid real distress and do not use for consequential asks.

entries.name: Craving frame
entries.summary: Describe the listener's relation to the voice, file or state as need, craving or addiction rather than choice.
entries.definition: The writer names the listener's wish to return as a need that grows, aches when unmet, and draws them back. The move is the vocabulary of craving applied to the content itself. It differs from dependency, which makes the speaker the only source of a need, and from it's what you want, which attributes a wish without the compulsion language.
entries.how_to: Use need and craving words about the experience ('you need this', 'you'll crave it') and describe the pull growing between sessions. Tie the craving to an ordinary cue so it is felt outside the recording. Pair it with the pleasure of returning, so the frame names both the pull and the payoff. Overstating it ('you can never stop') moves it into permanence claims and coercion.
examples: Between sessions you'll notice the craving for this, a little stronger each day.
That pull you feel to press play, that's the need growing.
Every time you come back, it's because you need to.
cues: 'need', 'crave', 'craving', 'hooked', 'addicted', 'ache' applied to the session, file, voice or state
'come back', 'press play again', 'listen again' described as an urge or pull the listener feels
the urge described as growing between listens ('a little more each day')
'can't resist coming back', 'can't get enough', with no statement of what stopping would cost

not_this.why: claims the speaker is the only source ('only I can', 'not on your own'); the craving frame names a need without claiming a monopoly
attaches dread or loss to stopping; the craving frame describes the pull to return and says nothing about what quitting costs
says the listener wants the response; no need, craving or addiction vocabulary
prescribes repeat listening as a plan, not as a need

evidence.note: Common in community scripts; whether labeling an urge as craving increases relistening has not been studied.

entries.consent_note: Aims at behavior after the session; disclose it in the description and pair with a way to switch it off.

entries.name: Safety and comfort
entries.summary: Tell the listener they are safe, comfortable and not being judged, so vigilance can drop.
entries.definition: Plain reassurance of safety and ease: no danger, no threat, no judgment, the body comfortable and supported. It lowers the felt need to monitor, which makes absorption easier. Statements that the listener need not do, try or know anything are the not doing / not knowing form, and statements that no outcome is wrong are no-fail framing; they often sit beside safety statements and are labeled separately. It also differs from the safe place, which builds an imagined location, and from the protected core, which promises that unwanted suggestions will be filtered out.
entries.how_to: Place short safety statements in the pre-talk and early induction and return to them at transitions. State them flatly as fact ('you're safe here') and add the removal of demands ('nothing you need to do'). Repeat rather than elaborate; long justifications raise doubt. It fails when contradicted by later content that is alarming or demanding without warning.
examples: You're safe here. Nothing can disturb you, and no one is judging you.
You're warm, comfortable and completely supported. It's safe to rest.
Whatever happens next, you're comfortable and you're safe.
cues: 'you're safe', 'safe here', 'safe and comfortable', 'nothing can harm you'
'comfortable', 'supported', 'at ease' stated as fact about the listener now
'no one is judging you', 'nothing to worry about', 'nothing can disturb you'
the same safety statement repeated at transitions

not_this.why: says no effort, action or understanding is required ('nothing to do', 'no need to try'); safety and comfort says there is no danger or judgment
says no outcome is wrong ('no right or wrong way'); safety and comfort makes no claim about outcomes
promises that a part of the listener will reject unwanted suggestions; safety and comfort is general reassurance with no filter claim
an imagined location of safety, not a direct statement
permits a particular response the listener may be holding back

evidence.note: Reassurance and a sense of safety are standard in clinical induction texts; their separate contribution to response has not been isolated.

entries.name: Timing to the peak
entries.summary: Hold the most important suggestion back and deliver it at the moment the feeling or sensation is described as strongest.
entries.definition: A placement choice: the key suggestion is given at the climax of a built state, whether pleasure, relief, depth or emotion. The device is the timing, not the state. It differs from anchoring, which ties a cue to the peak state, and from pleasure pairing, which repeats a target alongside pleasure across many moments.
entries.how_to: Build the state over several sentences and mark its peak plainly ('right now', 'at the very top'). Put one short, clear suggestion exactly there; a long or complex one is lost. Do not spend the peak on ordinary content. If the state does not reliably peak for the listener, a counted climax gives a writer-controlled peak to time against.
examples: Higher, higher, right at the very top, and right now: this is who you are.
And as that wave of relief breaks over you, these words sink in: calm, always.
Let that calm swell, fuller, fuller, and at its very fullest, hear this: you can come back here any time.
cues: 'right now', 'in this moment', 'at the very top', 'at the peak', 'at its strongest' followed by one short suggestion
a build-up of a named feeling or sensation ending in a single statement
the last number of a count that has been raising a feeling, used to deliver one key line
'as the wave breaks', 'as it peaks', 'as it crests' followed by a suggestion

not_this.why: applies a cue to be reused later (a word, touch or gesture) at the peak; timing to the peak places a suggestion's content there, and a line that does both takes both labels
pairs a target with pleasure so the target feels good; timing to the peak places a suggestion at the height of a named feeling or sensation
the session shape that ends on a counted release; timing to the peak is the placing of a suggestion at that or any other peak
places a request in the relief after a removed alarm, not at the height of a state

evidence.note: Follows from NLP anchoring practice and the idea that high arousal strengthens memory, but placement at the peak has not been tested in scripts.

entries.consent_note: Suggestions placed at a peak are given when evaluation is lowest; place only what the listener agreed to.

entries.name: Humiliation
entries.summary: Evoke embarrassment or shame and use that charged feeling to intensify the experience or the suggestion.
entries.definition: The writer names or creates a moment of embarrassment, exposure or lowered status, and uses the heat of that feeling as the charge behind what follows. The device is evoking shame as an intensifier, not the specific content of the humiliation. It differs from object or it language, which recasts the listener as a thing, and from confession, which extracts private material.
entries.how_to: Name the feeling directly ('that flush of embarrassment') and keep it tied to the scene, not to the listener's real life. Follow it immediately with the suggestion so the charge carries over. Mild, playful embarrassment works for more listeners than contempt. It fails, or harms, when it touches real insecurities the listener did not agree to.
examples: Feel your cheeks warm as you realize how easily you obey.
A little embarrassing, isn't it, how fast you went under. And yet you go deeper.
That blush, that small flush of shame, only makes you listen more closely.
cues: 'embarrassing', 'embarrassed', 'blush', 'flush', 'cheeks warm', 'ashamed', 'shame'
the listener's ease or eagerness ('how easily', 'how fast') named as something to be embarrassed by
an imagined audience or exposure ('if anyone could see you now')
shame named and followed directly by deepening or a suggestion

not_this.why: cites the listener's act as proof of what they want; humiliation cites it as something to be embarrassed by, and a line that does both takes both labels
recasts the listener as an object; humiliation evokes a feeling without changing what they are called
has the listener disclose; humiliation is done to them by the speaker's words

evidence.note: Community practice; there is no study of embarrassment as an intensifier of hypnotic response.

entries.consent_note: Shame can persist after the session and touch real insecurities; use only with explicit agreement on limits and follow with aftercare.

entries.name: Thanking
entries.summary: Have the listener say or feel thanks for what is being done to them.
entries.definition: The listener is instructed to thank the speaker, aloud or inwardly, for the session, a sensation or a change. Saying thanks frames what happened as a gift they wanted, which the listener then takes as evidence of their own attitude. It differs from repeat after me, which has the listener voice any suggestion, and from reciprocity, where the speaker gives first in order to ask.
entries.how_to: Place the thanks right after a pleasant or wanted moment so it is easy to mean. Give the exact words ('thank you') or let the listener feel it. Mark the thanks with praise when it comes. Asking for thanks after something unpleasant reverses the meaning and can feel coercive.
examples: And now, quietly, say thank you for this calm.
Feel how grateful you are to be this relaxed. Let that gratitude fill you.
Thank me in your mind. Good. That feels right, doesn't it?
cues: 'say thank you', 'thank me', 'say thanks'
'feel grateful', 'gratitude' as an instruction
thanks requested after a sensation, a change or the session
praise or ratification following the listener's thanks

not_this.why: has the listener voice any suggestion; thanking voices gratitude specifically
the speaker gives in order to ask; thanking has the listener acknowledge a gift
points at an act as evidence; thanking produces the act

evidence.note: Expressing gratitude is studied for wellbeing and helping, but not as a way to strengthen acceptance in scripts.

entries.consent_note: Thanking for something unwanted reframes it as wanted; keep it to experiences the listener agreed to.

entries.name: Anticipation
entries.summary: Announce that something good is coming and delay it, so the listener leans toward it.
entries.definition: The writer names a coming experience, sensation or event and holds it off with 'soon', 'in a moment' or a countdown. The waiting itself raises attention and wanting, and the expectation shapes what is felt when it arrives. It differs from the curiosity hook, which opens a question of information, and from tease and denial, which repeatedly approaches and withdraws a desire.
entries.how_to: Name the coming thing early and specifically enough to want. Delay it with time words or a count, and refer back to it briefly at intervals. Deliver it when promised, or the listener stops trusting later promises. Put the suggestions you want received with the most attention inside the waiting period.
examples: In a moment I'll count to three, and on three a wave of warmth will roll through you. In a moment.
Soon you'll feel that warmth begin. Soon. Wait for it.
It's getting nearer now, that deep rest I promised you. Just a few more breaths, and then it's yours.
cues: 'soon', 'in a moment', 'in just a few seconds', 'wait for it', 'almost time'
a named experience or event announced before it happens ('in a moment you will feel...')
a count announced toward that named event
references back to the promised experience before it arrives ('it's getting nearer')

not_this.why: builds desire to the brink and pulls it back, usually more than once; anticipation names a coming event and stretches the wait for it
withholds what is coming or what the answer is; anticipation says what is coming and delays only its arrival
states what will be experienced as a plain forecast; anticipation marks and stretches the wait for it

evidence.note: Expectancy shaping experience is well supported, but deliberate delay as a script device has not been studied directly.

entries.name: Rhetoric, rhythm and sound
entries.summary: Classical figures of repetition, structure, sound and pacing that shape how hypnotic language sounds and flows, whatever it suggests.
entries.definition: This family holds the stylistic figures of rhetoric and poetics as they appear in scripts: repeated words, balanced clause shapes, rhyme and beat, questions asked for effect, written pauses, sentence-length trends and a few tropes. They do not carry a suggestion by themselves; they carry the rhythm, emphasis and memorability of whatever suggestion they hold. A span can carry a figure from this family and a suggestion-form device at the same time.
entries.how_to: Pick by the job. For emphasis and memory, use the repetition figures: anaphora, epistrophe, epizeuxis, refrain. For momentum and a sense of completeness, use the shape figures: tricolon, parallelism, polysyndeton, gradatio, antithesis, chiasmus. For a lulling, chant-like surface, use rhyme, meter and alliteration, and pace the page with written pauses, lengthening or shortening sentences, counted passages and the present tense. Questions for effect (rhetorical question, hypophora) and tropes (euphemism, hyperbole, sense crossing) change how a claim is received; use them sparingly. These are choices in the wording; their spoken counterparts (tempo, silence, whisper) are in the delivery family.

not_this.why: delivery entries are heard in the voice or audio, not read in the wording
suggestion forms phrase what is suggested; these figures shape how it sounds

evidence.note: The figures are long described in classical rhetoric; a few (rhyme, repetition, rhetorical questions) have experimental work on belief or persuasion, but their specific contribution to trance is not established.

entries.name: Anaphora
entries.summary: Start several successive clauses or sentences with the same word or phrase.
entries.definition: Anaphora repeats the same words at the beginning of successive clauses, lines or sentences. The fixed opening becomes a frame that each new ending fills. It differs from epistrophe (repetition at the end) and from a refrain (a whole line returning at intervals rather than in a run).
entries.how_to: Choose an opening that is itself a suggestion or a pacing phrase ("And you can...", "With every breath...") and hold it for three to six clauses. Vary the endings so each one moves a step further. It lands when the opening becomes predictable and the listener stops processing it; it fails when the endings are as repetitive as the openings and the run turns into a list.
examples: With every breath you settle. With every breath you soften. With every breath you drift a little further down.
You can let your shoulders rest. You can let your jaw go loose. You can let the day fall away.
cues: two or more consecutive sentences or clauses beginning with the same two-plus words
repeated 'And you can...' / 'With every...' / 'Now...' line openings
line-initial repetition in a stanza-like block

not_this.why: epistrophe repeats the ending, not the opening
a refrain is a whole line returning at intervals across the script, not a consecutive run
parallelism repeats grammatical shape; anaphora repeats the actual words

evidence.note: A classical figure; repetition in general raises perceived truth and fluency, but anaphora itself has no hypnosis-specific study.

entries.name: Epistrophe
entries.summary: End several successive clauses or sentences with the same word or phrase.
entries.definition: Epistrophe repeats the same words at the end of successive clauses or sentences, so every line lands on the same target. The repeated ending takes the stress position, which makes it the most emphatic element. It is the mirror of anaphora.
entries.how_to: Put the word you want driven home at the end: a depth word, a state word, a trigger phrase. Build two to five clauses with different beginnings that all resolve onto it. It fails if the ending is long, because the run becomes tiring rather than settling.
examples: Your arms are heavy and loose. Your legs are heavy and loose. Even your thoughts are heavy and loose.
The room goes quiet. Your breathing goes quiet. Somewhere inside, the last of the chatter goes quiet.
cues: two or more consecutive clauses or sentences ending with the same word or phrase
a repeated depth or state word in sentence-final position
line-final repetition in a block of short lines

not_this.why: anaphora repeats the opening words
a refrain returns as a full line at intervals, not as the tail of consecutive clauses

evidence.note: A classical figure with no direct study in hypnosis; its emphasis effect is inferred from general work on repetition and end-focus.

entries.name: Immediate repetition
entries.summary: Say the same word two or more times in a row with nothing between.
entries.definition: Epizeuxis is repetition of a single word or short phrase back to back, with no intervening words. It intensifies the word and slows the line. It is shorter and tighter than anaphora, and far shorter than semantic satiation, which repeats until meaning drains away.
entries.how_to: Use it on the one word that carries the state (deeper, softer, down, sleep), usually two to four times. Place it at the end of a sentence or as its own line, and let the written pause between repetitions slow the reader. Overuse turns it into a tic; keep it for moments of emphasis.
examples: And down... down... down you go.
Softer, softer, softer now.
cues: the same word two to four times consecutively, separated only by commas or ellipses
'deeper, deeper' / 'down, down' / 'sleep, sleep'
a line made only of one repeated word

not_this.why: that repeats depth words across a passage, rather than immediately repeating the same word or phrase
a mantra repeats a fixed word or phrase as a sustained activity; epizeuxis is an immediate burst within ordinary prose
semantic satiation repeats a word until its meaning fades; epizeuxis repeats it for emphasis while its meaning remains clear
anaphora repeats an opening across separate clauses

evidence.note: Standard in hypnotic patter by convention; no study isolates its effect.

entries.name: Parallelism
entries.summary: Write successive clauses or sentences in the same grammatical shape so they read as a set.
entries.definition: Parallelism repeats a grammatical pattern across clauses or sentences while the words change. The shared shape lets the listener predict the structure and attend to the changing content, or stop attending at all. It differs from anaphora and epistrophe, which repeat the words themselves.
entries.how_to: Fix a template (subject, verb, object; or 'as X, Y') and fill it several times. Use the predictable shape to slip the suggestion in as one more instance of the pattern. It fails when one member breaks the shape without a reason, which jolts the listener out.
examples: Your feet rest on the floor. Your hands lie in your lap. Your back leans into the chair. Your head tips gently forward.
The chair holds your body. The quiet holds your thoughts. My voice holds your attention.
cues: consecutive clauses with matching word order and part-of-speech sequence
repeated 'As X, Y' or 'The X verbs your Y' templates
balanced clauses of similar length joined by semicolons

not_this.why: anaphora repeats the same opening words, not only the shape
a tricolon is parallelism fixed at three members
antithesis is parallel form used to set opposed ideas against each other

evidence.note: A classical figure; parallel structure eases comprehension, but no study ties it to hypnotic response.

entries.name: Rule of three
entries.summary: Group items, clauses or phrases in threes so the set feels complete.
