theory.writer_takeaway: When redefining a term, use it consistently in its new sense rather than arguing for it; repeated use does the work that argument would invite resistance to.

theory.name: Illocutionary force
theory.summary: What an utterance does, such as ordering, permitting, promising or asking, as distinct from what it literally says.
theory.claim: 'You might want to close your eyes' is grammatically a statement about possibility but functions as a request. Force can be direct or indirect, and listeners respond to the force rather than the grammar. Indirect forms soften directives while keeping their effect.
theory.evidence_note: A foundational concept in pragmatics; research on indirect requests supports that listeners readily recover the intended force.
theory.writer_takeaway: Choose the grammatical form for tone but keep the force clear; indirect phrasing lowers resistance only if the listener still knows what is being asked.

theory.name: Speech-act theory
theory.summary: The theory that saying things is a way of doing things, and that utterances succeed or fail depending on social conditions.
theory.claim: Utterances perform acts: naming, declaring, promising, commanding. Some acts, like renaming, take effect by being said if the right conditions hold, such as standing to make the declaration and uptake by the hearer. The theory classifies acts and the conditions under which they succeed.
theory.evidence_note: A long-standing, widely used framework in philosophy of language; it is a classification scheme rather than a predictive model.
theory.writer_takeaway: When the script declares a change (a new name, a role, a rule), set up the conditions that make the declaration feel valid: the listener's consent and the speaker's standing.

theory.name: Begging the question
theory.summary: An argument that assumes the very conclusion it is supposed to support.
theory.claim: The conclusion appears, usually reworded, as a premise: 'you are going deep because your mind is sinking deeper'. The reasoning looks complete but adds no support. Circularity is easy to miss when the restatement uses different words.
theory.evidence_note: A long-recognized fallacy and uncontroversial as a logical point. Experimental work on circular reasoning is limited; it suggests that how acceptable a circular argument seems depends on the dialogue context and on whether the repeated claim has already been granted, not simply on rewording.
theory.writer_takeaway: A circular 'because' can make a suggestion feel justified at no cost, but it is fragile under scrutiny; it works best when the listener is absorbed rather than evaluating.

theory.name: Enthymeme
theory.summary: An argument with a premise left unstated, which the listener supplies.
theory.claim: Classical rhetoric's enthymeme omits a premise the audience is expected to fill in: 'you're relaxing, so you're ready'. Because the listener supplies the missing step, they rarely examine it. The step they supply is usually one they already believe.
theory.evidence_note: A classical concept accepted in modern argumentation theory, though what exactly counts as an enthymeme is debated.
theory.writer_takeaway: This construct duplicates the device 'Unstated premise'; leave out a premise only when the listener will reliably supply the one you intend.

theory.name: Enthymematic persuasion
theory.summary: The idea that arguments persuade better when listeners complete them, because self-supplied premises are not scrutinized.
theory.claim: When people supply a missing premise, the conclusion feels partly self-generated, and people counterargue less against their own contributions. This links the classical enthymeme to research on self-generated arguments and self-persuasion.
theory.evidence_note: The idea is plausible but the persuasion research does not favor it in general: reviews of studies comparing stated and unstated conclusions mostly find the stated conclusion at least as persuasive. Any advantage for leaving the step out appears limited to engaged listeners who actually draw the inference, and it fails when they do not.
theory.writer_takeaway: Leave gaps only where the listener will fill them the way you intend; otherwise state the conclusion outright.

theory.name: Argument from consensus
theory.summary: Treating the fact that many people believe or do something as a reason to believe or do it.
theory.claim: 'Everyone who listens to this goes deeper' offers numbers as evidence. As a logical argument it is weak, but as a heuristic it often works because consensus correlates with truth. People lean on it most when they are uncertain.
theory.evidence_note: Uncontroversial as a fallacy. The underlying social-proof effect is well supported, though some classic demonstrations are smaller than popular accounts suggest.
theory.writer_takeaway: Consensus claims work best when the listener is unsure; specifics that make the claimed group feel real make them land harder.

theory.name: False dilemma
theory.summary: Presenting two options as the only ones when others exist.
theory.claim: A false dilemma narrows the choice so both offered options serve the speaker. It is a classic informal fallacy. In hypnotic language the same structure appears as the double bind and the illusion of choice.
theory.evidence_note: Uncontroversial as a logical point; research on choice sets supports that which options are presented shapes what people choose.
theory.writer_takeaway: This construct duplicates the device of the same name; make both offered options acceptable outcomes and leave the constraint unspoken.

theory.name: Motte-and-bailey
theory.summary: Advancing a bold claim, retreating to a modest defensible one when challenged, then returning to the bold one.
theory.claim: The speaker holds an ambitious position (the bailey) and, when pressed, substitutes a modest, defensible version (the motte). Once the challenge passes, the ambitious claim returns. Both versions share a name, which hides the switch.
theory.evidence_note: A named pattern from philosophy, popularized online; it is an analytic tool rather than an experimentally studied effect.
theory.writer_takeaway: Recognize the pattern in material that alternates 'this is just relaxation' with strong transformation claims; keep what you claim consistent across the pre-talk and the body.
theory.source: Nicholas Shackel, The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology, Metaphilosophy (2005)

theory.name: Equivocation
theory.summary: Using one word in two senses within an argument so a conclusion seems to follow.
theory.claim: A word shifts meaning partway through: 'deep' as relaxed, then 'deep' as changed. Each step looks valid, but the conclusion depends on the shift. Words with two common senses make the shift easy to miss.
theory.evidence_note: A classic fallacy, uncontroversial as a logical point, with little distinct experimental work.
theory.writer_takeaway: Words with two senses let you carry a listener from an accepted meaning to a stronger one; this is also exactly what a critical listener catches.

theory.name: Moral reframing
theory.summary: Presenting a request in terms of the listener's own moral values rather than the speaker's.
theory.claim: People are more receptive to arguments framed in values they hold. Recasting a position in the listener's terms (care, loyalty, freedom, fairness) reduces the sense that it comes from an opposing camp.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by experiments in political psychology; effects are modest, and replications have found them smaller or inconsistent in some settings.
theory.writer_takeaway: Tie suggestions to values the listener already holds, stated in their words, rather than to the values that motivate you.

theory.name: Moralization
theory.summary: The process by which a preference becomes a moral value, making it more rigid and more emotionally charged.
theory.claim: Once something is a moral matter, people resist compromise, react to violations with anger or disgust, and expect others to share the view. Moralization can be driven by harm arguments and by emotional association.
theory.evidence_note: An established construct in moral psychology with experimental and longitudinal support; the mechanisms of change are still debated.
theory.writer_takeaway: Framing a behavior as right versus wrong makes it stick harder and makes lapses feel like violations; that rigidity is the cost, so use it sparingly and only with consent.

theory.name: Scope neglect
theory.summary: Emotional and evaluative responses barely change with the size of a quantity.
theory.claim: People's concern or willingness to pay changes little whether a problem affects two thousand or two hundred thousand. The response tracks the image or feeling the description evokes, not the quantity. Magnitude is processed coarsely unless amounts are compared side by side.
theory.evidence_note: Insensitivity to quantity is replicated in valuation and judgment research, though its size depends on how responses are elicited and it shrinks when quantities are compared directly. The related claim that a single identified case moves people more than statistics is a separate effect, and reviews find it small and dependent on conditions.
theory.writer_takeaway: Do not assume that a larger multiplier will make a suggestion more compelling; describe the intended change concretely.
theory.source: William H. Desvousges, F. Reed Johnson, Richard W. Dunford, K. Nicole Wilson and Kevin J. Boyle, Measuring Natural Resource Damages with Contingent Valuation, Contingent Valuation: A Critical Assessment (1993)

theory.name: Framing effect
theory.summary: Logically equivalent descriptions of the same choice lead people to choose differently.
theory.claim: Describing outcomes as gains or losses, or as amounts kept versus lost, shifts decisions. Loss frames tend to promote risk-taking and gain frames caution. The effect depends on listeners not translating between frames.
theory.evidence_note: Risky-choice framing (the original gain/loss decision problems) is robust and widely replicated, though smaller in within-person designs and among deliberating or expert decision makers. Framing a persuasive appeal around what is gained versus what is lost is a different case: reviews of that work find differences that are small or negligible.
theory.writer_takeaway: Choose the frame on purpose, what the listener gains by going along or what they lose by holding back, but treat it as a matter of tone and fit; the evidence that either frame persuades better is weak.

theory.name: Agenda-setting
theory.summary: What an audience thinks about is shaped by what a source covers and how often.
theory.claim: Media coverage shapes less what people think than what they think about. Topics that recur prominently come to be judged important. The research is on news media; applying it to a single script or a series of files is an extrapolation.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in media research over decades; effects are stronger for unfamiliar topics and weaker for those people experience directly.
theory.writer_takeaway: What the script returns to most becomes what matters to the listener; spend airtime on what you want weighted.

theory.name: Attribute salience
theory.summary: Which features of a topic are emphasized shapes how the topic is judged.
theory.claim: Beyond which topics get attention, which attributes are highlighted shapes evaluation: describing trance as 'effortless' rather than 'deep' changes what it is judged by. Salient attributes become the criteria.
theory.evidence_note: An extension of agenda-setting research (second-level agenda-setting) with supporting studies; less established than the first-level effect.
theory.writer_takeaway: Pick the attribute you want the listener to judge the experience by and keep it in the foreground.

theory.name: False balance
theory.summary: Presenting two sides as equally credible when the evidence strongly favors one.
theory.claim: Giving equal time to a fringe view signals that the question is open. Audiences infer uncertainty from the structure of the presentation, not just its content. This can make weak claims seem credible.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by content analyses of news coverage and some experimental work on how balance affects perceived consensus.
theory.writer_takeaway: 'Some say, others say' structure creates the impression of open debate; use it only where you mean the question to be open.

theory.name: Manufactured consensus
theory.summary: Creating the appearance that many people agree, through repetition, multiple voices or selective display.
theory.claim: A source can simulate agreement with repeated voices, staged testimonials or selective quotation. Listeners infer a real consensus and adjust their own view. The appearance works through the same channel as genuine social proof.
theory.evidence_note: The component effects (social proof, the illusory-truth effect of repetition) are well supported in laboratory work, including findings that one source repeating a claim can raise its perceived prevalence. Whether staged or coordinated fake consensus shifts beliefs outside the lab is less clear; studies of real campaigns report mixed and often small effects.
theory.writer_takeaway: This construct duplicates the variant of the same name; layered voices and 'so many others' framing simulate a crowd.

theory.name: Narrative transportation
theory.summary: Being absorbed in a story, with attention, imagery and feeling all directed into the story world.
theory.claim: Transported readers lose track of their surroundings, form vivid images and feel for the characters. Transportation is associated with story-consistent beliefs and less counterarguing. It depends on story quality and on the reader's general tendency to become absorbed.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported by experiments and meta-analysis; effects on beliefs are modest to moderate and depend on how they are measured.
theory.writer_takeaway: This construct underlies the device 'Story absorption'; vivid, coherent, concrete stories absorb more than abstract ones.

theory.name: Narrative persuasion
theory.summary: Stories change attitudes and beliefs, often by routes other than argument.
theory.claim: Narratives influence beliefs through absorption, identification and lowered resistance rather than through evidence. They can shift attitudes on matters the story only implies. Some studies find effects that persist or grow over time.
theory.evidence_note: Meta-analyses show small to moderate effects; delayed or growing effects are less consistent.
theory.writer_takeaway: When direct suggestion meets resistance, carry the message in a story and let a character's change make the point.
theory.source: Kurt Braddock and James Price Dillard, Meta-Analytic Evidence for the Persuasive Effect of Narratives on Beliefs, Attitudes, Intentions, and Behaviors, Communication Monographs (2016)

theory.name: Extended Elaboration Likelihood Model
theory.summary: A model holding that stories persuade by absorbing readers so they argue back less.
theory.claim: It extends the elaboration likelihood model to narrative: absorption and identification reduce counterarguing, so persuasive content embedded in a story meets less resistance. Stories whose persuasive intent is less obvious do this best.
theory.evidence_note: A widely cited framework with partial support; reduced counterarguing appears in some tests and not others.
theory.writer_takeaway: Keep the persuasive point inside the plot rather than stating it as a moral; an overt message breaks the absorption it relies on.

theory.name: Entertainment Overcoming Resistance Model
theory.summary: A model of how engaging stories lower reactance, counterarguing and the sense that a message does not apply to you.
theory.claim: Engagement with characters and plot weakens the defenses people use against persuasion: feeling pushed, arguing back, and dismissing the message as irrelevant. Identification, liking and parasocial bonds are named mechanisms.
theory.evidence_note: A synthesis framework with some supporting experiments; individual pathways are inconsistently supported.
theory.writer_takeaway: Give the listener a character to like and identify with, so the message arrives as that character's experience rather than your demand.
theory.source: Emily Moyer-Gusé, Toward a Theory of Entertainment Persuasion: Explaining the Persuasive Effects of Entertainment-Education Messages, Communication Theory (2008)

theory.name: Character identification
theory.summary: Taking a character's perspective, so their goals and feelings feel like one's own during the story.
theory.claim: Identification involves empathy, sharing the character's goals and a temporary loss of self-awareness. Readers who identify adopt the character's view more readily. Similarity helps but is not required.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by survey and experimental work; its measures overlap with transportation, and effects vary across studies.
theory.writer_takeaway: This construct duplicates the device of the same name; give the character the listener's situation so stepping into them is easy.

theory.name: Parasocial interaction
theory.summary: A one-sided sense of relationship with a media figure, experienced as if they were talking to you.
theory.claim: Audiences respond to performers who address them directly as if in a real interaction, and over time this can become a felt relationship. Direct address, personal disclosure and a consistent voice strengthen it.
theory.evidence_note: A long-standing concept with a large empirical literature; definitions and measures vary between studies.
theory.writer_takeaway: Direct address, disclosure and a consistent voice across files build a felt relationship; that bond adds influence, so do not use it to foster dependency.

theory.name: Suspension of disbelief
theory.summary: Audiences set aside skepticism in order to engage with a fiction.
theory.claim: People accept impossible premises within a fiction to enjoy it. The classic account treats this as a willing choice. Later psychological work suggests people do not actively suspend disbelief so much as fail to engage it while absorbed.
theory.evidence_note: A literary concept rather than a tested theory; related experimental work favors the not-engaging account over active suspension.
theory.writer_takeaway: Frame impossible content as fiction or play so the listener has no reason to evaluate it as fact.

theory.name: Transportation-induced counterarguing reduction
theory.summary: Absorption in a story takes up the mental resources that would otherwise go to arguing back.
theory.claim: When attention is occupied with following and imagining a story, less is left for critical evaluation of its claims. Reduced counterarguing is proposed as one route from transportation to belief change.
theory.evidence_note: Some experiments find counterarguing mediates transportation effects; others find the mediation weak.
theory.writer_takeaway: Place suggestions while the listener is most absorbed in the story, not at the moment you bring them out of it.

theory.name: Narrative coherence
theory.summary: Stories whose parts hang together are judged more believable.
theory.claim: People judge accounts by whether they fit together and match what they already know, not only by evidence. In legal settings, jurors build competing stories and favor the most coherent one. Coherence can outweigh accuracy.
theory.evidence_note: Fisher's narrative paradigm, which names coherence and fidelity as the tests people apply to stories, is a rhetorical framework and not an experimental finding. Empirical support comes from the story model of juror decision-making and from narrative comprehension research, where more coherent accounts are judged more credible.
theory.writer_takeaway: Keep the story's internal logic consistent; gaps and contradictions break belief faster than an implausible premise does.

theory.name: Narrative closure
theory.summary: Audiences want stories to resolve, and unresolved stories hold attention until they do.
theory.claim: Stories that withhold resolution create tension and curiosity. Resolution signals that the meaning is settled and releases attention.
theory.evidence_note: A concept from narrative theory and media studies with limited direct testing; the psychological need-for-closure literature is related but distinct.
theory.writer_takeaway: Withhold closure to hold attention through a section; close loops deliberately when you want the listener to settle.

theory.name: Zeigarnik effect
theory.summary: The claim that unfinished tasks are remembered better than finished ones.
theory.claim: Early studies reported that interrupted tasks were recalled more often than completed ones. The effect is widely cited to explain why open loops in stories and scripts hold attention.
theory.evidence_note: Replication is weak and inconsistent, and the effect as popularly stated is not reliably found; related findings on unfinished goals staying active have more support.
theory.writer_takeaway: Do not count on open loops to make content memorable; their attention-holding value is easier to defend than any memory benefit.
theory.source: Bluma Zeigarnik, Über das Behalten von erledigten und unerledigten Handlungen, Psychologische Forschung (1927)

theory.name: Expectation violation
theory.summary: Breaking what a listener expects captures attention and can make the moment more memorable.
theory.claim: Unexpected events trigger orienting and closer processing. Mild violations within an established pattern draw attention; large ones can disrupt or alarm.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in attention and memory research; effects depend on the size of the violation and the context.
theory.writer_takeaway: Establish a pattern first, then break it once at the moment you most need full attention.

theory.name: Event segmentation theory
theory.summary: People divide ongoing experience into discrete events, and the boundaries between events shape memory.
theory.claim: Perceivers keep a model of the current event and update it when predictions fail. Boundaries are moments of updating and tend to be well remembered, while content inside one event is bound together. Crossing a boundary can make material from the previous event harder to access.
theory.evidence_note: Segmentation and better memory for event boundaries are supported by behavioral and neuroimaging studies. The finding that crossing a boundary makes earlier material harder to access is less secure: it has replicated unevenly and appears mainly when memory is already under load. Its use to explain hypnotic amnesia is an extrapolation.
theory.writer_takeaway: Mark section changes clearly; content within a section binds together, and a strong boundary can help loosen access to what came before.

theory.name: Situation-model updating
theory.summary: Listeners build a mental model of a story's situation and update it as the story moves.
theory.claim: Readers track time, place, characters, goals and causes. A shift on any of these costs processing effort and forces an update of the model. Models include sensory detail as well as facts.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in reading research; dimensions vary in how closely readers track them.
theory.writer_takeaway: Change one dimension at a time when guiding imagery; too many shifts at once break the listener's picture.

theory.name: Moral exemplification
theory.summary: Stories teach values by showing characters rewarded or punished for what they do.
theory.claim: Audiences learn norms from seeing behavior and its consequences in narratives, much as in observational learning. A concrete exemplar carries more weight than an abstract statement of the rule.
theory.evidence_note: Builds on well-supported observational learning research; evidence for specific narrative effects on values is mixed.
theory.writer_takeaway: Show a character rewarded for the behavior you want rather than stating the rule.

theory.name: Cognitive load
theory.summary: Working memory has a small capacity, and tasks that demand more of it leave less for checking and evaluating.
theory.claim: Cognitive load theory holds that working memory can hold and process only a few new elements at once. Material that is complex, poorly organized or arriving in several streams consumes that capacity, and when load is high people learn less. The theory itself is about learning; that loaded people also evaluate messages less carefully is a separate finding from persuasion research, covered under distraction-induced persuasion and dual-process theory.
theory.evidence_note: The capacity limit is well established; the theory's finer distinctions between types of load are harder to measure and are debated in education research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Overload works by using up capacity, so the suggestion that follows must be short and simple enough to land with what is left.

theory.name: Working-memory interference
theory.summary: Two tasks that use the same mental resource, such as two verbal streams, disrupt each other more than tasks using different resources.
theory.claim: Working memory is modeled as several partly separate stores, including a verbal loop and a visuospatial store, under a shared executive. Tasks that compete for the same store interfere strongly; tasks that use different stores interfere less. Holding words in mind while hearing other words is a classic case of strong interference.
theory.evidence_note: The multi-component model and same-modality interference are robust and widely replicated.
theory.writer_takeaway: A counting or spelling task interferes most with verbal evaluation of the suggestions; a visual task leaves verbal processing freer.

theory.name: Attentional capture
theory.summary: Some events, such as sudden onsets or unexpected sounds, pull attention to themselves whatever the listener intends.
theory.claim: Attentional capture is the involuntary shift of attention to a stimulus because of its properties, such as abrupt onset, motion, loudness or personal relevance like one's own name. Capture can briefly override the current goal. How strongly it does so depends on what the person is set to look for.
theory.evidence_note: Capture by abrupt onsets is well replicated. Noticing one's own name in an unattended channel is also replicated, but only about a third of listeners do so in the classic studies. How far capture is truly independent of goals is still debated.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use sudden changes or the listener's name sparingly to pull drifting attention back, and expect the effect to be brief.

theory.name: Attentional blink
theory.summary: After noticing one target in a rapid stream, people often miss a second target that follows within about half a second.
theory.claim: When items arrive quickly in sequence, detecting one target briefly impairs detection of a second target arriving roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds later. A common explanation is that consolidating the first item into awareness takes time, though other accounts exist. Items inside the gap may still be partly processed without being reported.
theory.evidence_note: A robust laboratory effect with rapid visual and auditory streams; claims that it can be used to slip messages past awareness in ordinary speech go beyond the evidence.
theory.writer_takeaway: Ordinary speech is too slow for this to be a reliable way to hide suggestions; its practical relevance is mainly to fast visual material such as text flashes.

theory.name: Orienting response
theory.summary: A new or changed stimulus triggers an automatic turn of attention and brief alerting, which fades as the stimulus repeats.
theory.claim: The orienting response is the reflexive reaction to novelty: attention turns toward the change, and heart rate and arousal shift. Repetition of the same stimulus makes the response habituate. Any change in the stimulus restores it.
theory.evidence_note: A classic and well-supported finding in psychophysiology.
theory.writer_takeaway: Monotony lets orienting fade, which helps drift; a deliberate change re-engages attention. Decide which effect you want at each point.

theory.name: Prediction error
theory.summary: Learning and attention are driven by the gap between what was expected and what happened.
theory.claim: When an outcome differs from what was predicted, the difference is a prediction error. Errors draw attention and drive learning; fully predicted outcomes produce little new learning. Dopamine signals in the brain behave in a way that matches reward prediction error.
theory.evidence_note: Strongly supported in conditioning and neuroscience research, though how far one mechanism explains all learning is contested.
theory.writer_takeaway: A reward that surprises teaches more than one the listener saw coming; fully predictable rewards gradually stop strengthening anything.

theory.name: Predictive processing
theory.summary: A framework in which the brain constantly predicts its input, so perception is shaped by expectation as well as by the senses.
theory.claim: Predictive processing proposes that the brain generates predictions about incoming signals and updates mainly on mismatches. Strong prior expectations can shape what is perceived, especially when input is ambiguous or weak. Some authors use it to explain suggestion and placebo as expectations outweighing sensory evidence.
theory.evidence_note: Influential and broadly consistent with many findings, but as a general framework it is hard to test directly, and its application to hypnosis is largely theoretical.
theory.writer_takeaway: Faint or ambiguous sensations are easiest to reshape by expectation, so suggest sensations that are already uncertain rather than ones that contradict a clear signal.

theory.name: Processing fluency
theory.summary: Things that are easy to process feel more true, more familiar and more likeable.
theory.claim: Processing fluency is the subjective ease of perceiving or understanding something. People use that ease as a cue, judging fluent statements as more likely true and fluent things as more pleasant. Repetition, clear wording, rhyme and familiarity all raise fluency.
theory.evidence_note: The core effects, including the repetition-truth effect, are well replicated; some specific findings, such as rhyme-as-reason, rest on fewer studies.
theory.writer_takeaway: Simple, repeated, rhythmic wording makes a suggestion feel more true; hard wording invites scrutiny.

theory.name: Cognitive ease
theory.summary: A popular summary of fluency: when thinking feels easy, people relax their guard and accept more.
theory.claim: Cognitive ease names the felt state of easy processing. On this account, ease signals that all is well, so effortful checking is not engaged, while strain mobilizes it. It overlaps almost entirely with processing fluency.
theory.evidence_note: Rests on the fluency research; it is a popular framing rather than a separate construct, and some priming studies cited alongside it have failed to replicate.
theory.writer_takeaway: Treat this as processing fluency: keep the key suggestion easy to take in.

theory.name: Dual-process theory
theory.summary: Thinking runs on a fast, automatic mode and a slow, deliberate one, and influence often works through the fast one.
theory.claim: Dual-process theories divide cognition into fast, intuitive processes and slow, effortful ones that need working memory. Deliberate checking is limited and is skipped when people are distracted, tired or unmotivated. Persuasion models built on this predict that surface cues matter more when deliberate processing is low.
theory.evidence_note: Widely used and supported in broad outline, but the clean two-system division is criticized as an oversimplification.
theory.writer_takeaway: Surface cues such as authority, repetition and confidence carry more weight when the listener is not analyzing; the content itself matters more when they are.

theory.name: Cognitive dissonance
theory.summary: Holding conflicting beliefs, or acting against one's beliefs, is uncomfortable, and people often change beliefs to match what they did.
theory.claim: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort of inconsistency between cognitions, especially between action and attitude. People reduce it by changing the attitude, adding justifications, or discounting the conflict. The effect is strongest when the act feels freely chosen and is not explained by outside reward.
theory.evidence_note: A foundational and much-replicated idea, though some classic paradigms have had mixed recent replications and rival explanations such as self-perception exist.
theory.writer_takeaway: When the listener freely does a small thing, point it out; their wish to be consistent does more than added reasons would.

theory.name: Distraction-induced persuasion
theory.summary: Mild distraction during a message can increase agreement by blocking counterarguments, when the message is weak.
theory.claim: Distraction reduces the listener's ability to generate counterarguments. For weak or disagreeable messages this raises acceptance; for strong messages it can lower acceptance by blocking favorable thoughts too. Heavy distraction stops the message from being understood at all.
theory.evidence_note: Supported in persuasion research, with the reversal for strong messages part of the standard finding; effects are moderate and depend on the level of distraction.
theory.writer_takeaway: Distraction helps only if the suggestion is still understood; keep the main suggestion clear while occupying attention elsewhere.
theory.source: Richard E. Petty, Gary L. Wells and Timothy C. Brock, Distraction Can Enhance or Reduce Yielding to Propaganda: Thought Disruption Versus Effort Justification, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1976)

theory.name: Attentional tunneling
theory.summary: Under strong focus or stress, attention narrows onto one thing and other information drops out.
theory.claim: Attentional tunneling is the narrowing of attention onto a single source or task, with neglect of other cues. High arousal, high workload and compelling displays promote it. People in it often fail to notice even salient events outside the focus.
theory.evidence_note: Well documented in applied attention research such as aviation, and related to older findings that arousal narrows the range of cues used.
theory.writer_takeaway: Narrow focus on the voice or one sensation crowds out the room; describe the narrowing as it happens rather than demanding it.

theory.name: Task-set inertia
theory.summary: A mental task set lingers after a switch, so a sudden switch leaves a moment of slowed, less organized processing.
theory.claim: Switching between tasks has a cost: the previous task set persists for a time and interferes with the new one. Responses right after a switch are slower and more error-prone. Preparation time reduces this switch cost but does not remove it.
theory.evidence_note: Task-switch costs are robust, but they are measured as brief slowing on simple laboratory tasks, and the inertia account competes with other explanations of those costs. Whether a switch creates a window of heightened suggestibility has not been established.
theory.writer_takeaway: An abrupt switch can interrupt an expected response; if you put an instruction after it, keep the instruction short and clear. Any added persuasive effect from the timing is untested.
theory.source: Alan Allport, Elizabeth A. Styles and Shulan Hsieh, Shifting Intentional Set: Exploring the Dynamic Control of Tasks, Attention and Performance XV (1994)

theory.name: Pattern interruption
theory.summary: Practitioner term: breaking an automatic action midway leaves a moment of uncertainty that a suggestion can fill.
theory.claim: In hypnosis and NLP practice, interrupting an over-learned sequence such as a handshake is said to leave the person briefly without a next step and open to direction. This duplicates the device pattern interrupt and its rapid-induction variants. The research analogues are task-switch costs and the orienting response.
theory.evidence_note: Supported mainly by demonstration; the underlying switch-cost and orienting effects are real, but the size of any window of heightened suggestibility has not been measured.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; deliver the instruction immediately and keep it to one or two words.

theory.name: Hypnotic induction
theory.summary: The procedure that defines a hypnosis context; it adds a modest increase in response over the same suggestions given without it.
theory.claim: An induction is whatever opening procedure is presented as hypnosis, often relaxation and focusing suggestions. Research finds it raises responsiveness only modestly compared with the same suggestions given without one. Much of its effect appears to come from labeling the situation as hypnosis and the expectations that brings.
theory.evidence_note: Well studied; the modest added effect is consistent, and different induction styles, including alert ones, produce similar results.
theory.writer_takeaway: The induction's main job is to set expectation and focus; its specific content matters less than its credibility to the listener.

theory.name: Hypnotizability
theory.summary: A stable trait: people differ widely in how strongly they respond to hypnotic suggestions, and their ranking stays similar over years.
theory.claim: Hypnotizability is measured with standardized scales that give a series of suggestions and count the responses. Scores are spread across the population, with a minority highly responsive and a minority barely responsive. Scores are highly stable over long periods.
theory.evidence_note: Trait stability over decades is among the best-established findings in hypnosis research. Skills-training programs have reported sizeable gains in scale scores, but whether those gains reflect genuinely changed experience or compliance is contested.
theory.writer_takeaway: Write so that low responders still have a good experience; no-fail framing and covering all possibilities protect them.

theory.name: Hypnotic suggestibility
theory.summary: Responsiveness to suggestions given after a hypnotic induction; largely the same ability as responding without one.
theory.claim: Hypnotic suggestibility is the degree to which a person experiences suggested changes after an induction. It correlates strongly with responsiveness to the same suggestions given without induction. The induction adds a modest increment.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported; the strong correlation with nonhypnotic suggestibility is a central finding.
theory.writer_takeaway: Much of what a script does would work without the word hypnosis; the label mainly adds expectation.

theory.name: Nonhypnotic suggestibility
theory.summary: Responsiveness to imaginative suggestions given without any hypnotic induction.
theory.claim: People respond to suggestions for changes in movement, sensation and perception even when hypnosis is not mentioned. This imaginative suggestibility correlates strongly with hypnotic suggestibility. It shows that the capacity to respond lies mostly in the person and the suggestion, not the trance label.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported.
theory.writer_takeaway: Waking and conversational suggestion can work for responsive listeners; an announced induction is optional.

theory.name: Direct verbal suggestion
theory.summary: Plainly worded suggestions can produce real changes in perception, movement and experience in responsive people.
theory.claim: A verbal suggestion is a communication that invites a change in experience or behavior that feels involuntary. In responsive people, direct suggestions alter pain, perception and motor control, with measurable brain correlates. The change is felt as happening rather than being done.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in laboratory studies of highly hypnotizable participants.
theory.writer_takeaway: Plain direct suggestions are effective; they do not need disguising to work for responsive listeners.

theory.name: Indirect suggestion
theory.summary: The claim that implied, permissive suggestions work better than direct ones; research does not support a general advantage.
theory.claim: In the Ericksonian tradition, indirect suggestion conveys the response through implication, story or permission and is said to avoid resistance. Laboratory comparisons generally find indirect and direct wording produce similar responses. Indirect wording may suit some listeners or reduce the sense of being ordered.
theory.evidence_note: Controlled studies largely fail to find the claimed superiority; the advantage is mostly practitioner belief.
theory.writer_takeaway: Choose indirect or direct wording for tone and the listener's preference, not on the assumption that indirect is stronger.

theory.name: Response expectancy theory
theory.summary: Expecting a response helps produce it: believing something will happen can generate the experience directly.
theory.claim: Response expectancies are expectations about one's own automatic responses, such as pain relief or relaxation. The theory holds that such expectations are self-confirming and are a main cause of hypnotic and placebo effects. Changing the expectation changes the response.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported for placebo and hypnosis; expectancy explains a substantial share, but not all, of the variation in hypnotic response.
theory.writer_takeaway: Tell the listener specifically what they will experience, and give early easy successes that confirm the expectation.

theory.name: Cold control theory
theory.summary: Hypnotic responses are intended actions the person does not recognize as intended, so they feel involuntary.
theory.claim: Cold control theory says hypnotic response uses normal executive control but lacks the higher-order thought that one is intending it. The action happens; the awareness of willing it is missing. Highly hypnotizable people are proposed to be good at this selective lack of awareness.
theory.evidence_note: A cognitive theory with some supporting experiments; it is one of several competing accounts.
theory.writer_takeaway: Describe responses as happening by themselves; drawing attention to doing them works against the effect.

theory.name: Higher-order thought theory
theory.summary: A theory of consciousness: a mental state is conscious when one is aware of being in it.
theory.claim: Higher-order thought theory holds that a state becomes conscious when accompanied by a thought about that state. Applied to hypnosis, it underlies accounts in which suggested actions are performed without awareness of intending them. It is a general theory of consciousness, not a hypnosis theory as such.
theory.evidence_note: A respected but contested philosophical position; its application to hypnosis is developed mainly through cold control theory.
theory.writer_takeaway: Treat it as background for cold control: the response is real, and the sense of doing it is what the suggestion removes.

theory.name: Dissociated control theory
theory.summary: Suggestion is said to trigger behavior directly, bypassing ordinary executive control.
theory.claim: Dissociated control theory proposes that in hypnosis, subsystems of control can be set off directly by suggestion with weaker top-down oversight. This would explain why responses feel effortless and automatic. It differs from accounts in which only the awareness of control is altered.
theory.evidence_note: Influential but with mixed support; some predictions, such as reduced executive involvement, have not held up consistently.
theory.writer_takeaway: Same practical advice as other automaticity accounts: frame responses as happening on their own.

theory.name: Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis
theory.summary: Hypnotic behavior is explained by ordinary social and cognitive factors such as expectation, motivation, attitude and role-taking.
theory.claim: Sociocognitive theory rejects a special trance state. Responses arise from people's beliefs about hypnosis, their motivation to respond, how they interpret suggestions, and the role they adopt. The experiences can still be genuine and felt as involuntary.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported on many points, especially the roles of expectancy and context; the state versus nonstate debate has largely converged on a mix of both.
theory.writer_takeaway: What the listener believes hypnosis is, and wants it to be, drives the response; framing, pre-talk and role matter as much as technique.
theory.source: Nicholas P. Spanos, Hypnotic Behavior: A Social-Psychological Interpretation of Amnesia, Analgesia, and ‘Trance Logic’, Behavioral and Brain Sciences (1986)

theory.name: Trance logic
theory.summary: The proposed tolerance, in hypnosis, of logical contradictions, such as seeing a hallucinated person alongside the real one.
theory.claim: Trance logic was proposed as a hallmark of hypnosis: subjects accept contradictions between suggested and real perceptions without distress. An example is reporting that a hallucinated person is transparent. Later work found simulators and nonhypnotized people often respond similarly.
theory.evidence_note: Not established as a distinct marker of hypnosis; studies with control groups weakened the original claim.
theory.writer_takeaway: Do not rely on listeners ignoring contradictions; keep suggested perceptions consistent where it matters.
theory.source: Martin T. Orne, The Nature of Hypnosis: Artifact and Essence, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology (1959)

theory.name: Posthypnotic suggestion
theory.summary: Suggestions given during hypnosis can produce responses after it ends, often to a cue and sometimes without awareness of why.
theory.claim: Posthypnotic suggestions specify a later response tied to a cue. Responsive people often carry them out, sometimes with amnesia for the suggestion and with invented reasons for their behavior. The effects tend to weaken over time without reinforcement.
theory.evidence_note: Well documented in laboratory research with responsive people; long-lasting effects without rehearsal are less supported than practitioner claims suggest.
theory.writer_takeaway: Tie the response to a clear cue, rehearse it in session, and expect it to need refreshing.

theory.name: Abreaction
theory.summary: The release of strong emotion when recalling a painful memory, once thought to be curative in itself.
theory.claim: Abreaction is the intense emotional discharge that can accompany recalling or reliving distressing events. Early psychodynamic theory held that this discharge cures symptoms. Later practice treats it as something that may happen and must be handled, not a goal in itself.
theory.evidence_note: The claim that catharsis cures is poorly supported; emotional release without further processing can leave people worse off.
theory.writer_takeaway: Regression and revivification can surface strong emotion unexpectedly; include a way to stop, settle and reorient.

theory.name: Hypnotic amnesia
theory.summary: Responsive people can fail to recall events from hypnosis when told to forget, and recall returns when the suggestion is cancelled.
theory.claim: Suggested amnesia is a reversible failure to retrieve, not erasure: the material comes back on a prearranged cue. It occurs in a minority of people and is often partial. Forgotten material can still influence behavior.
theory.evidence_note: Well documented in laboratory studies; spontaneous complete amnesia is rarer than popular depictions suggest.
theory.writer_takeaway: Expect amnesia suggestions to be partial for most listeners, and frame them so partial forgetting still counts.

theory.name: Ericksonian confusion technique
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: deliberately confusing talk followed by a clear suggestion the listener grabs for relief.
theory.claim: Erickson described piling up ambiguous, contradictory or irrelevant statements until the listener wants clarity, then giving a simple suggestion that resolves the confusion. This duplicates the device confusion technique and its variants. The proposed mechanism is the drive to escape uncertainty.
theory.evidence_note: Supported mainly by case reports and practice; laboratory work on the related disrupt-then-reframe effect gives indirect support.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; the relief only works if the closing instruction is truly simple.

theory.name: Confusion-restructuring
theory.summary: Practitioner term: confuse first, then supply a new frame while the listener is searching for meaning.
theory.claim: Confusion-restructuring pairs a disruption of understanding with an immediate new interpretation. The listener, wanting coherence, takes the offered frame. It overlaps with disrupt-then-reframe in persuasion research and with the confusion technique.
theory.evidence_note: Disrupt-then-reframe has laboratory and field support, almost all of it from brief sales and donation requests; whether it carries over to a hypnotic script has not been tested. The practitioner version is unmeasured.
theory.writer_takeaway: Treat it as confusion technique or disrupt then reframe; the new frame must come immediately after the disruption.

theory.name: Milton Model
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: NLP's catalog of Erickson's artfully vague language patterns, listed here as separate devices.
theory.claim: The Milton Model collects language patterns observed in Erickson's work: nominalizations, unspecified verbs, presuppositions, embedded commands, binds and ambiguities. Vagueness lets the listener fill in content from their own experience. Here it is a collection, not a device; each pattern has its own entry.
theory.evidence_note: The patterns are real linguistic forms; claims that the set is especially hypnotic have little controlled evidence.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the individual device entries; vagueness should leave room for the listener, not hide what is being suggested.
theory.source: Bandler & Grinder (1975), Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, Vol. 1

theory.name: Meta Model
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: NLP's set of questions for recovering the specific detail behind vague language.
theory.claim: The Meta Model sorts vague language into deletions, generalizations and distortions and pairs each form with a question that recovers the specifics. It was built as a therapy tool, loosely on transformational grammar, and came first; the Milton Model was later presented as its inverse, using the same forms deliberately. It names the forms listed here under artful vagueness.
theory.evidence_note: Its categories are drawn from linguistics; the therapeutic claims are not well tested.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use it as an editing checklist: each vague form you keep should be kept on purpose.
theory.source: Bandler & Grinder (1975), The Structure of Magic, Vol. 1

theory.name: Pacing and leading
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: state verifiable things first, then a suggestion that borrows their credibility; duplicates devices.
theory.claim: Pacing and leading means matching the listener's current experience with true statements before introducing a new one. The accepted statements are said to build momentum that carries the suggestion. This duplicates the devices pacing and pacing and leading.
theory.evidence_note: Plausibly related to fluency and consistency effects; the specific sequence has not been well tested in controlled research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; paced statements must actually be true for the listener or they cost credibility.

theory.name: Embedded commands
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary for commands placed inside longer sentences; duplicates the device.
theory.claim: Embedded commands are imperative phrases placed inside a longer sentence, often marked by tone. Practitioners claim they bypass conscious evaluation. This duplicates the devices embedded command and analog marking.
theory.evidence_note: Controlled evidence that embedded commands act outside awareness is weak; any effect is likely through ordinary suggestion and repetition.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; do not expect a hidden command to work where an open one would not.

theory.name: Conversational hypnosis
theory.summary: Practitioner term for inducing trance within ordinary-sounding talk, without an announced induction.
theory.claim: Conversational hypnosis refers to using Ericksonian language patterns in everyday conversation to produce absorption and responsiveness. It duplicates the conversational and unannounced induction devices. Commercial courses often overstate its power to influence unwilling people.
theory.evidence_note: Research on nonhypnotic suggestibility shows suggestion can work without the label; claims of covert control over others are not supported.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the induction device entries; absorption still depends on the listener's engagement.

theory.name: Utilization
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: whatever the listener brings or does is accepted and used in service of the goal.
theory.claim: Erickson's utilization principle treats the listener's behavior, beliefs, resistance and surroundings as material for the process rather than obstacles. Distractions become deepeners and resistance becomes participation. It duplicates the device utilization and its variants.
theory.evidence_note: A practice principle supported by clinical reports rather than controlled tests.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; name likely distractions in advance and give each one a role.

theory.name: Therapeutic double bind
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: offering choices that all lead to the desired response; duplicates the double bind device.
theory.claim: The therapeutic double bind gives alternatives that all lead to the intended outcome, such as going into trance now or in a moment. It borrows the term from family-systems theory, where a double bind was a harmful contradictory demand. It is listed here as double bind with variants.
theory.evidence_note: The clinical form is practitioner-reported; controlled evidence that these constrained choices improve hypnotic responding is lacking. Studies of choice in other contexts offer indirect support at most.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; a bind is easy to see through when the options are obviously equivalent.

theory.name: Interspersal technique
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: suggestion words scattered through unrelated talk; duplicates the device.
theory.claim: Interspersal places suggestion words or phrases within a narrative on another topic, often marked by voice. Erickson described it for pain relief. It duplicates the devices interspersal and analog marking.
theory.evidence_note: Clinical reports only; any effect is likely through repetition and priming rather than concealment.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entry; scattered words work best when they also make sense in the surrounding story.

theory.name: Metaphorical suggestion
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: suggestions carried by a story whose structure mirrors the wanted change; duplicates the metaphor device.
theory.claim: Metaphorical suggestion delivers the target response through a story or image that parallels it, leaving the listener to draw the connection. It is said to avoid resistance and engage imagination. It is listed here as metaphor and its variants.
theory.evidence_note: Research on narrative transportation supports story-based persuasion in general; the specific therapeutic claims rest on practice.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; the parallel should be close enough that the listener feels it without being told.

theory.name: Analog marking
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: setting words apart by tone or pause so they form a second message; duplicates the device.
theory.claim: Analog marking uses nonverbal cues such as tone, pause or volume to set particular words apart. The marked words are said to be processed as a separate message. It is listed here as analog marking.
theory.evidence_note: Marking clearly draws attention to words; claims that the second message works outside awareness lack controlled support.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entry; in a written script, mark the words with stage directions so the performer knows to set them apart.

theory.name: Anchoring (NLP)
theory.summary: Practitioner vocabulary: tying a state to a cue at its peak, NLP's version of conditioning; duplicates devices.
theory.claim: NLP anchoring captures an intense state and associates it with a touch, word or image, so the cue later recalls the state. Practitioners claim a single pairing can be enough. It is a form of classical conditioning and duplicates the devices anchoring and trigger installation.
theory.evidence_note: Conditioning itself is well established; NLP's claims of reliable one-trial anchors are not supported by controlled research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the device entries; rehearse the cue several times rather than relying on one pairing.

theory.name: Reframing
theory.summary: Changing the meaning given to an experience changes how people feel about it and respond to it.
theory.claim: Reframing places the same facts in a different frame of meaning or context. A sensation, behavior or event judged one way can be judged differently under a new frame. Related research on cognitive reappraisal shows that reinterpreting a situation alters the emotional response.
theory.evidence_note: Reappraisal is well supported in emotion research; therapy-specific reframing techniques have less direct evidence.
theory.writer_takeaway: Offer the new meaning as a natural reading of what the listener already feels, not as a correction.

theory.name: Rapport matching
theory.summary: People unconsciously mimic one another, and being mimicked can increase liking; NLP built a deliberate matching technique on this.
theory.claim: Spontaneous mimicry of posture, gesture and speech occurs in ordinary interaction and goes with smoother rapport and liking. NLP turned this into deliberate matching of breathing, tempo and language. Deliberate matching that is noticed can backfire.
theory.evidence_note: Mimicry effects are documented, though some replicate less strongly than first reported; NLP's specific claims have less support.
theory.writer_takeaway: In recorded audio, match the pace and breathing the listener is likely to have, and slow gradually rather than abruptly.

theory.name: Social proof
theory.summary: People use what others are doing as evidence of what is correct, especially when unsure.
theory.claim: When a situation is ambiguous, people look to the behavior of others to decide what to believe or do. The effect is stronger when the others seem similar to the observer and when many of them act the same way.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in lab and field work on conformity and norm-based messaging. Effects are often modest and depend on the reference group seeming credible and similar.
theory.writer_takeaway: Describe other listeners like this one already doing or feeling the target response, and make them sound similar to the listener rather than generic.

theory.name: Informational social influence
theory.summary: Accepting other people's judgments as real information about how things are.
theory.claim: People conform because they believe others know something they do not. This kind of influence changes private belief, not only public behavior, and is strongest when the task is hard or the situation unclear.
theory.evidence_note: A long-standing, well-replicated distinction in social psychology, though in practice it is usually mixed with normative influence and hard to separate cleanly.
theory.writer_takeaway: A listener's uncertainty about what trance feels like is an opening: say what others typically experience, and that report becomes the template for their own experience.

theory.name: Normative social influence
theory.summary: Going along with others to be accepted or to avoid disapproval.
theory.claim: People conform to fit in with a group they value, even when they privately disagree. It changes outward behavior more than private belief and depends on the group being present or salient.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported; the Asch line-judgment studies are the standard example, with conformity rates varying by culture, era and group setup.
theory.writer_takeaway: Signal belonging and approval for the target response, but expect this to produce compliance more readily than conviction; pair it with devices that build private belief.

theory.name: Descriptive norms
theory.summary: Beliefs about what most people actually do.
theory.claim: A descriptive norm is a perception of common behavior. Making one salient pulls behavior toward it, including in the wrong direction when a message stresses how many people do the unwanted thing.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported by field studies on littering and energy use; effects are reliable but usually small.
theory.writer_takeaway: State the target response as what people typically do, and never stress how often listeners fail or resist, since that makes failure the norm.

theory.name: Injunctive norms
theory.summary: Beliefs about what other people approve or disapprove of.
theory.claim: An injunctive norm concerns what is approved rather than what is common. It works through anticipated approval or disapproval and can offset an unhelpful descriptive norm.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in the same research line as descriptive norms; strongest when the norm is made salient at the moment of choice.
theory.writer_takeaway: Where the target behavior is not yet common, make the approval of it explicit instead of claiming that everyone does it.

theory.name: Reciprocity principle
theory.summary: People feel obliged to return favors, gifts and concessions.
theory.claim: Receiving something creates a felt debt that people want to repay, often with more than they received. The norm is found across cultures and covers concessions as well as gifts.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported as a social norm; specific sales applications vary in strength, and the obligation weakens when the gift looks like a tactic.
theory.writer_takeaway: Give something first, such as comfort, praise or a pleasant experience, before asking, and keep the gift from feeling transactional.

theory.name: Commitment and consistency
theory.summary: Once people take a stand, they feel pressure to act in line with it.
theory.claim: People want their words, actions and self-image to agree with each other. Commitments that are active, public, effortful and freely chosen bind most strongly.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported through consistency theories and commitment research; effect size depends heavily on whether the commitment felt freely chosen.
theory.writer_takeaway: Collect small, explicit, self-chosen agreements early and refer back to them later; framing each as the listener's own choice is what makes it hold.

theory.name: Authority principle
theory.summary: People defer to those who appear to have legitimate expertise or power.
theory.claim: Signals of authority such as titles, confident tone and expert framing increase both compliance and belief, often without the listener checking whether the authority is relevant.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in general; Milgram's obedience studies are the famous case, though how to interpret them is still argued over.
theory.writer_takeaway: Establish credible competence early and speak with calm certainty; irrelevant or borrowed authority works less well on listeners who notice it.

theory.name: Liking principle
theory.summary: People are more easily persuaded by those they like.
theory.claim: Liking is raised by similarity, compliments, familiarity, cooperation and attractiveness, and greater liking makes requests and claims easier to accept.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported overall; individual components such as similarity and compliments have solid but variable evidence.
theory.writer_takeaway: Build warmth and similarity before the main suggestions; a voice the listener likes earns more than a voice that is merely competent.

theory.name: Scarcity principle
theory.summary: Things seem more valuable when rare, limited or about to be lost.
theory.claim: Opportunities look more desirable as they become less available. Losing access is felt more strongly than gaining it, and things that have just become scarce are wanted most.
theory.evidence_note: Supported, but results in consumer research are mixed and depend on the scarcity seeming real; partly explained by reactance and loss aversion.
theory.writer_takeaway: Present the state or experience as special and not always available, and avoid scarcity claims the listener can see through.

theory.name: Unity principle
theory.summary: People yield more to someone they see as part of their own group.
theory.claim: Shared identity, not just similarity, increases influence. Being 'of' the same family, place or group makes the influencer's interests feel like one's own.
theory.evidence_note: Proposed later as an addition to the original six principles; it draws on solid in-group research but has had less direct testing as a distinct principle.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use 'we' and shared-identity language that places speaker and listener in one group, rather than only stressing that they are alike.

theory.name: Foot-in-the-door
theory.summary: Agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a larger one.
theory.claim: Agreeing to a small request raises the chance of agreeing to a larger, related one later. The usual explanation is self-perception: the first act of compliance shifts the person's self-image toward being someone who agrees or helps. A wish to stay consistent with the earlier act is the main rival account.
theory.evidence_note: Replicated many times, but the average effect is small and inconsistent; it works best when the first act is freely chosen and the two requests are related.
theory.writer_takeaway: Open with easy, nearly certain requests and make each feel freely chosen, so it changes self-image and not just behavior.

theory.name: Door-in-the-face
theory.summary: Refusing a large request makes people more likely to accept a smaller one that follows.
theory.claim: After a large request is refused, a smaller one feels like a concession, and people reciprocate by agreeing. The contrast also makes the second request look smaller.
theory.evidence_note: Replicated with a modest average effect; it depends on the same person making both requests with little delay between them.
theory.writer_takeaway: Ask for more than you need first, then retreat to the real request as a visible concession.

theory.name: Low-ball
theory.summary: Getting agreement first and then raising the cost often keeps the agreement.
theory.claim: Once people commit to a decision, they tend to stay with it even after the terms get worse, because the commitment has generated its own supporting reasons.
theory.evidence_note: Replicated in lab and field settings; it runs on commitment and weakens when the change in terms feels deceptive.
theory.writer_takeaway: Secure agreement to the easy version, then add requirements; listeners who notice the move tend to resent it.

theory.name: Pre-suasion
theory.summary: What a person is attending to just before a message shapes how they receive it.
theory.claim: Directing attention to a concept before a request makes related responses more likely. The moment before the message is treated as part of the message.
theory.evidence_note: A popular synthesis of attention and priming research; some of the behavioral priming findings it relies on have not replicated well.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use the title, description and opening lines to point attention at the ideas that will make later suggestions feel natural.

theory.name: Illusory truth effect
theory.summary: Statements heard before feel more true than new ones.
theory.claim: Repetition makes a statement easier to process, and people read that ease as a sign of truth. The effect occurs even for statements people could know are false.
theory.evidence_note: Robust and well replicated; relevant prior knowledge reduces the effect but does not remove it.
theory.writer_takeaway: Repeat the key beliefs across the script in recognizable wording so that by the end they feel familiar and therefore true.

theory.name: Mere-exposure effect
theory.summary: Repeated exposure to something makes people like it more.
theory.claim: Simple repeated exposure, without any reward, raises liking for a stimulus. The effect appears even when the exposures are not consciously noticed.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported, though the gain levels off and can reverse with heavy repetition or boredom.
theory.writer_takeaway: Repeated listening and recurring phrases build fondness for the voice and its words; vary enough to avoid tedium.

theory.name: Familiarity heuristic
theory.summary: People treat what feels familiar as safer, better or more correct.
theory.claim: Familiarity is used as a shortcut for judging truth, safety and quality. The feeling of familiarity is easily credited to the content being right.
theory.evidence_note: Supported indirectly by fluency and mere-exposure research; the term itself is used loosely across studies.
theory.writer_takeaway: Make new ideas feel familiar by tying them to experiences the listener already knows before asking them to accept those ideas.

theory.name: Availability heuristic
theory.summary: People judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.
theory.claim: Events that are easy to recall or imagine are judged more frequent or probable. Vivid, recent or emotional examples therefore count for more than they should.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported; one of the core heuristics in judgment and decision research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Make the target outcome vivid and easy to picture so it seems likely; a vague promise weighs less than a concrete image.

theory.name: Priming
theory.summary: Exposure to one stimulus changes how a later stimulus is processed.
theory.claim: Activating a concept makes related concepts quicker to come to mind and more likely to shape interpretation of what follows.
theory.evidence_note: Semantic and repetition priming are robust; many social or behavioral priming findings have failed to replicate, so claims that a single word changes behavior deserve doubt.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use word choice to make target ideas easy to reach, but do not expect a lone primed word to carry a suggestion by itself.

theory.name: Affective priming
theory.summary: A brief emotional stimulus colors how the next thing is evaluated.
theory.claim: A positive or negative prime speeds evaluation of a following target with the same valence and can bias how that target is judged.
theory.evidence_note: Well documented in reaction-time tasks; effects on real-world attitudes are smaller and less certain.
theory.writer_takeaway: Put warm, pleasant wording directly before the ideas you want the listener to view favorably.
theory.source: Russell H. Fazio, David M. Sanbonmatsu, Martha C. Powell and Frank R. Kardes, On the Automatic Activation of Attitudes, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1986)

theory.name: Evaluative conditioning
theory.summary: Pairing a neutral thing with something liked or disliked changes how much it is liked.
theory.claim: When a stimulus is repeatedly paired with a positive or negative one, it takes on that valence. This changes liking rather than expectation, and it can persist after the pairings stop.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported by meta-analysis with moderate effects; whether awareness of the pairing is needed remains debated.
theory.writer_takeaway: Pair target words, states or behaviors repeatedly with pleasant experience so they become liked for their own sake.

theory.name: Spreading activation
theory.summary: Activating one concept in memory partly activates related concepts.
theory.claim: Memory is modeled as a network of linked concepts. Activation spreads along the links, so mentioning one idea makes its associates more available.
theory.evidence_note: An influential model that accounts for much semantic priming data; it is a framework rather than a single tested claim.
theory.writer_takeaway: Choose words and images whose associations point toward the goal, since every term brings its neighbors to mind as well.

theory.name: Source-monitoring error
theory.summary: Misremembering where a memory or idea came from.
theory.claim: People infer the source of a memory from its features. Imagined events, suggestions and real experiences can be confused, especially when the content is vivid and source cues are weak.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported framework that accounts for many false-memory and misattribution findings.
theory.writer_takeaway: Ideas that are vivid and phrased in the listener's own voice can later feel self-generated; that is how suggested beliefs come to feel owned.

theory.name: Misinformation effect
theory.summary: Misleading information given after an event distorts memory of the event.
theory.claim: Information supplied after an experience can be absorbed into the memory of it, changing the details people later report.
theory.evidence_note: Robust and widely replicated; whether the original memory is replaced or just harder to retrieve is debated.
theory.writer_takeaway: Telling the listener what they 'just felt' shapes what they remember feeling; use it for ratification and take care with claims about past events.

theory.name: Continued influence effect
theory.summary: Corrected misinformation keeps shaping reasoning after the correction.
theory.claim: Even after accepting a retraction, people keep relying on the false information, especially when it filled a gap in a causal story. Corrections work better when they supply an alternative explanation.
theory.evidence_note: Well replicated; giving an alternative account reduces the effect but rarely removes it.
theory.writer_takeaway: When replacing a belief, give a new explanation that fills the gap instead of only denying the old one.
theory.source: Hollyn M. Johnson and Colleen M. Seifert, Sources of the Continued Influence Effect: When Misinformation in Memory Affects Later Inferences, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition (1994)

theory.name: Sleeper effect
theory.summary: A message from a discounted source can gain influence over time.
theory.claim: When a persuasive message arrives with a cue that discounts it, its impact can rise later as the cue is forgotten while the message is remembered.
theory.evidence_note: Contested for decades; it appears only under specific conditions and is not a general rule.
theory.writer_takeaway: Do not rely on it, but note that disclaimers such as 'it is only a fantasy' may fade from memory faster than the content they frame.

theory.name: Social learning theory
theory.summary: People learn behavior by watching others and the consequences those others receive.
theory.claim: Learning happens through observation and imitation, not only through direct reinforcement. Attention, retention, ability to reproduce and motivation govern whether a modeled behavior is adopted.
theory.evidence_note: A broad, well-established framework; observational learning itself has strong support.
theory.writer_takeaway: Show a model performing the target response and being rewarded for it, ideally a model the listener identifies with.

theory.name: Algorithmic amplification
theory.summary: Recommendation systems can push some content far beyond the audience it would reach on its own.
theory.claim: Platforms that rank content by predicted engagement send certain material to wider audiences, which shapes what ideas seem common and familiar to viewers.
theory.evidence_note: Partly documented, but strong claims, for example about radicalization pathways, are disputed and evidence varies by platform.
theory.writer_takeaway: Titles, tags and descriptions decide who arrives and with what expectations; this acts on distribution, not on the script text.

theory.name: Engagement-based selection bias
theory.summary: Content that provokes strong reactions is over-represented in what people see.
theory.claim: When selection favors attention-grabbing material, people encounter a skewed sample, which distorts their beliefs about what is typical.
theory.evidence_note: Not an established named effect; the label describes an inference from how ranked feeds are built, and it overlaps heavily with algorithmic amplification. There is some empirical support that ranked feeds over-represent provocative material, but how much this distorts beliefs about what is typical remains uncertain.
theory.writer_takeaway: Listeners who arrive through feeds may hold exaggerated expectations; manage them with explicit expectation setting early in the script.

theory.name: Psychological reactance
theory.summary: When people feel their freedom is threatened, they push back to restore it.
theory.claim: A perceived threat to freedom of choice creates a motivation to resist the pressure, sometimes by doing the opposite of what was asked.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported; forceful, controlling language reliably raises reactance across many studies.
theory.writer_takeaway: Use permissive wording and explicit statements of freedom to lower reactance; heavy commands invite pushback from many listeners.

theory.name: Counterarguing
theory.summary: Producing objections to a message while hearing it.
theory.claim: Listeners actively generate thoughts against a message, and the number and strength of those counterarguments predict how little they are persuaded.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported in cognitive-response research on persuasion.
theory.writer_takeaway: Reduce counterarguing by occupying attention, answering objections in advance, or using indirect forms that give nothing to argue with.

theory.name: Epistemic vigilance
theory.summary: People have built-in ways of checking whether to trust what they are told.
theory.claim: Humans evaluate both the source and the content of what they hear to avoid being misled. This filtering is what keeps communication useful even though deception is possible.
theory.evidence_note: A theoretical framework with supporting evidence from developmental and reasoning research rather than a single measured effect.
theory.writer_takeaway: Claims that contradict obvious experience trigger checking, while plain truths pass easily; lead with what the listener can verify.

theory.name: Persuasion Knowledge Model
theory.summary: What people know about persuasion tactics shapes how they respond to them.
theory.claim: When people recognize a message as a persuasion attempt, they reinterpret it and may resist. This knowledge builds over a lifetime of exposure to tactics.
theory.evidence_note: Influential framework with good support in consumer research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Experienced listeners recognize techniques; naming a technique openly can build trust or invite resistance depending on how it is framed.

theory.name: Persuasion resistance
theory.summary: The general set of ways people avoid being persuaded.
