theory.claim: Resistance includes reactance, distrust, scrutiny and inertia. Persuaders can either lower these sources of resistance or increase the pull of the message, and the two approaches work differently.
theory.evidence_note: A synthesis built on well-supported components rather than one tested effect.
theory.writer_takeaway: Plan for resistance directly: lower its sources instead of only adding pressure.

theory.name: Inoculation theory
theory.summary: Exposure to weakened counterarguments builds resistance to later persuasion.
theory.claim: Like a vaccine, a mild attack on a belief together with its refutation prepares people to resist stronger attacks later.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported, including recent work on prebunking misinformation.
theory.writer_takeaway: Raise likely doubts early in a mild form and resolve them, so that later doubts feel already answered.
theory.source: William J. McGuire, Inducing Resistance to Persuasion: Some Contemporary Approaches, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology (1964)

theory.name: Forewarning effect
theory.summary: Warning people that a persuasion attempt is coming makes them resist it more.
theory.claim: Warning people that they are about to be persuaded usually reduces the message's impact. A warning about the topic and position lets them prepare counterarguments, and works better with a delay; a warning about persuasive intent raises resistance at once. On topics people care little about, a warning can instead shift them toward the expected message in advance.
theory.evidence_note: Supported, though effects vary with how involved the person is and the topic.
theory.writer_takeaway: Announcing persuasive intent can backfire; frame what follows as an experience to have rather than an argument to accept.
theory.source: Jonathan L. Freedman and David O. Sears, Warning, Distraction, and Resistance to Influence, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1965)

theory.name: Counter-attitudinal processing
theory.summary: How people process messages that oppose their existing attitudes.
theory.claim: Messages against a person's attitude are scrutinized harder and judged weaker, while agreeable messages pass with less checking.
theory.evidence_note: The core finding, that opposing arguments are scrutinized longer and rated weaker than agreeable ones, is well supported under the names disconfirmation bias and biased assimilation. The stronger claim that mixed evidence pushes attitudes further apart has replicated less consistently. The name used here is not the literature's standard term.
theory.writer_takeaway: Start from points the listener already accepts and move toward contested ones gradually.

theory.name: Motivated reasoning
theory.summary: People reason toward the conclusions they want to reach.
theory.claim: Wanting a conclusion affects which evidence people seek and how they judge it, within the limits of what they can justify as reasonable.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported; its role in political belief is sometimes overstated relative to the simpler effect of prior beliefs.
theory.writer_takeaway: Tie target beliefs to what the listener already wants; their desire supplies reasons the script does not have to state.

theory.name: Confirmation bias
theory.summary: Favoring information that fits what one already believes.
theory.claim: People seek, interpret and remember evidence in ways that support their existing beliefs.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported, though the term covers several distinct processes that are studied separately.
theory.writer_takeaway: Once a belief is planted, invite the listener to watch for signs of it; they will tend to find them.

theory.name: Belief perseverance
theory.summary: Beliefs persist even after the evidence for them is discredited.
theory.claim: Once people have explained a belief to themselves, the explanation keeps it alive after the original evidence is withdrawn.
theory.evidence_note: Well replicated; asking people to explain the opposite reduces it.
theory.writer_takeaway: Have the listener produce their own reasons for a belief; self-generated explanations make it last.

theory.name: Attitude bolstering
theory.summary: Defending a belief by recalling reasons that support it.
theory.claim: When challenged, people bring supporting thoughts to mind instead of rebutting the challenge directly.
theory.evidence_note: Identified as a common resistance strategy in self-report studies; less studied than counterarguing.
theory.writer_takeaway: A direct challenge may prompt listeners to rehearse reasons for their existing belief. Link the suggestion to a belief they already hold.
theory.source: Robert P. Abelson, Modes of Resolution of Belief Dilemmas, Journal of Conflict Resolution (1959)

theory.name: Source derogation
theory.summary: Resisting a message by discrediting the person who delivers it.
theory.claim: Instead of engaging with the content, people question the credibility or motives of the speaker.
theory.evidence_note: Supported as a common resistance strategy in self-report research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Protect the speaker's credibility: avoid claims that make the voice seem uninformed or plainly manipulative.
theory.source: Julia Z. Jacks and Kimberly A. Cameron, Strategies for Resisting Persuasion, Basic and Applied Social Psychology (2003)

theory.name: Metacognitive monitoring
theory.summary: Watching and judging one's own thinking.
theory.claim: People track their own mental states, such as confidence and ease of processing, and use those signals to make judgments about what is true or known.
theory.evidence_note: Well established in memory and learning research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Point out signs of a response that listeners can notice, then offer an interpretation of what those signs mean; that interpretation can shape how they judge the experience.

theory.name: Cognitive decoupling
theory.summary: Keeping an imagined possibility separate from what one believes is real.
theory.claim: Hypothetical thinking and engagement with fiction require holding a representation apart from one's model of reality, so it can be explored without being accepted as fact.
theory.evidence_note: A theoretical construct introduced to explain pretend play and later adopted in dual-process accounts of reasoning; its operation is inferred from behavior in pretense and reasoning tasks. The separation is not complete: content encountered in fiction can still shift real-world beliefs.
theory.writer_takeaway: Fiction and as-if frames rely on decoupling: listeners will engage with content they would reject as a factual claim.

theory.name: Conditional regard
theory.summary: Approval given only when someone behaves as wanted, which makes their sense of worth depend on meeting the condition.
theory.claim: When a parent, partner or authority gives warmth only after compliance and withdraws it after failure, the recipient learns that their worth is contingent. This tends to produce compliance driven by internal pressure (guilt, anxiety to earn approval) rather than by choice. The pattern produces short-term conformity alongside resentment and fragile self-esteem.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by a body of developmental studies on parental conditional regard, mostly self-report and correlational; the link to introjected (pressured) motivation replicates fairly consistently across cultures.
theory.writer_takeaway: Praise that is explicitly tied to obedience works as leverage but carries pressure, not warmth; know which you are writing. In consensual scripts, pair contingent approval with unconditional reassurance in aftercare so the contingency stays inside the fiction.

theory.name: Attachment theory
theory.summary: People form bonds to caregivers that act as a secure base, and the quality of those bonds shapes later closeness and dependence.
theory.claim: Humans have an attachment system that seeks proximity to a protective figure under threat. Repeated experience with caregivers produces working models (secure, anxious, avoidant) that carry into adult relationships. Threat activates the system, so distress tends to increase clinging to whoever is available as a source of safety.
theory.evidence_note: Core claims about infant attachment and adult attachment styles are well supported, though styles measured by self-report are less stable than popular accounts suggest, and attachment-style typing is heavily over-popularized.
theory.writer_takeaway: Distress can prompt people to seek comfort from trusted others; this may help explain why comfort following tension can strengthen a bond. Whether a recorded voice can become an attachment figure in the technical sense is untested. Use the secure-base pattern for wellbeing scripts and treat its use to cultivate dependency as a coercive move.

theory.name: Rejection sensitivity
theory.summary: Some people anxiously expect rejection, notice cues of it quickly and react strongly, often by trying harder to please.
theory.claim: Rejection sensitivity is a disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive and overreact to rejection. Highly sensitive people may accommodate others more to avoid disapproval, or respond with hostility. The trait varies between people and is shaped by past experiences of rejection.
theory.evidence_note: Measured with a standard questionnaire and supported by many correlational and some experimental studies; effects are moderate and depend on context.
theory.writer_takeaway: Threats of withdrawn approval or abandonment land much harder on some listeners than others; a writer cannot see who is listening. Keep such threats clearly inside the fiction and close with explicit reassurance.

theory.name: Intermittent reinforcement
theory.summary: Rewards that come only sometimes produce behavior, and attachment, that persists longer than rewards that come every time.
theory.claim: Behavior reinforced on a partial schedule is more resistant to extinction than behavior reinforced every time (the partial reinforcement extinction effect). In relationships, unpredictable alternation of warmth and coldness is proposed to strengthen attachment to the inconsistent partner. The relational extension builds on, but is less directly tested than, the laboratory finding.
theory.evidence_note: The laboratory partial-reinforcement effect is among the most robust findings in learning research; its application to traumatic bonding in relationships rests on fewer, mostly correlational studies.
theory.writer_takeaway: Rewarding every response teaches fast but fades fast; occasional, unpredictable reward keeps a habit going. Hot-and-cold alternation is the same mechanism applied to affection and belongs to the coercive patterns.
theory.source: Charles B. Ferster and B. F. Skinner, Schedules of Reinforcement, Appleton-Century-Crofts (1957)

theory.name: Investment model of commitment
theory.summary: People stay committed when satisfaction is high, alternatives look poor, and they have already invested a lot.
theory.claim: Commitment to a relationship is predicted by three things: satisfaction, the perceived quality of alternatives, and the size of investments (time, effort, shared identity) that would be lost by leaving. Commitment can stay high even when satisfaction is low, if alternatives look worse and investments are large.
theory.evidence_note: Well supported by meta-analysis across romantic, work and other relationships; mostly correlational and self-report.
theory.writer_takeaway: Scripts that raise invested effort, belittle alternatives or cut the listener off from others are working the commitment levers, not satisfaction. Naming those moves helps a writer tell bonding from entrapment.

theory.name: Equity theory
theory.summary: People feel uneasy when what they give and get in a relationship is out of balance, and act to restore balance.
theory.claim: People compare their ratio of contributions to rewards with the other party's. Being under-benefited produces resentment; being over-benefited produces guilt. Both push people to restore balance, either by changing behavior or by reinterpreting what was given.
theory.evidence_note: Supported in workplace and relationship research, more clearly for people who feel under-benefited than for those who feel over-benefited, whose discomfort is weaker and more easily explained away. Individual differences in equity sensitivity are large, and the model predicts poorly in close relationships where people stop keeping score.
theory.writer_takeaway: A gift or favor creates a felt debt the listener wants to repay, which is why giving first precedes asking. Thanking and gratitude moves work partly by making the listener feel over-benefited.

theory.name: Self-determination theory
theory.summary: Motivation is strongest and healthiest when people feel autonomous, competent and connected to others.
theory.claim: The theory holds that three basic needs, autonomy, competence and relatedness, support self-motivated behavior and wellbeing. It distinguishes controlled motivation (pressure, guilt, contingent reward) from autonomous motivation (choice, value, interest). Controlling rewards can undermine interest in an activity that was already enjoyed.
theory.evidence_note: A large, broadly supportive literature across education, health and work; the undermining effect of rewards on intrinsic motivation is debated and depends on reward type.
theory.writer_takeaway: Framing a response as the listener's choice and showing them they are capable increases follow-through after the session. Heavy pressure produces compliance in the moment but less lasting change.

theory.name: Epistemic trust
theory.summary: Trusting that a person is a reliable source of knowledge, so their statements are accepted and learned without checking.
theory.claim: People learn much of what they know by accepting what trusted others tell them. Cues such as being addressed by name, eye contact and being shown care (ostensive cues) are proposed to open epistemic trust, so information is taken as relevant and generalizable. The concept has been used to explain both learning in therapy and vulnerability to manipulation.
theory.evidence_note: Developmental studies show that children use cues about informants when deciding whom to learn from. The claim that ostensive cues such as eye contact and being addressed by name open a special channel for learning comes mainly from infant research and remains debated. Adult epistemic trust has been studied, but the specific claim that these cues make an adult listener accept a recorded voice's statements has not been established. Clinical extensions associated with Fonagy and colleagues remain under test.
theory.writer_takeaway: On this account, direct address, the listener's name and visible care are what mark statements as personally relevant knowledge and not just words; treat that as a reasonable working assumption, not a measured effect. Whatever openness a listener gives is exactly what makes an unreliable source dangerous, so do not spend it on false claims about the real world.

theory.name: Trust calibration
theory.summary: Trust is well calibrated when it matches how reliable a source actually is; over-trust and under-trust both cause errors.
theory.claim: People adjust trust in a source according to its track record and signals of competence. Trust is calibrated when it tracks actual reliability. Early accurate statements raise trust, which then carries over to later statements that cannot be checked.
theory.evidence_note: Developed mainly in research on trust in automation and in advice-taking; well supported in those settings, extended here by analogy.
theory.writer_takeaway: Several checkable true statements build trust that the next unverifiable one may borrow; this is the usual rationale offered for pacing and leading, by analogy and without direct test. A writer who overstates potency spends trust that later suggestions need.

theory.name: Diagnosticity
theory.summary: How strongly a piece of evidence points to one conclusion over another; people often overweight evidence that is not very diagnostic.
theory.claim: Evidence is diagnostic when it is much more likely under one hypothesis than under its alternative. People tend to treat any evidence consistent with their hypothesis as confirming it, even when the evidence would occur anyway. Ordinary relaxation signs, for example, are taken as proof of trance though they occur in any resting person.
theory.evidence_note: The concept comes from Bayesian reasoning; the failure to weigh diagnosticity (pseudodiagnosticity) is well documented in judgment research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Listeners will accept low-diagnostic evidence (heavy limbs, slower breathing, lost time) as proof of trance if the script calls it proof. Convincers built on things that happen anyway are cheap and effective; know that this is what they are.
theory.source: Michael E. Doherty, Clifford R. Mynatt, Ryan D. Tweney and Michael D. Schiavo, Pseudodiagnosticity, Acta Psychologica (1979)

theory.name: Confounding variable
theory.summary: A hidden factor that affects both the supposed cause and the outcome, making one look like it caused the other.
theory.claim: When two things vary together, a third factor may drive both. Without controlling for it, a study, or a listener, wrongly credits the first thing with causing the second. In hypnosis, expectation, motivation and relaxation are frequent confounds for claims that a specific technique worked.
theory.evidence_note: A basic methodological concept, not a contested finding.
theory.writer_takeaway: When judging whether a device works, remember that expectation and the listener's motivation travel with almost every device. Do not credit a technique for an effect the frame or the listener's eagerness may have produced.

theory.name: Demand characteristics
theory.summary: Cues in a situation that tell people what response is expected, which they then tend to produce.
theory.claim: Participants pick up the hypothesis from the setting, instructions and experimenter, and many try to be good subjects by behaving as they think is wanted. Orne raised this specifically for hypnosis research, where cues about how a hypnotized person acts shape what hypnotized people do. Expected behavior and genuine effect become hard to separate.
theory.evidence_note: Widely accepted and demonstrated in classic studies including simulator designs; the size of demand effects varies and is hard to estimate in general.
theory.writer_takeaway: Every expectation the script states is also a cue for what to perform, and listeners will often perform it. Expectation setting is a device precisely because demand works.

theory.name: Observer effect
theory.summary: People behave differently when they know they are being watched or measured.
theory.claim: Being observed changes behavior, often toward what the observer is assumed to want. The popular Hawthorne effect is one version. Self-observation can have a similar effect: monitoring one's own behavior changes it.
theory.evidence_note: Reactivity to observation is real, but the original Hawthorne studies are weak evidence and the term is over-popularized; effects vary widely by setting.
theory.writer_takeaway: Telling the listener they are being watched, or asking them to watch and report on themselves, changes behavior through that alone. Self-policing works partly this way.

theory.name: Ecological validity
theory.summary: Whether findings from a lab setting hold up in the real situations they claim to describe.
theory.claim: A result can be reliable in a controlled study yet fail to generalize to ordinary settings, because the task, people or context differ. Persuasion and hypnosis findings often come from students in brief lab sessions, not from listeners alone with an audio file over weeks.
theory.evidence_note: A methodological concept; the specific gap between lab hypnosis research and recorded self-directed listening has not been well studied.
theory.writer_takeaway: Treat effect claims from lab studies as a starting point; a recorded script heard alone at night is a different setting. Test on real listeners where possible.

theory.name: Construct validity
theory.summary: Whether a measure actually captures the thing it claims to measure.
theory.claim: A test can be consistent yet measure something other than its label. Measures of hypnotizability, for example, mostly score responses to suggestions, which overlaps with but is not identical to any proposed trance state. Mislabeling a measure leads to wrong conclusions about what changed.
theory.evidence_note: A basic methodological concept; its application to the trance-state debate is long-standing and unresolved.
theory.writer_takeaway: A suggestibility test shows that a listener responds to suggestions; it does not prove a special state. Use such tests as convincers, but do not mistake them for a depth gauge.

theory.name: Classical conditioning
theory.summary: After repeated pairing, a neutral cue comes to trigger the response originally produced by what it was paired with.
theory.claim: When a neutral stimulus reliably predicts a meaningful one, the neutral stimulus comes to evoke a response on its own. Learning depends on the cue predicting the outcome, not on mere co-occurrence, and the response weakens if the cue is repeatedly presented alone. Many claims about hypnotic triggers assume this mechanism without testing it.
theory.evidence_note: One of the best established findings in psychology. Whether verbal-only pairing in a recording produces true conditioning, as opposed to suggestion and expectation, is largely untested.
theory.writer_takeaway: Present the cue just before the state, repeatedly, and keep firing it with the state afterward, or it extinguishes. Expect that much of what scripts call conditioning also runs on expectation.

theory.name: Operant conditioning
theory.summary: Behavior followed by good consequences becomes more likely; behavior followed by bad consequences becomes less likely.
theory.claim: The frequency of a behavior is shaped by its consequences: reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it. Timing matters, since consequences that follow closely are more effective, and the schedule of reinforcement affects how fast behavior is learned and how long it lasts. Complex behavior can be built by reinforcing successive approximations.
theory.evidence_note: Extremely well established in animals and humans. In a recording, reinforcement is suggested rather than delivered, so effects depend on the suggested reward feeling real.
theory.writer_takeaway: Deliver the suggested reward immediately after the response, mark the exact moment, and reinforce small steps first. Suggested punishment teaches avoidance and should be used sparingly.

theory.name: Ideomotor effect
theory.summary: Thinking vividly about a movement can produce small real movements without any felt intention to move.
theory.claim: Imagining or expecting a movement primes the motor system, and slight movements can follow that the person does not experience as willed. This explains pendulums, Ouija boards and dowsing. Hypnotic arm levitation and finger signals are proposed to use the same route.
theory.evidence_note: Well demonstrated (for example in facilitated communication and table-turning studies); the sense of non-volition is real but the movement is produced by the person.
theory.writer_takeaway: Describe the movement vividly and in progress, not as a command, so the listener imagines it rather than decides it. Small movements come easier than large ones.
theory.source: William Benjamin Carpenter, On the Influence of Suggestion in Modifying and Directing Muscular Movement, Independently of Volition, Royal Institution of Great Britain (1852)

theory.name: Self-perception theory
theory.summary: People infer their own attitudes and traits partly by watching what they themselves do.
theory.claim: When inner states are weak or ambiguous, people read them off their own behavior, much as an outside observer would. Doing something without strong external pressure leads to the conclusion that one wanted to. The theory competes with cognitive dissonance theory as an explanation of attitude change after behavior.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by many studies, especially for weakly held attitudes; less applicable when attitudes are strong. Related facial-feedback findings have had replication trouble.
theory.writer_takeaway: Get a small act first, then point at it as evidence of what the listener is or wants. The less the script visibly pushed, the more the listener credits the act to themselves.

theory.name: Misattribution of arousal
theory.summary: Physical arousal from one source can be mistaken for an emotion caused by something else nearby.
theory.claim: Bodily arousal is ambiguous, and people label it using whatever explanation is at hand. Arousal from fear, exercise or excitement can be read as attraction, anger or excitement about a different target. Labels supplied by the setting therefore shape which emotion is felt.
theory.evidence_note: Classic studies (two-factor theory, the suspension-bridge study) are well known, but replications have been mixed and effects are smaller and less reliable than popular accounts suggest.
theory.writer_takeaway: Tell the listener what a sensation means while it is happening; ambiguous arousal takes the label it is given. Do not rely on it as a strong effect.

theory.name: State-dependent memory
theory.summary: Material learned in a particular bodily or mental state is recalled better when that state returns.
theory.claim: Recall improves when the internal state at retrieval matches the state at learning, for example sobriety or intoxication, mood, or arousal. The context-dependent version applies to the external setting. Practitioners often invoke this to explain why material from one session comes back in the next, but hypnosis has not been shown to act as a state in this sense.
theory.evidence_note: Reliable for drug states; mood-dependent memory is weaker and inconsistent. Effects are generally modest and shrink when strong retrieval cues are present. Its use to explain hypnotic recall and posthypnotic amnesia is an extrapolation: suggested amnesia depends on the suggestion being given and lifts on a cue, which a state-dependency account does not predict.
theory.writer_takeaway: Reinstate the same wording, cues and setting used when a suggestion was given if you want it recalled; matching cues is the well-supported part. Do not count on the difference between trance and waking to produce forgetting; if you want amnesia, suggest it.

theory.name: Elaboration likelihood model
theory.summary: Persuasion takes a careful route when people are motivated and able to think, and a shortcut route when they are not.
theory.claim: When motivation and ability to process a message are high, attitudes change through careful evaluation of arguments (central route) and the change tends to last. When either is low, people rely on peripheral cues such as source attractiveness, number of arguments or mood, and the change is weaker and less stable. Distraction, fatigue and low involvement push processing toward the peripheral route.
theory.evidence_note: Influential and widely supported, though criticized as hard to falsify because route is often inferred from the outcome; the single-route unimodel is a competing account.
theory.writer_takeaway: Overload, distraction and relaxation lower scrutiny, which helps cues like authority and repetition work; but change made that way fades unless it is reinforced or later endorsed by the listener's own thinking.

theory.name: Neodissociation theory
theory.summary: Hilgard's theory that hypnosis divides awareness, so part of the mind carries out or registers things the conscious part does not notice.
theory.claim: Hilgard proposed that cognitive control systems are organized in a hierarchy, and hypnosis lets some subsystems run without the executive's awareness. His hidden observer demonstrations, where a part of the subject reported pain that the hypnotized subject denied, were taken as evidence. Later dissociated-control versions say hypnosis weakens executive monitoring rather than splitting awareness.
theory.evidence_note: Remains a major theory of hypnosis, but the hidden observer has been shown to depend on how it is suggested, which supports sociocognitive critics; the debate is unresolved.
theory.writer_takeaway: Suggestions that one part acts while another watches or forgets fit how highly responsive listeners describe hypnosis. Phrasing that splits doer from observer gives the listener a frame for the response to feel unwilled.

theory.name: Absorption (trait)
theory.summary: A stable tendency to become deeply engrossed in experiences such as music, stories, nature or imagery.
theory.claim: Some people readily lose themselves in sensory and imaginative experiences, to the point of not noticing their surroundings. Absorption is measured by the Tellegen Absorption Scale and correlates modestly with hypnotizability. It also predicts how deeply people are transported by stories.
theory.evidence_note: Reliably measured; its correlation with hypnotizability is consistent but modest and partly depends on testing context.
theory.writer_takeaway: Rich sensory detail and immersive imagery will work very well for some listeners and barely at all for others. Offer more than one route in, such as a physical or ideomotor route alongside imagery.

theory.name: Placebo effect
theory.summary: Improvement that comes from believing in and expecting a treatment, not from the treatment's specific ingredient.
theory.claim: Expectation, conditioning from past treatments and the care surrounding treatment can produce real changes, especially in pain, nausea and other subjective symptoms. Placebo effects can work even when people are told they are taking a placebo. The nocebo effect is the same mechanism producing harm from negative expectation.
theory.evidence_note: Real and well documented for subjective outcomes like pain, but often overstated for objective disease outcomes; some apparent placebo improvement is regression to the mean.
theory.writer_takeaway: Stating in advance that a technique is strong, or that an imagined substance causes the effect, works through expectation. Negative warnings can produce the very effects they describe.

theory.name: Ironic process theory
theory.summary: Trying not to think of something keeps it active, so it returns more, especially under stress or mental load.
theory.claim: Suppressing a thought runs two processes: an effortful one that looks for distractions and an automatic one that checks for the unwanted thought. The checking process keeps the thought primed. When mental load or stress reduces effort, the thought rebounds.
theory.evidence_note: The basic rebound effect is replicated but the effect size in meta-analysis is small and varies widely with method.
theory.writer_takeaway: Telling a listener not to think of or not to do something brings it to mind; a negative suggestion uses this on purpose. For thought replacement, give a positive target to attend to instead of a ban.

theory.name: Effort justification
theory.summary: People come to value what they had to work or suffer for, to make the effort seem worth it.
theory.claim: Spending effort or enduring discomfort on something creates pressure to see it as valuable, because otherwise the effort was wasted. This is usually explained as dissonance reduction. Severe initiations make groups seem more attractive to those who go through them.
theory.evidence_note: Classic initiation studies and later work support the effect, though some replications are mixed and alternative explanations (such as contrast with relief) exist.
theory.writer_takeaway: Asking the listener to work, wait or endure before the payoff increases how much they value it. The same mechanism powers hazing and dependency, so use it knowingly.

theory.name: Labeling effect
theory.summary: Telling people they have a trait makes them more likely to act in line with it.
theory.claim: Attributing a trait to someone (you are a helpful person, a good listener) increases later behavior consistent with the label. The label changes self-perception, which then guides behavior. Labels work best when plausible and given before the behavior is requested.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by field and lab studies, with moderate effects; the strength depends on credibility of the label and on whether the person accepts it.
theory.writer_takeaway: Name the trait first, then ask for behavior that fits it. Keep the label believable relative to what the listener has already done.
theory.source: Robert E. Kraut, Effects of Social Labeling on Giving to Charity, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (1973)

theory.name: Imagination inflation
theory.summary: Imagining an event that never happened increases confidence that it really did happen.
theory.claim: Repeatedly imagining an event makes it more familiar and more detailed, which people then mistake for memory. Imagination inflation is one route by which false memories form. Suggestive procedures, including hypnosis, increase this risk.
theory.evidence_note: Robustly demonstrated in the lab, with modest effects; full false memories form in a minority of participants, and the clinical implications have been heavily debated.
theory.writer_takeaway: Asking the listener to imagine something in detail makes it feel more real and more remembered. Scripts that suggest past events or that a trait was always so are using this; do not use it on real autobiographical memory outside clear fiction.

theory.name: Automaticity
theory.summary: Well-practiced responses run fast, without effort or awareness, and can be triggered by cues in the environment.
theory.claim: Repeated practice makes behaviors efficient and less dependent on conscious intention, so they can run while attention is elsewhere. Automatic processes can be started by environmental cues. Claims that subtle primes automatically drive complex social behavior are a separate, more contested strand.
theory.evidence_note: Skill and habit automaticity is well established. Many behavioral priming findings (for example elderly-priming and walking speed) have failed to replicate.
theory.writer_takeaway: Responses become automatic through repetition with a consistent cue, not through being described as automatic once. Drill and practice schedules matter more than a single strong suggestion.
theory.source: John A. Bargh, The Four Horsemen of Automaticity: Awareness, Intention, Efficiency, and Control in Social Cognition, Handbook of Social Cognition (1994)

theory.name: Habituation
theory.summary: Response to a repeated, unchanging stimulus weakens over time; a change in the stimulus restores attention.
theory.claim: Organisms reduce their response to stimuli that repeat without consequence. A novel or changed stimulus restores the response (dishabituation) and triggers an orienting reaction. Habituation is distinct from fatigue and from extinction.
theory.evidence_note: Among the most basic and robust findings in behavioral science.
theory.writer_takeaway: Monotony lets vigilance lapse, which helps induction; but repeated suggestions also lose impact. Vary wording, tone or rhythm to keep key lines from fading into background.

theory.name: Mere-agreement effect / acquiescence
theory.summary: People tend to agree with statements regardless of content, and a run of agreements makes further agreement easier.
theory.claim: Acquiescence bias is a tendency to answer yes or agree, documented in survey research. Persuasion practice adds the claim that a sequence of agreements builds momentum toward accepting a final request. The momentum claim is the basis of the yes set.
theory.evidence_note: Acquiescence bias in surveys is well documented. Experimental support for yes-set momentum is thin and mixed; it is largely practitioner lore.
theory.writer_takeaway: Easy agreements lower friction, but do not expect a chain of yeses alone to carry an unwelcome request. The final step still needs to fit what came before.

theory.name: Critical faculty (Elman)
theory.summary: Practitioner model saying hypnosis bypasses a critical part of the mind that normally screens suggestions.
theory.claim: Elman defined hypnosis as bypassing the critical faculty and establishing selective thinking. The model pictures a gatekeeper that evaluates incoming ideas and must be relaxed, overloaded or tricked for suggestions to pass. It is a teaching model, not a measured structure.
theory.evidence_note: No direct empirical support for a discrete critical faculty; reduced evaluative monitoring in hypnosis has partial support from research on executive control, but the gatekeeper picture is a simplification.
theory.writer_takeaway: Treat bypass the critic as a description of what many devices try to do, not as a switch. Listeners still reject suggestions that clash with their values.
theory.source: Dave Elman, Findings in Hypnosis, Westwood Publishing (1964)

theory.name: Implementation intentions
theory.summary: If-then plans that tie a specific action to a specific situation make people more likely to follow through on a goal they already hold.
theory.claim: Forming a plan of the form 'when situation X arises, I will do Y' links a cue to a response, so the situation triggers the behavior with less deliberation. This closes the gap between intending and acting. It works best for people who already hold the goal.
theory.evidence_note: Supported by a large literature and meta-analysis with medium effects; some recent preregistered replications find smaller effects.
theory.writer_takeaway: Tie a post-session behavior to a concrete everyday cue and have the listener rehearse the if-then pairing. Vague 'you will' suggestions do less.

theory.name: Motivating operations
theory.summary: Conditions such as deprivation or satiation change how valuable a reward is, and so how hard someone works for it.
theory.claim: In behavior analysis, a motivating operation alters the effectiveness of a reinforcer and the frequency of behavior that has produced it. Deprivation makes a reinforcer more effective (establishing operation); satiation makes it less effective (abolishing operation). Value is not fixed but depends on recent access.
theory.evidence_note: Well established in applied behavior analysis and animal research.
theory.writer_takeaway: Withholding or delaying a reward raises its pull; giving too much of it drains that pull. Plan the order of deprivation and reward rather than offering rewards freely.
theory.source: Jack Michael, Distinguishing Between Discriminative and Motivational Functions of Stimuli, Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior (1982)

theory.name: Variable-ratio schedules
theory.summary: Rewarding after an unpredictable number of responses produces high, steady response rates that resist stopping.
theory.claim: On a variable-ratio schedule, reward comes after a varying number of responses around an average. This produces high, steady rates with few pauses and strong resistance to extinction. It is the schedule of slot machines and is linked to compulsive behavior.
theory.evidence_note: Schedule effects are very well established in laboratory work; their direct role in gambling disorder is supported but combined with other factors.
theory.writer_takeaway: Unpredictable rewards keep a listener responding and returning more than predictable ones. That is effective and also the core of compulsion, so name it when it is used.

theory.name: Sunk-cost effect
theory.summary: People continue a course of action because of what they have already spent on it, even when stopping would be better.
theory.claim: Prior investment of money, time or effort increases willingness to continue, though past costs cannot be recovered and should not affect the decision. Explanations include wanting to avoid waste and to justify past choices. The effect is stronger when the person made the original decision.
theory.evidence_note: The sunk-cost effect appears in hypothetical and real decisions, but its size varies with the task and how prior investment is framed. Early claims that children and animals do not show it have been challenged by later studies, with mixed results across tasks and ages.
theory.writer_takeaway: Reminding the listener how far they have come makes stopping feel like waste. It is a legitimate motivator for a series, and coercive when used to block leaving.

theory.name: Contrast effect
theory.summary: Something is judged by comparison with what came just before it, so a prior extreme shifts the judgment the other way.
theory.claim: Perception and judgment are relative: warm water feels hot after cold water, and a moderate request seems small after a large one. The preceding item sets a standard that the next one is compared against. Contrast operates for sensations, prices, requests and emotional states.
theory.evidence_note: Perceptual contrast is robust; social and request contrast effects are supported but depend on the comparison being salient and relevant.
theory.writer_takeaway: Place a suggestion right after its opposite: tension before relaxation, a big ask before a smaller one, alarm before relief. The contrast does part of the work.
theory.source: Muzafer Sherif, Daniel Taub and Carl I. Hovland, Assimilation and Contrast Effects of Anchoring Stimuli on Judgments, Journal of Experimental Psychology (1958)

theory.name: Anchoring effect (judgment)
theory.summary: An initial number or reference point pulls later estimates toward it, even when the reference is irrelevant.
theory.claim: When people estimate a quantity after seeing a number, their estimate stays near that number and adjusts insufficiently. This happens even with arbitrary anchors. This is a different concept from NLP anchoring, which is a conditioned cue.
theory.evidence_note: One of the most replicated judgment effects, though effects with incidental anchors are smaller and less reliable than with considered anchors.
theory.writer_takeaway: A stated number for depth, duration or frequency sets the scale the listener judges by. Do not confuse this with installing an anchor as a trigger; they share a name and nothing else.

theory.name: Cognitive fluency of rhyme (rhyme-as-reason)
theory.summary: Statements that rhyme are judged more true than the same claims stated without rhyme, because they are easier to process.
theory.claim: Easy processing (fluency) is misread as a sign of truth or familiarity. Rhyme, repetition, clear type and simple wording all increase fluency. McGlone and Tofighbakhsh found rhyming aphorisms rated more accurate than non-rhyming versions with the same meaning.
theory.evidence_note: The rhyme-as-reason study is a single well-known experiment with limited replication; the broader fluency and illusory-truth effects are well replicated.
theory.writer_takeaway: Repetition and easy wording reliably make a line feel more familiar and more true; rhyme may add to that, on thinner evidence. Put the core suggestion in the simplest, most fluent phrasing in the script and repeat it.

theory.name: Self-reference effect
theory.summary: Information related to oneself is remembered better than other information.
theory.claim: Judging whether a word describes oneself produces better recall than judging its meaning or sound. Self-relevant material gets richer encoding and connects to an organized body of self-knowledge. The effect extends to material framed as about 'you'.
theory.evidence_note: Robust and confirmed by meta-analysis.
theory.writer_takeaway: Frame suggestions as about the listener and in their own voice; first- and second-person phrasing is remembered better than general statements.

theory.name: Generation effect
theory.summary: Information people produce themselves is remembered better than the same information read or heard.
theory.claim: Generating a word or answer, even from a simple cue, leads to better memory than reading it. The finding is about memory. The further idea that people believe and own what they produce themselves comes from separate research on self-persuasion and is not part of this effect.
theory.evidence_note: Well replicated in memory research with moderate effects; it depends on the generation task being meaningful.
theory.writer_takeaway: Invite the listener to supply an answer or missing word. When they actually generate it, they may remember it better than if they had only heard it; whether it feels more like their own idea is a separate claim.

theory.name: Spacing effect
theory.summary: Repetitions spread out over time produce stronger, longer-lasting learning than the same repetitions massed together.
theory.claim: Learning distributed across sessions is retained much better than learning crammed into one session. Gaps between repetitions force retrieval and strengthen memory. The optimal gap grows with how long the material must be retained.
theory.evidence_note: One of the most robust findings in memory research, replicated for over a century.
theory.writer_takeaway: A key suggestion repeated across several sessions and spaced through a script outlasts the same suggestion repeated many times in a row. Prescribe repeat listening rather than relying on one long file.
